  • Christian nurture and formation. Children take on the religion of their parents; festivals, rites of passage, worship and Christian values stick for life; church teaching, education, parental influence and the religious community all reinforce it, as does cultural pressure to conform.

subsections.heading: The criticisms of the arguments — and the replies
subsections.html:
Spec 1.6 · Responses to reasons for belief; lack of clear evidence that God exists

  • Every argument needs a named critic — a 12-marker on the proofs is really a question about their objections.
  • Russell against first cause — Aquinas exempts God from the very rule the argument rests on; infinite regress is simpler.
  • Hume against design — why include so much evil, and why not natural processes instead of a designer?
  • Darwin vindicates Hume — the eye could evolve by natural selection, so no designer is required.
  • Religious experience is subjective — and if it is ineffable it cannot convey any concrete belief about God.
ArgumentThe named objection
First cause (Aquinas)Bertrand Russell (1872–1970) criticised it for contradicting itself: Aquinas says there is no uncaused cause, then makes an exception for the primary cause without justifying it. Russell thought it made more sense to accept an infinite regress of cause and effect. Two further objections: even if the argument works it need not point to God, because the universe could have self-existence; and it tells us almost nothing about the nature of that cause, so it is of little use to a believer.
Design (Paley)David Hume (1711–1776) asked why a designer felt the need to include so much evil and suffering in his product, and suggested the universe could have come into being through natural processes. Darwin's evidence appears to vindicate him: organs such as the eye could have evolved through natural selection over a long period, with no designer required.
Religious experienceThe experience is subjective, so it is out of reach of rational examination — convincing for the person who had it, very hard to use to persuade anyone else. The problem is worse if the experience is ineffable, because an experience beyond description cannot convey a concrete belief about the nature of God.

✗ "Some people disagree with the first cause argument." — unnamed objections score at the bottom.
✓ "Russell objected that Aquinas exempts God from the very rule the argument depends on, and argued that an infinite regress of cause and effect is the simpler conclusion."

Russell against first cause and Hume against design are the two names to bank. One each, plus the reply, and the appraisal writes itself.

More detail

A 12-marker on the arguments for God is really a question about their critics, so each argument needs a named objection attached to it.

subsections.heading: Religious experience, miracles, atheism and agnosticism
subsections.html:
Spec 1.6 · Experiences such as conversion; reasons for atheism and agnosticism

  • Revelation, not reason — many believe because they have heard, seen or felt God’s presence.
  • Otto, James and Buber — the numinous; experience as the foundation of belief; God known through personal encounter.
  • Three types — direct experience (Exodus 3), conversion (Acts 9; Bishop Hugh Montefiore) and miracles.
  • Lourdes, 1858 — Bernadette Soubirous’s visions and the spring at Massabielle, where pilgrims claim cures.
  • Atheism’s five reasons — no evidence, science suffices, control of nature, the problem of evil, conflicting truth claims.
  • Feuerbach and Freud — God as a projection of man, and belief as a neurosis against the terrors of nature.

Two conversions, in their own words

"Now as he was going along and approaching Damascus, suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to him, 'Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?' He asked, 'Who are you, Lord?' The reply came, 'I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.'" — Acts 9:1–7
Used to argue: the model conversion — a direct encounter that changed a persecutor into the Church's greatest missionary.

"One dark wintry afternoon, I was sitting alone in my study at school. I suddenly became aware of a figure in white whom I saw pretty clearly in my mind's eye. I heard the words, 'follow me'. Instinctively, I knew that this was Jesus… It was an indescribably rich event that filled me afterwards with an overpowering joy. I could do no other than follow those instructions." — Bishop Hugh Montefiore (1920–2005)
Used to argue: conversions still happen, and happen to people who knew nothing about Jesus beforehand — which answers the "it is just upbringing" objection.

ArgumentCounter-argument
Religious experiences are so widespread and so transformative that they are best explained by God actually existing.They are private and unverifiable, and can be explained psychologically.
Conversions such as St Paul's changed whole lives and founded the Church.Conversion can be the product of upbringing, emotion or social pressure.
Belief founded on experience is personal and direct, not second-hand.If experience were required, most believers would have no grounds for faith — yet they believe through nurture, scripture and reason.
More detail

The argument from religious experience says that God is known through revelation, not only through reason.

Many people believe because they have felt God's presence — by hearing him, seeing him or feeling his support in everything they do. Such experiences range from visions to healing to an overwhelming sense of love, and may be vividly described or ineffable (beyond description). Rudolf Otto (1869–1937) called them numinous — the sense of wonder and awe we feel in the presence of something greater than ourselves. William James (1842–1910) regarded religious experience as the foundation of religious belief, and Martin Buber (1878–1965) argued that because God is personal he is known only through personal encounters. The three types: direct experience of God (Moses and the burning bush, Exodus 3), conversion (St Paul on the road to Damascus, Acts 9; Augustine; C. S. Lewis; Bishop Hugh Montefiore), and miracles.

A miracle is an inexplicable event in which God dramatically intervenes: a physical or mental healing, a special sign that changes the course of a life, or an act that saves someone from a specific danger. Jesus's ministry was characterised by miracles that overcame the forces of nature, expelled demons, healed, or brought people back from the dead; the incarnation — Jesus being both truly human and truly divine — and the resurrection, Christ overcoming the powers of death, are themselves miracles. Christians believe miracles still happen, and Roman Catholics point to Lourdes, a town in the south of France at the foot of the Pyrenees: in 1858 Bernadette Soubirous had a number of visions of the Virgin Mary in the Grotto of Massabielle and was told to dig nearby, where she found a spring. Pilgrims who bathe in or drink the water claim to have been cured of their ailments.

Why some Christians are cautious about miracles: they can look like God acting arbitrarily, favouring some and not others; many claims have natural or psychological explanations; and some Christians hold that God works through the ordinary laws of the universe rather than breaking them. Atheists explain them as coincidence, misreporting or the placebo effect.

Atheism literally means "without or no God": an atheist believes there is no God or gods. Most atheists regard themselves as realists, facing the world as it really is and giving a naturalistic account of the existence and functioning of the universe. The reasons: there is no reliable empirical evidence for God, and one should only believe what there is good evidence for; everything in the universe can be explained satisfactorily by scientific observation, research and experiment, so God is unnecessary and there need be no great design or ultimate purpose; advances in science and medicine, and human ability to control the environment, remove the need for God; the problem of evil suggests an imperfect world full of design flaws, and God's apparent non-intervention supports the conclusion that he is not there; religious truth claims conflict between religions and within them, so believers cannot say what God is like or what he expects, and that conflict is dangerous — as in Israel/Palestine and Northern Ireland, and in atrocities committed in God's name. As atheists put it, God was once the explanation for what we did not understand, and now it is God who needs explaining.

Two named explanations of why people believe: Ludwig Feuerbach (1804–1872) argued that happiness is our primary desire and only seems secure if God exists to reward the virtuous and punish the wicked, so humanity imagined a God and gave him every quality we admire — intelligence, goodness, love. His conclusion: what man is in need of, he makes his God, so God is no more than a projection of man. Sigmund Freud (1856–1939) argued religion is a mental defence against the threatening aspects of nature: rather than face the terrors of life people believe in a protecting power, which is really a magnification and projection of the child's earliest memory of a parent — so belief in God is a symptom of neurosis, curable when one learns to face the world without illusions. A non-religious upbringing is itself a factor.

Agnosticism is not knowing whether God exists. Agnostics are unconvinced by theistic arguments but equally unconvinced by Freud or Feuerbach, and do not think evil conclusively disproves God. They may feel there is no positive empirical evidence either way, that the philosophical arguments are evenly balanced (first cause against the problem of evil), that it is not irrational to think some unknown cause lies behind the universe, and that both believers and atheists are guilty of intellectual arrogance in claiming a certainty nobody has.

subsections.heading: The problem of evil and Christian responses to it
subsections.html:
Spec 1.7 · The Problem of Evil and Suffering; theodicy

  • Hick’s definition — "physical pain, mental suffering and moral wickedness"; learn it word for word.
  • Moral and natural evil — caused by moral agents, or by the natural order; deforestation blurs the line.
  • The inconsistent triad — Hume and Mackie: omnipotence, omniscience and omnibenevolence cannot all hold while evil exists.
  • Evidential and experiential — the sheer amount of evil, and meeting it first-hand with prayers unanswered.
  • Augustinian and Irenaean theodicies — evil as privation after the Fall; evil as soul-making towards God’s likeness.
  • Plantinga, Satan and mystery — the Freewill Defence and eschatological verification; prayer, forgiveness and charity in practice.

Evil and suffering in scripture

Adam and Eve exercise freewill by disobeying God, and are banished from Eden. — Genesis 3
Used to argue: evil enters creation through the misuse of human freewill, not through God.

"Your enemy the devil prowls around like a lion looking for someone to devour." — 1 Peter
Used to argue: evil comes from Satan tempting and corrupting humanity.

"Then Satan answered the Lord, 'Does Job fear God for nothing?… But stretch out your hand now, and touch all that he has, and he will curse you to your face.' The Lord said to Satan, 'Very well, all that he has is in your power; only do not stretch out your hand against him!'" — Job 1:9–12
Used to argue: in the Old Testament Satan is God's servant, whose role is to test people's faith — so suffering can be a test rather than a disproof.

When Job demands an answer, God replies from the whirlwind, "Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?" — Job
Used to argue: suffering is a mystery, and humans are not placed to judge God.

"The devil had already put it into the heart of Judas son of Simon Iscariot to betray him." — John 13:2
Used to argue: by the time of Jesus Satan had become a hostile supernatural force who tempts and possesses people and works to thwart God's plans.

"We know that in everything God works for good with those who love him, who are called according to his purpose." — Romans 8:28
Used to argue: suffering is not meaningless; God works through it for a purpose, so it is not evidence against him.

"Happy are those whose way is blameless, who walk in the law of the Lord… With my whole heart I seek you; do not let me stray from your commandments." — Psalm 119:1–10
Used to argue: the solution to evil is obedience to God, guided by the Law, the prophets and the example of Jesus.

Argument: evil counts against GodCounter-argument
The inconsistent triad (Hume, J. L. Mackie): an omniscient God knows evil exists, an omnipotent God can remove it, an omnibenevolent God wants to — yet evil exists, so God lacks one of those attributes.The Freewill Defence (Plantinga): God chose to limit himself in order to give humanity freewill, so he created the possibility of evil, not evil itself. Strong on moral evil — but silent on earthquakes and disease.
Natural evil is the sharpest form: God is the creator, so volcanoes, droughts and disease trace back to him rather than to any human misuse of freedom.The Augustinian theodicy fills that gap: evil is a privation, not a thing God made, and natural evil is the corruption of nature that followed the Fall (Genesis 3). Its weakness: why would a good creation choose to disobey?
The evidential problem: the sheer amount and gratuitousness of evil — the Holocaust, the Killing Fields of Cambodia, the Soviet Gulag — makes a wholly good, all-powerful God improbable rather than merely puzzling.The Irenaean theodicy makes evil purposeful: God created the world immature, and suffering develops charity and compassion so we grow into the likeness of God. Its weakness: nurturing love would build souls better than pain, and it lessens the significance of Jesus.
The experiential problem: a believer who meets suffering first-hand, or watches innocent children suffer, and prays without any answer, may find belief impossible to sustain.Christians answer with mystery and eschatological verification — "Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?" (Job) — and with Romans 8:28: "in everything God works for good with those who love him."
Non-religiously, it is easier to attribute suffering to evolution and to human freedom, and much moral evil has been done in religion's name — the Crusades, the atrocities of Isis.Christian responses are practical, not merely theoretical: prayer, forgiveness and charity, following Jesus, who healed the sick, and the parable of the Sheep and the Goats (Matthew 25:31–46) — and Jesus's own suffering means God does not stand outside it.

✗ Describing the problem of evil for twelve marks and never appraising either side.
✗ "Christians say evil comes from freewill." — true, but it answers only moral evil.
✓ "The Freewill Defence accounts for moral evil, but it cannot explain earthquakes or disease; the Augustinian theodicy fills that gap by tracing natural evil to the corruption of nature after the Fall."

Naming Augustine, Irenaeus and Plantinga and saying what each one gets wrong is the difference between level 3 and level 4.

More detail

John Hick defined evil as "physical pain, mental suffering and moral wickedness"; for Christians it is whatever is opposed to God and his purposes.

That definition is worth learning word for word, because it gives you a named scholar in the first line of a 6-marker. Evil is what causes suffering and harm to God's creation.

  • Moral evil — suffering caused by moral agents, deliberately or through negligence: bullying, lying, cheating, murder, rape.
  • Natural evil — suffering caused by events that have nothing to do with people: the natural order of the world producing volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, droughts, floods, disease and death.

The line between them is not as clean as it looks, and saying so earns credit: given human interference in the natural world, many recent natural disasters actually stem from human decisions, so the suffering they cause may really be a form of moral evil — floods and mudslides caused by widespread deforestation are the standard example.

The logical problem of evil, posed by Hume and J. L. Mackie as an inconsistent triad: if God is omnipotent and omniscient he knows evil exists and can stop it; if he is omnibenevolent he will want to stop it; yet evil exists. So either God is not good, or not all-powerful — and either answer destroys the Christian understanding of God. Set out as an argument: if God existed there would be no evil; evil exists; therefore God cannot exist.

Two further forms are worth naming. The evidential problem relies on the amount and often gratuitous nature of evil, which makes an omnipotent, omniscient and wholly good God improbable — the Jewish Holocaust during the Second World War, the Killing Fields of Cambodia and the Soviet Gulag are the standard illustrations. The experiential problem arises when a person meets evil first-hand and suffers, or watches a loved one or innocent children suffer; it is compounded if they pray for help and no response seems to come.

A theodicy is a theory that tries to explain the existence of evil in God's good creation. The two to learn:

TheodicyThe argumentThe weakness
Augustinian (soul-deciding) — Augustine, 354–430Evil does not exist in itself; it is a privation — a corruption or absence of good — and is not created by God. It originates in the freewill of angels and humans who turn their backs on God (Genesis 3). Moral evil comes from human disobedience; natural evil is the corruption of nature that followed the Fall.Why would a good creation choose to disobey? And does calling evil an "absence of good" do justice to real suffering?
Irenaean (soul-making) — Irenaeus, 130–202God created the world immature and innocent, not perfect. Humans are made in God's image but must have freewill, or we would be robots. Evil, moral and natural, develops qualities such as charity and compassion, so we grow into the likeness of God, helped by Jesus's example, ready for heaven.It lessens the significance of Jesus, and why would God use evil to build souls when nurturing love would work better?

Other Christian responses: the Freewill Defence — Alvin Plantinga (b.1932) argues a good, omnipotent God can co-exist with evil because he gave humanity the freedom to choose between good and evil; in other words God chose to limit himself in order to give humanity the gift of freewill, so he did not create evil but created the possibility for evil to occur. Evil and suffering are caused by people misusing that gift, and it is human decisions that cause hunger, poverty, pollution, disease and war (though this does not explain natural evil). Satan — in the Old Testament Satan is God's servant testing faith, as in Job; in the New Testament he is God's adversary, tempting Jesus in the wilderness, possessing individuals and prompting Judas; some Christians therefore perform exorcisms, while others hold Satan is the personification of the evil within each of us. Mystery — evil is beyond human understanding and the answer may come in heaven, which is eschatological verification.

Practical responses, which are what "how do religious people cope with suffering?" wants, and the booklet reduces them to three: prayer — to understand what God wants, to trust that he is listening, and to intercede for victims; Christians hold that no sincere prayer goes unheard or unanswered, and that an apparently unanswered prayer means only that we cannot understand God's reply. Forgiveness — forgiving those who caused the suffering and encouraging them to seek God's forgiveness, "turning the other cheek" to end the cycle of hatred and bitterness. Charity — giving time, money and expertise to relieve suffering caused by natural and moral evil, following Jesus, who healed the sick, and the parable of the Sheep and the Goats (Matthew 25:31–46), in which helping those in need is helping him. Add acceptance, the hope of an afterlife, the support of a priest and the church, focusing on agape and on Jesus's own suffering, taking action against the causes of suffering — and, honestly, anger at God.

Non-religious explanations and responses. Atheists and humanists cannot believe a good, omnipotent God would design a world containing earthquakes and disease; they find it easier to attribute bad things to evolution or to human beings misusing their freedom. They also point out, ironically, how much moral evil has been done in the name of religion — the Crusades, the atrocities of Isis, and religions that forbid contraception. Their responses are practical: use science, meteorology and geology to prevent or mitigate natural disasters; use psychology, education, legislation and a greater sense of social justice to reduce moral evil and prevent crime; and, accepting that some suffering is inevitable, invest in treatment and care — therapies and support for mental ill health, palliative care for the terminally ill. The underlying argument is that we should improve the world ourselves rather than wait to be compensated in heaven, which Marx called an opiate.

The statement to evaluate is almost always some form of "evil disproves God". Learn it in pairs, with the appraisal built into each row:

subsections.heading: Suffering as punishment for sin and as proof of faith
subsections.html:
Spec 1.7 · Evil and suffering and the purpose of life, with particular reference to suffering as punishment for sin and proof of faith

  • Two spec readings, pulling opposite ways — suffering as what sin deserves, and suffering as the test of faith.
  • Punishment: Genesis 3:16–19 — pain, toil and death imposed after the Fall; the Augustinian theodicy generalises it.
  • Proof of faith: Job — Satan acts as God’s servant, testing whether Job fears God "for nothing"; his faith holds.
  • God’s answer is no answer — "Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?"
  • Link it to purpose — on the Irenaean account life’s purpose is growth into God’s likeness, and suffering is the means.
ArgumentCounter-argument
Suffering as punishment makes God just: sin has consequences, and Genesis 3 says so explicitly.It punishes the innocent. Children, and Job himself, suffer without having sinned — which is exactly the objection the Book of Job exists to raise.
Suffering as a test gives it purpose, and Job's endurance is the model Christians are given.A God who tests people by torturing them is hard to call omnibenevolent, and nurturing love would develop faith better than pain.
Both readings preserve God's omnipotence and omniscience: nothing happens outside his purpose (Romans 8:28).Both make God the author of suffering, which is the problem the Freewill Defence was invented to avoid.
Jesus's own suffering shows God does not stand outside it — so suffering can be redemptive rather than punitive.The evidential problem still stands: no amount of soul-making or testing accounts for the Holocaust or the Killing Fields.

✗ "Christians think suffering is a punishment from God." — one of two spec readings, given as if it were the whole teaching.
✓ "Some Christians read suffering as the punishment sin deserves, tracing it to the Fall (Genesis 3:16–19); others read it as a test that proves faith, as in Job, where Satan acts as God's servant — and the two readings disagree about whether the sufferer deserved it."

If a question mentions the purpose of life, link suffering to it: on the Irenaean account the purpose of life is to be built into the likeness of God, and suffering is the means.

More detail

The spec names two specific Christian readings of suffering, and they pull in opposite directions: suffering as what sin deserves, and suffering as the test that proves faith.

Suffering as punishment for sin. The line runs straight out of Genesis 3: Adam and Eve freely disobey, fall from God's grace, and the consequences — pain in childbearing, toil, thorns and thistles, and return to the dust (Genesis 3:16–19) — are imposed as punishment. For some Christians Original Sin is a spiritual inheritance, so all humanity bears the consequence; for others the story describes the universal human condition. The Augustinian theodicy generalises it: natural evil exists because human disobedience ruined the perfection God created, so the order of nature was lost, bringing natural disasters, disease and death. The practical implication is the one the Psalmist draws — the answer to suffering is to obey God, who has given us the Ten Commandments and has even become incarnate to show by example the life he expects (Psalm 119:1–10).

Suffering as proof of faith. The Book of Job gives the alternative. Satan appears there as God's servant, whose role is to test whether Job fears God "for nothing" (Job 1:9–12); God permits the test, Job's faith holds, and when Job demands an explanation God answers only "Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?". On this reading suffering is neither deserved nor meaningless but a trial through which faith is proved — which connects directly to the Irenaean theodicy, where evil develops charity and compassion and grows us into the likeness of God, and to Romans 8:28: "in everything God works for good with those who love him."

The must-knows

Three readings of Genesis: fundamentalist (literal), conservative (broadly true, not literal), liberal (metaphorical and symbolic).

Six attributes of God: omnipotent, omniscient, omnibenevolent, omnipresent, eternal, immutable.

The Trinity: one substance, three persons — Father the creator, Son the saviour, Spirit the sanctifier. Evidence: Jesus's baptism (Matthew 3:13–17) and the Nicene Creed.

Four arguments for God: first cause (Aquinas), design (Paley's watch), ontological (Anselm), religious experience (Otto, James, Buber).

Two types of evil: moral (caused by humans) and natural (caused by nature). Two theodicies: Augustinian soul-deciding, Irenaean soul-making.

Named thinkers you can bank: Augustine, Aquinas, Calvin, Anselm, Paley, Plantinga, Irenaeus, Hick, Schweitzer, Polkinghorne, Armstrong, Otto, James, Buber — and for the other side Plato, Darwin, Sartre, Freud, Hobbes, Mill, Singer, Dawkins, Feuerbach, Baggini, Russell, Hume, Spinoza, Mackie.

Who first said it: Big Bang — Friedman (1922), expanded by the priest Lemaître (1927). Steady state — Bondi, Gold and Hoyle (1948). Evolution — Darwin, On the Origin of the Species (1859). Evil defined — Hick: "physical pain, mental suffering and moral wickedness".

Named Church sources: Pope John Paul II, Sollicitudo Rei Socialis (1988) and the Methodist Conference (1991) on the environment; the Christian Declaration on Nature (Assisi, 1986); Roman Catholic Catechism 2417 on animals; the Church of England on animal research; Special Agenda IV (Manchester Diocese, 2010) on science; the Nicene Creed on the Trinity.

Determinism's named studies: DARPP-32 (2009), Bouchard's twins (1970s–80s), Kempermann (genes switched on and off), Libet (1980s). Hard determinism in one line: Spinoza.

Every 12-marker: arguments for, arguments against, at least one religion named, appraisal of each argument, justified conclusion with your own opinion.

The 12-mark frame

Paragraph 1 — restate the statement and say what turns on it. One or two sentences: what the claim actually asserts, and which Christian belief it threatens. "The claim that [science has disproved creation / we have no freewill / humans are superior to animals] matters because it bears directly on [the authority of Genesis / accountability at judgement / the imago Dei]."

Paragraph 2 — the strongest case FOR, with teaching and scripture. One named argument, its evidence, then your appraisal of it. "A fundamentalist Christian would argue…" · "Calvin's doctrine of predestination supports this, because…" · "This argument is strong because it rests on Genesis 1:28 itself, but it is weakened by…"

Paragraph 3 — the strongest case AGAINST, with teaching and scripture. Same shape, opposite side. "However, a liberal Christian would respond…" · "Polkinghorne replies that Genesis answers why rather than how…" · "Russell's objection is more damaging still, because…"

Paragraph 4 — where Christians disagree with each other. This is the paragraph that separates level 4 from level 3, and in this module it is always available. "Christians do not speak with one voice here: fundamentalists read Genesis literally, whereas conservative and liberal Christians…" · "The Roman Catholic Catechism (2417) permits what a minority of Christians reject outright…" · "A Christian who follows Natural Law would argue…, but a situation ethicist would respond…"

Paragraph 5 — a conclusion that decides. Weigh the arguments against each other, then state your own view and why. "On balance, the argument from… is the stronger, because…" · "Although the evidential problem of evil remains unanswered, 'proves' is too strong a word, and I therefore disagree with the statement." Never finish with "both sides have good points".

The marks are in the appraisal, not the list. Each argument needs a named source — Aquinas, Paley, Augustine, Irenaeus, Plantinga, Hick, Catechism 2417, the Nicene Creed — and a sentence saying how good that argument actually is.

subsections.heading: Quotes to learn
subsections.html:
Front of the card is the topic and the reference; the back is the words and what they prove. These are the twenty that earn marks across spec 1.1–1.7 — in Religious Studies the quotation is the mark.

Creation — Genesis 1:1–3"In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. The earth was without form and void and the darkness was upon the face of the deep; and the spirit of God was moving over the face of the waters."Used to argue: the universe is not an accident — God is its source, and he gives shape and form to chaos
Creation is good — Genesis 1"God saw that it was good."Used to argue: creation has intrinsic value, so it must not be exploited — the foundation of every stewardship answer
Imago Dei — Genesis 1:27"So God created humankind in his image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them."Used to argue: human beings are unique, have intrinsic worth, and are set apart from animals
Dominion — Genesis 1:28"God blessed them and said to them, 'Be fruitful and increase in number; fill the earth and subdue it. Rule over the fish in the sea and the birds in the sky and over every living creature that moves on the ground.'"Used to argue: either human dominance over creation — "subdue" and "rule over" — or, read as stewardship, human responsibility for it
Stewardship — Genesis 2:15"The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to till it and keep it."Used to argue: humanity's role is to look after God's creation — the clearest stewardship verse in Genesis
The planet as a gift — Sollicitudo Rei Socialis 1988"The earth and all life on it is a gift from God given to us to share and develop, not to dominate and exploit… We must consider the welfare of future generations in our planning for and utilisation of the earth's resources."Used to argue: the Roman Catholic position — the planet is held in trust, so consumption must be balanced against conservation
Animals and the Church — Catechism 2417"God entrusted animals to the stewardship of those whom he created in his own image. Hence, it is legitimate to use animals for food and clothing… Medical and scientific experimentation on animals is a moral practice if it remains within reasonable limits and contributes to caring for or saving human lives."Used to argue: the Catholic position exactly — use is permitted, cruelty and sentimentality are not. Set it against Singer on speciesism
Science and religion — Polkinghorne"Genesis is not there to give short, technical answers about how the universe began. It gives us the big answer that things exist because of God's will. One can perfectly well believe in the Big Bang, but believe in it as the will of God the creator."Used to argue: science answers how and Genesis answers why — the wording to quote on compatibility
The soul — Genesis 2:7"…then the Lord God formed man of the dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and man became a living being."Used to argue: unlike other creatures, humans are given a non-physical element, interpreted as the soul — and depend on God for life
The soul survives death — Ecclesiastes 12:7"And the dust returns to the ground it came from, and the spirit returns to God who gave it."Used to argue: something non-physical survives the death of the body
The soul outranks the body — Matthew 10:28"Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell."Used to argue: the soul is distinct from the body and matters more — the dualist's New Testament text
Greed — 1 Timothy 6:10"For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil, and in their eagerness to be rich some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pains."Used to argue: greed, not poverty, is a source of human wrongdoing — and note the exact wording, "a" root of "all kinds of" evil
Freewill — Deuteronomy 30"I have set before you life and death, so choose life."Used to argue: God puts a real choice before human beings, so freewill is genuine and judgement is just
Original Sin limits freewill — Romans 7:18–19"For I have the desire to do what is good, but I cannot carry it out... the evil I do not want to do — this I keep on doing."Used to argue: St Paul's own account of Original Sin — freewill survives the Fall but is damaged by it
Hard determinism — Spinoza"In the mind there is no absolute or free will; but the mind is determined to will this or that by a cause, which has been determined by another cause, and this last by another cause, and so on until infinity."Used to argue: hard determinism — behaviour is wholly determined by prior causes, so there is no freewill and no ethical accountability
Monotheism — Exodus 20:2–3"I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. You shall have no other gods before me."Used to argue: God has revealed himself as one, so he alone is worthy of worship — the first move in any monotheism answer
The Trinity — Matthew 3:13–17"This is my Son, whom I love; with him I am well pleased."Used to argue: at Jesus's baptism the Father speaks, the Son is baptised and the Spirit descends as a dove — all three persons acting together, the key evidence for the doctrine
Conversion — Acts 9:1–7"Now as he was going along and approaching Damascus, suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to him, 'Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?' He asked, 'Who are you, Lord?' The reply came, 'I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.'"Used to argue: the model religious experience — a direct encounter that turned a persecutor into the Church's greatest missionary
Evil defined — John Hick"Physical pain, mental suffering and moral wickedness."Used to argue: learn it word for word — it puts a named scholar in the first line of any answer on evil
Suffering has a purpose — Romans 8:28"We know that in everything God works for good with those who love him, who are called according to his purpose."Used to argue: suffering is not meaningless — God works through it, so it is not evidence against him. The reply to the evidential problem

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
OmnipotentAll-powerful — God can do anything
OmniscientAll-knowing and all-seeing, including the future
OmnibenevolentAll-loving
OmnipresentPresent everywhere at once
TranscendentBeyond and outside creation, and outside time
ImmanentPresent and active within the world and people's lives
Imago DeiMade in the image of God (Genesis 1:27) — the source of human uniqueness and intrinsic worth
StewardshipThe duty to protect and safeguard God's creation for future generations
DominionRule over creation, given to humanity in Genesis 1:28
CreationismThe belief that the biblical accounts of creation are literally true
DualismThe view that a human being is composed of body and soul
PhysicalismThe view that the real world is nothing more than the physical world — no soul, no afterlife
ConcupiscenceThe pull towards satisfying our passions, which Augustine traced to the Fall
Original SinThe inherited consequence of the Fall — all humanity is born inclined to sin
SinAny action that goes against the law of God
FreewillThe ability to make genuine choices and so be held responsible for them
DeterminismThe view that human choices are fixed by prior causes — genes, upbringing or brain chemistry
PredestinationCalvin's teaching that God chose before birth who would be saved (the elect) and who damned (the reprobate)
MonotheismBelief in one God
PolytheismBelief in many gods
Ultimate realityThe supreme, final and fundamental power in all reality; the underlying cause of all existence
AtheismThe belief that God does not exist
AgnosticismThe view that we cannot know whether God exists
NuminousOtto's word for the sense of awe and wonder at being in the presence of a greater being
MiracleAn inexplicable event in which God intervenes — a healing, a sign, or a rescue from danger
Moral evilSuffering caused by human beings, deliberately or by negligence
Natural evilSuffering caused by natural events, such as disease or earthquakes
TheodicyA theory that tries to explain the existence of evil in God's good creation
PrivationAugustine's claim that evil is an absence or corruption of good, not a thing God made
AgapeSelfless, unconditional love — the Christian ideal of love of neighbour
HamartiaThe Greek word for sin — to "miss the mark", to fall short of God's goals for humanity
Ex nihiloCreation out of nothing
Ex materiaCreation out of pre-existing matter
Young Earth CreationismThe belief that the earth and all life were created in six days, about 10,000 years ago
Old Earth CreationismThe earth is about four billion years old, but all life was directly created by God in countless separate acts
Apparent goodAquinas: something mistaken for a real good, because the Fall damaged human reasoning
GraceGod's undeserved love — what humanity fell from in Genesis 3
Hard determinismAll human behaviour is wholly determined by external factors, so there is no freewill and no accountability
Soft determinismBehaviour is caused, but a person acting according to their own character and not compelled is still meaningfully free
LibertarianismThe view that although character is caused, the moral self is free and can choose between self-interest and duty
Psychosomatic unityThe human being understood as body and soul together, not a soul housed in a body
Anthropic principleThe conditions for human life are so improbably fine-tuned that the universe looks designed for us
Infinite regressAn endless chain of causes — what the first cause argument says cannot be followed back forever
TritheismThe error of treating the Trinity as three gods rather than one
UnitarianismThe error of treating the differences between the three persons as merely superficial
GlossolaliaSpeaking in tongues — one of the gifts of the Holy Spirit
Eschatological verificationThe claim that the problem of evil will only be answered after death

questions.promptHtml: Why do many Christians accept the Big Bang and evolution, when the Bible gives a different account?
questions.answerHtml:
Because they do not read Genesis as a scientific report. Conservative and liberal Christians treat it as broadly true or as metaphorical — an answer to why there is something rather than nothing, not how it happened. On that reading a "day" could be billions of years, and the Big Bang and natural selection become the means God used.

They can also point to authority: the Catholic Church accepts the Big Bang, which was first proposed by the priest Georges Lemaître, and the Church of England encouraged members to see God's design achieved through the laws of the universe and the process of evolution.

The exam line: science asks how, religion asks why. Fundamentalist Christians reject the compromise and read Genesis literally, explaining fossils by Noah's flood or the Apparent Age theory.

questions.promptHtml: Why do Christians believe they have a responsibility for the planet, and what is the strongest objection to saying that duty is specially theirs?
questions.answerHtml:
Why: God created the planet and "saw that it was good", so it has intrinsic value; Genesis 1:28 is read as stewardship, a duty to safeguard creation for future generations; Revelation warns of judgement for those who "destroy the earth"; and the Catholic Church calls the planet a gift to be "shared and developed, not to dominate and exploit".

The objection: non-religious people reach exactly the same duty without scripture — obligation to future generations, justice for the poorest, and the practical need to keep the earth habitable. If the conclusion is identical, the religious reasons add motivation rather than obligation.

A second objection comes from inside Christianity: Genesis 1:28 also says "dominion" and "subdue", which some scholars argue has licensed exploitation, and some Christians prioritise the next life over this one.

questions.promptHtml: What is the strongest objection to the claim that human beings have a soul?
questions.answerHtml:
The interaction problem: if the soul is non-material, it is very hard to explain how it could act on physical matter — how a non-physical thing moves a hand or receives a thought.

Supporting objections: there is no scientific evidence of a soul; the Old Testament makes no clear reference to "souls" and says little about life after death; and the usual evidence — near-death experiences, spiritualism, remembered lives — has naturalistic explanations and cannot be replicated.

The Christian reply: Genesis 2:7 and Genesis 1:27, Ecclesiastes 12:7 and Matthew 10:28, and the Catechism's definition of the soul as "the spiritual principle in man". Some Christians avoid the problem altogether by teaching bodily resurrection rather than an immortal soul.

questions.promptHtml: Why do Christians think people do wrong, when God made them good?
questions.answerHtml:
Because of the Fall. Genesis 3 describes Adam and Eve freely disobeying God, and that fall from grace produces Original Sin, which affects all humanity: we are born inclined to sin, and the image of God in us is distorted. Paul puts it exactly — "the evil I do not want to do, this I keep on doing" (Romans 7:18–19).

Aquinas gives a gentler version: humans naturally desire the good, but the Fall damaged our reasoning, so we mistake an apparent good for a real good. Augustine's version is harsher — concupiscence, the body pulling against the soul.

The named root causes to list are selfishness, greed, ignorance and sin.

questions.promptHtml: If God is omniscient, how can we be free? Give the Christian answers.
questions.answerHtml:
The problem: if God knew before Genesis exactly what you would choose, you were never really free — you were always going to do it.

  1. Knowledge is not compulsion. God knows what we will do but does not force us; he may know all possible outcomes, or the end result but not the route we take.
  2. Self-limitation. God has the capacity for omniscience but limits it, so that freedom is genuine.
  3. Timelessness. God is outside time, so he does not know it "before" it happens; all things are present to him, and he knows what we are freely choosing now.

Why it matters: without freewill there is no accountability, no need for the incarnation and crucifixion, and judgement day becomes unjust — which is why most Christians defend freedom even at the cost of a weaker account of foreknowledge.

questions.promptHtml: Why do Christians believe in one God, and why is the Trinity not a contradiction of that?
questions.answerHtml:
One God: God revealed himself that way. In the Ten Commandments he declares that he alone is God and alone is worthy of worship (Exodus 20:2–3), and Jesus endorsed it in telling his followers to love the Lord God with all their heart, mind and soul. Philosophically, the order and unified laws of the world suggest a single designer, and a perfect being cannot have a rival.

The Trinity: God is one substance, three persons. The three work as one — at Jesus's baptism the Father speaks, the Son is baptised and the Spirit descends as a dove (Matthew 3:13–17). The Nicene Creed states the belief formally.

The objection worth knowing: critics ask whether a religion with a Trinity is genuinely monotheistic at all. The answer is the distinction between substance and person.

questions.promptHtml: What is the strongest objection to Paley's design argument, and to Aquinas's first cause argument?
questions.answerHtml:
Against design: natural selection explains apparent design without a designer — complexity is built up by a blind process over immense time. Evolution is also cruel and wasteful, which fits a loving designer badly. And the analogy is weak: we know watches are made, but we have no second universe to compare this one with.

Against first cause: the argument stops the chain of causation exactly where it suits itself. If everything must have a cause, so must God; if something can be uncaused, why not the universe? Science can explain the universe's origin and operation without invoking God, and the theory is simpler without him.

The reply: the first cause must be different in essence — uncaused — and a universe arising from nothing by chance is, Christians argue, less plausible than a creator.

questions.promptHtml: Why does the existence of evil challenge belief in God, and which Christian response is strongest?
questions.answerHtml:
The challenge is the inconsistent triad: an omniscient God knows evil exists, an omnipotent God can remove it, an omnibenevolent God wants to. Evil exists. So God lacks one of those attributes — and any of those conclusions destroys the Christian God.

The responses, appraised: the Freewill Defence (Plantinga) is strong on moral evil — God created the possibility of evil, not evil itself — but says nothing about earthquakes or disease. The Augustinian theodicy covers that gap, tracing natural evil to the corruption of nature after the Fall, but struggles to explain why a good creation would disobey. The Irenaean theodicy makes evil purposeful — soul-making — but asks why God could not build souls through love instead, and reduces the significance of Jesus.

A judgement: the Irenaean theodicy handles both kinds of evil and fits the idea of a world that develops us, which makes it the most complete — though the sheer scale of evil in the evidential problem remains the hardest thing for any of them to answer.

questions.promptHtml: Explain why evil and suffering cause problems for Christians. (6)
questions.answerHtml:
Evil undermines the Christian understanding of God's nature, which is the inconsistent triad set out by Hume and J. L. Mackie 1: an omniscient God knows evil exists, an omnipotent God could remove it, and an omnibenevolent God would want to 1

Since evil plainly exists, the believer appears forced to give up either God's goodness or his power, and either answer destroys the God of the Creeds 1

The evidential problem makes it worse: the sheer scale and gratuitousness of suffering, such as the Holocaust and the Soviet Gulag, is hard to reconcile with any loving purpose 1

The experiential problem is personal: a Christian who meets suffering first-hand and prays without any answer may find belief impossible to sustain 1

Natural evil is the sharpest difficulty, because the Freewill Defence cannot explain earthquakes or disease, which Christians attribute to God's own creation 1

questions.promptHtml:
"If God is omnipotent then we have no freewill."

Do you agree? Give reasons for your answer, showing you have considered another point of view. In your answer you should refer to at least one religion. (12)
questions.answerHtml:
The real paper marks this in levels, so treat the plan below as a target for coverage rather than a tick list.

Arguments for: God's power means he can do anything, including controlling every human mind and preventing people from making their own choices 1

This power is evident in the doctrine of creation: God commands the world and humanity into existence, creates humans in his image and moulds Adam before giving him the breath of life, showing complete power over humanity 1

Calvin's predestination endorses it: God has already determined who is saved and who is damned, so his sovereignty leaves us nothing to control 1

Omniscience reinforces omnipotence — if God knew before Genesis what we would choose, we were always determined to choose it 1

Arguments against: without freewill human beings have no accountability or individuality, which prevents God from having a full, fruitful and personal relationship with them 1

The doctrine of creation itself describes the Fall of Adam and Eve (Genesis 3) because they chose to disobey, which indicates real freedom despite God's power 1

Without freewill humanity cannot sin, so the incarnation and crucifixion of Christ become unnecessary 1

It also undermines judgement day: people cannot be judged for deeds orchestrated by an omnipotent being 1

Christian teaching to anchor it: the Roman Catholic Church teaches that God made us in his image and able to control our own actions, and Deuteronomy 30 sets life and death before us and tells us to "choose life" 1

Christians answer the foreknowledge problem by saying God knows without compelling, limits his own foresight, or stands outside time so that all our free choices are simply present to him 1

Conclusion: although it looks logical that an omnipotent God would negate freewill, that does not fit the Christian belief in a fruitful, personal relationship between God and humanity 1

An omnipotent God has chosen to create beings with freewill so that they can genuinely accept or reject his offer of relationship; after the Fall he sent the Law, the prophets and his Son to restore it, and it is the decision to accept that redemption on which people are judged — so I disagree with the statement 1

questions.promptHtml:
"Humans are superior to animals."

Do you agree? Give reasons for your answer, showing you have considered another point of view. In your answer you should refer to at least one religion. (12)
questions.answerHtml:
Level marked on the real paper — the plan is a target for coverage, not a tick list.

Arguments for: Christians hold that humanity alone shares in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), which gives human beings a unique status among creatures 1

Genesis 1:28 tells humanity to "rule over" and "subdue" the animals — the concept of dominion — and God creates the universe for humans, telling them to be fruitful and multiply 1

Revelation is given to humans, not animals: God became flesh as a human being in the incarnation (John 1:14), and many Christians hold that salvation (John 3:16) is offered only to humanity 1

Non-religiously, humans have evolved into the dominant species through intelligence, reasoning and self-awareness, and animals cannot exercise moral responsibility, so they cannot hold rights 1

Arguments against: animals can suffer and feel pain, so Peter Singer argues they have moral worth and that treating them differently is "speciesist" 1

Evolution shows commonality: we share common ancestors and a high percentage of DNA with higher primates, so we differ by degree rather than in kind 1

Higher primates have complex thought and identity rivalling young children, which makes a sharp human/animal line hard to defend 1

Many Christians read Genesis 1:28 as stewardship rather than hierarchy, and Albert Schweitzer argued for a "reverence for all life" 1

Christian teaching to anchor it: animals are part of a creation God "saw was good", so exploiting them is against God's will and the Bible condemns cruelty to animals 1

Yet most Christians still accept that animals may be used for food, labour and some medical testing, provided they are treated humanely — which is a claim of superiority in practice 1

Conclusion: the biological case for commonality is strong, and the arguments from suffering show that superiority cannot mean animals may be treated as things 1

But the Christian teaching that humanity alone bears the image of God, receives revelation and is offered salvation gives human beings a distinct role and a distinct responsibility; I therefore agree that humans are superior in status, but only in the sense that stewardship makes them accountable for the creatures beneath them 1

questions.promptHtml:
"Suffering proves God does not exist."

Do you agree? Give reasons for your answer, showing you have considered another point of view. In your answer you should refer to at least one religion. (12)
questions.answerHtml:
Level marked on the real paper — the plan is a target for coverage, not a tick list.

Arguments for: if God is good and all-powerful he has both the means and the inclination to prevent suffering, yet suffering occurs, which suggests he does not exist 1

Hume and Mackie set this out as the inconsistent triad, and the conclusion follows: if God existed there would be no evil; evil exists; therefore God cannot exist 1

God is the creator, so natural evil — disease, earthquakes, death — traces back to him rather than to human freewill 1

The evidential problem adds weight: the scale and gratuitousness of the Holocaust or the Gulag go far beyond anything a loving purpose could require 1

Arguments against: a great deal of suffering is caused by the misuse of human freewill, so Plantinga's Freewill Defence shows that a good God can co-exist with evil because he created only the possibility of it 1

Augustine argued evil is not a thing God made but a privation — a corruption of good — originating in the free choice of angels and humans to turn from God in Genesis 3 1

Irenaeus argued God deliberately made the world imperfect so that suffering could develop charity and compassion and build us into the likeness of God 1

Some Christians answer with mystery: in Job, God rebukes human demands for an explanation with "Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?", and the answer may only come in heaven 1

Christian teaching to anchor it: suffering is not meaningless in Christianity, because Jesus himself suffered, and Christians respond practically with prayer, forgiveness and charity rather than treating suffering as a disproof 1

Appraisal: the Freewill Defence is strong on moral evil but silent on natural evil; the Augustinian theodicy covers natural evil but must explain why a good creation disobeyed; the Irenaean theodicy covers both but makes God the author of suffering 1

Conclusion: suffering is the most serious challenge to belief in God, and the evidential version of the problem is not fully answered by any theodicy 1

But "proves" is too strong: the theodicies show the existence of God and the existence of evil are not logically contradictory, so suffering makes belief harder to hold rather than impossible, and I therefore disagree with the statement 1

questions.promptHtml: Explain religious and non-religious views about the commonality of human beings and other animals. (6)
questions.answerHtml:
Many non-religious people stress commonality on the basis of evolutionary theory: humans evolved from a common ancestor with the higher primates and share a high percentage of their DNA 1, a similarity so close that it should guide how we treat other animals, which is why this group tends to favour animal rights 1

Peter Singer goes further, arguing that all animals including humans have the same moral worth because they all make decisions and all feel pain, so it is "speciesist" to think only humans are valuable 1

Christians who accept evolution are also open to commonality, valuing animals both because God created them and declared them good and because of that shared heritage; the concept of stewardship endorses it, and Albert Schweitzer said Christians should have a reverence for all life 1

But most Christians accept commonality only up to a point: humanity alone is created in the image of God, which marks a genuine point of difference, because human beings have a spiritual dimension and can be in a relationship with God 1

That relationship was solidified by the incarnation, when God revealed himself in human form, and the death and resurrection of Jesus point to a salvation offered to humanity alone — which is why some Christians emphasise human dominance over the rest of the animal kingdom 1

Give both sides of the non-religious view and both sides of the Christian view: that symmetry is what the "religious and non-religious" wording is asking for.

questions.promptHtml:
"The life of an animal is as valuable as a human life."

Do you agree? Give reasons for your answer, showing you have considered another point of view. In your answer you should refer to at least one religion. (12)
questions.answerHtml:
Level marked on the real paper — the plan is a target for coverage, not a tick list.

Arguments for: animals are part of a creation God made and declared good, so a minority of Christians argue they are as intrinsically valuable as humans and oppose both research on animals and eating them 1

Scripture extends the duty of care to animals: "A righteous man has regard for the life of his beast" (Proverbs 12:10), and Jesus taught that not even the death of a single sparrow goes unnoticed by God 1

The Messianic vision of Isaiah 11:6–8 looks forward to wolves and sheep living together in peace and a child safe with a poisonous snake — God's intended end for creation is harmony, not exploitation 1

Non-religiously, Peter Singer argues animals have the same moral worth because they make choices and feel pain, and evolution shows commonality — a shared ancestor and a high percentage of shared DNA — so the difference is one of degree, not kind 1

Arguments against: Christians hold that animals were not created in God's image and do not have a soul, so they cannot have the spiritual relationship with God that human beings can 1

Genesis 1:28 gives humanity the command to "fill the earth and subdue it" and to "rule over" every living creature, which most Christians read as a real difference in status 1

The Roman Catholic Church warns its members not to be sentimental about animals or grant them too much importance: human beings are of greater value, and while people suffer every effort should go on relieving that suffering 1

Non-religiously, humanity's intelligence, reasoning and self-awareness make it the dominant species, and animals act on instinct and exercise no moral responsibility, so they cannot hold rights in the way humans do 1

Christian teaching to anchor it: the Roman Catholic Catechism (2417) states that God entrusted animals to the stewardship of those made in his image, so it is legitimate to use them for food and clothing and to experiment on them "within reasonable limits" where this saves human lives 1

The Church of England takes the same balance from the other direction, recognising the need for some animal research while affirming that responsible stewardship requires all animals to receive "careful and sympathetic treatment, both during their lives and in the manner of their dying" 1

Conclusion: the arguments from suffering and from commonality are strong enough to rule out treating animals as mere things, and both Churches accept that cruelty is wrong 1

But "as valuable" is too strong for the Christian position: humanity alone bears the image of God, has a soul and is offered salvation, and both Churches permit the use of animals for food and essential medicine — so I disagree with the statement, while holding that stewardship makes humans accountable for how they use that greater status 1

Genesis 1:28 gives humanity the command to "fill the earth and subdue it" and to "rule over" every living creature, which most Christians read as a real difference in status

The Roman Catholic Church warns its members not to be sentimental about animals or grant them too much importance: human beings are of greater value, and while people suffer every effort should go on relieving that suffering

Non-religiously, humanity's intelligence, reasoning and self-awareness make it the dominant species, and animals act on instinct and exercise no moral responsibility, so they cannot hold rights in the way humans do

Christian teaching to anchor it: the Roman Catholic Catechism (2417) states that God entrusted animals to the stewardship of those made in his image, so it is legitimate to use them for food and clothing and to experiment on them "within reasonable limits" where this saves human lives

The Church of England takes the same balance from the other direction, recognising the need for some animal research while affirming that responsible stewardship requires all animals to receive "careful and sympathetic treatment, both during their lives and in the manner of their dying"
Conclusion: the arguments from suffering and from commonality are strong enough to rule out treating animals as mere things, and both Churches accept that cruelty is wrong

But "as valuable" is too strong for the Christian position: humanity alone bears the image of God, has a soul and is offered salvation, and both Churches permit the use of animals for food and essential medicine — so I disagree with the statement, while holding that stewardship makes humans accountable for how they use that greater status

drill.intro:
How to answer each part — Paper 1

3 marks (AO1) — no explanation is required. Give three focused and distinct points; brief, clear reasons are ideal. Do not develop them.

4 marks (AO1) — these always ask for two points of information which require some development. The development must add value to the point while still answering the question posed, so each point scores 1 and its development scores 1. An example is often the quickest way to develop a point.

6 marks (AO1 + AO2) — these always ask you to explain. Explain and develop the issue, drawing out the influence and significance of the religion, beliefs and values. Level marked: the top level needs religious terms used accurately, a comprehensive explanation, and an assured account of significance. Even where no number is given, explain more than one reason; if told to choose a religion, name it and stay inside it.

12 marks (AO1 + AO2) — the synoptic assessment. Draw on a number of ideas and arguments from across the course, then evaluate and appraise each argument as you make it. Consider every aspect of the question, do not neglect the alternative viewpoint no matter how weak it is, refer to at least one religion (humanist and atheist views give perspective but do not count as that reference), and judge the value of the arguments to reach a fully justified conclusion.

The four parts of a real Question 1 — 3, 4, 6 and 12 marks — three of each in D1–D12, and a fourth set of each in D13–D16. The 6- and 12-mark answers are level marked on the real paper, so the mark points below are a target for coverage, not a tick list — but hitting them all will put you in the top level.

modules.title: Life and Death
modules.standfirst: Section 2 of Paper 1: Beliefs and Values — 25 marks in parts worth 3, 4, 6 and 12, and the longest section on the course: death and destiny (2.1–2.2) — physicalism and dualism, resurrection, judgement, heaven, hell, purgatory, linear against cyclical views and the meaning of life — then the ethics that follow from the sanctity of life (2.3–2.8) — abortion, euthanasia, sexual relationships, homosexuality, marriage, cohabitation, divorce, family life, childlessness, fertility treatment, genetic engineering, contraception, celibacy and adoption. Almost every question turns on one of two things: whether something survives death, or whether the sanctity of life is absolute.

subsections.html:
Two questions run through the whole section. Is death the end? — which is physicalism against dualism, and the evidence each side uses. And what is life for? — which is salvation against a meaning you make yourself. Christian teaching is the spine of every answer, but the non-religious views are examined just as hard, so learn both halves of each pair.

What they actually ask

From the seven June papers 2019–2025, Paper 1 Section 2 (Questions 3 and 4 — you answer one). This is the section that most reliably asks about relationships rather than the afterlife: marriage breakdown has appeared in every single year.

  • Divorce, remarriage and marriage breakdown — all seven years. "three possible consequences of divorce" (2019); "the attitudes its followers have towards divorce" (2020); "Religious people should never divorce" (2021); "three attitudes to remarriage" (2022); "two attitudes to divorce" and "three ways religious people may respond to problems in a marriage" (2023); "two attitudes to remarriage" and "two ways religious people may respond to family breakdown" (2024); "differing attitudes to remarriage" (2025).
  • The meaning and purpose of life — religious and non-religious — six of seven. "In order for life to have meaning and purpose a person must be religious" (2019); "three non-religious ideas about the meaning and purpose of life" (2020); "two religious beliefs about the meaning and purpose of life" (2021); "two non-religious beliefs about the meaning and purpose of life" and "two of its beliefs that may give life purpose" (2022); "the ideas non-religious people have about the meaning and purpose of life" (2023); "its teachings about the meaning and purpose of life" (2024).
  • Children, childlessness, fertility, contraception and adoption — all seven years. "the differing attitudes of religious people to the issue of childlessness" (2019); "two reasons why some people decide not to have children" and "three rights children should have" (2020); "what its followers believe about fertility treatments" (2021); "All religious people should have children" (2022); "three reasons why some people choose not to have children" and "Religious people should never use contraception" (2023); "Religious people should adopt children" (2024); "two non-religious attitudes to adoption" (2025).
  • Marriage, sex outside marriage and cohabitation — "two attitudes its followers hold about sex outside marriage" (2019); "No-one should have sex outside of marriage" (2020); "three purposes of sexual relationships" (2021); "three attitudes to cohabitation" and "what its followers believe about the purpose of marriage" (2022); "three reasons why marriage may be important to religious people" (2024); "differing religious responses to sex outside marriage" (2025).
  • Homosexuality and same-sex relationships — "Heterosexual relationships are the best model for society" (2019); "two different attitudes to homosexuality" (2020); "Attitudes to same sex relationships are changing" (2021); "how religious people may respond to same-sex relationships" (2024); "two attitudes religious people may have to same-sex relationships" (2025).
  • Family life, roles and the generations — "why family life is important for many religious people" (2019); "It is the responsibility of a family to look after their elderly relatives" (2020); "why family life is important to its followers" (2021); "A nuclear family is the best model for society" (2022); "two beliefs about the role of women in the family" (2023); "three ways religious people can support families" (2025).
  • Abortion, euthanasia and the value of life — "two reasons why its followers believe it is important to reduce suffering" (2019); "the attitudes its followers may have towards abortion" (2020); "three things the law says about abortion in one named country" and "two differing attitudes to euthanasia" (2021); "the beliefs its followers may have about euthanasia" (2022); "Allowing an abortion may be the most loving thing to do" (2023); "three non-religious beliefs about the value of human life" (2024); "Euthanasia should be legalised" (2025).
  • Life after death and judgement — "three reasons why some non-religious people believe in life after death" (2019); "two beliefs about the consequences of cause and effect on life after death" (2022); "why religious people may believe in life after death" (2023); "This life is all there is" (2024); "A God centred life is needed for an afterlife in paradise" (2025).

subsections.heading: Is death the end? Physicalism, dualism and the two cases
subsections.html:
Spec 2.1 · Non-religious beliefs and views about death and human destiny · Immortality of the soul · Whether or not there is an afterlife; why some believe and others do not

  • Physicalism: you are your body — thought and feeling come from the brain, so death ends the person.
  • No scientific evidence of a soul — damaged brains lose reasoning and recall, which physicalists read as proof.
  • Why people believe anyway — the desire to go on living and the fear of death; Marx called religion an opiate.
  • Dualism: body and soul — the body deteriorates and dies, but the soul is the permanent part of the person.
  • Plato: becoming and being — the changing body belongs to one realm, the indivisible immortal soul to the other.
  • Some atheists accept an afterlife — on Platonic, psycho-somatic grounds, citing near-death experiences, spiritualism and reincarnation.
Argument for an afterlifeCounter-argument
The Bible clearly states that "eternal life" is on offer, and Christians treat it as authoritative.Religious claims rest on holy books whose sources have never been verified.
Jesus's physical resurrection is evidence that death is not a permanent state.Consciousness is physical brain activity; death destroys the brain and the body.
Psychics, mediums, ghosts and communication with the dead.These all have rational, psychological explanations.
Near-death experiences, and evidence that brain activity continues after the heart stops.Near-death experiences can be explained by physical processes in a dying brain.
Life cannot be called good or just unless there is another life in which justice is dispensed — the good rewarded, the wicked punished.There is simply a lack of good-quality empirical evidence for any of it.
If humans have non-material souls, that lends support to something continuing after death.There are problems with the idea itself: what exactly continues, and would it still be you?
Belief in an afterlife comforts the bereaved and gives life meaning.One may benefit more from accepting life as it is and making the most of it; the belief is driven by fear of death.

✗ "Non-religious people don't believe in life after death." — the spec explicitly asks why some do.
✓ "Some atheists and Humanists accept an afterlife on Platonic grounds, holding that we are psycho-somatic beings whose souls belong to the realm of being."

Read the question's wording. A 4-marker that says "non-religious" and gets Christian teaching scores nothing — this is the single most common error flagged in the school's model-answer feedback.

More detail

Death as the end: physicalism

Physicalism is the view that each person is only a living, physical body, so death marks the end of that individual's existence.

  • We are capable of thought and feeling because of the functions of our brains, not because of a soul.
  • A loss of brain function or efficiency affects our ability to relate to people and to recall our past — when brains deteriorate, reasoning and self-control wane.
  • There is no scientific evidence of a soul or spirit.
  • Consciousness is physical brain activity, and death plainly destroys the brain and the material body.
  • Therefore there is no afterlife.

Physicalists add a sharper point about why people believe in an afterlife: the belief is caused by the desire to go on living, by fear of death, and by an inability to imagine a world without us. Marx went further — the promise of a next life can be used by the ruling classes to control communities, which is why he called religion an opiate.

Body and soul: dualism and Plato

Spec 2.1 · Immortality of the soul

Dualism is the view that a human being is composed of body and soul: the body deteriorates and dies, but the soul is the permanent part of the person.

Plato distinguished two realms. The body changes and so belongs to the realm of becoming; the soul is a simple entity that cannot be broken into parts and is not subject to change, so it belongs to the realm of being. For Plato the immortal soul continues to exist after the death of the body.

This matters in RS because the argument is not only religious. Some atheists and Humanists accept an afterlife because they think human beings are psycho-somatic entities — body and soul together — and they appeal to Plato rather than to scripture. They may also point to paranormal evidence:

  • Near-death experiences — reports of consciousness continuing while the body is clinically dying.
  • Spiritualism — psychics, mediums, communication with the dead, ghosts.
  • Reincarnation and remembered lives.
  • Some evidence that brain activity continues after the heart stops.

Belief in an afterlife may also simply be beneficial: it gives life meaning and it comforts those whose loved ones have died.

Is there an afterlife? The two cases

Spec 2.1 · Whether or not there is an afterlife; why some believe and others do not

This is the table that writes the 12-markers, so learn it in pairs.

subsections.heading: Why Christians believe in life after death
subsections.html:
Spec 2.1 · Christian beliefs about resurrection and the nature of life after death

  • Four reasons, in order — God’s omnipotence and omnibenevolence, Jesus’s teaching, Jesus’s resurrection, and dualism.
  • God can and wants to — he created us once, so he can create us again, and he loves us enough to want to.
  • John 3:16 is the hinge — eternal life is God’s offer, received through faith in Jesus.
  • Resurrection, not just an immortal soul — Paul’s "spiritual bodies" (1 Corinthians 15); Matthew 27:52 has bodies raised.
  • Christians split on what survives — an immortal soul influenced by Greek thought, or God resurrecting body and soul together.

The quotes that do the work

"For God so loved the world that he gave his only son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life." — John 3:16
Used to argue: eternal life is God's offer, received through faith in Jesus.

"The dust returns to the ground it came from, and the spirit returns to God who gave it." — Ecclesiastes 12:7
Used to argue: something non-physical survives the death of the body.

St Paul describes the dead being raised as "spiritual bodies". — 1 Corinthians 15
Used to argue: Christian hope is resurrection, not merely an immortal soul.

"The tombs also were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised." — Matthew 27:52
Used to argue: scripture describes bodily resurrection, not disembodied spirits.

More detail

Christian belief in an afterlife rests on the nature of God, the teaching and resurrection of Jesus, and a dualistic understanding of the person.

  1. The omnipotence and omnibenevolence of God — he created us once and he can create us again, and he loves us enough to want to.
  2. Jesus taught it, and his atoning work on the cross made it possible for humanity to be with God in the next life.
  3. Jesus's resurrection shows that death is not a permanent state.
  4. Dualism — we are body and soul, and the soul can continue to exist with God.

Christians divide on what survives. Some teach an immortal soul superior to the body, influenced by Greek thought. Others reject that as unbiblical and as detracting from humanity's dependence on God: to experience life after death we depend on God's love and power, and just before judgement God resurrects those who have died, body and soul together — which is what happened to Jesus.

subsections.heading: The End Time: eschatology and the millennium
subsections.html:
Spec 2.1 · Christian teachings about the Last Judgement

  • Eschatology — the study of Christian teaching about the End Time, or Eschaton, based on Revelation.
  • Four millennial positions — millennialism, premillennialism, postmillennialism and amillennialism each read the thousand years differently.
  • Naming two is the mark — it shows the divergent views within the religion that the mark scheme rewards.
More detail

Eschatology is the study of Christian teachings about the End Time, or Eschaton, and it is based on the apocalyptic teachings of the book of Revelation.

PositionWhat it teaches
MillennialismChrist will rule the earth for 1,000 years, a time of peace and justice; then the dead will be resurrected to be judged with the living.
PremillennialismThings will get steadily worse, with Satan torturing humanity (the Tribulation), before God defeats Satan — which marks the beginning of Jesus's rule.
PostmillennialismThe millennium started with Jesus's resurrection; things gradually improve until there is enough peace and justice for Jesus to return and fully realise God's kingdom.
AmillennialismThe millennium began with the incarnation and will end with the return of Jesus to judge the living and the dead.

You will not be asked to choose between them, but naming two shows the examiner you know Christians read Revelation differently — which is exactly the "divergent views within the religion" the mark scheme rewards.

subsections.heading: Resurrection and judgement
subsections.html:
Spec 2.1 · Judgement; the law of cause and effect in relation to life after death

  • Resurrected and judged together — at the Eschaton the dead rise and stand with the living before Jesus.
  • Three grounds of judgement — belief in God, acceptance of Jesus’s sacrifice, and obedience to his commandments.
  • Faith: "whoever believes in the Son has eternal life" — salvation is grace, not something earned.
  • Works: the Sheep and the Goats — judged on feeding the hungry and visiting prisoners (Matthew 25:31–40).
  • James settles it — "faith without works is dead", so works are the evidence of faith rather than a rival to it.
  • A 6-marker wants consequences — charity, forgiveness, obedience, confession and missionary work.

The basis of judgement

In the parable of the Sheep and the Goats, those who fed the hungry, clothed the poor, helped the sick and visited prisoners are told that "what you do for the least of these, you do for me", and are counted righteous; those who ignored the needy are cursed. — Matthew 25:31–40
Used to argue: judgement is on good works, so Christians must act now.

"Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life." — John's gospel
Used to argue: judgement is on faith, not on earning salvation.

"Faith without works is dead." — James
Used to argue: the two cannot be separated — faith must show itself in action.

Argument: salvation is by faithCounter-argument: works matter too
"Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life", and John 3:16 makes eternal life the gift given to whoever believes — nothing is said about earning it.The parable of the Sheep and the Goats (Matthew 25:31–40) judges people entirely on what they did for the hungry, the sick and the imprisoned: "what you do for the least of these, you do for me."
Salvation is grace — God's unearned gift.
