Protestants who emphasise faith alone argue that we cannot buy our way into heaven and the Church cannot intercede for us.James settles it from the other side: "Faith without works is dead." A faith that changes nothing is no faith at all, so works are the evidence of faith rather than a rival to it.
Historically this is the Reformation objection: the medieval practice of selling indulgences implied the Church held the keys to heaven, which Protestants rejected as making salvation something purchased.Roman Catholic teaching keeps both: judgement is on belief in God, acceptance of Jesus's sacrifice and obedience to his commandments — and purgatory exists precisely because most people are not yet pure enough for heaven.
If works could save, Christ's sacrifice would not have been necessary — which is the same objection Protestants make to purgatory.A faith with no consequences has no effect on how Christians live now. Belief in judgement is supposed to produce charity, forgiveness, obedience, confession and missionary work, and a 6-marker on judgement wants exactly those consequences.

✗ "Christians go to heaven and non-Christians go to hell." — too crude, and it ignores the faith-versus-works debate entirely.
✓ "Judgement rests on faith in Christ, but the parable of the Sheep and the Goats makes good works the evidence of that faith, which is why James insists faith without works is dead."

A 6-marker on "how belief in judgement affects Christian lives" wants consequences: charity, forgiveness, obedience to the commandments, confession, missionary work. Describing judgement without saying what it makes people do stays in level 2.

More detail

At the beginning of the Eschaton the dead will be resurrected and judged alongside the living by Jesus.

Judgement is based on belief in God, acceptance of Jesus's sacrifice, and obedience to God's commandments. God will judge all either at the end of life or at the end of the world; all people are sinful, and salvation is a gift through Christ.

Cause and effect in a Christian frame: faith in Jesus plus good works leads to reward in the afterlife. Some Protestants emphasise faith alone — we cannot buy our way into heaven, and the Church cannot intercede for us. Others point to James to insist that works matter too. Where other religions are concerned, some Christians are exclusivists and hold that salvation is only for Christians; others disagree.

"Faith is all a Christian needs to be saved" is the 12-marker this subsection exists for. Learn it in pairs:

subsections.heading: Heaven and hell
subsections.html:
Spec 2.1 · Christian beliefs about heaven and hell

  • Heaven is the reward — eternal communion with God and no sin or suffering; Jesus likens it to a wedding feast.
  • Three readings of heaven — a real place, this world transformed, or a symbol of relationship with God.
  • Hell is eternal punishment — Revelation’s "lake of fire"; Dante’s Inferno imagines nine circles.
  • Four readings of hell — literal torture, annihilation, a symbol of separation from God, or empty.
  • Universalism — hell as correction with eventual salvation for all; Luke 16:19–31 tells against it.
  • Exclusivists — hold heaven is only for Christians, which leaves the problem of those never told.
Argument: hell is incompatible with a loving GodCounter-argument
Eternal punishment with no hope of redemption is disproportionate to any finite human sin, and an omnibenevolent God could not will it — so if hell exists it must be empty.God is just as well as loving. Judgement would be meaningless if every outcome were the same, and Revelation describes wrongdoers "thrown into the lake of fire".
Universalists treat hell as a place of correction rather than punishment, and expect eventual universal salvation — which keeps judgement without making God a torturer.Jesus's own teaching tells against it: in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31) the afterlife is eternal and the fate is fixed, with no crossing between the two states.
Hell need not be a place at all. Read as annihilation — simply ceasing to exist — or as a symbol of separation from God, the objection loses most of its force, and Christians lose nothing they need.If hell is only a symbol, so is heaven, and the whole point of judgement weakens; exclusivists go further and hold that heaven is only for Christians.
God does not send anyone there: hell is the consequence of a free choice to reject God's love, so the freewill God gave is what makes it possible, not a failure of his goodness.That reply is only as strong as the account of freewill behind it — and it still leaves the problem of those who never heard the offer at all, which is why many Christians reject exclusivism.
More detail

Heaven is described as paradise and hell as a place of torment — but Christians disagree about whether either is a place at all.

Heaven. It is the reward for faith and/or good works; the kingdom of God fully experienced; eternal life in everlasting communion with God; a shared community with no sin, evil, suffering or death. Jesus likens it to a banquet or wedding feast, and Revelation describes "a rainbow, resembling an emerald, encircling the throne of God". The interpretations:

  • Heaven is a real place, a higher metaphysical world.
  • Heaven is this world transformed after the day of judgement.
  • Heaven is a symbol of eternal life in positive relationship with God, not a location.
  • Some see it in terms of bodily resurrection, others as a higher world of souls.
  • Exclusivists hold that it is only for Christians.

Hell. It is eternal punishment for the wicked — the immoral and non-believers — with no hope of redemption; the domain of the devil. Revelation describes wrongdoers being "thrown into the lake of fire", and Dante's Inferno imagines nine circles, with Limbo first, over the gate of which is written "abandon hope all you who enter here". The interpretations:

  • Hell is a literal place of eternal torture.
  • Hell is annihilation — simply ceasing to exist.
  • Hell is a symbol of separation from God: existing without divine love and peace.
  • Hell is incompatible with the love of God, so if it exists it must be empty.

Some Christians find eternal punishment impossible to square with a just God, and so treat hell as a place of correction, expecting eventual universal salvation — universalism. Against that, the book of Revelation and some of Jesus's own teaching — the parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31) — describe the afterlife as eternal and one's fate as fixed.

"A loving God would not send anyone to hell" is the 12-marker here, and it is answered from inside Christianity rather than against it:

subsections.heading: Purgatory
subsections.html:
Spec 2.1 · Religious beliefs about the nature of life after death

  • A Roman Catholic belief — after judgement the righteous are purified of their sins before entering heaven.
  • The "final purification of the elect" — developed in the medieval period, because most are not pure enough for heaven.
  • Prayers for the dead — the process can be shortened, so relatives are encouraged to pray.
  • The Protestant objection — not in the Bible, salvation is by faith alone, and it implies Christ’s sacrifice was insufficient.
  • The standard 4-marker — "two different Christian beliefs about purgatory": one from each column, each developed.
More detail

Purgatory is a Roman Catholic belief that after judgement the righteous spend time being purified of their sins before entering heaven.

It was developed during the medieval period to explain how someone who had sinned could still be saved: most people are not pure enough to enter heaven immediately and need purification. The Roman Catholic Church calls it the "final purification of the elect". Because the process can be shortened, relatives are encouraged to pray for the dead.

Catholic beliefProtestant objection
Purification is needed before a sinful person can stand in God's presence.There is no mention of purgatory in the Bible, so it is rejected as unbiblical.
Prayers of the living can help those in purgatory.Salvation comes through faith in Christ alone, not through the works of humanity.
It explains how a just God can save imperfect people.It implies Christ's sacrifice was not sufficient on its own.

This is the standard 4-mark question on this section — "explain two different Christian beliefs about purgatory" — so learn one point from each column, each developed.

subsections.heading: Linear and cyclical views of human existence
subsections.html:
Spec 2.1 · Linear and cyclical views; immortality of the soul, resurrection, rebirth and judgement

  • Linear (Christian) — one life, one death, one resurrection and one judgement, then heaven or hell.
  • Cyclical — deeds decide rebirth into a higher or lower form, or escape from the cycle altogether.
  • Hinduism: atman, karma, moksha — the soul is released and reincarnated, aiming to unite with Brahman.
  • Buddhism: no soul at all — anicca, anatta and dukkha; the skandhas separate, so only consequences survive.
  • Compare on four themes — identity, judgement, opportunity and the problem of evil.
  • Paper 1 rule — your named religion must be Christianity; other traditions only supply the alternative view.
More detail

Christianity holds a linear view of human existence; the cyclical view belongs to Eastern religions, and the contrast is what the exam wants.

The linear view (Christian): you are born, you live, you die; at the End Time the dead are resurrected and stand with the living to be judged on their belief in and acceptance of God and on their life choices; they then experience either eternity in heaven or eternal damnation in hell. Death is the end of human life, and there is one life and one judgement.

The cyclical view: a person's deeds determine whether they are reborn into a higher or lower form of life, or escape the cycle of birth and rebirth altogether.

TraditionWhat it teaches
HinduismWe are psycho-somatic beings; each living being has an atman (soul), the permanent aspect of the individual. At death the atman is released and reincarnated; the type of creature depends on karma — one's actions. The aim is moksha, freedom from the cycle of samsara, so the atman unites with Brahman, the World Soul.
BuddhismThe idea of a psycho-somatic unity is an illusion — there is no soul. Every individual suffers three universal symptoms: anicca (change), anatta (no soul) and dukkha (suffering or dissatisfaction). Extinguishing greed and selfishness by following the Noble Eightfold Path brings enlightenment and nirvana; otherwise at death the skandhas separate and merge with others to form new beings, so only our consequences survive.

Compare them on the four themes the lesson sets out — and note that on Paper 1 your named religion must be Christianity, with other traditions used only to supply the alternative viewpoint:

ThemeLinear (Christian)Cyclical
IdentityThe same person is resurrected and judged, so identity is preserved.Hinduism preserves the atman; Buddhism does not, so arguably nothing of "you" continues.
JudgementOne judgement by a just God, based on faith and works.No judge is needed — karma operates as an impersonal law of cause and effect.
OpportunityOne life only, which makes this life urgent and valuable.Many lives, which allows progress over time but may reduce urgency.
The problem of evilSuffering is hard to reconcile with an omnipotent, benevolent God.Suffering is explained as the consequence of deeds in a previous life.

subsections.heading: Christian teachings on the meaning and purpose of life
subsections.html:
Spec 2.2 · Eternal life, the kingdom of God, salvation, Jesus as lord and saviour; salvation by faith versus works

  • Meaning comes from creation and salvation — we were made by God and are offered eternal life through Christ.
  • Aquinas: the supreme good is God — not happiness, but a positive relationship with the God who made us.
  • Augustine: we cannot save ourselves — so we must put our trust in Christ.
  • Love, kingdom and self-denial — love God and neighbour, build the kingdom, take up your cross daily (Luke 9:23).
  • Christian hedonism — the purpose of humanity is to enjoy God lavishly, by knowing, worshipping and serving him.
  • Salvation: faith, works or both — John 3:16 against the Sheep and the Goats, with James insisting on both.

Salvation: faith or works?

"For God so loved the world that he gave his only son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life." — John 3:16
Used to argue: salvation comes by faith, as a gift of God's grace.

"What you do for the least of these, you do for me." — Matthew 25:31–40
Used to argue: salvation is shown in works — how we treat the needy.

"Faith without works is dead." — James
Used to argue: the two belong together; faith that changes nothing is no faith at all.

More detail

For Christians the meaning and purpose of life come from the doctrines of creation and salvation: we were made by God, and we are offered eternal life through Christ.

  • Created by God (Genesis) — we are part of God's plan, and meaning comes from that.
  • To praise and serve God. Aquinas argued that the supreme good for a human being is not happiness but a positive relationship with God: we are alive because God created us, and seeking God out and experiencing him gives life meaning.
  • Salvation and forgiveness — accepting Christ's sacrifice on the cross and living by God's commandments. Augustine held that we cannot save ourselves and must put our trust in Christ.
  • Love and Christian ethical practice — the greatest commandment to love God and love your neighbour.
  • Building the kingdom of God — aiming to transform the earth so that it reflects God's kingdom.
  • Self-denial — "Whoever wants to be my disciple must deny themselves and take up their cross daily and follow me." (Luke 9:23)
  • Christian hedonism — the primary purpose of humanity is to enjoy God lavishly, by knowing, worshipping and serving him.

Salvation is achieved through the grace of God, faith, worship and love. Protestants who emphasise faith alone argue that we cannot buy our way into heaven and the Church cannot intercede; others insist, with James, that good works are required evidence.

subsections.heading: Non-religious meaning and purpose — and whether the question even helps
subsections.html:
Spec 2.2 · Non-religious ideas about the meaning and purpose of life; whether life can have meaning only for religious people

  • Six named positions — Darwinian survival, Aristotle’s flourishing, hedonism and Epicurus, Bentham, Sartre, Nietzsche.
  • Sartre: radical freedom — no God means no script, so we must choose and invent meaning for ourselves.
  • Nietzsche: nihilism — God is dead, values are baseless, and all meaning and purpose are false.
  • Epicurus is the mild version — minimise pain and live a happy, tranquil life.
  • Humanist views do not count as the religion — a 12-marker still needs reference to at least one religion.
  • Marx: religion as an opiate — a false higher meaning that distracts people from social progress.
Argument: life has meaning only for religious peopleCounter-argument
Without God there is no absolute meaning or purpose — declare "God is dead" with Nietzsche and you slip into nihilism.Even with no absolute, objective answer, we can still create our own purpose and meaning.
Only an afterlife can give ultimate purpose to this life.Happiness is a purpose most people accept, and it does not depend on God existing.
There is no reason to act morally if there is no God, which leads to a selfish worldview.Being religious may actually be damaging — a false sense of purpose can stop us appreciating this life.
Without God, life is random, chaotic and cruel.Aristotle, Bentham and Sartre all give workable accounts of purpose with no God in them at all.
Argument: the questions get in the wayCounter-argument
"Meaning" and "purpose" are human inventions, so the question has no answer.To know how to improve the world we must first know what ultimate values we are aiming at.
Asking abstract philosophical questions detracts from actually living a full life.These questions have troubled humans for centuries precisely because they matter.
People need practical help, not theoretical discussion of ultimate purpose.Religious people would call them fundamentally important — eternal life may be at stake.
Marx criticised religion as an opiate, distracting people from social progress with the false promise of a higher meaning.A sense of purpose is arguably crucial for psychological health and wellbeing.

✗ Answering "life has meaning only for religious people" by describing Christian beliefs about heaven for a page.
✓ Give the case for, the case against, appraise each one, name at least one religion, and finish with a justified conclusion and your own opinion.

In the 12-markers, humanist and atheist views give useful perspective — but on their own they do not count as the reference to one religion the question requires.

Everything below this line is new ground

Spec points 2.3 to 2.8 have not been taught in class yet and no lesson slides exist for them, so the seventeen subsections that follow were built from the Edexcel 4RS1 specification and the school's Section 2 revision booklet rather than from John's own lessons — check them against the lessons when they happen.

More detail

Non-religious accounts of meaning do not appeal to God, and the spec expects you to name the thinkers.

  • Darwinian — the purpose of life is to survive and reproduce.
  • Aristotle — the purpose is to flourish: living and doing well allows the full expression of the human intellect.
  • Hedonism — pleasure is the most important intrinsic good (hedone is Greek for pleasure). Epicurus argued a milder version: minimise pain and live a happy, tranquil life.
  • Bentham and the utilitarians — value lies in seeking the greatest good for the greatest number.
  • Sartre — if God is dead there is no script or plan; there is no external, fixed meaning, so we must choose and invent meaning for ourselves. Radical freedom.
  • Nietzsche — God is dead, all values are baseless and reason is impotent; all meaning and purpose are false. Nihilism.

The spec also asks about the claim that these questions get in the way of living well and improving the world:

subsections.heading: The sanctity of life
subsections.html:
Spec 2.3 · Christian teachings about the sanctity of life and the particular value of human life; non-religious beliefs about the value of life — not yet taught in class — built from the specification

  • Life is a sacred gift from God — intrinsically valuable, so it must be protected, and it is not ours to end.
  • Two halves the exam wants — worth does not depend on usefulness, and God gives life and takes it away.
  • Imago Dei is the ground — Genesis 1:27 gives every human being intrinsic moral worth.
  • Jeremiah 1:5 is the anti-abortion text — God knew you and set you apart before you were born.
  • Catholic teaching is the strongest form — Natural Law’s "preserve life"; protected absolutely from the moment of conception.
  • Liberals hold a weaker form — the presumption is against ending life, but agape may make it the most loving option.

The scripture that carries sanctity of life

"So God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them." — Genesis 1:27
Used to argue: imago Dei — every human being shares in the image of God, which gives all human life intrinsic moral worth.

"You shall not murder." — Exodus 20:13
Used to argue: taking innocent human life is directly forbidden by the Decalogue.

"Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, before you were born I set you apart." — Jeremiah 1:5
Used to argue: God knows and has a plan for a person before birth, so the unborn child is already in relationship with him. This is the key anti-abortion text.

"For you created my inmost being; you knit me together in my mother's womb." — Psalm 139:13
Used to argue: God is the maker of life in the womb; later in the psalm, "I am fearfully and wonderfully made" (139:14).

"The LORD gave and the LORD has taken away; may the name of the LORD be praised." — Job 1:21
Used to argue: both the beginning and the end of a life are God's decision, not ours.

"Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have received from God? You are not your own." — 1 Corinthians 6:19
Used to argue: the body is held in trust from God, so it is not simply ours to dispose of.

✗ "Sanctity of life means life is really important."
✓ "Sanctity of life means life is a sacred gift from God, intrinsically valuable because humans are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27), and therefore not ours to end."

A 6-marker on sanctity of life wants two developed teachings with scripture attached — not a list of verses with no explanation of what each one establishes.

More detail

Sanctity of life is the belief that life is a sacred gift from God: it is intrinsically valuable, so it must be protected, and it is not for human beings to decide when it ends.

Two halves to the belief, and the exam wants both:

  1. Life is intrinsically valuable — its worth does not depend on how useful, healthy or happy the person is. It comes from God.
  2. Life is not ours to end — God gives it and God takes it away, so decisions about death belong to him.

The Roman Catholic position is the strongest form of the belief. Natural Law gives preserve life as a primary precept, and an ordered society is one in which human life is protected. The Catechism teaches that human life is sacred because from its beginning it involves the creative action of God, and that it must be respected and protected absolutely from the moment of conception.

More liberal Christians hold a weaker form. Life is still sacred and the presumption is always against ending it — but in a tragic case, ending a life may be the most loving option, and love (agape) is the one absolute. This is situation ethics, and it is where almost all the internal Christian disagreement in 2.3 comes from.

Non-religious views on the value of life do not appeal to God, and they are examined just as hard:

  • Utilitarians value a life for the happiness it contains, so quality of life rather than mere biological life is what matters.
  • Peter Singer argues that human life is not intrinsically more valuable than animal life; what matters morally is self-awareness and the capacity to suffer, which a foetus or a brain-dead patient may lack.
  • Most non-religious people still hold human life to be of very high value: the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) states in Article 3 that everyone has the right to life.
  • The warning example of judging some lives less valuable than others is Nazi Germany's racial ideology — which both religious and non-religious thinkers use as a reason to keep the value of human life absolute.
Sanctity of lifeQuality of life
Life is a gift from God and valuable in itself, whatever its condition.A life of unrelieved suffering may not be a benefit to the person living it.
Imago Dei applies to every human being equally, so no one may be written off.Judging by quality allows compassion to override a rule that can cause harm.
Once you start grading lives by quality you have no clear line to stop at.Medicine already makes quality-of-life judgements, for example in withdrawing futile treatment.

subsections.heading: Relieving suffering
subsections.html:
Spec 2.3 · Christian teachings and non-religious beliefs about the importance of relieving suffering — not yet taught in class — built from the specification

  • Relieving suffering is a duty — Jesus healed the sick, and judgement itself is described in terms of the needy.
  • Three Christian reasons — the Sheep and the Goats, Jesus’s example with lepers, and "love your neighbour".
  • Healing is a gift of the Spirit — Jesus gave the disciples authority to heal, and Christians claim miracles today.
  • Non-religious reasons — utilitarian happiness, science and medicine, and freedom from avoidable pain as a right.
  • The tension to name — relieving suffering and protecting life pull opposite ways in abortion and euthanasia.
More detail

Christians treat the relief of suffering as a duty, because Jesus healed the sick and because judgement itself is described in terms of how the needy were treated.

Christian reasons to relieve sufferingNon-religious reasons to relieve suffering
The parable of the Sheep and the Goats makes care of the sick the basis of judgement — "whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me" (Matthew 25:40).For utilitarians, reducing suffering directly increases the general happiness, so it is the clearest moral duty there is.
Jesus set the example: he healed lepers and other outcasts, which was radical because sickness was associated with sin and exclusion.Modern science and medicine are seen as the main means of reducing suffering, and supporting them is a moral priority.
It follows from the commandment to "love your neighbour as yourself" (Mark 12:31).Freedom from avoidable pain is treated as a human right.
Healing is one of the gifts of the Holy Spirit; Jesus gave the disciples authority to heal, and many Christians claim healing miracles today.Suffering has no purpose or redemptive value, so there is no reason to preserve it.

Note the tension the examiner is looking for: a Christian has both a duty to relieve suffering and a duty to protect life. In abortion and euthanasia those two duties pull in opposite directions, and which one wins is exactly what Christians disagree about.

subsections.heading: Abortion: the law and the arguments
subsections.html:
Spec 2.3 · The nature of abortion, current legal arrangements, and differing attitudes to abortion among religious and non-religious people — not yet taught in class — built from the specification

  • Abortion — deliberately ending a pregnancy before the foetus could survive independently.
  • Abortion Act 1967 — two doctors must agree, "in good faith", that one of the legal grounds is met.
  • 24 weeks, or up to birth — risk to health to 24 weeks; grave injury, risk to life or serious disability to birth.
  • Neither banned nor on demand — abortion outside those grounds remains unlawful in the UK.
  • Against: sanctity of life — Exodus 20:13, Jeremiah 1:5, Natural Law, life from conception, the "culture of death".
  • For: the most loving option — liberals and, in strictly limited cases, the Church of England accept the lesser evil.

✗ "Christians are against abortion."
✓ "Most Christians begin from the sanctity of life and so oppose abortion, and Roman Catholic teaching rejects it absolutely from conception — but liberal Christians and, in strictly limited circumstances, the Church of England accept that it may be the most loving or least harmful option."

Naming denominations is the quickest way into the top level. "Some Christians… other Christians…" is worth less than "Roman Catholics… Anglicans…".

More detail

Abortion is the deliberate ending of a pregnancy before the foetus can survive independently, and the Christian argument turns on whether the sanctity of life is absolute or can be outweighed by the most loving outcome.

The law in the UK (the spec requires current legal arrangements in a named country):

  • Governed by the Abortion Act 1967. Two doctors must agree, "in good faith", that one of the legal grounds is met.
  • Up to 24 weeks (the limit set by amendment in 1990): risk to the physical or mental health of the pregnant woman, or to that of her existing children, greater than the risk of continuing the pregnancy.
  • Up to birth: risk of grave permanent injury to the woman's physical or mental health; risk to her life; or a substantial risk that the child would be seriously disabled.
  • Abortion remains unlawful outside those grounds, so the UK neither bans it nor allows it on demand.
Christian arguments against abortionChristian arguments for allowing it
It breaks the sanctity of life: life is God's gift, and Exodus 20:13 forbids killing. Conservative Christians call abortion a form of murder.Liberal Christians argue it can be the most loving option — situation ethics — for instance where the pregnancy results from rape, or where the woman's life is in danger.
God knows and plans for the child before birth (Jeremiah 1:5; Psalm 139:13), so the unborn child is already a person in relationship with him.Quality of life should also weigh: a child facing a very short and painful life, or a family that cannot cope, are morally relevant facts.
Catholic teaching adds Natural Law — preserve life, reproduce, keep an ordered society — and holds that life begins at conception, so the embryo is not "just a bundle of cells".Some Christians do not regard the early foetus as a full person, and so do not treat early abortion as the taking of a human life.
Abortion is said to devalue human life generally; John Paul II's Evangelium Vitae describes a "culture of death".Others hold that the decision belongs to the individual conscience before God, not to the church or the state.
There are better alternatives — adoption, fostering, and proper support for the mother.The Church of England holds that abortion is a great moral evil, but accepts that in strictly limited circumstances it may be the lesser of two evils, for example where mother and child would otherwise both die.
Non-religious arguments for allowing abortionNon-religious arguments against
Utilitarians: abortion may produce the greatest happiness for everyone concerned, including the existing family.It conflicts with the doctor's duty to do no harm, which the Hippocratic oath expresses.
The child might have a very poor quality of life, or the pregnancy might damage the welfare of the mother or her other children.It destroys a potential life that could have been a long and happy one.
Personal autonomy: John Stuart Mill's harm principle says we may do as we wish provided we do not harm others, and many argue a woman has fundamental rights over her own body.Rights need not be religious: if the foetus is a human being, or at least a potential person, it can be argued it already has a right to life.
Some deny the early foetus moral significance at all; Singer argues moral status depends on self-awareness, not species membership.Better alternatives exist — more effective contraception, social support for pregnant women, and easier adoption.

subsections.heading: Euthanasia: the law and the arguments
subsections.html:
Spec 2.3 · The nature of euthanasia, current legal arrangements, and differing attitudes to euthanasia among religious and non-religious people — not yet taught in class — built from the specification

  • Euthanasia — bringing about a gentle death to end suffering; the vocabulary is marked to the word.
  • Voluntary, non-voluntary, involuntary — at the person’s request, decided for them, or against their wishes.
  • Active, passive, assisted suicide — a deliberate act, withdrawing treatment, or providing someone else the means.
  • Suicide Act 1961 — suicide is no crime, but assisting carries up to 14 years, so euthanasia is illegal here.
  • Belgium and the Netherlands since 2002 — the lawful contrast country the spec allows you to name.
  • Palliative care is the alternative — St Christopher’s Hospice, founded 1967 by Dame Cicely Saunders, a Christian.

✗ Writing a 12-marker on euthanasia that is all about how sad suffering is.
✓ Every paragraph should carry a named argument — sanctity of life, autonomy, slippery slope, most loving option — and then appraise it before moving on.

Also keep the words straight: assisted suicide is not euthanasia, and withdrawing futile treatment is not what the Catholic Church calls murder.

More detail

Euthanasia is bringing about a gentle death to end suffering, and the vocabulary is marked to the word.

Kind of euthanasiaWhat it means
Voluntary euthanasiaThe person's life is ended at their own clear and repeated request.
Non-voluntary euthanasiaThe person cannot express a wish — for example someone in a persistent vegetative state — and the decision is taken for them.
Involuntary euthanasiaThe person's life is ended against their wishes. Almost everyone on both sides rejects this.
Active euthanasiaA deliberate act, such as a lethal injection, causes the death.
Passive euthanasiaDeath follows from withdrawing or withholding treatment that is keeping the person alive.
Assisted suicideSomeone else provides the means, but the person ends their own life.
Palliative care and hospicesThe main alternative: controlling pain and caring for the dying rather than ending life. St Christopher's Hospice was founded in 1967 by Dame Cicely Saunders, a Christian.

The law in the UK: the Suicide Act 1961 means suicide and attempted suicide are no longer crimes, but assisting a suicide remains an offence carrying up to 14 years in prison, and actively ending another person's life is murder or manslaughter — so euthanasia is illegal. For contrast, the spec allows another named country: euthanasia has been lawful under strict safeguards in Belgium and the Netherlands since 2002.

Christian arguments against euthanasiaChristian arguments for allowing it
It breaks the sanctity of life — God gives and takes away life (Job 1:21), and Exodus 20:13 forbids killing. Conservative Christians call it a form of murder.Liberal Christians argue it can be the most loving option where suffering is intense and death is near, which is situation ethics applied to the end of life.
Catholic teaching: it breaks the Natural Law precept to preserve life, and the Catechism states that an act or omission which, of itself or by intention, causes death in order to eliminate suffering is murder.Quality of life must be weighed as well as sanctity of life; a Christian is not obliged to keep a body alive at all costs.
Suffering can have meaning in Christian thought — it can be shared with Christ's suffering — and life should be protected to the very end.Some argue that a patient who is brain-dead or permanently unconscious is no longer living a human life in any full sense.
There is a better alternative: hospices and good palliative care, which relieve the suffering without ending the life.God gave human beings free will and conscience, so some Christians hold the decision belongs to the person and their family before God.
Legalising it devalues human life and pressures the vulnerable — again the "culture of death" argument.Even opponents often accept withdrawing disproportionate treatment: Catholic teaching permits discontinuing medical procedures that are burdensome and futile, which is not the same as killing.
Non-religious arguments for allowing euthanasiaNon-religious arguments against
Utilitarian: ending unbearable and untreatable suffering increases happiness and reduces pain overall.It conflicts with the duty of doctors to do no harm, and many in the medical profession oppose it for that reason.
Autonomy: Mill's harm principle, and the claim that we have a fundamental right to choose the time and manner of our own death.The slippery slope: legalising voluntary euthanasia may lead on to non-voluntary and then involuntary killing.
It is unjust that people who are too disabled to end their own lives are denied a choice others have.Practical difficulties: who would qualify, who would police it, and how would the vulnerable be protected from pressure by family or doctors?
Experience in countries where it is legal, such as Belgium since 2002, is used to argue that safeguards can work.The alternative is to fix end-of-life care — better palliative care and hospice provision — rather than to offer death.

subsections.heading: Christian teaching on love and sexual relationships
subsections.html:
Spec 2.4 · Christian teaching about love, the nature and importance of sexual relationships, and attitudes to sex outside marriage; atheist and Humanist attitudes and Christian responses — not yet taught in class — built from the specification

  • Agape is the starting point — selfless, self-giving love, defined by how it behaves rather than how it feels.
  • "The greatest of these is love" — 1 Corinthians 13:13, which liberals make the test of any relationship.
  • Three purposes of sex — procreation (Genesis 1:28), union as one flesh (Genesis 2:24), and faithful love.
  • Unitive and procreative belong together — the Catholic Natural Law reasoning that decides most of this topic.
  • Three Christian positions — Catholic and evangelical prohibition, Anglican pastoral ideal, liberal and Quaker conscience.
  • Humanists: consent, honesty, no harm — marital status is irrelevant, though adultery still breaks a promise.

Love: the passage the whole topic rests on

"Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud." — 1 Corinthians 13:4
Used to argue: Christian love is defined by how it behaves, not by how it feels — which is why it can be commanded.

"And now these three remain: faith, hope and love. But the greatest of these is love." — 1 Corinthians 13:13
Used to argue: love outranks every other virtue; liberal Christians use this to make love the test of whether any relationship is good.

"Love your neighbour as yourself." — Mark 12:31
Used to argue: the second greatest commandment, and the ground of every Christian duty to another person.

Sex belongs in marriage: the texts used

"Flee from sexual immorality." — 1 Corinthians 6:18, followed by "your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit" (6:19)
Used to argue: against promiscuity and casual sex — the body is God's, not a thing to use.

"You shall not commit adultery." — Exodus 20:14
Used to argue: faithfulness within marriage is a direct commandment.

"Anyone who looks at a woman lustfully has already committed adultery with her in his heart." — Matthew 5:28
Used to argue: Jesus extends the commandment from the act to the intention.

"But if they cannot control themselves, they should marry, for it is better to marry than to burn with passion." — 1 Corinthians 7:9
Used to argue: Paul directs sexual desire into marriage rather than outside it.

Argument: sex belongs only in marriageCounter-argument
Natural Law: sex has a unitive and a procreative purpose which belong together, and marriage is the only relationship ordered to both. Roman Catholic and conservative evangelical teaching holds all sex outside marriage wrong.Liberal and Quaker Christians hold that what matters is the quality of the relationship — commitment, faithfulness, honesty and mutual respect — and that the decision belongs to individual conscience before God.
Scripture directs desire into marriage: "flee from sexual immorality" and "your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit" (1 Corinthians 6:18–19), and Paul's concession that "it is better to marry than to burn with passion" (1 Corinthians 7:9).Those texts address promiscuity rather than committed unmarried partners, and 1 Corinthians 13 makes love, not marital status, the test of a relationship — "the greatest of these is love."
Marriage is a covenant made before God in which the couple promise to forsake all others, so sex outside it breaks a promise or anticipates one not yet made — and Jesus extends the commandment on adultery to the intention (Matthew 5:28).The Church of England keeps marriage as the ideal but takes a pastoral rather than a condemning view of people whose lives do not fit it, and in practice welcomes cohabiting couples who come to be married.
Christians reply to the non-religious case that it underrates the vulnerability of sex and the good of lifelong commitment, that children do best in stable marriages, and that treating sex as merely private risks treating people as means to pleasure.Atheist and Humanist attitudes, which the spec names: sex is a natural good, and what makes it right or wrong is consent, honesty and the avoidance of harm. Mill's harm principle finds nothing wrong where both consent — though adultery is still judged wrong, because it breaks a promise.
More detail

Christian teaching on relationships starts from agape — selfless, self-giving love — and places sexual relationships inside lifelong, faithful, monogamous marriage.

The purposes of sex in Christian teaching:

  • Procreation — "Be fruitful and increase in number; fill the earth" (Genesis 1:28).
  • Union — "they become one flesh" (Genesis 2:24): sex consummates and seals the marriage.
  • An expression of faithful love between husband and wife, and a strengthening of their bond.
  • In Catholic teaching the unitive and procreative purposes belong together and should not be separated, which is Natural Law reasoning.

Where Christians differ:

  • Roman Catholic and conservative evangelical: all sex outside marriage — pre-marital sex, promiscuity, adultery — is wrong; Natural Law and scripture are decisive.
  • Anglican: marriage remains the ideal and the proper place for sex, but the church takes a pastoral view of people whose lives do not fit the ideal.
  • Liberal and Quaker: what matters most is the quality of the relationship — commitment, faithfulness, honesty and mutual respect — and the decision is a matter of individual conscience.

Atheist and Humanist attitudes, which the spec names explicitly: sex is a natural, biological and emotional good; what makes it right or wrong is consent, honesty and the avoidance of harm rather than marital status; Mill's harm principle applies, so consenting adults may choose freely; sex before marriage and contraception are unproblematic; adultery is still usually judged wrong, because it breaks a promise and harms people. Christian responses: that this underrates the vulnerability of sex and the good of lifelong commitment, that children do best in stable marriages, and that treating sex as merely private risks treating people as means to pleasure.

Changing patterns of relationships between the sexes. Conservative Christians argue that the pattern was set by God in Genesis and should not change — the man as provider, the woman as homemaker. Others point to what has actually changed: women in paid work, the financial need for two incomes, contraception, and the acceptance of a man staying at home. Liberal Christians read the change as good: all are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27), "there is neither… male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28), and it is for each couple to negotiate their roles.

"Sex should only take place within marriage" is the standard 12-marker on 2.4, and it is the one place where the Christian columns split most clearly:

subsections.heading: Homosexuality: the range of Christian teaching
subsections.html:
Spec 2.4 · Different Christian teachings and attitudes towards homosexuality; religious and non-religious attitudes to human sexuality, including heterosexuality and homosexuality — not yet taught in class — built from the specification

  • The disagreement is about reading the Bible — write both sides with the texts each uses, and do not editorialise.
  • Against: Leviticus 18:22 and Romans 1:26–27 — plus Mark 10:6–9 grounding marriage in male and female.
  • For: Genesis 1:27, 1 Corinthians 13, Galatians 3:28 — God’s image, judged by love, the old categories dissolved.
  • Interpretive arguments — Jesus says nothing; the holiness code is not kept; the Church revised slavery and women.
  • Catechism 2357–2359 — acts "intrinsically disordered", people accepted with "respect, compassion, and sensitivity", called to chastity.
  • Quakers 2009, Methodists 2021, CofE 2023 — same-sex marriages, then marriages, then Prayers of Love and Faith.

The texts used by Christians who hold that same-sex sexual acts are wrong

"Do not have sexual relations with a man as one does with a woman; that is detestable." — Leviticus 18:22 (older translations: "it is an abomination")
Used to argue: the Old Testament law explicitly prohibits same-sex acts.

Paul writes that "God gave them over to shameful lusts" (1:26), and that the men "abandoned natural relations with women and were inflamed with lust for one another" (1:27). — Romans 1:26–27
Used to argue: the prohibition is not only Old Testament; Paul treats such acts as contrary to nature.

"But at the beginning of creation God 'made them male and female.' … 'and the two will become one flesh.' … Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate." — Mark 10:6–9, with Genesis 1:27 and Genesis 2:24
Used to argue: Jesus grounds marriage in the creation of male and female, so sexual complementarity is part of God's design. This is also the Natural Law argument: sex ordered to procreation.

The destruction of Sodom — Genesis 19 — is traditionally cited too, though many scholars read its sin as inhospitality and attempted gang rape rather than homosexuality as such.

The texts and arguments used by Christians who affirm same-sex relationships

"So God created mankind in his own image." — Genesis 1:27
Used to argue: gay people are made in God's image like everyone else, so they cannot be treated as defective.

"Love is patient, love is kind…" — 1 Corinthians 13, with "Love your neighbour as yourself" (Mark 12:31)
Used to argue: the test of a relationship is whether it shows this kind of love; a faithful, committed same-sex relationship passes it.

"There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus." — Galatians 3:28
Used to argue: in Christ the old categories of exclusion no longer determine a person's standing.

Interpretive arguments: Jesus says nothing about homosexuality; the Leviticus holiness code also forbids things Christians no longer observe; Romans 1 is read in context as concerning idolatry and exploitative practice rather than loving partnerships; and the Church has revised its reading of scripture before, on slavery and on the status of women.

Argument: same-sex relationships should be acceptedCounter-argument
Gay people are made in God's image like everyone else (Genesis 1:27), so they cannot be treated as defective; Galatians 3:28 says the old categories of exclusion no longer determine a person's standing in Christ.Leviticus 18:22 prohibits same-sex acts explicitly, and the prohibition is not only Old Testament: Romans 1:26–27 has Paul treating such acts as contrary to nature.
The test of a relationship is whether it shows the love of 1 Corinthians 13 and "love your neighbour as yourself" (Mark 12:31) — and a faithful, committed same-sex relationship passes it.Natural Law: Jesus grounds marriage in the creation of male and female (Mark 10:6–9, with Genesis 1:27 and 2:24), so sexual complementarity and the ordering of sex to procreation are part of God's design.
Interpretive arguments: Jesus says nothing on the subject; the Leviticus holiness code also forbids things Christians no longer observe; Romans 1 can be read as about idolatry and exploitation rather than loving partnerships; and the Church has revised its reading of scripture before, on slavery and on the status of women.Conservative evangelicals reply that this is reading the culture back into the text. Popular opinion does not override revelation, and a church is not free to set aside what scripture treats as authoritative on sexual ethics.
Churches have already decided it: the Quakers have celebrated same-sex marriages since 2009, the Methodist Church in Britain since 2021, and Archbishop Desmond Tutu compared the exclusion of gay people to apartheid — so it is not incompatible with Christian faith.The Roman Catholic position distinguishes the person from the act: homosexual acts are "intrinsically disordered" (Catechism 2357), but people with a homosexual inclination "must be accepted with respect, compassion, and sensitivity" (2358) and are called to chastity (2359). Being gay is not a sin; the acts are.
Non-religiously: orientation is not a choice, Mill's harm principle means consenting adults harm no one, equality law treats such discrimination as unjust, and exclusion has caused real harm.The Church of England shows how unsettled this is: its doctrine still holds marriage to be the union of one man and one woman and expects clergy in same-sex relationships to be celibate, yet in 2023 the House of Bishops commended Prayers of Love and Faith for same-sex couples. The Church remains openly divided — which is itself the point to make.

✗ "The Church thinks homosexuality is a sin."
✓ "Roman Catholic teaching holds homosexual acts to be intrinsically disordered while insisting gay people be treated with respect and compassion; the Church of England keeps its doctrine of marriage but since 2023 commends prayers of blessing; Quakers have celebrated same-sex marriages since 2009."

✗ Also wrong: "Christians used to be against it but now they accept it." The disagreement is live and present-tense, inside and between denominations.

More detail

Christians disagree sharply about same-sex relationships, and the disagreement is fundamentally about how to read the Bible. Write both sides with the texts each actually uses, and do not editorialise — the mark scheme rewards the range of views, not your sympathies.

Church or traditionWhere it stands
Roman CatholicHomosexual acts are "intrinsically disordered" (Catechism 2357). But people with a homosexual inclination "must be accepted with respect, compassion, and sensitivity" (2358) and are called to chastity (2359). Being gay is not itself a sin; sexual acts are.
Church of EnglandDoctrine still holds marriage to be the union of one man and one woman, and clergy in same-sex relationships are expected to be celibate. Homophobia is condemned. In 2023 the House of Bishops commended Prayers of Love and Faith, prayers of blessing that may be used with same-sex couples, without changing the Church's doctrine of marriage. The Church remains openly divided.
Quakers (Religious Society of Friends)Affirming. Britain Yearly Meeting decided in 2009 to celebrate same-sex marriages on the same basis as any other, treating the commitment itself as what matters.
Methodist Church in BritainVoted in 2021 to permit same-sex marriages in its churches, while allowing ministers who disagree not to conduct them.
Conservative evangelicalHolds the traditional teaching on the authority of scripture; some affirming evangelicals disagree, which is why the label is not uniform.
Individual voicesArchbishop Desmond Tutu, an Anglican, campaigned openly for the acceptance of gay people and compared their exclusion to apartheid.

Non-religious attitudes: sexual orientation is not a choice; Mill's harm principle means consenting adults harm no one; equality and human rights law treat discrimination on grounds of sexuality as unjust; and Humanists generally judge relationships by consent, honesty and care rather than by gender. Christian responses run both ways: conservatives reply that popular opinion does not override revelation, while affirming Christians say the same conclusion is reached from scripture itself.

D23 is the 12-marker — "everyone should accept homosexual relationships" — and the whole answer lives in these pairs. Note that both columns are Christian: that is what makes it a top-band answer.

subsections.heading: Marriage and its purposes
subsections.html:
Spec 2.5 · Christian teachings about marriage and its purposes, marriage vows and monogamy; the roles and status of partners within marriage — not yet taught in class — built from the specification

  • A lifelong, monogamous, public covenant — made before God, and a sacrament in the Catholic and Orthodox churches.
  • Four purposes — God’s gift in creation, the foundation of family life, the place for sex, mutual comfort and children.
  • "What God has joined together, let no one separate" — Mark 10:9; marriage is God’s act, so it is permanent.
  • The vows are unconditional — "for better, for worse… till death us do part", the basis of the case against divorce.
  • Rings, declarations, proclamation — the outward signs of vows that forsake all others for life.
  • Ephesians 5 splits the roles question — 5:22 submission against 5:21 mutual submission and 5:25 sacrificial love.

The marriage texts

"That is why a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh." — Genesis 2:24
Used to argue: marriage is part of God's plan in creation, and it creates a single new unit.

"Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate." — Mark 10:9, in Mark 10:6–9
Used to argue: marriage is God's act, not merely the couple's, which is why it is permanent. The priest echoes it at the proclamation.

The vows: "to have and to hold from this day forward; for better, for worse, for richer, for poorer, in sickness and in health, to love and to cherish, till death us do part." — Church of England marriage service
Used to argue: the commitment is unconditional and lifelong, which is the whole basis of the Christian objection to divorce.

Jesus attended the wedding at Cana and turned water into wine there. — John 2:1–11
Used to argue: Jesus honoured marriage, and his first sign was given at one.

More detail

For Christians marriage is a lifelong, monogamous, public covenant made before God — and in the Catholic and Orthodox churches it is a sacrament, an outward sign of God's grace.

The purposes, as the Church of England marriage service sets them out: marriage is a gift of God in creation; it is the foundation of family life; it is the proper place for a sexual relationship; and it exists for the couple's mutual comfort, help and delight, and for the bringing up of children.

  • Monogamy — one partner, because the two become one flesh.
  • The declarations — each is asked whether they will love, comfort, honour and protect the other, "forsaking all others", as long as they both shall live.
  • The rings — an outward and visible sign of the vows and of unending love.
  • The proclamation — the priest joins their hands: "those whom God has joined together let no one separate".

The roles and status of partners is a divergent-views question, and Ephesians 5 is where both sides go:

Conservative readingLiberal reading
Ephesians 5:22 — "Wives, submit yourselves to your own husbands as you do to the Lord" — with the husband as head of the household.Ephesians 5:21 comes first — "Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ" — so the passage teaches mutual submission.
Genesis 2:18: God made a "helper suitable for him", which is read as a complementary rather than identical role.Genesis 1:27: both male and female are made in God's image, so they are of equal status.
1 Timothy 2:12 — Paul does not permit a woman "to assume authority over a man" — and Jesus chose twelve male disciples.Galatians 3:28 — "neither… male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" — and scripture has strong women: Deborah as judge, Mary Magdalene as first witness of the resurrection.
"Equal but different": equal worth, distinct God-given roles, with the woman's role centred on the home and children.Ephesians 5:25 sets the real standard for husbands — "love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her" — which is sacrificial, not domineering.

Non-religious views of marriage: it is a free choice and a legal contract; a public sign of love and commitment; it brings legal and financial advantages; it is a good but not the only place to raise children; and same-sex couples should have equal access to it.

subsections.heading: Cohabitation, sex outside marriage and same-sex marriage
subsections.html:
Spec 2.5 · Attitudes to cohabitation and same-sex marriage; attitudes to sex outside marriage including pre-marital sex, promiscuity and adultery — not yet taught in class — built from the specification

  • Marriage is the standard everything is judged against — but churches differ over how to treat those who fall short.
  • Adultery is condemned across all denominations — Exodus 20:14, Matthew 5:28, and Jesus’s one ground for divorce.
  • Cohabitation is not mentioned in the Bible — the argument runs through sex outside marriage, and attitudes have softened.
  • Civil partnerships 2005, same-sex marriage 2013 — first marriages 2014; Scotland 2014, Northern Ireland 2020.
  • The quadruple lock — bars the Church of England from conducting same-sex marriages and protects other bodies.
  • Churches that do marry same-sex couples — Quakers, the United Reformed Church 2016, Scottish Episcopal 2017, Methodists 2021.
More detail

Christian teaching treats marriage as the proper place for sex, so cohabitation, pre-marital sex, promiscuity and adultery are judged against that standard — but the churches differ over how to respond to people whose lives do not match it.

PracticeChristian teachingNon-religious views
AdulteryForbidden by Exodus 20:14 and by Jesus in Matthew 5:28; it breaks the vow to forsake all others, and Matthew 19:9 treats it as the one ground Jesus allows for divorce. Condemned across all denominations.Almost always judged wrong too, because it breaks a promise freely made and harms the partner and any children — though a few couples agree open relationships.
PromiscuityAgainst "flee from sexual immorality" and "your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit" (1 Corinthians 6:18–19), and against the importance of marriage.A matter of free choice between consenting adults, with practical cautions about sexually transmitted infections and emotional harm.
Pre-marital sexCatholics and conservative evangelicals hold it wrong: Natural Law places sex within marriage, and Paul directs desire into marriage (1 Corinthians 7:9). Liberals treat it as a matter of conscience within a committed relationship.Normal and acceptable; it can test compatibility, and the harm principle finds nothing wrong where both consent.
CohabitationThe Bible does not mention it directly; the argument runs through sex outside marriage. "Marriage should be honoured by all" (Hebrews 13:4) is cited for keeping marriage as the ideal. In practice attitudes have softened — many couples who cohabit go on to marry in church, and Anglican clergy generally welcome them rather than refuse them.Widely accepted: it offers freedom, tests a relationship, and avoids the cost of a wedding. The main caution is practical — cohabiting partners have weaker legal protection than spouses if they separate.

Same-sex marriage. Keep the law and the churches separate, and be precise about which churches do what.

  • The law: civil partnerships were introduced in the UK in 2005. The Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 made same-sex marriage legal in England and Wales, with the first marriages in 2014; Scotland followed in 2014 and Northern Ireland in 2020. The Act also contains protections — the so-called quadruple lock — which bar the Church of England from conducting same-sex marriages and protect other religious organisations from being compelled to.
  • Churches that marry same-sex couples: the Quakers (from their 2009 decision), the United Reformed Church (2016), the Scottish Episcopal Church (2017) and the Methodist Church in Britain (2021).
  • Churches that do not: the Roman Catholic Church, which teaches that marriage is by its nature between a man and a woman and ordered to the procreation of children; the Church of England, whose doctrine of marriage is unchanged though it agreed prayers of blessing for same-sex couples in 2023; and the Orthodox churches.
Arguments for same-sex marriageArguments against
Equality: if marriage is a public good, denying it to some couples treats them as lesser; Galatians 3:28 is used to the same effect by affirming Christians.Jesus grounds marriage in male and female in Mark 10:6–9, so changing the definition changes what Christians believe marriage is.
Marriage is about lifelong, faithful, self-giving love, and 1 Corinthians 13 sets no condition about gender.Natural Law: marriage is ordered to procreation, which a same-sex union cannot achieve by its own nature.
Churches have already recognised it — Quakers, the URC and the Methodists in Britain — so it is not incompatible with Christian faith.Scripture is treated as authoritative on sexual ethics (Leviticus 18:22; Romans 1:26–27), and a church is not free to set it aside.
Gay people are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27), and excluding them from marriage has caused real harm.The Catholic Church distinguishes respecting gay people, which it requires, from blessing a union it does not regard as marriage.

subsections.heading: Divorce, annulment and remarriage
subsections.html:
Spec 2.6 · Christian teachings about annulment, divorce and remarriage; attitudes to the breakdown of marriage and its implications — not yet taught in class — built from the specification

  • Three strands in the New Testament — no divorce (Mark 10:9), adultery only (Matthew 19:9), desertion (1 Corinthians 7:15).
  • Catholic: annulment, not divorce — a declaration that no valid marriage ever existed; remarriage barred while a spouse lives.
  • Amoris Laetitia (2016) — Pope Francis encouraged pastoral discernment case by case.
  • Church of England since 2002 — a priest may, at their own discretion, marry a divorced person in church.
  • Orthodox: a concession to human weakness — remarriage is allowed, but the second service is deliberately penitential.
  • Annulment is not divorce — saying so is an easy mark.

The three strands in scripture

"Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate." — Mark 10:9
Used to argue: no divorce at all. Marriage is God's act, so no human authority can undo it.

"I tell you that anyone who divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another woman commits adultery." — Matthew 19:9, in Matthew 19:3–9
Used to argue: divorce is permitted on the single ground of adultery or sexual immorality.

Paul writes that if an unbelieving partner leaves, the believer "is not bound". — 1 Corinthians 7:15
Used to argue: divorce is not ideal but can be accepted where the marriage has effectively ended, which is the most flexible of the three.

Argument: divorce is always wrongCounter-argument
"Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate" (Mark 10:9). Marriage is God's act, not merely the couple's, so no human authority can undo it — which is why the Roman Catholic Church holds that a valid, consummated sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved at all.Jesus himself allows an exception: "anyone who divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality…" (Matthew 19:9). If adultery is a ground, divorce cannot be always wrong, and Paul adds a third strand — if an unbelieving partner leaves, the believer "is not bound" (1 Corinthians 7:15).
The vows are unconditional and lifelong — "for better, for worse… till death us do part" — so breaking them breaks a promise made before God, which is why a religious person may feel real guilt.The Church of England holds that divorce falls short of God's intention but that marriages do break down and people need compassion rather than condemnation; since 2002 a priest may at their discretion marry a divorced person in church.
Catholic teaching offers annulment instead — a declaration that no valid marriage ever existed, through deceit, coercion or incapacity at the time of the vows — so a way out exists without conceding that a true marriage can end.Critics reply that annulment reaches the same outcome by another route, and the Orthodox churches are more honest about it: they permit divorce as a concession to human weakness, with a deliberately more penitential second ceremony.
Divorce has real consequences, which is itself an argument for permanence: two households, disputes over children, higher welfare and housing costs, and concern about children's education and wellbeing.Staying in a loveless or abusive marriage harms everyone, including the children. Situation ethics asks only what is most loving, and Pope Francis's Amoris Laetitia (2016) itself encouraged pastoral discernment case by case.

✗ "Catholics don't believe in divorce and other Christians do."
✓ "Catholics hold that a valid sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved, so they offer annulment rather than divorce; Anglicans permit remarriage in church at the priest's discretion; Orthodox churches allow remarriage with a more penitential service."

Annulment and divorce are not the same thing, and saying so is an easy mark.

More detail

Christians disagree about divorce because the New Testament itself contains three different positions, and the denominations have each built on a different one.

ChurchDivorceRemarriage
Roman CatholicA valid, consummated sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved, so a civil divorce does not end it in the eyes of the Church. Instead the Church may grant an annulment — a declaration that no valid marriage ever existed, for example because of deceit, coercion or incapacity at the time of the vows.Not permitted while the first spouse lives and no annulment has been granted; those who remarry civilly have traditionally been barred from communion, although Pope Francis's Amoris Laetitia (2016) encouraged pastoral discernment case by case.
Church of EnglandDivorce falls short of God's intention, but the Church recognises that marriages do break down and that people need compassion rather than condemnation.Since 2002 a priest may, at their own discretion, marry a divorced person in church while a former spouse is still living; clergy who decline may instead offer a service of prayer and dedication after a civil marriage.
Methodist and other free churchesAccept that marriages fail and that people change; the emphasis is on support rather than penalty.Generally allowed in church.
OrthodoxPermits divorce as a concession to human weakness, and has services acknowledging it.Allowed, but the second ceremony is deliberately more subdued and penitential than the first.

Non-religious attitudes: divorce is sad and regrettable and should not be undertaken lightly, but it is sometimes necessary — people change, and staying in a loveless or abusive marriage harms everyone, including the children. The law allows it, and the priority is to protect the children's interests.

Implications for individualsImplications for societyImplications for religious communities
Financial loss and often two households to run; disputes over access to children; childcare problems; the strain of starting again; for a religious person, guilt at having broken a vow made before God.The breakdown of family units; higher welfare and housing costs; concern about the effects on children's education and wellbeing; a changing pattern of family life.It challenges the teaching that marriage is permanent; divorced members may feel judged or excluded; and it places more responsibility on churches to provide guidance, counselling and practical support.

"Divorce is always wrong" is the 12-marker, and the strongest answers argue it out of scripture itself:

subsections.heading: Family structures and responsibilities
subsections.html:
Spec 2.7 · Christian teachings about family life and its importance; responsibilities within the family including between generations; the rights of children; the changing nature of family life; the roles of men and women — not yet taught in class — built from the specification

  • The family is the basic unit — where faith is first handed on, which Catholic teaching calls the "domestic church".
  • Five family types — nuclear, extended, single-parent, reconstituted and same-sex parent families.
  • Duties run both ways — Exodus 20:12 to honour parents; Ephesians 6:4 gives parents patience and instruction.
  • 1 Timothy 5:8 — failing to provide for your own household is called a denial of the faith.
  • Children have standing — "let the little children come to me" (Mark 10:14) supports talk of children’s rights.
  • Why Christians disagree — biblical authority, and the weight each church gives scripture, tradition, reason and experience.

Christian teaching on family responsibilities

"Honour your father and your mother, so that you may live long in the land the LORD your God is giving you." — Exodus 20:12
Used to argue: respect for parents is a commandment, and it continues into their old age — the duty between generations.

"Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right." … "Fathers, do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord." — Ephesians 6:1, 6:4
Used to argue: the duty runs both ways. Children owe obedience; parents owe their children patience and a religious upbringing — and the same pairing appears in Colossians 3:20–21.

"Anyone who does not provide for their relatives, and especially for their own household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever." — 1 Timothy 5:8
Used to argue: providing for family, including elderly relatives, is a religious obligation and not merely a kindness.

"Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them, for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these." — Mark 10:14
Used to argue: children have real standing in Christian thought, which supports talk of children's rights — to care, protection, education and a faith upbringing.

Argument: the traditional family is what children needCounter-argument
Marriage is established in creation — "a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh" (Genesis 2:24) — and exists partly for the bringing up of children, so the nuclear family is the God-given shape.Genesis 1:27 makes all people equally in God's image and Galatians 3:28 dissolves the old categories, so liberal Christians read the family's function rather than its shape as what scripture requires — and single-parent, reconstituted and same-sex parent families can perform it.
Catholic teaching calls the family the domestic church: it is where children are taught to pray, brought to baptism and raised in the faith, so the church's future depends on it. In Natural Law it is also the building block of an ordered society.Churches already support families of every shape through rites of passage, Sunday schools, marriage preparation, the Mothers' Union and food banks — which suggests the duty is to sustain the family in front of you, not to enforce one model of it.
Conservatives read Ephesians 5:22–23, Genesis 2:18 and 1 Timothy 2:12 as giving distinct, complementary roles, with Catholic teaching praising the particular gifts mothers bring; "equal but different" is the phrase.Ephesians 5:21 comes first — "submit to one another out of reverence for Christ" — and 5:25 tells husbands to love sacrificially. The Church of England's position is broadly that it is for the couple to decide, provided the children's needs come first.
When family life breaks down the costs are real: financial strain, disrupted contact with children, instability and poorer wellbeing, higher welfare costs, and more demand on churches for counselling.Non-religious views, and the law, make the welfare of the child paramount: what matters is whether a household can love and care for a child. Children also have rights of their own — "let the little children come to me" (Mark 10:14).
Duties run between generations as well as down: "honour your father and your mother" (Exodus 20:12), and 1 Timothy 5:8 calls failing to provide for one's household a denial of the faith.Christians themselves disagree, and saying why earns a mark: it comes down to the authority of the Bible — whether its first-century social instructions are binding or culturally conditioned — and the weight each church gives to scripture, tradition, reason and present-day experience.
More detail

Christianity treats the family as the basic unit of society and as the place where faith is first handed on — which is why Catholic teaching calls it the "domestic church".

Type of familyWhat it means
NuclearParents and their children living in one household.
ExtendedThe nuclear family plus other relatives, for example a grandparent living with them.
Single-parentOne parent, of either sex, raising children alone — through choice, bereavement, separation or divorce.
Reconstituted (step-family)Two families joined after divorce or bereavement, so step-parents and step-siblings live together.
Same-sex parent familiesA couple of the same sex raising children, by adoption, fostering or fertility treatment — accepted by some churches and not by others, for the reasons set out in 2.4 and 2.5.

Why the family matters in Christian teaching: it is where children are taught to pray, brought to baptism and raised in the faith, so Catholic teaching calls it the domestic church; it is the building block of an ordered society in Natural Law; and marriage, which Genesis 2:24 establishes, exists partly for the bringing up of children.

The roles of men and women in the family divide along the same lines as the roles within marriage: conservatives read Ephesians 5:22–23, Genesis 2:18 and 1 Timothy 2:12 as giving distinct, complementary roles, with Catholic teaching praising the particular gifts mothers bring to family life; liberals read Genesis 1:27 and Galatians 3:28 as establishing equality and leave the division of work to the couple. The Church of England's position is broadly that it is for the couple to decide, provided the children's needs come first.

Why Christians disagree at all comes down to two things, and saying so explicitly is worth a mark: the authority of the Bible — whether its first-century social instructions are binding or culturally conditioned — and the different weight each church gives to scripture, tradition, reason and present-day experience.

When family life breaks down, the consequences for the individuals are financial strain, disrupted contact with children, instability and poorer wellbeing; for society, higher welfare costs and concern about children's outcomes; and for churches, more demand for counselling and support. Non-religious views agree that stable families matter for children's welfare, but see no reason the family must take one particular shape.

The 12-marker is usually "a child needs a mother and a father" or "the family is the most important part of society". Both are argued from the same two columns:

subsections.heading: How churches sustain family life
subsections.html:
Spec 2.7 · Ways in which Christian communities help to sustain family life, support the upbringing of children and keep families together, particularly through local churches — not yet taught in class — built from the specification

  • The examiner wants named provisions — concrete activities, each with what it actually does for the family.
  • Rites of passage — baptism, confirmation, marriage and funerals tie the family into the congregation.
  • Teaching the children — Sunday schools, children’s liturgy, youth groups and church schools.
  • Preparation and counselling — marriage preparation courses, parenting classes, and Catholic Marriage Care.
  • Mothers’ Union — an Anglican organisation that exists to support marriage and family life.
  • Practical help — food banks, toddler groups, debt advice and holiday clubs run out of church halls.

✗ "The church helps families by praying for them." — true, but on its own it is one thin point.
✓ Name specific provisions — baptism and the other rites of passage, Sunday school, marriage preparation, Mothers' Union, food banks — and then say what each one does for the family. That is point plus development, which is how the 4-markers are scored.

More detail

This is the practical subsection of the section, and the examiner wants concrete church activities rather than general goodwill.

  • Rites of passage — baptism or christening, confirmation, marriage and funerals mark the turning points of family life, in joy and in grief, and tie the family into the congregation.
  • Teaching the children — Sunday schools, children's liturgy, youth groups and church schools support parents in passing on the faith.
  • Preparation and counselling — marriage preparation courses before a church wedding, parenting classes, and pastoral counselling from a priest or vicar; Catholic Marriage Care offers relationship counselling specifically.
  • Keeping marriages together — the Mothers' Union, an Anglican organisation, exists to support marriage and family life, and many churches run groups for parents and for couples in difficulty.
  • Practical help — food banks, toddler groups, debt advice and holiday clubs run out of church halls, which relieve exactly the pressures that break families apart.
  • Community — church socials and shared meals that bring families together and reduce isolation, especially for single parents, the bereaved and the elderly.

subsections.heading: Childlessness and deciding not to have children
subsections.html:
Spec 2.8 · Religious and non-religious beliefs and attitudes to childlessness; decisions not to have children and the reasons for such decisions — not yet taught in class — built from the specification

  • Keep the two kinds apart — involuntary childlessness is no sin; voluntary childlessness is the contested one.
  • Against: Natural Law and Genesis 1:28 — reproduction is a primary precept, and children are a reward (Psalm 127:3).
  • Unitive and procreative — Catholic teaching makes openness to children part of what the couple consent to.
  • For: Matthew 19:12 — Jesus honours those who renounce marriage for the kingdom, so it cannot be wrong in itself.
  • "Mutual comfort, help and delight" — the Church of England service makes a childless marriage a complete marriage.
  • Four responses to involuntary childlessness — prayer and support, acceptance of God’s will, fertility treatment, adoption or fostering.

The scripture both sides use

"Be fruitful and increase in number; fill the earth and subdue it." — Genesis 1:28
Used to argue: having children is a command given in creation, not simply an option — the strongest text against choosing childlessness.

"Children are a heritage from the LORD, offspring a reward from him." — Psalm 127:3
Used to argue: children are a gift and a blessing, so a marriage that shuts them out is refusing something God offers.

"It is not good for the man to be alone." — Genesis 2:18
Used to argue: companionship is itself a purpose of marriage, so a childless marriage is still fulfilling what marriage is for.

"Others have renounced marriage because of the kingdom of heaven." — Matthew 19:12
Used to argue: Jesus treats a life without marriage or children as a legitimate — even honoured — Christian calling, which is the key text for the other side.

✗ "Christians think you have to have children."
✓ "Catholic teaching holds marriage to be unitive and procreative, so a marriage closed to children is defective — but Matthew 19:12 honours those who renounce marriage for the kingdom, and most Protestant churches leave family size to the couple's conscience."

Also keep involuntary and voluntary childlessness apart. A question about "Christian attitudes to childlessness" that only talks about IVF has answered half of it.

More detail

Christianity has traditionally treated children as a blessing and procreation as one of the purposes of marriage, so childlessness raises a real question — and Christians disagree sharply over whether a couple may deliberately choose it.

Keep the two kinds apart, because the arguments are different:
