  1. Involuntary childlessness — the couple want children and cannot have them. No Christian treats this as a sin; the question is what may be done about it.
  2. Voluntary childlessness — the couple choose not to have children. This is the contested one.

Reasons people decide not to have children: they do not want them; they are infertile or have difficulty conceiving; there is a risk of passing on a genetic disease; careers matter more to them; the financial cost, and the freedom of life without them; and for some, concern about population or the environment.

Christian arguments against choosing childlessnessChristian arguments for allowing the choice
Natural Law: to reproduce is one of the primary precepts, so a marriage deliberately closed to children frustrates a purpose God built into it.Conscience: the decision belongs to the couple before God, who know their own health, circumstances and capacity.
Genesis 1:28 commands it, and Psalm 127:3 calls children a reward — so refusing them refuses a gift.Free will: God gave human beings the freedom to choose, and forcing parenthood on an unwilling couple serves no one, least of all a child.
Catholic teaching holds marriage to be both unitive and procreative, and openness to children is part of what the couple consent to; some evangelical Christians put it more bluntly, that to demand that marriage means sex but not children is to defraud the creator.Marriage also exists for the couple's "mutual comfort, help and delight", as the Church of England service puts it, so a childless marriage is a complete marriage.
Children are how faith is handed on — the family as the "domestic church" — so the church's future depends on them.Jesus and Paul had no children, and Matthew 19:12 honours those who renounce marriage for the kingdom, so childlessness cannot be wrong in itself.
A couple with the means to raise a child and no good reason not to may be acting selfishly rather than faithfully.A couple may serve God and others in other ways — fostering, adoption, ministry, caring for relatives — and situation ethics asks only what the most loving outcome is.

Non-religious attitudes:

  • Free will and personal choice — whether to have children is nobody else's business, and Mill's harm principle finds no one harmed by the decision.
  • Feminist arguments: a woman has control over her own body and no duty to reproduce; motherhood is an option, not an obligation.
  • A fulfilled life does not require children — careers, relationships and other commitments can supply purpose.
  • Practical reasons are treated as perfectly respectable: cost, housing, health, and concern about population and the environment.
  • Some still think a couple who can raise children well and choose not to are missing something, but almost nobody treats it as a moral wrong.

Christian responses to involuntary childlessness — this is the (b)-mark favourite, so have two ready with development: prayer and pastoral support from the church community; acceptance of God's will, as with the childless couples of scripture who were eventually blessed (Abraham and Sarah, Hannah, Elizabeth and Zechariah); fertility treatment, where the couple's church accepts it; and adoption or fostering, which almost every church positively commends.

subsections.heading: Fertility treatment: IVF, AIH, AID and surrogacy
subsections.html:
Spec 2.8 · Forms of fertility treatment to support successful conception; religious and non-religious attitudes to them — not yet taught in class — built from the specification

  • Two questions decide it — does the treatment separate sex from reproduction, and what happens to spare embryos.
  • AIH uses the husband’s sperm, AID a donor’s — many Christians accept the first and reject the second.
  • IVF, egg donation, surrogacy — fertilisation outside the body, a third party’s egg, another woman carrying the child.
  • Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 1990 — licenses clinics and sets a 14-day limit on research embryos.
  • Commercial surrogacy is unlawful — only reasonable expenses may be paid, and the arrangement is unenforceable.
  • Donum Vitae (1987) — the Catholic case: it separates the unitive from the procreative, and embryos are destroyed.

✗ "Christians are against IVF."
✓ "The Roman Catholic Church rejects IVF, because it separates the unitive from the procreative and because spare embryos are destroyed (Donum Vitae, 1987) — while Anglicans, Methodists and most Protestants accept it, treating medicine as a God-given means of healing and leaving the decision to the couple's conscience."

And get the initials right: AIH uses the husband's sperm, AID a donor's. Christians who accept the first often reject the second, and knowing why is the mark.

More detail

The vocabulary is marked to the word, and the Christian argument turns on two things: whether the treatment separates sex from reproduction, and what happens to the spare embryos.

TreatmentWhat it means
IVF (in vitro fertilisation)Egg and sperm are fertilised outside the body — "test-tube babies" — and an embryo is then implanted in the womb.
AIH (artificial insemination by husband)The husband's sperm is introduced into the wife artificially, so both gametes come from the married couple.
AID (artificial insemination by donor)A third party's sperm is used, because the husband's is not viable.
Egg donationA third party provides the egg, which is then fertilised and implanted.
SurrogacyAnother woman carries and gives birth to the child for the couple — sometimes called "rent a womb".

The law in the UK: fertility treatment and embryo research are regulated under the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 1990 (amended 2008), which licenses clinics and sets a 14-day limit on keeping a research embryo. Surrogacy is lawful but commercial surrogacy is not — under the Surrogacy Arrangements Act 1985 a surrogate may be paid only reasonable expenses, and the arrangement is not legally enforceable.

Christian arguments against fertility treatmentChristian arguments for it
It separates the unitive from the procreative: sex is meant to join the couple and to make children, and IVF makes a child without the act that unites. This is the Natural Law objection, and it is the heart of the Catholic case — set out in Donum Vitae (1987).God works through science. Medicine is a God-given means of healing, and infertility is a condition like any other; on this view the scientist is, as liberal Christians put it, a kind of priest of nature doing God's work.
Playing God: conception is God's decision about when and whether a life begins, and treatment takes it out of his hands.Situation ethics: giving a longed-for child to a couple who cannot conceive is plainly the most loving outcome, and agape is the only absolute.
Spare embryos. IVF creates more embryos than are implanted, and the rest are frozen, discarded or used in research. If life begins at conception, that breaks the sanctity of life.Not every Christian holds that a pre-implantation embryo has full moral status; a former Archbishop of York argued that embryos and sperm before fertilisation have no moral status of their own.
AID and egg donation bring a third party's genetic material into a marriage; Catholic teaching has called this a kind of mechanical adultery, because the child is not the fruit of the couple's own union.AIH keeps both gametes within the marriage, so many Christians who reject AID accept it — nothing has entered the marriage from outside.
Surrogacy is said to break the bond of marriage, to treat a child as a commodity, and to treat egg, sperm and womb as things to be bought.Genesis 1:28 blesses having children, so helping a couple to do what God commands is cooperating with him, not defying him.
It encourages family forms the church does not recognise, by letting single people and same-sex couples have children.Conscience: this is a medical decision for the couple before God, not one the church should take for them.
Non-religious arguments for fertility treatmentNon-religious concerns
It relieves real suffering and produces a wanted child — a clear utilitarian gain in happiness.Identity: a child conceived with a donor egg or sperm may struggle with not knowing, or only later discovering, where half their genetic inheritance came from.
Reproductive autonomy: the decision belongs to the people involved, and Mill's harm principle finds no third party harmed.Because one donor's gametes may be used for several families, there is a small risk that two genetically related people meet and form a relationship without knowing they are related.
The law already permits and regulates it, with licensed clinics, counselling and limits.Surrogacy: the risk of psychological harm to the surrogate, who may not want to give up the child — which is one reason commercial surrogacy is illegal in the UK.
It is simply treatment for a medical condition, and refusing it to some people is unjust.Cost and access: private treatment is expensive and NHS provision varies, so the better-off get more chances.

subsections.heading: Genetic engineering and cloning
subsections.html:
Spec 2.8 · Forms of genetic engineering to support successful conception; Christian beliefs and teachings about genetic engineering, and non-religious attitudes — not yet taught in class — built from the specification

  • Healing or playing God — the whole division is whether this continues Jesus’s healing or usurps the creator.
  • Six terms — genetic engineering, gene therapy, embryo screening, therapeutic cloning, reproductive cloning, "designer babies".
  • Therapeutic against reproductive cloning — many Protestants accept the first because it heals, and reject the second.
  • Reproductive cloning is banned — the Human Reproductive Cloning Act 2001 outlaws it in human beings in the UK.
  • Eugenics is the shared worry — religious and non-religious alike fear deciding which lives are worth starting.
More detail

Genetic engineering is the deliberate alteration or selection of an organism's genes, and Christian responses divide over whether this is healing — which Jesus commanded — or playing God.

TechniqueWhat it means
Genetic engineeringAltering the genes of a living thing, including a human embryo, to change its characteristics or remove a fault.
Gene therapyCorrecting a faulty gene in order to treat or prevent a disease.
Embryo screeningTesting embryos created by IVF for genetic conditions, and implanting only the unaffected ones.
Therapeutic cloningCloning cells — not a person — to grow tissue for treating illness or replacing damaged organs.
Reproductive cloningCloning cells in order to produce a new individual genetically identical to the donor. Banned in human beings in the UK by the Human Reproductive Cloning Act 2001.
"Designer babies"The feared end point: choosing a child's characteristics rather than curing a disease. This is the eugenics objection.
Conservative Christian viewLiberal Christian view
Playing God. Creation belongs to God, and remaking a human being usurps the creator's role.Stewardship and healing. God gave human beings reason and the capacity to heal; using it to cure disease continues the work Jesus began when he healed the sick.
It breaks the sanctity of life, because embryos are created, screened, used and destroyed in the process.Not all Christians hold that an early embryo has the full moral status of a person, so research on it is not the taking of a life.
God saw that his creation was "very good" (Genesis 1:31), so it should not be redesigned.Situation ethics: if the outcome is a healthy child and a cured patient, that is what agape requires.
Roman Catholic teaching rejects human cloning as immoral and unnecessary, and objects to any procedure that treats an embryo as material.Many Protestant churches draw the line between therapeutic cloning, which they accept because it heals, and reproductive cloning, which they reject.
It opens the road to eugenics — selecting people rather than curing them — and to deciding which lives are worth having.Christians should fight the abuse, not the technology: the right response is strict regulation, which the UK already has.

Non-religious attitudes: broadly supportive and regulated rather than principled. Therapeutic cloning and embryo research are lawful under licence in the UK, and a utilitarian will point out that eliminating inherited disease produces an enormous gain in happiness. The standard non-religious worry is the same as the Christian one at the far end: eugenics — designer babies, the quiet judgement that some lives are not worth starting, and unease about the kind of society that would create.

subsections.heading: Contraception
subsections.html:
Spec 2.8 · Contraception; Christian beliefs and teachings about contraception including reasons for and against it, and non-religious attitudes — not yet taught in class — built from the specification

  • The clearest denominational split in the section — Catholics forbid artificial methods, Protestants leave it to conscience.
  • Artificial against natural — condom, pill, coil, implant and sterilisation, against natural family planning and abstinence.
  • Humanae Vitae (1968) — every marital act must remain open to the transmission of life.
  • Lambeth 1930 — the Church of England accepted contraception in marriage where there is a morally sound reason.
  • Responsible parenthood — only have the children you can feed, house and raise; no verse forbids contraception.
  • The lesser of two evils — it prevents unwanted pregnancies, and therefore abortions, and the spread of HIV.

✗ "Catholics are not allowed contraception."
✓ "Catholic teaching forbids artificial contraception, because Natural Law makes sex both unitive and procreative (Humanae Vitae, 1968) — but it permits natural family planning, where the couple restrict sex to infertile days."

✗ "The Bible says contraception is wrong." No verse addresses it. The argument runs through Natural Law and the procreative purpose of marriage, and saying so is worth more than inventing a quotation.

More detail

This is the clearest denominational split in the whole section: the Roman Catholic Church forbids artificial contraception and permits natural methods, while Anglicans and most Protestants leave it to the couple's conscience.

  • Artificial contraception — a device, drug or operation that prevents conception: the condom, the pill, the IUD or coil, implants, sterilisation.
  • Natural contraception — avoiding conception without any device, by restricting sex to the woman's infertile days: the rhythm or calendar method, now usually called natural family planning. Total abstinence counts too.
Christian arguments against artificial contraceptionChristian arguments for it
Natural Law: sex has a procreative and a unitive purpose, and artificial contraception deliberately destroys the first while keeping the second. Catholic teaching in Humanae Vitae (1968) holds that every marital act must remain open to the transmission of life, and treats artificial contraception as intrinsically wrong.The Church of England accepted contraception within marriage at the 1930 Lambeth Conference where there is a morally sound reason for limiting a family, and later treated family planning as a matter for the couple's own conscience.
God decides when a person conceives, and contraception takes that decision from him — the same "playing God" argument as in 2.3.Responsible parenthood: a couple should only have the children they can feed, house and raise properly, and the Bible nowhere forbids contraception.
Children are a blessing (Psalm 127:3) and Genesis 1:28 commands being fruitful, so planning them away works against God's purpose for marriage.The lesser of two evils: contraception prevents unwanted pregnancies — and therefore abortions — and prevents the spread of sexually transmitted infections, including HIV.
Some methods may act after fertilisation rather than before it, which on the Catholic view of conception makes them abortive rather than contraceptive.Situation ethics: if using contraception is the most loving thing to do for the couple, their existing children and the wider family, then agape permits it.
It is said to encourage sex outside marriage and promiscuity by removing the consequences.Conscience and freedom: most Protestant churches hold that this is a private decision and not a matter of doctrine at all.
But note: the Catholic objection is to artificial methods. Natural family planning is permitted, because the couple do not interfere with the act itself.Critics of the Catholic position reply that the intention is identical in both cases, so the distinction is about the means and not the purpose.

Non-religious attitudes:

  • A straightforward matter of choice for the couple; Mill's harm principle finds nobody else harmed.
  • Far better than bringing unwanted children into the world, and a basic tool of public health against HIV and other infections.
  • A feminist issue: contraception gave women control over their own bodies, and with it education, careers and a real say in family size.
  • The only caution is that it should be used responsibly — reliably, and with regard to a partner's health.

subsections.heading: Celibacy
subsections.html:
Spec 2.8 · Celibacy, including reasons for and against it and differing attitudes to it — not yet taught in class — built from the specification

  • Celibacy is a calling, not a rule — the settled choice to abstain from sex and usually from marriage.
  • Celibacy is not chastity — chastity is the right ordering of sexual behaviour for whatever state you are in.
  • Who takes the vow — Latin-Church Catholic priests, monks and nuns; Anglican and Methodist clergy may marry.
  • Orthodox practice — married men are ordained as parish priests, but bishops are chosen from the celibate.
  • For: 1 Corinthians 7:1 and 7:32–33 — Paul’s own preference, and undivided attention to the Lord’s affairs.
  • Against: Genesis 1:28 and 2:18 — be fruitful, and it is not good to be alone; Peter was a married man.

The celibacy texts

"It is good for a man not to touch a woman." — 1 Corinthians 7:1
Used to argue: Paul's own preference for celibacy — the foundational text for treating it as an ideal.

"An unmarried man is concerned about the Lord's affairs — how he can please the Lord. But a married man is concerned about the affairs of this world." — 1 Corinthians 7:32–33
Used to argue: the celibate person can give God undivided attention, which is the practical case for clerical celibacy.

"Others have renounced marriage because of the kingdom of heaven. The one who can accept this should accept it." — Matthew 19:12
Used to argue: Jesus commends celibacy and says it is not for everyone — both halves matter.

"But if they cannot control themselves, they should marry… it is better to marry than to burn with passion." — 1 Corinthians 7:9
Used to argue: celibacy is a gift given to some, not a demand made of all. Even Paul concedes the point.

✗ "Christians have to be celibate until they are married."
✓ That is chastity, not celibacy. Celibacy is the settled choice to abstain from sex and usually from marriage; chastity is the right ordering of sexual behaviour for whatever state you are in — which for an unmarried Christian means abstinence, and for a married one means faithfulness.

✗ "All priests are celibate." Only Roman Catholic priests of the Latin Church, monks and nuns. Anglican and Methodist clergy marry, and Orthodox parish priests may be married men.

More detail

Celibacy is choosing to abstain from sexual activity and usually from marriage, and in Christianity it is treated as a particular calling rather than a general rule.

Who it applies to: Roman Catholic priests of the Latin Church, and monks and nuns, take a vow of celibacy. Anglican, Methodist and other Protestant clergy may marry; the Orthodox churches ordain married men as parish priests but choose their bishops from among the celibate. Catholic and conservative evangelical teaching also calls gay Christians to celibacy, as set out in 2.4.

Reasons for celibacyReasons against it
Undivided service: without a spouse and children, a priest, monk or nun is free for prayer, ministry and the people they serve (1 Corinthians 7:32–33).Not everyone can do it. Paul himself says that those who cannot control themselves should marry (1 Corinthians 7:9), so requiring it of all clergy sets up people to fail.
Imitating Christ: Jesus was celibate, and Matthew 19:12 treats renouncing marriage for the kingdom as a genuine calling.Genesis 1:28 commands being fruitful, and Genesis 2:18 says it is not good for a person to be alone — so marriage, not celibacy, is the created norm.
Paul's preference: "it is good for a man not to touch a woman" (1 Corinthians 7:1), and he wished others could be as he was.Most Protestants reject compulsory clerical celibacy as a human rule rather than a biblical one; the Reformers argued a married minister understands family life better.
Special standing: Revelation describes those who "did not defile themselves with women" as following the Lamb, which has been read as giving the celibate a particular place in heaven.Peter and the other apostles were married — Jesus heals Peter's mother-in-law (Mark 1:30) — so celibacy was never a condition of leading the church.
Discipline: self-denial is a Christian virtue, and giving up something good for God is an act of devotion.It is an unnatural denial of a God-given part of being human, and a rule imposed rather than freely chosen can do real damage.

Non-religious attitudes: celibacy is simply a matter of choice, and nobody else's business. It can let a person concentrate on study, work or other commitments; a relationship can be committed and close without sex; and some people are asexual, so for them it is not a sacrifice at all. The usual non-religious criticism is not of chosen celibacy but of required celibacy, imposed by an institution on people who did not choose it for themselves.

subsections.heading: Adoption and fostering
subsections.html:
Spec 2.8 · Adoption and fostering, including religious and non-religious attitudes to them — not yet taught in class — built from the specification

  • Adoption is permanent, fostering temporary — adoption transfers parental responsibility legally and for good.
  • James 1:27 — looking after orphans and widows is the mark of pure and faultless religion.
  • Ephesians 1:5 — adoption is Paul’s own image for salvation, so adopting mirrors what God has done.
  • Jesus was raised by Joseph — cited to show a family is made by love and commitment, not by genetics.
  • The standing alternative — to abortion, to childlessness, and to fertility treatments that discard embryos.
  • Welfare of the child is paramount — the legal principle; same-sex adoption lawful since 2005, equality regulations 2007.

Why Christians support adoption

"Religion that God our Father accepts as pure and faultless is this: to look after orphans and widows in their distress." — James 1:27
Used to argue: caring for children who have no one is not optional charity but the test of real religion.

"A father to the fatherless… God sets the lonely in families." — Psalm 68:5–6
Used to argue: placing a child in a family is God's own work, so Christians doing it are joining in with him.

"He predestined us for adoption to sonship through Jesus Christ." — Ephesians 1:5
Used to argue: adoption is the image Paul uses for salvation itself — Christians are adopted children of God, so adopting a child mirrors what God has done for them.

"Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me." — Matthew 25:40
Used to argue: the Sheep and the Goats makes care of the vulnerable the basis of judgement, and a child in care is exactly who is meant.

✗ "Adoption is when you look after someone else's child for a while."
✓ That is fostering. Adoption transfers parental responsibility permanently and legally. Mixing them up costs a definition mark in part (a).

In a 12-marker on childlessness, contraception or abortion, adoption is the point that turns an argument into an evaluation — "there is an alternative, and here it is" — so keep it in reserve for every one of them.

More detail

Adoption and fostering are the alternative that almost every Christian argument in this section ends up recommending — against abortion, against childlessness, and against the fertility treatments the churches find difficult.

  • Adoption — parental responsibility is transferred permanently and legally to the adoptive parents, and the child becomes a full member of the new family.
  • Fostering — temporary care in a family home while legal responsibility stays with the birth parents or the local authority; the child may return home or go on to be adopted.

Two further arguments come up constantly and are worth having ready. First, Jesus himself was raised by a man who was not his biological father, which Christians cite to show that a family is made by love and commitment rather than by genetics. Second, adoption is the standing alternative: many Christians argue it is preferable to abortion, and preferable to fertility treatments that create and discard embryos — a childless couple can still raise a child, and a child who needs a family gets one.

"Every Christian with the means should foster or adopt" — for— against
James 1:27 makes looking after orphans the mark of pure religion, and Matthew 25:40 ties judgement to care for the vulnerable.The Bible commends caring for the vulnerable without specifying how; giving, fostering support, or helping a struggling family can meet the same duty.
Thousands of children are waiting for a permanent family, and the need is real and immediate.Not every household is suited to it. A placement that breaks down can harm the child more than waiting would.
Christians are themselves adopted children of God (Ephesians 1:5), so the practice reflects the gospel.Christians also have duties to their own children, their parents and their work (1 Timothy 5:8), and these can rightly come first.
Christian teaching that opposes abortion is much stronger when the same Christians offer the alternative they recommend.A duty is too strong a word for something that must be freely and carefully chosen; most churches call it a vocation, not an obligation.

Where Christians have disagreed: adoption by same-sex couples. In England and Wales unmarried and same-sex couples have been able to adopt since 2005, and the equality regulations of 2007 removed the ability of agencies to refuse them. Some Catholic adoption agencies closed or separated from the Church rather than comply. The arguments are the ones from 2.4 and 2.5: on one side the welfare of a child who needs a family now, and gay people as equally made in God's image; on the other the church's doctrine that marriage is between a man and a woman, and the claim that a child is best placed with a mother and a father.

Non-religious attitudes are strongly supportive, and the governing principle in law is that the welfare of the child is paramount — so what matters is whether the household can love and care for the child, not its shape. The usual non-religious additions: adoption is an answer to childlessness that does not need medical technology; it reduces the harm of children growing up in institutional care; and the process should be made quicker and less obstructive.

The must-knows

The two positions on death: physicalism (we are only a physical body, so death ends us) and dualism (body and soul, and the soul persists).

Four reasons Christians believe in an afterlife: God's omnipotence and omnibenevolence; Jesus taught it; Jesus's resurrection; dualism.

Three destinations: heaven, hell and — for Roman Catholics only — purgatory, which Protestants reject as unbiblical.

Linear versus cyclical: one life, one judgement (Christian) against rebirth determined by deeds (Hinduism, Buddhism).

Faith or works: John 3:16 for faith, the Sheep and the Goats for works, James to tie them together.

Named thinkers: Plato, Aquinas, Augustine for the religious side; Aristotle, Epicurus, Bentham, Sartre, Nietzsche, Marx for the non-religious side.

Every 12-marker: for, against, appraisal of each argument, at least one religion named, justified conclusion with your own opinion.

The 12-mark frame

The same five paragraphs work for both halves of this section, but the vocabulary changes. Use the afterlife column for 2.1–2.2 questions and the ethics column for 2.3–2.8.

Paragraph 1 — restate the statement and say what turns on it. Afterlife: "The claim that death is the end matters because Christian hope, judgement and the whole point of living well depend on something surviving." Ethics: "The claim that [abortion / euthanasia / choosing childlessness] is always wrong turns on whether the sanctity of life is absolute, or whether agape can override it."

Paragraph 2 — the strongest case FOR, with teaching and scripture, then appraise it. Afterlife: "A Christian would argue that eternal life is God's offer — 'whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life' (John 3:16) — and that Jesus's resurrection shows death is not permanent. This is strong within the faith, but it rests on the authority of a text the critic does not accept." Ethics: "A Christian who follows Natural Law would argue that preserving life is a primary precept, and that life is sacred from conception because every human bears the image of God (Genesis 1:27). This is the most consistent position, because it needs no judgement about whose life is worth living."

Paragraph 3 — the strongest case AGAINST, with teaching and scripture, then appraise it. Afterlife: "However, a physicalist would respond that consciousness is brain activity and death destroys the brain, so there is nothing left to survive; near-death experiences have naturalistic explanations. This is the stronger evidential position, though it cannot disprove an afterlife either." Ethics: "However, a situation ethicist would respond that agape is the only absolute, so in a tragic case the most loving act may be the one that ends a life — and Christians also have a duty to relieve suffering, which here pulls against the duty to preserve life."

Paragraph 4 — where Christians disagree with each other. Name the denominations; "some Christians… other Christians…" is worth less. "Roman Catholics hold that…, while the Church of England accepts that in strictly limited circumstances…" · "Catholics believe in purgatory as the final purification of the elect, which Protestants reject as unbiblical." · "Quakers have celebrated same-sex marriages since 2009, whereas the Roman Catholic Church teaches that marriage is by its nature between a man and a woman."

Paragraph 5 — a conclusion that decides. Weigh the arguments, state your own view, and give the reason. "On balance, the argument from autonomy is strong, but the slippery-slope objection has not been answered, so I agree only with the limited version of the statement." · "Because the paranormal evidence is unverifiable, I find the physicalist case stronger on the evidence — though it does not touch the Christian argument from the nature of God." Never end with "it depends what you believe".

Two things lose easy marks here. Humanist and atheist views give useful perspective but do not count as the reference to one religion. And in the ethics questions, adoption and palliative care are the alternatives that turn an argument into an evaluation — keep one of them in reserve for every one of them.

subsections.heading: Quotes to learn
subsections.html:
Front of the card is the topic and the reference; the back is the words and what they prove. Twenty quotes covering the whole of spec 2.1–2.8 — four on death and judgement, then the texts the ethics questions are argued with.

Eternal life — John 3:16"For God so loved the world that he gave his only son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life."Used to argue: eternal life is God's offer, received through faith in Jesus — the single most useful verse in this module
Something survives death — Ecclesiastes 12:7"The dust returns to the ground it came from, and the spirit returns to God who gave it."Used to argue: something non-physical survives the death of the body — the dualist's text against physicalism
Judgement on works — Matthew 25:31–40"Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me."Used to argue: the parable of the Sheep and the Goats makes judgement rest on good works, so Christians must act now — also the key text for relieving suffering and for adoption
Faith and works — James"Faith without works is dead."Used to argue: faith and works cannot be separated — the line that settles the faith-versus-works 12-marker without choosing a side
Sanctity of life — Genesis 1:27"So God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them."Used to argue: imago Dei — every human being shares in God's image, which gives all human life intrinsic worth. Also used by affirming Christians on homosexuality, and for equality within marriage
Do not kill — Exodus 20:13"You shall not murder."Used to argue: taking innocent human life is directly forbidden by the Decalogue — the first move against both abortion and euthanasia
Life in the womb — Psalm 139:13"For you created my inmost being; you knit me together in my mother's womb."Used to argue: God is the maker of life in the womb, so the unborn child is already his — the key anti-abortion text, with "I am fearfully and wonderfully made" (139:14)
Life is not ours to end — Job 1:21"The LORD gave and the LORD has taken away; may the name of the LORD be praised."Used to argue: both the beginning and the end of a life are God's decision, not ours — the key anti-euthanasia text
Love defined — 1 Corinthians 13:4, 13:13"Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud." … "And now these three remain: faith, hope and love. But the greatest of these is love."Used to argue: Christian love is defined by how it behaves, not how it feels, which is why it can be commanded — and it outranks every other virtue, which is how liberal Christians make love the test of a relationship
Love your neighbour — Mark 12:31"Love your neighbour as yourself."Used to argue: the second greatest commandment, and the ground of every Christian duty to another person — relieving suffering, family responsibility, and the affirming case on sexuality
Adultery — Exodus 20:14 and Matthew 5:28"You shall not commit adultery." … "Anyone who looks at a woman lustfully has already committed adultery with her in his heart."Used to argue: faithfulness is a direct commandment, and Jesus extends it from the act to the intention — and Matthew 19:9 makes adultery the one ground he allows for divorce
Same-sex acts in the Law — Leviticus 18:22"Do not have sexual relations with a man as one does with a woman; that is detestable."Used to argue: the traditional Christian prohibition, with Romans 1:26–27. The reply: the same holiness code forbids things Christians no longer observe, and Jesus says nothing on the subject
One in Christ — Galatians 3:28"There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus."Used to argue: in Christ the old categories of exclusion no longer determine standing — used for equal roles in marriage and the family, for women's status, and by Christians who affirm same-sex relationships
Marriage as one flesh — Genesis 2:24"That is why a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh."Used to argue: marriage is part of God's plan in creation and creates a single new unit — the basis of monogamy, and of the Natural Law case on sex
Marriage is permanent — Mark 10:9"Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate."Used to argue: marriage is God's act and not merely the couple's, so no human authority can undo it — the Catholic case against divorce, and the priest's words at the proclamation
The one ground for divorce — Matthew 19:9"I tell you that anyone who divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another woman commits adultery."Used to argue: the second scriptural strand — divorce is permitted on the single ground of adultery, which is why the New Testament itself leaves Christians divided
Honour your parents — Exodus 20:12"Honour your father and your mother, so that you may live long in the land the LORD your God is giving you."Used to argue: respect for parents is a commandment that continues into their old age — the duty between generations, with Ephesians 6:1–4, where the duty runs both ways
Be fruitful — Genesis 1:28"Be fruitful and increase in number; fill the earth and subdue it."Used to argue: having children is a command given in creation — the strongest text against deliberate childlessness and against artificial contraception, with Psalm 127:3, "children are a heritage from the LORD"
Renouncing marriage — Matthew 19:12"Others have renounced marriage because of the kingdom of heaven. The one who can accept this should accept it."Used to argue: Jesus treats a life without marriage or children as a legitimate calling — and says it is not for everyone. The key text for celibacy and for voluntary childlessness
Orphans and widows — James 1:27"Religion that God our Father accepts as pure and faultless is this: to look after orphans and widows in their distress."Used to argue: caring for children who have no one is the test of real religion — the case for adoption and fostering, the alternative every ethics answer in 2.3 and 2.8 ends up recommending

equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: faithfulness is a direct commandment, and Jesus extends it from the act to the intention — and Matthew 19:9 makes adultery the one ground he allows for divorce

equations.name: Same-sex acts in the Law — Leviticus 18:22
equations.formula: "Do not have sexual relations with a man as one does with a woman; that is detestable."
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: the traditional Christian prohibition, with Romans 1:26–27. The reply: the same holiness code forbids things Christians no longer observe, and Jesus says nothing on the subject

equations.name: One in Christ — Galatians 3:28
equations.formula: "There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus."
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: in Christ the old categories of exclusion no longer determine standing — used for equal roles in marriage and the family, for women's status, and by Christians who affirm same-sex relationships

equations.name: Marriage as one flesh — Genesis 2:24
equations.formula: "That is why a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh."
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: marriage is part of God's plan in creation and creates a single new unit — the basis of monogamy, and of the Natural Law case on sex

equations.name: Marriage is permanent — Mark 10:9
equations.formula: "Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate."
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: marriage is God's act and not merely the couple's, so no human authority can undo it — the Catholic case against divorce, and the priest's words at the proclamation

equations.name: The one ground for divorce — Matthew 19:9
equations.formula: "I tell you that anyone who divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another woman commits adultery."
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: the second scriptural strand — divorce is permitted on the single ground of adultery, which is why the New Testament itself leaves Christians divided

equations.name: Honour your parents — Exodus 20:12
equations.formula: "Honour your father and your mother, so that you may live long in the land the LORD your God is giving you."
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: respect for parents is a commandment that continues into their old age — the duty between generations, with Ephesians 6:1–4, where the duty runs both ways

equations.name: Be fruitful — Genesis 1:28
equations.formula: "Be fruitful and increase in number; fill the earth and subdue it."
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: having children is a command given in creation — the strongest text against deliberate childlessness and against artificial contraception, with Psalm 127:3, "children are a heritage from the LORD"

equations.name: Renouncing marriage — Matthew 19:12
equations.formula: "Others have renounced marriage because of the kingdom of heaven. The one who can accept this should accept it."
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: Jesus treats a life without marriage or children as a legitimate calling — and says it is not for everyone. The key text for celibacy and for voluntary childlessness

equations.name: Orphans and widows — James 1:27
equations.formula: "Religion that God our Father accepts as pure and faultless is this: to look after orphans and widows in their distress."
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: caring for children who have no one is the test of real religion — the case for adoption and fostering, the alternative every ethics answer in 2.3 and 2.8 ends up recommending

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
PhysicalismThe view that the real world is nothing more than the physical world — no soul, no afterlife
DualismThe view that a person is composed of body and soul, the soul being the permanent part
Immortality of the soulThe belief that the soul is not subject to change or death and continues to exist after the body dies
ResurrectionGod raising the dead to life, body and soul, just before judgement — as happened to Jesus
EschatologyThe study of Christian teachings about the End Time
The EschatonThe End Time itself, when the dead are raised and judged
The Last JudgementJesus judging the resurrected dead alongside the living on faith, acceptance of his sacrifice and obedience to God
HeavenEternal life in communion with God — the kingdom of God fully experienced, with no sin, suffering or death
HellEternal punishment or separation from God for the wicked, with no hope of redemption
PurgatoryThe Roman Catholic belief in a final purification of the elect after judgement, before entering heaven
UniversalismThe belief that hell is a place of correction and that there will eventually be universal salvation
MillennialismThe belief that Christ will rule the earth for 1,000 years of peace and justice before the resurrection of the dead
Linear viewExistence runs once — birth, life, death, resurrection, judgement, heaven or hell
Cyclical viewExistence repeats: deeds determine rebirth into a higher or lower form, or escape from the cycle
ReincarnationThe atman being reborn into another body after death
KarmaThe principle that a person's actions determine the form of their rebirth
MokshaFreedom from samsara, the cycle of life, so the atman can unite with Brahman
NirvanaThe state reached on enlightenment, escaping the cycle of rebirth
SalvationBeing saved from sin and brought to eternal life with God, through the grace of God, faith, worship and love
GraceGod's unearned gift — salvation cannot be bought or deserved
Eternal lifeLife with God that does not end, offered to whoever believes in the Son (John 3:16)
The kingdom of GodGod's rule, which Christians work to reflect on earth and expect to be fully realised at the End Time
Near-death experienceA report of consciousness continuing while the body is clinically dying, used as evidence for an afterlife
HedonismThe view that pleasure is the most important intrinsic good
NihilismNietzsche's view that all values are baseless and life has no meaning
ExclusivismThe belief that salvation is only available to members of one's own religion
Sanctity of lifeThe belief that life is a sacred gift from God, intrinsically valuable and not ours to end
Quality of lifeThe measure of how good or bearable a life is for the person living it, used to weigh against sanctity of life
Imago Dei"In the image of God" — the teaching from Genesis 1:27 that gives every human life its particular worth
AgapeSelfless, self-giving, unconditional love — the love that is commanded rather than felt, and the Christian standard for every relationship
Situation ethicsThe approach that treats agape as the one absolute and judges each act by whether it is the most loving in that situation
Natural LawAquinas's approach: God built purposes into human nature that reason can discover, giving primary precepts such as preserve life, reproduce, live in an ordered society
The DecalogueThe Ten Commandments, including "you shall not murder" (Exodus 20:13) and "you shall not commit adultery" (Exodus 20:14)
AbortionThe deliberate ending of a pregnancy before the foetus can survive independently
EuthanasiaBringing about a gentle death to end suffering — literally "a good death"
Voluntary euthanasiaA life ended at the person's own clear and repeated request
Non-voluntary euthanasiaA life ended when the person cannot express a wish, so the decision is taken for them
Involuntary euthanasiaA life ended against the person's wishes — rejected by almost everyone on both sides
Active euthanasiaDeath caused by a deliberate act, such as a lethal injection
Passive euthanasiaDeath that follows from withdrawing or withholding life-sustaining treatment
Assisted suicideSomeone else provides the means, but the person ends their own life — illegal in the UK under the Suicide Act 1961
Palliative careControlling pain and caring for the dying rather than ending life — the main Christian alternative to euthanasia
HospiceA place providing palliative care for the dying; St Christopher's was founded in 1967 by Dame Cicely Saunders, a Christian
CovenantA binding, solemn agreement made before God — which is how Christians describe marriage, and why it is not treated as an ordinary contract
SacramentAn outward sign of inward grace; marriage is a sacrament for Catholics and Orthodox, but most Protestants treat it as a covenant instead
MonogamyMarriage to one partner only, because "they become one flesh" (Genesis 2:24)
AdulterySex with someone other than one's marriage partner — forbidden by Exodus 20:14, and the one ground Jesus allows for divorce (Matthew 19:9)
PromiscuityHaving many casual sexual partners
Pre-marital sexSex before marriage, between people who are not married to each other
CohabitationLiving together as a couple without being married
Civil partnershipA legally recognised union giving rights similar to marriage, introduced in the UK in 2005
AnnulmentA Catholic declaration that no valid marriage ever existed — for example through deceit, coercion or incapacity at the time of the vows. Not a divorce
RemarriageMarrying again while a former spouse is still living; allowed in Anglican churches at the priest's discretion since 2002
Nuclear familyParents and their children in one household
Extended familyThe nuclear family plus other relatives, for example a grandparent living with them
Reconstituted familyA step-family — two families joined after divorce or bereavement, so step-parents and step-siblings live together
Domestic churchCatholic teaching that the family is a church in miniature, where faith is first taught and handed on
ChildlessnessHaving no children, whether involuntarily (unable to conceive) or voluntarily (by choice)
IVFIn vitro fertilisation — egg and sperm fertilised outside the body, then the embryo is implanted in the womb
AIHArtificial insemination by husband — both gametes come from the married couple
AIDArtificial insemination by donor — a third party's sperm is used
SurrogacyAnother woman carries and gives birth to the child for the couple; commercial surrogacy is illegal in the UK
Genetic engineeringDeliberately altering or selecting genes to change characteristics or remove a fault
Therapeutic cloningCloning cells, not a person, to grow tissue for treating illness
Reproductive cloningCloning to produce a new, genetically identical individual — banned in humans in the UK since 2001
EugenicsSelecting which people are born on the basis of desired characteristics — the "designer baby" objection
Artificial contraceptionA device, drug or operation preventing conception — condom, pill, IUD, implant, sterilisation. Forbidden by Catholic teaching
Natural contraceptionAvoiding conception without any device, by restricting sex to infertile days — the rhythm method or natural family planning. Permitted by Catholic teaching
CelibacyThe settled choice to abstain from sexual activity, usually also from marriage, often for religious reasons
ChastityThe right ordering of sexual behaviour for your state in life — abstinence if unmarried, faithfulness if married. Not the same as celibacy
AdoptionPermanent, legal transfer of parental responsibility — the child becomes a full member of the new family
FosteringTemporary care in a family home, with legal responsibility staying with the birth parents or local authority

questions.promptHtml: Why do Christians believe in life after death?
questions.answerHtml:
From the nature of God: he is omnipotent, so having created us once he can create us again; and omnibenevolent, so he wants to.

From Jesus: he taught that there is life after death, and his atoning work on the cross made it possible for humanity to be with God. His own physical resurrection shows death is not permanent.

From the nature of the person: Christians are dualists — we are body and soul, and the soul can continue to exist with God (Ecclesiastes 12:7).

From scripture's authority: the Bible plainly states that eternal life is on offer — "whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life" (John 3:16).

questions.promptHtml: What is the strongest objection to belief in an afterlife?
questions.answerHtml:
That consciousness is physical brain activity. If thought, memory and personality depend on the brain — and we can watch them fail as the brain fails — then death, which destroys the brain, destroys the person. No separate thing is left to continue.

Supporting objections: there is no good-quality empirical evidence; psychics, mediums, ghosts and near-death experiences all have rational psychological explanations; and there is a conceptual problem — what exactly would continue, and would it still be you?

The debunking move: belief in an afterlife is itself explained as a desire to go on living, fear of death, and an inability to imagine a world without us — and, for Marx, as a tool of social control.

questions.promptHtml: Why do some non-religious people believe in an afterlife, when they do not believe in God?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the argument for a soul need not be religious. Some atheists and Humanists hold that human beings are psycho-somatic entities — body and soul — and appeal to Plato: the body belongs to the changing realm of becoming, while the soul is simple, unchanging and belongs to the realm of being, so it survives the body.

They may also point to paranormal evidence: near-death experiences, spiritualism and communication with the dead, remembered lives, and evidence that brain activity continues after the heart stops.

Finally, the belief can be defended on its effects: it gives life meaning and it comforts the bereaved.

questions.promptHtml: Why do Christians disagree about hell?
questions.answerHtml:
Because eternal punishment is hard to reconcile with a just and loving God. If hell is endless torture for a finite life, the punishment seems disproportionate, which undermines God's justice; and if God is omnibenevolent, some argue hell must be incompatible with his love, so if it exists it must be empty.

The alternatives: hell as annihilation — simply ceasing to exist; hell as a symbol of separation from God, existing without divine love and peace; or hell as a place of correction, leading eventually to universal salvation.

Against all of that stands scripture: Revelation describes wrongdoers "thrown into the lake of fire", and the parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31) presents the afterlife as eternal with one's fate fixed.

questions.promptHtml: Why do Protestants reject purgatory?
questions.answerHtml:
Two reasons, and both are worth a mark. First, it is not in the Bible — it was developed in the medieval period, and Protestants who take scripture as the sole authority find no basis for it.

Second, it conflicts with salvation by faith alone. If a person can be purified over time, and if the prayers of the living can shorten that process, then salvation starts to look like something achieved by human works — and that implies Christ's sacrifice was not sufficient on its own.

The Catholic case: most people are not pure enough to enter God's presence immediately, so a "final purification of the elect" explains how a just God can still save imperfect people.

questions.promptHtml: How does a linear view of existence differ from a cyclical one, and what does each do better?
questions.answerHtml:
Linear (Christian): one life, then resurrection and a single judgement, then heaven or hell. Cyclical: deeds determine rebirth into a higher or lower form until one escapes the cycle.

Linear does better on identity and urgency. The same person is raised and judged, so identity is preserved; and because there is only one life, the choices made in it matter absolutely.

Cyclical does better on the problem of evil and on opportunity. Suffering is explained as the consequence of deeds in a previous life, no judge is needed because karma works as an impersonal law, and there are further chances to improve.

Each has a cost: the linear view must explain why a good God permits suffering and eternal punishment; the Buddhist version of the cyclical view has no soul, so it is unclear that anything of you continues at all.

questions.promptHtml: How does belief in judgement change the way a Christian actually lives?
questions.answerHtml:
It makes present behaviour consequential. In the parable of the Sheep and the Goats, the righteous are those who fed the hungry, clothed the poor, helped the sick and visited prisoners — "what you do for the least of these, you do for me" — so charity, service and care for the needy become urgent rather than optional.

It also encourages obedience to God's commandments, forgiveness of others, confession of sin, and evangelism, since judgement is based on belief in God and acceptance of Jesus's sacrifice.

The tension to note: Christians who emphasise faith alone argue that works cannot buy salvation; those who follow James reply that "faith without works is dead", so works are the evidence of real faith.

questions.promptHtml: Can life have meaning without God? Give the strongest argument on each side.
questions.answerHtml:
Strongest "no": without God there is no absolute, objective meaning. Nietzsche followed the point through — if God is dead, all values are baseless and reason is impotent, which is nihilism. Religious meaning is also underwritten by an afterlife, so only it can give ultimate purpose to this life.

Strongest "yes": meaning does not have to be objective to be real. Sartre argues that with no script we must choose and invent our own purpose; Aristotle grounds it in flourishing, and Bentham in the greatest good for the greatest number. Happiness is a purpose almost everyone accepts, and it does not depend on God existing.

A judgement: the "no" side wins on absolute meaning and loses on lived meaning. Most people find purpose in relationships, work and happiness regardless of belief — so a fair conclusion is that religion supplies a kind of meaning that atheism cannot, without being the only source of meaning there is.

questions.promptHtml: Why do two Christians reading the same Bible reach opposite conclusions on euthanasia?
questions.answerHtml:
Because they start from different texts and give them different weight. One begins with "you shall not murder" (Exodus 20:13) and "the LORD gave and the LORD has taken away" (Job 1:21), and concludes that life is God's to end. The other begins with "love your neighbour as yourself" (Mark 12:31) and with Jesus relieving suffering wherever he found it, and concludes that leaving someone in agony is the less Christian act.

Because they disagree about how the Bible works. A conservative Christian reads it as giving absolute rules that hold whatever the consequences. A liberal Christian reads it as giving one absolute principle — agape — and treats the rules as generally reliable guidance about how to apply it. That is situation ethics, and it is the single biggest cause of internal Christian disagreement in this whole section.

Because the duties genuinely conflict. A Christian has a duty to protect life and a duty to relieve suffering, and in a terminal case the two point in opposite directions. Neither side is ignoring scripture; they are ranking two scriptural duties differently.

And because authority differs. Catholics read scripture through the magisterium and Natural Law, which gives a settled official answer; Protestants who hold to scripture alone, with no teaching authority above the individual conscience, end up with a range of answers instead.

questions.promptHtml: Why do sanctity of life and quality of life pull against each other?
questions.answerHtml:
Because they locate value in different places. Sanctity of life says the worth of a life is intrinsic — it comes from God, through imago Dei (Genesis 1:27), and so it does not change when the person's health, usefulness or happiness changes. Quality of life says worth depends on the content of the life: what it is actually like to be that person now.

So they give opposite answers in the hard cases. On a sanctity view, a patient in unrelieved pain still has a life of full and equal value, so ending it is a wrong done to them. On a quality view, a life of nothing but suffering may be no benefit to the person living it, so insisting it continue is the cruelty.

Each has a real cost. Sanctity of life risks preserving suffering it could relieve, and it has to explain why an absolute rule should win when it causes harm. Quality of life risks the slippery slope: once lives are graded, there is no obvious line to stop at, and someone has to do the grading.

Can a Christian hold both? Many do, and saying how is worth the top marks. The presumption is always for life; but Christians are not obliged to preserve a body at all costs, and Catholic teaching itself permits withdrawing burdensome or futile treatment while forbidding any act intended to cause death. Good palliative care is the practical attempt to honour both at once — raise the quality of the life without ending it.

questions.promptHtml: Why has Christian teaching on homosexuality and same-sex marriage split the churches, rather than changing across all of them together?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the churches answer two separate questions and disagree on both. First: are the biblical prohibitions (Leviticus 18:22; Romans 1:26–27) binding today, or are they culturally conditioned in the way the Bible's instructions on slavery are now taken to be? Second: what is marriage — if Jesus grounds it in male and female (Mark 10:6–9), then extending it is not a reform but a change of definition.

Because each church has a different decision-making structure. The Roman Catholic Church has a teaching authority that can hold a settled position, and Natural Law gives it a reasoned one: sex is ordered to procreation. The Quakers decide by the discernment of the meeting, which is why they moved first, in 2009. The Church of England has to carry General Synod, the bishops and a worldwide communion with it, which is why it has kept its doctrine of marriage while commending prayers of blessing from 2023.

Because the law deliberately left it to them. The Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 included the "quadruple lock", which bars the Church of England from conducting same-sex marriages and protects other religious bodies from being compelled. So a change in civil law did not force a change in doctrine, and the churches diverged: the URC in 2016, the Scottish Episcopal Church in 2017, the Methodist Church in Britain in 2021.

The underlying point, and it is worth a mark: Christians differ because they give different weight to scripture, tradition, reason and present-day experience. Affirming Christians lead with agape and Galatians 3:28; traditional Christians lead with scripture and the created order. Note that the disagreement is live and present-tense — it is not a case of the old view giving way to a new one.

questions.promptHtml: Why is an annulment not simply a Catholic form of divorce?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the two do opposite things. A divorce ends a marriage that existed. An annulment declares that no valid marriage ever existed — for example because one party was coerced, was deceived about something fundamental, or lacked the capacity to consent at the time of the vows.

Why the Church needs the distinction. Catholic teaching holds marriage to be a sacrament, and that in a valid, consummated sacramental marriage it is God who joins the couple: "what God has joined together, let no one separate" (Mark 10:9). If God did the joining, no human court can undo it, so a civil divorce changes the couple's legal position without ending the marriage in the eyes of the Church. Annulment does not claim to undo God's act; it examines whether the act ever took place.

The practical consequence. Without an annulment a Catholic who remarries civilly is, on the Church's teaching, still married to the first spouse — which is why remarriage has traditionally barred people from communion, though Amoris Laetitia (2016) encouraged pastoral discernment case by case.

The criticism, which belongs in a 12-marker: that annulment is a legal device producing the same outcome as divorce while allowing the Church to say it has not permitted one. The reply is that the grounds are genuinely different — an annulment turns on what was true at the wedding, a divorce on what has happened since.

questions.promptHtml: Why do many Christians accept AIH but reject AID and surrogacy?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the objection is about who is involved, not about using medicine. In AIH both egg and sperm come from the married couple, so the child is still the fruit of their own union and nothing has entered the marriage from outside. In AID and egg donation a third party's genetic material comes into the marriage, and Catholic teaching has called this a kind of mechanical adultery. In surrogacy a third party's body is involved as well.

Three further objections stack up on the AID and surrogacy side: the child risks being treated as a commodity that has been bought, rather than received as a gift; it is said to weaken the exclusive bond of marriage; and it makes it straightforward for single people and same-sex couples to have children, which some churches regard as cutting the child's upbringing loose from marriage as they understand it.

But notice this is not the Catholic position. Catholic teaching rejects AIH too, because any technique that conceives a child apart from the marital act separates the unitive from the procreative — that is the Natural Law argument of Donum Vitae (1987). The AIH-but-not-AID line is the Protestant middle ground: medicine may help a couple to conceive, but only their own gametes may be used.

The replies, for the other side of the answer: that situation ethics makes giving a longed-for child the most loving act available, whatever the source of the gametes; that God works through science, so a donor is simply part of the means; and that donor conception is regulated in the UK, with counselling and limits, precisely to manage the risks about identity and consent.

questions.promptHtml: Why would a church treat celibacy as a higher calling when Genesis commands people to be fruitful?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the New Testament adds something Genesis does not have. Genesis 1:28 blesses marriage and children in creation; Jesus and Paul then speak of a second, narrower calling. Jesus says some "have renounced marriage because of the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 19:12), and Paul says plainly that "it is good for a man not to touch a woman" (1 Corinthians 7:1). Jesus himself was celibate, so the church has an example as well as a text.

Because of the practical argument Paul makes. "An unmarried man is concerned about the Lord's affairs… a married man is concerned about the affairs of this world" (1 Corinthians 7:32–33). Without a spouse or children, a priest, monk or nun is free for prayer and ministry and belongs to the whole community rather than to one household — which is the Catholic case for clerical celibacy.

Note how the church limits the claim. Celibacy is treated as a gift given to some, not a rule for all: Matthew 19:12 adds "the one who can accept this should accept it", and Paul concedes that those who cannot control themselves "should marry". So it is a higher calling in the sense of a fuller renunciation, not a judgement that marriage is second-rate — marriage is still a sacrament in Catholic teaching.

The objections, which make the other half of a 12-marker: that Genesis 2:18 says it is not good to be alone; that Peter and the other apostles were married, so celibacy was never a condition of church leadership; that Protestants regard compulsory clerical celibacy as a human rule with no biblical warrant, and argue a married minister understands family life better; and that a requirement imposed rather than freely chosen can do real harm. Non-religious critics make the same distinction — they object to required celibacy, not to anyone choosing it.

questions.promptHtml: Explain why religious people differ in their views about the afterlife. (6)

They read scripture differently. Some Christians, influenced by Greek thought, teach an immortal soul that survives the body 1, while others reject that as unbiblical and as detracting from our dependence on God, holding instead to the resurrection of body and soul described in 1 Corinthians 15 1

They differ over hell: some take Revelation's "lake of fire" literally, while others treat hell as annihilation or as separation from God, and universalists argue it is a place of correction leading to eventual universal salvation 1

questions.promptHtml:
"The notion of an afterlife is pure fantasy."

Do you agree? Give reasons for your answer, showing you have considered another point of view. In your answer you should refer to at least one religion. (12)
questions.answerHtml:
The real paper marks this in levels, so treat the plan below as a target for coverage rather than a tick list.

Arguments for: there is a lack of good-quality empirical evidence for any afterlife, and we should not believe what the evidence does not support 1

Physicalism explains the person entirely: thought and feeling are functions of the brain, and when the brain deteriorates so do memory and personality, so death destroys the person 1

The usual evidence collapses under examination — mediums, ghosts and near-death experiences all have rational psychological explanations 1

The belief is better explained as wish-fulfilment: a desire to go on living, fear of death, an inability to imagine a world without us — and, for Marx, a tool by which the ruling classes control communities 1

Arguments against: Christians point to the authority of the Bible, which states plainly that eternal life is on offer (John 3:16) 1

Jesus's physical resurrection is presented as evidence that death is not a permanent state, and Matthew 27:52 describes bodies being raised 1

A moral argument: life cannot be called good or just unless there is another life in which justice is dispensed, the good rewarded and the wicked punished 1

Dualism supports it philosophically — Plato argued the soul is simple and unchanging, so it survives the body, and some atheists and Humanists accept an afterlife on exactly these grounds 1

Christian teaching to anchor it: belief rests on the nature of God — an omnipotent God who created us can create us again, and an omnibenevolent God wants us with him 1

Appraisal: calling it "fantasy" assumes that only empirical evidence counts, which begs the question against religious claims; but the conceptual problem is real — it is unclear what continues, or whether it would still be the same person 1

Conclusion: the sceptical case is strong on evidence, and the explanations of why people believe are persuasive 1

But "pure fantasy" overstates it: Christian belief is grounded in a reasoned account of God's nature and in the resurrection of Jesus, and the demand for justice is a serious argument — so I would say the afterlife is unproven rather than fantasy 1

questions.promptHtml:
"Heaven means being with God, not a place."

Do you agree? Give reasons for your answer, showing you have considered another point of view. In your answer you should refer to at least one religion. (12)
questions.answerHtml:
Level marked on the real paper — the plan is a target for coverage, not a tick list.

Arguments for: many Christians treat heaven as a symbol of eternal life in positive relationship with God rather than a location 1

The descriptions in Revelation — a rainbow like an emerald encircling the throne of God — are apocalyptic imagery, and reading them literally misunderstands the genre 1

What is promised is communion with God, with no sin, evil, suffering or death; those are relational descriptions, not geographical ones 1

Some Christians expect heaven to be this world transformed after the day of judgement, which again makes it a state of affairs rather than another place 1

Arguments against: many Christians do hold heaven to be a real place, a higher metaphysical world 1

Christian teaching about bodily resurrection points that way: raised bodies, as in 1 Corinthians 15 and Matthew 27:52, need somewhere to be 1

Jesus likens heaven to a banquet or wedding feast, which are physical, located and shared events 1

Heaven is also described as a shared community, which suggests more than a private relationship between an individual soul and God 1

Christian teaching to anchor it: the disagreement runs through the Church — some see heaven in terms of bodily resurrection, others as a higher world of souls, and exclusivists add that it is open only to Christians 1

Appraisal: the "place" reading takes scripture at its word but struggles with where such a place could be; the "relationship" reading fits a transcendent God but risks making heaven so abstract it offers little comfort to the bereaved 1

Conclusion: since God is transcendent and beyond space and time, communion with him cannot really be a matter of location, so the statement captures the heart of the belief 1

But the two are not opposed: the language of place is how Christians express the reality of resurrection and shared community, so I agree that heaven is primarily being with God, while holding that the imagery of place is doing necessary work rather than being a mistake 1

questions.promptHtml:
"Life has meaning and purpose only for religious people."

Do you agree? Give reasons for your answer, showing you have considered another point of view. In your answer you should refer to at least one religion. (12)
questions.answerHtml:
Level marked on the real paper — the plan is a target for coverage, not a tick list.

Arguments for: without God there is no absolute or objective meaning; Nietzsche followed the thought through to nihilism, in which all values are baseless 1

Ultimate purpose seems to require an afterlife: if death ends everything, nothing we do has lasting significance 1

Some argue there is no reason to act morally without God, which leads to a selfish worldview and makes life random, chaotic and cruel 1

Christianity supplies a complete answer: we were created by God, our purpose is to know, worship and serve him, and salvation through Christ gives a goal beyond this life (John 3:16) 1

Arguments against: meaning does not have to be objective to be real — even with no absolute answer, people can create their own purpose, as Sartre argued 1

Aristotle grounded purpose in flourishing, and Bentham in the greatest good for the greatest number, neither of which needs God 1

Happiness is a purpose most people accept, and it plainly does not depend on God existing 1

Religion may even be damaging here: a false sense of purpose can stop people appreciating this life, and Marx called religion an opiate that distracts from real social progress 1

Christian teaching to anchor it: Aquinas held that the supreme good for a human being is not happiness but a positive relationship with God, and Augustine that we cannot save ourselves and must trust in Christ — which is precisely the kind of meaning the non-religious views cannot supply 1

Appraisal: the religious case is strong on ultimate meaning and weak as a claim about all meaning, since it has to say that billions of non-believers lead meaningless lives, which does not match what they report 1

Conclusion: the word "only" is what sinks the statement 1

Religion offers a kind of meaning — absolute, God-given and extending beyond death — that non-religious accounts cannot match, and Christians would say that is the meaning that matters; but purpose found in flourishing, love, work and the happiness of others is real meaning too, so I disagree with the statement as it stands 1

questions.promptHtml: Identify three grounds on which the Abortion Act 1967 permits an abortion in the UK. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
A risk to the physical or mental health of the pregnant woman 1

A risk to the physical or mental health of her existing children 1

questions.promptHtml: Explain two reasons why many Christians oppose euthanasia. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
It breaks the sanctity of life 1: life is a gift from God, and as Job says, "the LORD gave and the LORD has taken away", so the timing of death is God's decision and not ours 1

Also accepted: hospices and palliative care relieve the suffering without ending the life; legalising it would devalue human life and pressure the vulnerable.

questions.promptHtml: Explain two different Christian attitudes to same-sex marriage. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
The Roman Catholic Church teaches that marriage is by its nature between a man and a woman, so it does not marry same-sex couples 1: Jesus grounds marriage in male and female in Mark 10:6–9, Natural Law orders marriage to procreation, and the Catechism calls homosexual acts intrinsically disordered while still requiring that gay people be treated with respect and compassion 1

The Quakers have celebrated same-sex marriages on the same basis as any other since their decision in 2009 1, because they judge a relationship by its commitment and faithful love rather than by the gender of the couple, and hold that gay people are made in God's image like everyone else (Genesis 1:27) 1

Also accepted: the Methodist Church in Britain permitted same-sex marriages in 2021; the Church of England keeps its doctrine of marriage but agreed prayers of blessing in 2023.

questions.promptHtml: Explain two ways in which a local church helps to sustain family life. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
Through the rites of passage 1: baptism, confirmation, marriage and funerals mark the turning points of family life, in celebration and in grief, and bind the family into the wider congregation that supports it 1

Through teaching and practical support for parents 1: Sunday schools and youth groups help parents pass on the faith, while marriage preparation courses, parenting classes and counselling — Catholic Marriage Care, for example, or the Anglican Mothers' Union — help keep couples together 1

Also accepted: food banks, toddler groups and debt advice relieving the pressures that break families apart; church socials reducing isolation.

questions.promptHtml: Explain why Christians have different attitudes to abortion. (6)
questions.answerHtml:
All Christians start from the sanctity of life: life is a gift from God, humans are made in his image (Genesis 1:27), and "you shall not murder" (Exodus 20:13) 1

Conservative Christians treat that principle as absolute. Roman Catholic teaching holds that life begins at conception, that Natural Law requires us to preserve life, and that the Catechism demands protection of life from the moment of conception — so abortion is never permissible 1

They support this from scripture that treats the unborn child as already known to God: "before I formed you in the womb I knew you" (Jeremiah 1:5) and "you knit me together in my mother's womb" (Psalm 139:13) 1

Liberal Christians give more weight to the second Christian duty, the relief of suffering, and to love as the one absolute. On situation ethics, abortion may be the most loving option — for instance after rape, or where the mother's life is at risk 1

They may also hold that the early foetus is not yet a full person, or that the decision belongs to the individual conscience before God rather than to the church 1

The Church of England sits between the two: it holds abortion to be a great moral evil, but accepts that in strictly limited circumstances it may be the lesser of two evils — which shows the disagreement is ultimately about whether sanctity of life can ever be outweighed by quality of life 1

questions.promptHtml: Explain Christian teachings about marriage and its purposes. (6)
questions.answerHtml:
Marriage is part of God's plan in creation: "a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh" (Genesis 2:24), so it creates a single new unit rather than a private arrangement 1

It is God's act and therefore permanent — "what God has joined together, let no one separate" (Mark 10:9) — which is why the vows run "for better, for worse… till death us do part" 1

In the Catholic and Orthodox churches marriage is a sacrament, an outward sign of God's grace, which raises it above a legal contract; Jesus honoured marriage by attending the wedding at Cana (John 2:1–11) 1

Its purposes, as the Church of England marriage service sets them out, include the couple's mutual comfort, help and delight — marriage is a lifelong partnership, not only an institution for children 1

It is the proper place for a sexual relationship: sex unites the couple and is open to procreation, which in Catholic Natural Law teaching are two purposes that belong together 1

And it is the foundation of family life — the place for bringing up children in the faith, which is why Catholic teaching calls the family the domestic church and why marriage matters to the wider community and not only to the couple 1
