questions.promptHtml: Explain why Christians think family life is important. (6)
questions.answerHtml:
The family is part of God's design: marriage in Genesis 2:24 exists partly for the bringing up of children, so family life is how the creation ordinance is carried out 1

It is where faith is handed on — children are brought to baptism, taught to pray and raised "in the training and instruction of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:4) — which is why Catholic teaching calls the family the domestic church 1

The Decalogue itself protects it: "honour your father and your mother" (Exodus 20:12) makes respect for parents a commandment, and the duty continues into their old age 1

The duty runs both ways: children owe obedience (Ephesians 6:1), and parents must not exasperate their children but bring them up patiently (Ephesians 6:4; Colossians 3:20–21) 1

Providing for relatives is treated as a test of faith — "anyone who does not provide for their relatives… has denied the faith" (1 Timothy 5:8) — so caring for the elderly and the vulnerable in the family is a religious obligation 1

And in Natural Law the family is the building block of an ordered society, which is why churches invest heavily in sustaining it through rites of passage, Sunday schools, marriage preparation and counselling 1

questions.promptHtml:
"Sanctity of life matters more than quality of life."

Do you agree? Give reasons for your answer, showing you have considered another point of view. In your answer you should refer to at least one religion. (12)
questions.answerHtml:
Level marked on the real paper — the plan is a target for coverage, not a tick list.

Arguments for: life is a sacred gift from God, so its value does not depend on its condition; humans are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27), which gives every life intrinsic worth 1

The decision belongs to God, not to us — "the LORD gave and the LORD has taken away" (Job 1:21) — and "you shall not murder" (Exodus 20:13) admits no exception for suffering 1

Catholic Natural Law requires us to preserve life, and the Catechism teaches that life must be protected from conception to the very end; abandoning that for quality of life produces what John Paul II called a culture of death 1

Practically, once lives are graded by quality there is no clear place to stop, and the people judged to have the lowest quality of life are the ones least able to defend themselves 1

Arguments against: Christians also have a duty to relieve suffering, which Jesus modelled in healing the sick and which judgement itself is measured by (Matthew 25:40) — and sanctity of life can leave someone trapped in agony 1

On situation ethics, love is the one absolute, so the most loving option may be to end a pregnancy or a life of unbearable suffering; liberal Christians read 1 Corinthians 13 this way 1

Utilitarians argue the value of a life lies in the experience it contains, so a life of unrelieved pain is not a benefit to the person living it 1

Even opponents already make quality-of-life judgements: Catholic teaching permits withdrawing treatment that is burdensome and futile, which concedes that mere biological life is not the only thing that matters 1

Christian teaching to anchor it: the Church is genuinely divided — Roman Catholic teaching treats sanctity of life as absolute from conception to natural death, while the Church of England and liberal Protestants accept that in strictly limited circumstances ending a life may be the lesser evil 1

Appraisal: the sanctity argument is strongest as a protection — it refuses to let anyone be written off — but weakest when it demands that suffering be prolonged for the sake of a principle the sufferer does not share 1

Conclusion: the two are not really rivals in most cases, since good palliative care serves both; the statement only bites in the tragic cases where they genuinely conflict 1

In those cases I would keep sanctity of life as the default, because a society that starts weighing lives is dangerous to the weakest — but I would allow the compassionate exceptions the Church of England already recognises, so I agree with the statement as a presumption rather than as an absolute 1

questions.promptHtml:
"Everyone should accept homosexual relationships."

Do you agree? Give reasons for your answer, showing you have considered another point of view. In your answer you should refer to at least one religion. (12)
questions.answerHtml:
Level marked on the real paper — the plan is a target for coverage, not a tick list.

Arguments for: gay people are made in God's image like everyone else (Genesis 1:27), so affirming Christians argue they cannot be treated as defective 1

If love is the greatest Christian virtue (1 Corinthians 13:13) and the test is "love your neighbour as yourself" (Mark 12:31), a faithful and committed same-sex relationship meets it 1

The traditional texts are contested: Jesus says nothing about homosexuality, the Leviticus holiness code also forbids things Christians no longer observe, and Romans 1 is read in context as about idolatry and exploitation rather than committed partnerships 1

Churches have already changed their reading of scripture on slavery and on the status of women, and Galatians 3:28 is used to argue that in Christ the old categories of exclusion no longer stand; non-religiously, orientation is not a choice and Mill's harm principle finds no victim 1

Arguments against: conservative Christians hold that scripture prohibits same-sex sexual acts — Leviticus 18:22 calls it detestable, and Paul describes men and women abandoning "natural relations" (Romans 1:26–27) 1

Jesus grounds marriage in the creation of male and female and in the two becoming one flesh (Mark 10:6–9, citing Genesis 1:27 and 2:24), so sexual complementarity is taken to be part of God's design 1

On Natural Law, sex is ordered to procreation within marriage, which is why Catholic teaching calls homosexual acts intrinsically disordered while insisting that gay people themselves be accepted with respect, compassion and sensitivity (Catechism 2357–2358) 1

There is also a freedom-of-conscience argument against the word "everyone": requiring universal acceptance of any sexual ethic overrides the right of religious believers to hold a different view 1

Christian teaching to anchor it: the Church is openly split — the Roman Catholic Church and most conservative evangelicals hold the traditional teaching, while Quakers have celebrated same-sex marriages since 2009 and the Methodist Church in Britain since 2021; the Church of England keeps its doctrine of marriage but agreed prayers of blessing in 2023, and figures such as Desmond Tutu campaigned for full acceptance 1

Appraisal: the conservative case is strong on the plain sense of specific texts and weak on why those texts are binding when neighbouring ones are not; the affirming case is strong on love and on the image of God and weaker on Jesus's own appeal to male and female in Mark 10 1

Conclusion: the sticking point is "everyone". Accepting gay people — refusing to abuse, exclude or discriminate against them — is something all the churches now say they require, and the Catholic Catechism says it explicitly 1

But accepting the relationships as equivalent to marriage is a doctrinal judgement Christians are still making in good faith on both sides, so I agree that everyone should accept gay people and treat them equally in law, while holding that "everyone" cannot reasonably be made to share one theological conclusion 1

questions.promptHtml:
"Religious people should never divorce."

Do you agree? Give reasons for your answer, showing you have considered another point of view. In your answer you should refer to at least one religion. (12)
questions.answerHtml:
Level marked on the real paper — the plan is a target for coverage, not a tick list.

Arguments for: Jesus is explicit — "what God has joined together, let no one separate" (Mark 10:9) — so marriage is God's act and no human authority can undo it 1

The vows are unconditional: "for better, for worse, for richer, for poorer, in sickness and in health… till death us do part", made in the presence of God, so divorce breaks a promise to God as well as to a spouse 1

Catholic teaching follows this through: a valid, consummated sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved, so the Church offers annulment — a declaration that no valid marriage existed — rather than divorce 1

Divorce also has real costs beyond the couple: financial loss, disputes over children, higher welfare costs, instability for children, and damage to the family as the building block of society 1

Arguments against: the New Testament itself is not united. Matthew 19:9 allows divorce for sexual immorality, and Paul says that if an unbelieving partner leaves, the believer "is not bound" (1 Corinthians 7:15) 1

Love is the greatest commandment, and forcing someone to remain in an abusive or loveless marriage is neither loving nor protective of the children — on situation ethics, divorce can be the most loving option 1

Most churches accept this in practice: the Church of England has since 2002 allowed priests to marry a divorced person in church at their discretion, Methodists permit remarriage, and the Orthodox churches allow it with a more penitential service 1

Non-religiously, divorce is regrettable but sometimes necessary, the law allows it, and the children's interests are better served by ending a destructive marriage than by preserving its form 1

Christian teaching to anchor it: the churches' divergence follows the three strands in scripture — Mark 10 for no divorce, Matthew 19 for adultery as a ground, 1 Corinthians 7 for the most flexible position — and the Catholic alternative is annulment rather than permission 1

Appraisal: the "never" position honours the vow and protects the weaker partner from being discarded, but it struggles with abuse and desertion, and it makes the Church look as though it values an institution more than the people inside it; the permissive position is compassionate but risks treating lifelong vows as provisional 1

Conclusion: "never" is too strong even by the Bible's own standards, since Jesus himself allows an exception in Matthew 19:9 and Paul allows another 1

So I disagree with the statement: religious people should treat marriage as lifelong and enter it expecting never to divorce, and a church is right to make that the teaching — but where a marriage has become harmful, the Anglican and Orthodox approach of compassion with seriousness seems more faithful to Christian love than an absolute prohibition 1

drill.intro:
How to answer each part — Paper 1

3 marks (AO1) — no explanation is required. Give three focused and distinct points; brief, clear reasons are ideal. Do not develop them.

4 marks (AO1) — these always ask for two points of information which require some development. The development must add value to the point while still answering the question posed, so each point scores 1 and its development scores 1. An example is often the quickest way to develop a point.

6 marks (AO1 + AO2) — these always ask you to explain. Explain and develop the issue, drawing out the influence and significance of the religion, beliefs and values. Level marked: the top level needs religious terms used accurately, a comprehensive explanation, and an assured account of significance. Even where no number is given, explain more than one reason; if told to choose a religion, name it and stay inside it.

12 marks (AO1 + AO2) — the synoptic assessment. Draw on a number of ideas and arguments from across the course, then evaluate and appraise each argument as you make it. Consider every aspect of the question, do not neglect the alternative viewpoint no matter how weak it is, refer to at least one religion (humanist and atheist views give perspective but do not count as that reference), and judge the value of the arguments to reach a fully justified conclusion.

Three of each part of a real Question 2 — 3, 4, 6 and 12 marks — twice over: D1–D12 on spec 2.1–2.2, then D13–D24 on 2.3–2.7. The 6- and 12-mark answers are level marked on the real paper, so the mark points below are a target for coverage, not a tick list.

modules.title: Peace and Conflict
modules.standfirst: Section 3 of Paper 1 Beliefs and Values — war and its causes, pacifism, Just War, holy war, weapons of mass destruction, terrorism, peace and forgiveness, bullying, sin and crime, punishment and capital punishment, in one 25-mark question (3, 4, 6 and 12 marks) where the marks live in the quotations and the named examples: Micah's swords into ploughs, Aquinas' conditions, Corrymeela, the Brighton bombing.

subsections.html:
Six spec areas sit under this one question: conflict and war (3.1), peace and reconciliation (3.2), bullying (3.3), sin and crime (3.4), punishment (3.5) and capital punishment (3.6). They share one spine — Christianity holds both a retributive strand from the Old Testament and a forgiving strand from Jesus, and almost every 12-marker here is really asking which strand wins.

What they actually ask

From the seven June papers 2019–2025, Paper 1 Section 3 (Questions 5 and 6 — you answer one). Capital punishment and sin-versus-crime appear in every single year, and capital punishment often twice in the same paper.

  • Capital punishment — all seven years. "Capital punishment is never justified" (2019); "three purposes for the death penalty" (2020); "two reasons why some non-religious people support capital punishment" (2021); "the attitudes its followers may have to capital punishment" and "The death penalty may be the lesser of two evils" (2022); "three beliefs about capital punishment" and "why some of its followers support the use of capital punishment" (2023); "why some non-religious people are against capital punishment" and "why some of its followers are opposed to capital punishment" (2024); "three reasons why society may support capital punishment" and "two reasons why some of its followers are opposed to capital punishment" (2025).
  • Sin and crime — the difference, and whether sins should be crimes — all seven years. "the differences between sins and crimes" (2019); "two types of sins and their consequences" and "All sins should be crimes" (2020); "three crimes" and "Crimes are worse than sins" (2021); "three sins" (2022); "two differences between sins and crimes" (2023); "Sins should be against the law" (2024); "three non-religious attitudes to crime" and "Committing a crime is always sinful" (2025).
  • Punishment, its aims and reform — "why some people think reform is the most important aim of punishment" (2019); "the attitudes to punishment in this religion" (2020); "two reasons why society may need to punish offenders" (2021); "two religious attitudes towards the aims of punishment" and "There is no point in punishment if it does not change the wrongdoer" (2022); "three benefits of reforming criminals" (2023); "three reasons why society punishes criminals" (2024).
  • Peace, peacemaking, forgiveness and reconciliation — all seven years. "three things a religious organisation may do to work for peace" (2019); "the teachings about the importance of forgiveness in this religion" (2020); "three ways religious organisations may work for world peace" and "Religion is the best hope for world peace" (2021); "two religious attitudes to the importance of peace" and "the importance of forgiveness in this religion" (2022); "Religious people should be peacemakers" (2023); "two ways religions can promote peacemaking" (2024); "the role of religion in peacemaking" (2025).
  • Bullying — and inclusion — six of seven. "three types of bullying" and "two reasons why its followers believe bullying is wrong" (2019); "why its followers do not agree with bullying" (2021); "three possible responses to bullying" (2022); "its attitude towards bullies" and "It is impossible to prevent bullying" (2023); "two reasons why bullying happens" (2024); "two teachings about why inclusion is important" and "Bullying should be a crime" (2025).
  • War, conflict and pacifism — "two contrasting attitudes towards war held by its followers" and "All religious people should oppose conflict" (2019); "three causes of conflict" and "All religious people should be pacifists" (2020); "its teachings about war" (2021); "two ways religion may lead to conflict" (2023); "three causes of conflict" and "Sometimes war is the only way to achieve peace" (2024); "the issues that may cause conflict" (2025).

What has not come up: no paper in these seven years asked directly about Just War theory, holy war, weapons of mass destruction or terrorism by name — they are reached only through the general "teachings about war" and "causes of conflict" stems. Learn them as material for those stems, not as topics of their own.

subsections.heading: Conflict and war — causes, consequences, and whether religion is to blame
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1 · Lesson 2, Revision Booklet 3 p.6

  • Conflict defined — a serious disagreement between two parties; large-scale conflict has five standard causes.
  • The five causes — politics or ideology, resources, nationalism or ethnicity, religion, and history or culture.
  • Three current conflicts — Russia–Ukraine (2014, full invasion 2022), Israel/Palestine (since 1948), Ethiopia's civil war (2020).
  • Consequences carry figures — WWII killed over 60 million, 60% civilians; Syria drove three million refugees into Turkey and Lebanon.
  • Religion is rarely the real cause — most wars come from misused freewill, and the twentieth century's worst were political and ethnic.
  • Non-religious response — give the UN stronger powers; Situation Ethics does whatever resolves the conflict with least harm.
ArgumentCounter-argument
Holy books can be used by believers to justify conflict — "Proclaim this among the nations: Prepare for war!" (Joel 3:9)Any conflict instigated by believers rests on an incorrect interpretation of the religion's doctrines
Religion is central to a devotee's identity, so it is worth dying for — and many religions venerate their martyrsMost religions advocate peace; Jesus blesses the peacemakers
Many conflicts of the past have been over religionMost wars and genocides were caused by the misuse of freewill, not by religion
So ridding the world of religion would make it more peacefulThe 20th century's worst wars were political and ethnic, not religious
More detail

A conflict occurs when there is a serious disagreement between two parties, and large-scale conflicts have five standard causes: politics, resources, history, culture and religion. The spec names those five, so learn them as a list and attach an example to each.

CauseWhy it leads to conflictExample
Politics or ideologyGroups hold differing views about the policies that should govern a countryThe Korean War, begun in 1950, when North Korea invaded South Korea aiming to unite the whole country under communism; the Cold War — Communism versus Capitalism
ResourcesThe desire for another country's resources, such as oil, or access to themThe two Gulf Wars — many believe the West wanted to secure access to Middle Eastern oil reserves; German expansion in the 1930s for coal, gas and factories
Nationalism or ethnicityThe belief that one ethnic group or culture is superior, which can mean demanding a separate country or removing a minorityThe civil wars in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Kosovo; the attempted genocide of the Tutsis in Rwanda in 1994; World War II
ReligionDifferences between religions, and differences within one religion, and holy books used to justify violenceThe war involving Christians and Muslims in the Central African Republic; the civil war in Syria — government forces who are Shia Muslims against rebel forces who are Sunni Muslims
History and cultureOld grievances and clashing ways of life keep a dispute alive across generationsNorthern Ireland; the Crusades still cited today

The spec also requires three current areas of conflict. Learn these three with one sentence each — a bare name is not a described example:

  1. The Russo-Ukrainian War. Began in 2014, initially over the status of Crimea and parts of the Donbas; in February 2022 Russia launched a full-scale invasion. President Putin called it a "special military operation" defending ethnic Russians in the eastern Donbas, but speculation about his motives ranges from keeping Ukraine out of NATO to restoring the Russian Empire. Cause: politics and resources.
  2. Israel / Palestine. Both Israelis and Palestinians claim the same land. Since the annexation of the land in 1948 there have been several wars, most recently in Gaza in May 2021. Israel occupies the Palestinian West Bank and has allowed Israelis to settle there, and claims the whole of Jerusalem as its capital; Palestinians claim East Jerusalem as the capital of a future Palestinian state. Cause: religion, history and resources.
  3. Ethiopia. A civil war since 2020. Its roots lie in the Ethiopian system of government: Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's attempt to reform the government was not well received by the Tigray ethnic group. Cause: politics and ethnicity.

Consequences are a favourite 3-mark question, and each one has a figure attached if you want the development mark. Death and injury, especially among civilians — in World War II more than 60 million people were killed, and 60% of the deaths were civilians. Mass migration — the Syrian conflict drove more than three million refugees into Turkey and Lebanon and on into Europe, and over 900,000 Rohingya have fled to Bangladesh, often into huge refugee camps. The cost — weapons and military personnel are expensive, and the disruption to a country's economy can be crippling. Damage to infrastructure — roads, hospitals and schools. Disrupted education. And the burden on neighbouring countries, providing shelter, health care and education for refugees.

The contested version — "Religion is the main cause of conflict" — comes up often enough that the two columns are worth memorising:

Non-religious responses to conflict: give the United Nations stronger powers so it can resolve conflicts quickly, and use Situation Ethics — do the most loving thing, whether that means sanctions or joining a war to end an invasion, whichever resolves the conflict with the least harm.

subsections.heading: Christian teachings on war — the Bible cuts both ways
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1 · Revision Booklet 3 p.6–7

  • Most Christians oppose war — but a minority allow taking up arms against an oppressor as a last resort.
  • The Bible against war — "Blessed are the peacemakers" (Matthew 5:9); Micah 4:3 beats swords into ploughshares.
  • The Bible for war — 1 Samuel 15:3 commands the destruction of the Amalekites; Joel 3:9 inverts Micah exactly.
  • Jesus' example cuts both ways — he died rather than fight, yet overturned the money changers' tables in righteous anger (Mark 11:15).
  • The individual-not-nation move — Jesus tells a person how to answer violence done to them, not a state what to do.
  • Three hundred years of pacifism — the early Church refused to fight at all; leaders condoned war once Rome turned Christian.

The Bible against war

"Blessed are the peacemakers." — Matthew 5:9. Used to argue that peacemaking, not fighting, is the Christian vocation.

"Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you." — Matthew 5:44. Used to argue that even an enemy is owed agape, which rules out killing them.

"If someone strikes you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also." — Matthew 5:39. Used to argue against retaliation of any kind.

"Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you; not as the world gives do I give to you." — John 14:27.

"Nation will not take up sword against nation, nor will they train for war any more." — Micah 4:3, foretelling the time when God's rule is established. Used to argue that God's ideal world is disarmed, so war can never be God's will. Isaiah calls the awaited Messiah the "Prince of Peace" (Isaiah 9:6–7).

Jesus' own example counts as evidence too: he was prepared to die rather than fight, and when arrested in the Garden of Gethsemane he did not resist and stopped his followers resisting. For the first three hundred years of the religion, Christians refused to fight in wars at all.

The Bible for war

"The LORD your God will drive out those nations before you… He will give their kings into your hand, and you will wipe out their names from under heaven." — Deuteronomy 7:22–24. Used to argue that God himself has commanded war.

"Proclaim this among the nations: Prepare for war! Rouse the warriors! Let all the fighting men draw near and attack. Beat your ploughshares into swords and your pruning hooks into spears. Let the weakling say, 'I am strong!'" — Joel 3:9–10. The prophets commanding the people to fight on God's behalf — and the exact inversion of Micah 4:3.

"Go now and fall on the Amalekites and destroy them, and put their property under ban. Spare no one: put them all to death, men and women, children and babes in arms, herds and flocks, camels and asses" — 1 Samuel 15:3.

"Greater love has no man than this that he lay down his life for his friends" — Jesus, in John. Used to argue that fighting to protect others is the highest form of love.

"Love your neighbour" — cuts both ways: to protect your neighbour you might need to fight for them.

✗ "Christians are against war because the Bible says so." — one unsupported assertion, no quotation, no acknowledgement of the other strand.
✓ "Most Christians oppose war, following Jesus' blessing of the peacemakers and Micah's vision of swords hammered into ploughs. However, others point to 1 Samuel 15, where God commands the destruction of the Amalekites, and argue force can be a last resort."

More detail

Most Christians think war is wrong and conflicts should be resolved peacefully, but a minority argue that as a last resort Christians may take up arms against an oppressor. The split exists because the Bible itself is divided, and an answer that quotes only one side is a half answer.

Two extra details earn credit. Jesus was occasionally prepared to use violence: he "overturned the tables of the money changers and the benches of those selling doves" in the Temple (Mark 11:15–16) — his righteous anger. And there is a long history of Christian leaders supporting governments in using force: once Christianity became a legal and then the official religion of the Roman Empire, Christian leaders were far more willing to condone warfare.

The standard move for Christians who accept war is this: Jesus' teaching on peace tells an individual how to respond to violence done to them; it does not tell a nation what to do when someone else is being made to suffer.

subsections.heading: Passive resistance and pacifism
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1, 3.2 · Lesson 3, Revision Booklet 3 p.7–8, 11

  • Pacifism defined — war and violence can never be justified, because human life is too valuable to put at risk.
  • Absolute versus conditional — absolutists rule out all violence; conditional pacifists admit extreme cases such as Hitler may leave no option.
  • The Quakers — the Religious Society of Friends, the named Christian absolutists, conscientious objectors in both World Wars.
  • Weapons of the Spirit — Quakers fight evil with truth, love and peace rather than weapons that harm and kill.
  • Gandhi and Martin Luther King — non-violence as the greatest force available to mankind, so passive resistance is power, not weakness.
  • Passive resistance in practice — strikes, boycotts, creative disorder, demonstrations and marches instead of fighting.

The Quakers' own declaration

"We utterly deny all outward wars and strife and fighting with outward weapons for any end or under any pretence whatsoever. And this is our testimony to the whole world."

— Declaration of the Society of Friends to Charles II (1661). The best evidence that pacifism is a settled Christian position and not a modern opinion.

The case for non-violence as a weapon

"Non-violence is the greatest force at the disposal of mankind. It is mightier than the mightiest weapon of destruction devised by the ingenuity of man."

— Mahatma Gandhi (1869–1948). Used to argue that passive resistance is not weakness but a different and stronger kind of power. Martin Luther King is the usual second example.

ArgumentCounter-argument
Human life is too valuable to risk; killing is always wrongSome evil can only be met with force — appeasement did not stop Hitler
Non-violent protest works: King's marches, Gandhi's campaigns, the fall of apartheidIt offers a weak response to a determined aggressor who is not watching public opinion
It keeps Christians faithful to Jesus' example and teachingIt is arguably hypocritical — refusing to fight while still benefiting from those who fight on your behalf
It breaks the cycle of violence rather than continuing itIt rules out a pre-emptive strike that might have saved lives
More detail

A pacifist believes war and violence can never be justified, because human life is so valuable that nothing can justify putting it at risk. Even fighting in self-defence is deemed wrong; there will always be another way to settle a conflict.

The word comes from the Latin pax (peace) and ficus (making). Pacifists also work to prevent war in the first place, by promoting justice and preserving religious and human rights — on the argument that denying people basic freedoms is what leads to conflict.

  • The word pacifism was coined by Emil Arnaud (1864–1921), a French peace campaigner, and adopted at the tenth Universal Peace Congress in Glasgow in 1901. The practice goes back as far as the Roman Empire — Seneca the Younger wrote against warfare.
  • A strong pacifist theme runs through Jesus' teachings, especially the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7), where he told his followers to turn the other cheek and love their enemies.
  • Pacifism also developed among Humanists: Erasmus argued strongly against war in In Praise of Folly (1509), and Rousseau, Kant and Bentham all spoke out against it, focusing on the waste of human resources. Leo Tolstoy (1828–1910) wrote The Kingdom of God is Within You, a history and defence of pacifism.
  • It was visible in the twentieth century in the conscientious objectors of both World Wars and in groups against nuclear weapons such as CND (the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament).
Kind of pacifistPosition
Absolute pacifistViolence is always wrong — human lives are too valuable, and there are better ways to resolve conflict
Conditional (or contingent) pacifistPrefers peaceful means, but recognises extreme cases — such as Hitler — may leave no option but war

The named Christian example is the Quakers — the Religious Society of Friends — who take the absolutist position. They accept there is evil in the world but deny it can be overcome by weapons that harm and kill; instead Christians should use the weapons of the Spirit — truth, love and peace. In both World Wars Quakers were conscientious objectors: refusing conscription, many served as medics, stretcher-bearers or fire-watchers, and some were imprisoned and fined.

Passive resistance is the practical form: strikes, boycotts, creative disorder, demonstrations and marches, which can be just as effective as fighting. Gandhi's claim is the standard quotation:

subsections.heading: Just War theory
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1 · Lesson 4, Revision Booklet 3 p.7

  • Just war defined — fought for the right reasons and in the right way; the theory sets when and how.
  • Augustine (354–430) — laid the roots: a right to go to war, and correct conduct during it.
  • Aquinas (1225–1274) — set the conditions: just cause, legitimate authority, right intention, last resort, strong chance of success.
  • Francisco de Vitoria (c.1483–1546) — added what happens after: the defeated nation restored so citizens resume daily life safely.
  • Three Latin headings — jus ad bellum, jus in bello, jus post bellum: going to war, fighting it, afterwards.
  • WWII is the worked example — Chamberlain declared war with Parliament's backing, to stop Hitler, after negotiation had failed.
ArgumentCounter-argument
The conditions give Christians a way to resist evil without abandoning conscienceIt is a compromise of Jesus' anti-war teaching — though others see his righteous anger in the Temple as support for it
WWII broadly met the conditions, so a just war is clearly possibleModern war can never be just: modern weaponry is devastating, unproportionate and indiscriminate
It restrains war, limiting who may be attacked and howIt is impossible to control soldiers' conduct in the heat of war
It demands care for the losers afterwards (jus post bellum)Deciding who is a bystander and who is involved is a subjective process
Without it, pacifism simply lets the aggressor winIt rules out a pre-emptive strike, and a "just" war can still lead to horrors afterwards — around a million civilians died in Iraq

Rowan Williams on modern warfare (2002)

"All violence works with that sort of distance, it depends on not seeing certain things. With the high-tech military methods we've got used to in recent years, there's a greater temptation to take for granted the view from a distance."

— the then Archbishop of Canterbury, comparing the suicide bomber and the high-tech soldier: both act from a distance at which you cannot meet someone's eyes. Used to argue that military action should now be considered "a lot further down the road" than fifty years ago — in other words, that modern weapons make last resort a much higher bar.

More detail

A just war is one fought for the right reasons and in the correct way; Just War theory defines when it is right to go to war and how that war should be fought. The spec asks for its history, so name the three authors — "some Christians say" scores nothing.

  • Augustine (354–430) laid the roots, at a time when Christianity was an official religion of a Roman Empire fighting wars across a huge territory. He set out two principles: the right to go to war and the correct conduct during war.
  • Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) developed and expanded Augustine's thought into four reasons that make it right to go to war and two principles governing conduct.
  • Francisco de Vitoria (c.1483–1546) added the principle about what should happen after a war: the defeated nation must be properly organised so its citizens can resume their daily lives in safety as quickly as possible.
  • Jus ad bellum — when it is right to go to war: a just cause; a legitimate authority; a right intention; as a last resort; with a strong chance of success.
  • Jus in bello — how the war is conducted: methods must be proportional; innocent people should not be attacked; prisoners treated fairly; weapons of mass destruction not used.
  • Jus post bellum — after the war: the losers treated humanely, and help given to get the people and the country back on their feet.
ConditionWorked example from Aquinas' conditions
Started by a legitimate or proper authorityA king or democratically elected government — Neville Chamberlain declared war on Hitler with the backing of Parliament
There must be a just causeTo right a wrong — to stop Hitler marching over Europe
There must be a good intentionMotives must be good and not selfish — the UK wanted to save Poland and rid Europe of fascism
War must be the last resortEverything must be done to avoid war — Chamberlain tried to negotiate with Hitler in the 1930s
No excessive force; proportional to the situationAvoid collateral damage and the killing of innocent civilians — the bombing of Dresden and the atomic bombs on Japan are both questioned

The theory is the outcome of many centuries of warring tribes and nations agreeing a code of behaviour to stop war becoming totally devastating to either side. Many Christians accept that as a last resort war can be justified to defeat a greater evil. Others have reservations, and the spec explicitly asks "whether Just War is possible":

subsections.heading: Holy war
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1 · Lesson 4, Revision Booklet 3 p.7–8

  • Three characteristics — a religious goal, authorised by a religious leader or God, and promising a spiritual reward.
  • The Crusades — the First Crusade (1095–1099), called by Pope Urban II to free Jerusalem, promising a plenary indulgence.
  • Old Testament episodes — the "wars of Yahweh" (Numbers 21:14), Moses and the Amalekites (Exodus 17), Jericho (Joshua 6).
  • St Bernard's defence — Jesus' peace commands applied to individuals, not to countries.
  • No holy war in the New Testament — its tone is agape, forgiveness and compassion, which is why early Christians were pacifists.
  • Most Christians reject it now — God is love, Jesus rejects violence, and the Pope has apologised for the Crusades.

Texts used to justify holy war

"Put on the whole armour of God" — used to argue that the Christian life is itself a kind of warfare.

"I did not come to bring peace but the sword." — Jesus. Used to argue that even Jesus expected conflict, not quiet.

St Bernard argued that Jesus' peace commands did not apply to countries, only to individuals — the standard move for separating personal pacifism from state violence.

More detail

A holy war is one in which religion is the driving force, and it has three defining characteristics. Learn all three — a 3-mark question on this is almost free marks.

  1. It must be fought to achieve a religious goal.
  2. It must be authorised by a religious leader or by God.
  3. It must promise a spiritual reward to those who fight in it.

The Christian example is the Crusades. The First Crusade (1095–1099) was called by Pope Urban II to free Jerusalem from Muslim control so Christian pilgrims could visit the city, including sites such as the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. Urban promised those who took part the reward of heaven, stating that anyone who died on Crusade would have their sins forgiven and go straight there — a plenary indulgence. They were known as milites Christi. All three characteristics are present, which is why this is the example to use.

The Old Testament supplies three more, and a named reference is worth more than a retelling:

  • The "wars of Yahweh" are mentioned in Numbers 21:14 — battles dedicated to God's plans for his people, in which God himself was involved.
  • Exodus 17:8–16 — the Amalekites attack the Israelites escaping Egypt. Moses holds the rod of God aloft on the hilltop, and while it is raised the Israelites have the upper hand; Aaron and Hur help him hold it up to secure victory, which is then dedicated to God.
  • Joshua 6 — the destruction of Jericho, the first target after crossing the Jordan into the promised land. The Israelites marched in silence around the city with the priests carrying the Ark of the Covenant, blew shofars, shouted at Joshua's signal so the walls collapsed, then killed all the inhabitants and dedicated the treasures to God.

Can war ever be holy? The Bible is ambiguous: those three Old Testament episodes against a New Testament with no tradition of holy war at all, whose tone is agape, forgiveness and compassion — which is why most early Christians were absolute pacifists. Holy war only began to be taught in the eleventh century, with the First Crusade, and by the end of the thirteenth century the idea had become less popular, as people came to think the Crusades were fought to gain territory and increase papal power.

Today most Christians reject it: God is love, Jesus rejects violence, and the Pope has apologised for the Crusades. Many would accept a war fought to defend people's rights, but regard a war fought for God as incompatible with a loving, compassionate and forgiving God. Some suggest the only acceptable holy war is one against injustice and evil.

subsections.heading: Weapons of mass destruction
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1 · Lesson 5, Revision Booklet 3 p.8–9

  • WMD defined — nuclear, chemical and biological weapons, able to inflict death and damage on a huge scale.
  • Nuclear facts — Hiroshima, 6 August 1945, killed 84,000; Nagasaki 40,000 more; nine states held about 15,700 warheads by 2015.
  • Banned by treaty — the Chemical Weapons Convention (1993), and the Biological Weapons Convention signed by 180 states.
  • Christians object — WMD deliberately target innocents, against the sanctity of life and the Christian duty of stewardship.
  • Deterrence is the exception — some Christians permit possession without use, which is why Christian countries keep arsenals.
  • Testing has its own ethics — Porton Down gave volunteers sarin in the 1950s; anthrax was released into the Northern Line in 1963–64.
ArgumentCounter-argument
Nuclear weapons may ironically prevent warfare: mutually assured destruction means they will never actually be usedThey threaten the world with extinction
Chemical and biological weapons target living beings while leaving infrastructure intact, and are cheaper than nuclear weaponsThey may have unforeseen effects — containing a chemical or biological release is very difficult
Possessing them deters attack, which is why so many states built themThey target indiscriminately — their whole purpose is huge destruction

The three statements worth quoting

"Though the monstrous power of these weapons act as a deterrent, it is to be feared that the mere continuance of nuclear tests undertaken with war in mind, will have fatal consequences for life on earth. Justice, right reason and humanity therefore, urgently demand that the arms race should cease; that the stockpiles that exist in various countries should be reduced equally… nuclear weapons should be banned."

— Pacem in Terris, the Roman Catholic Church.

"In nuclear war there would be no victors, only victims." — Pope Benedict XVI.

"The church has consistently considered any use or possession of nuclear weapons to be outside of what could ever be considered a just use of arms." — Stephen Cottrell, Archbishop of York, 2020. Note that he rules out possession as well as use, which is the sharper claim.

The two sides of research ethics

"It is not cruel to inflict on a few criminals sufferings which may benefit multitudes of innocent people throughout the centuries."

— Celsus, first century AD. Used to argue the utilitarian case for testing.

"The principle of medical and surgical morality consists in never performing on man an experiment which might be harmful to him to any extent, even though the result might be highly advantageous to science, i.e. the health of others."

— Claude Bernard (1813–1878). Used to argue that subjects must give informed consent and that risk must be minimal.

More detail

Weapons of mass destruction are nuclear, chemical and biological weapons, which have the capacity to inflict death and damage on a huge scale. Know one hard fact about each.

TypeWhat it isFacts that earn development marks
NuclearAtomic and thermonuclear bombs, developed towards the end of WWIIHiroshima, 6 August 1945 — 84,000 killed; Nagasaki three days later — 40,000 more. The hydrogen bomb is 1,000 times more powerful. The neutron bomb (1970s) uses radiation to kill people without harming buildings. By 2015 nine nations held about 15,700 warheads.
ChemicalToxic agents causing death or injury when inhaled, absorbed through the skin, or ingestedChoking agents (chlorine gas), blister agents (mustard gas), blood agents (hydrogen cyanide) and nerve agents (sarin, the most lethal). First used in modern warfare in WWI — over a million casualties, about 90,000 deaths. Banned by the Chemical Weapons Convention (1993), but believed used by Iraq against Iran and by the Syrian government.
BiologicalBacteria, viruses and fungi released to cause illness and deathIndiscriminate, capable of starting pandemics, and terrifying — even though they do not damage buildings. The Biological Weapons Convention was signed by 180 states.

Benefits and problems — the spec wants both:

Christian attitudes. The criteria for a just war or holy war make WMD very hard to justify: Christians are forbidden from killing innocents or vulnerable populations not involved in the war, and WMD deliberately target exactly those groups — the old, the young and women. Christians also appeal to the sanctity of life and to their role as stewards and custodians of God's creation — "the earth is the Lord's". Most therefore oppose their use and many favour working towards nuclear disarmament.

But some Christians think holding WMD as a deterrent while not necessarily using them is permissible, which is why many predominantly Christian countries hold nuclear arsenals.

Non-religious attitudes. Humanists would not support their use — human life is far too valuable — though some take a pragmatic line that in a world where nuclear weapons exist it is necessary to have them to deter an attack. Atheists are divided: some oppose them absolutely, and because they believe in no afterlife they think preserving this life and this planet matters even more; others argue WMD are a necessary means of self-defence, invoking Utilitarianism — an arsenal unlikely ever to be used extends the greatest happiness to the greatest number, because the fear of mutually assured destruction ironically keeps the peace. Situation Ethics may say "sometimes" — whichever course is most loving.

Testing WMD raises its own ethics. Nuclear tests have been atmospheric, underwater, exoatmospheric and underground; many countries signed the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty (1996), though India and Pakistan did not, and North Korea is the only country currently testing. Chemical and biological testing has used human subjects: Porton Down exposed volunteers to nerve agents including sarin in the 1950s; terminally ill patients were injected with Uranium 235 in the 1960s; a US navy ship sprayed microbes over San Francisco in 1950; anthrax spores were released into the Northern Line tunnels in 1963–64.

subsections.heading: Terrorism
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1 · Lesson 6, Revision Booklet 3 p.9–10

  • The UN definition — acts aiming to kill or seriously harm civilians, to intimidate a population or coerce a government.
  • Aims and forms — publicity, fear and intimidating authorities, through suicide bombings, car bombs, gun, knife and vehicle attacks.
  • The IRA and the Brighton bombing — Patrick Magee bombed The Grand Hotel in 1984 to kill Thatcher; five died, 31 injured.
  • The Army of God — an American Christian terrorist group formed in 1982, linked to abortion clinic bombings, arson and murder.
  • Freedom fighter or terrorist — Camilo Torres and Nelson Mandela show the label depends on who judges the cause.
  • Most Christians reject it — a campaign of terror cannot comply with biblical teaching on love, justice, peace and compassion.
ArgumentCounter-argument
It goes against Jesus' peace commands — "love your enemies"Some causes could be just: Nelson Mandela was branded a terrorist in his fight against apartheid
Just War reasoning rules it out — it can never meet the conditions of legitimate authority or no excessive forceUtilitarianism might permit it in very limited circumstances
Natural Law demands an ordered society, which terrorism destroysWhere a population has no vote, publicity may be the only leverage available
St Paul teaches Christians to obey their governments — "let everyone obey the ruling authorities"Obedience to an unjust government was exactly what oppressed groups were resisting
It can never be loving, and it breaches people's human rights—
Non-violent protest works — Martin Luther King; democratic means are sufficient to right wrongs—
More detail

The United Nations defines terrorism as any act which aims to cause death or serious harm to civilians, with the purpose of intimidating a group of people or a population, or compelling a government to abstain from or perform specific actions. The shorter definition is the illegal use of violence to further a cause. Saying "the UN defines it as" is worth doing — it shows the definition is not your own guess.

  • Forms: suicide bombings, car bombs, gun and knife attacks, and using vehicles as weapons.
  • Aims: to use acts of atrocity to gain publicity, cause fear and intimidate authorities into yielding to demands.

The named case study is the IRA and the Brighton bombing. The Irish Republican Army was established in Northern Ireland to protect the Catholic community; towards the end of the 1960s a breakaway group, the Provisional IRA, decided physical force was necessary. It ran a bombing campaign in Northern Ireland, clashing with the British Army and the Royal Ulster Constabulary, aiming to cause so much damage that British forces would withdraw. The campaign crossed the Irish Sea: about a month before the 1984 Conservative Conference, Patrick Magee planted a bomb in The Grand Hotel, Brighton, timed for the last night of the conference with the explicit aim of assassinating Margaret Thatcher. She survived; five people were killed and at least 31 injured.

Christians have been on both sides. The Army of God, an American Christian terrorist organisation formed in 1982 and committed to reducing abortions in America, has committed kidnap, attempted murder and murder, and has been associated with abortion clinic bombings and arsons; some Christians supported the aims and actions of the IRA. Some members of civil rights groups fighting social injustice have also used violence — regarding themselves as freedom fighters while their opponents called them terrorists, as with Camilo Torres. But the majority of Christians think terrorism cannot be justified morally — trying to force people to change their mindset or behaviour through a campaign of terror does not comply with the biblical teachings of love, justice, peace and compassion.

subsections.heading: Peace, reconciliation and forgiveness
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2 · Lesson 7, Revision Booklet 3 p.11–13

  • Peace defined — more than the absence of war: being in harmony with oneself and with others.
  • Three distinct ideas — justice is fairness, forgiveness is letting go of a grudge, reconciliation is restored friendly relations.
  • Gee Walker and Rev Julie Nicholson — one forgave her son's murderers; the other refused unrepentant 7/7 killers. Use the pair.
  • The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (1996) — Desmond Tutu's restorative justice body, which reconciled South Africa after apartheid.
  • Corrymeela — Ray Davey's inter-denominational centre at Ballycastle (1965), where Protestants and Catholics meet, share chores and face prejudice.
  • The United Nations (1945) — prevents conflict, helps parties make peace, deploys peacekeepers, and builds conditions for peace to hold.

The Prince of Peace

"For to us a child is born, to us a son is given… And he will be called Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. Of the greatness of his government and peace, there will be no end."

— Isaiah 9:6–7. Used to argue that peace is not incidental to the Messiah's work but his title.

The early Christian writers took the same line. Origen (185–254 AD) wrote that Christians had come "in accordance with the counsels of Jesus to cut down our warlike and arrogant swords of argument into ploughshares", having "become sons of peace for the sake of Jesus".

The forgiveness quotation to learn word-perfect

"Peter came to Jesus and asked, 'Lord, how many times shall I forgive my brother when he sins against me? Up to seven times?' Jesus answered, 'I tell you, not seven times, but seventy-seven times.'"

— Matthew 18:21–22. Used to argue that Christian forgiveness has no limit, which is why most Christians favour reform over revenge.

"It is mine to avenge; I will repay," says the Lord. — Romans 12:19. Used the other way: vengeance belongs to God, not to us.

Tutu on what reconciliation actually costs

"Forgiving and being reconciled to our enemies or our loved ones are not about pretending that things are other than they are… True reconciliation exposes the awfulness, the abuse, the hurt, the truth. It could even sometimes make things worse. It is a risky undertaking but in the end it is worthwhile, because in the end only an honest confrontation with reality can bring real healing."

— Archbishop Desmond Tutu. The best answer to "forgiveness is weakness": it is described here as risky and painful, not easy.

ArgumentCounter-argument
Jesus set no limit on forgiveness — "not seven times, but seventy-seven times" (Matthew 18:21–22) — and the Lord's Prayer makes being forgiven conditional on forgivingJesus also taught that forgiveness follows repentance — metanoia — so forgiving the unrepentant, as Rev Julie Nicholson argued, is empty
Christians have a duty to reconcile because of Jesus' example — his death on the cross reconciled humanity to God — and "First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift"Justice is a teaching too: "let justice roll on like a river" (Amos 5:24). Forgiving an offender can leave the victim without the fairness that peace actually requires
God is merciful and compassionate, and Christians who expect forgiveness on Judgement Day must forgive those who harm them — the parable of the unforgiving servant"It is mine to avenge; I will repay," says the Lord (Romans 12:19) — vengeance belongs to God, so the victim is not the one obliged to settle it
It works: the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (1996) used restorative justice to reconcile a divided South Africa and enable a free democracyTutu himself calls reconciliation "a risky undertaking" that "could even sometimes make things worse" — so it is not always the right course
Gee Walker forgave her son's murderers because she believed it was Jesus' command and willForgiveness with no consequence can look like condoning the crime, which is why most Christians want punishment alongside it rather than instead of it

✗ "Christians work for peace, for example a charity." — unnamed, so unmarkable.
✓ "Corrymeela, based in Ballycastle, runs residentials and school workshops to break down barriers between Protestants and Catholics." — named organisation, named place, named activity.

More detail

Peace is more than the absence of war or violence: it means being in harmony with oneself and others — say that, because the definition mark is for the second half. Christians treat peacemaking as a duty rather than a preference.

In the Old Testament the Jewish prophets look forward to the messianic era, a time of peace in which the Jews enjoy their full covenantal relationship with God and other nations follow their example. In the New Testament Jesus blesses the peacemakers in the Sermon on the Mount, discourages answering violence with violence, and tells his listeners to love their neighbour.

The spec asks for justice, forgiveness and reconciliation as three separate ideas. Keep them distinct:

IdeaWhat it meansTeaching
JusticeFairness — people getting what they deserve. Essential for peace, because it prevents resentment and civil unrest"But let justice roll on like a river, righteousness like a never-failing stream!" (Amos 5:24)
ForgivenessLetting go of a grudge, or absolving a wrong done to you. Christians believe that because God is merciful and compassionate they must show mercy too — and that if they expect God to forgive them on Judgement Day, they should forgive those who harm themMatthew 18:21–22 — forgive "not seven times, but seventy-seven times"; the Lord's Prayer, "Forgive us as we forgive…"; the Prodigal Son, whose God-like father forgives the son's rebellion
ReconciliationThe restoration of friendly relations. Christians feel a duty to reconcile people because of Jesus' example — his death on the cross reconciled humanity to God"First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift"; "Strive for peace with everyone" (Hebrews 12:14); "I give you a new commandment, that you love one another" (John 13:34–35)

St Paul regarded the ability to love as the greatest of all spiritual gifts: "Love is patient; love is kind; love is not envious or boastful or arrogant or rude… It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things" (1 Corinthians 13:1–7).

Real examples, which the examiner rewards heavily.

  • Gee Walker forgave her son's murderers; as a Christian she felt it was Jesus' command and will.
  • Rev Julie Nicholson refused to forgive the terrorists who killed her daughter in the 7/7 bombings — the guilty party had not repented, so she saw no point. A perfect counter-example for a 12-marker.
  • Desmond Tutu chaired the South African Truth and Reconciliation Commission in 1996, to deal with what had happened under apartheid (abolished in 1994). Witnesses identified as victims of gross human rights violations were invited to give statements about their experiences; perpetrators of violence could also testify and request amnesty from civil and criminal prosecution. By providing restorative justice it reconciled a divided community and helped the transition to a full and free democracy.

At a global level, the Roman Catholic Church — based in the independent state of the Vatican City — is a member of the United Nations in a non-voting capacity, with a permanent representative who can address the assembly. Other denominations are represented by the World Council of Churches, established in 1948 to seek unity, common witness and Christian service, and to bring about reconciliation in the world.

The one Christian organisation working for peace: Corrymeela. Founded by Ray Davey in 1965 and based at Ballycastle in county Antrim, Northern Ireland, which is divided along Protestant and Catholic lines. Its work is inter-denominational: Davey thought the buildings at Ballycastle could be a meeting place for people of any religious persuasion so all could be involved in the peace process. Visitors stay from two days to a week, share the domestic chores, are encouraged to mix, and join discussion groups that aim to challenge prejudices.

Its three stated aims are worth learning as a list:

  1. To be a sign that Protestants and Catholics can share in a common witness and ministry of reconciliation.
  2. To provide opportunities for meeting, dialogue and learning that dispel ignorance, prejudice and fear, and promote mutual respect, trust and co-operation.
  3. To support victims of violence and injustice, enable the healing of personal and social wounds, and promote new initiatives for social and political change.

Much of its work is in schools and youth groups, including workshops on conflict resolution and an international peace conference. Why? Because Jesus is the Prince of Peace, and because it puts the Bible's teaching on forgiveness into action. Davey said people are reminded as they leave Ballycastle that "Corrymeela begins when you leave" — the point being that the change has to happen back in their own community.

The United Nations was created in 1945, after the Second World War, with the central aim of maintaining international peace and security. It does this by working to prevent conflict, helping parties in conflict make peace, deploying peacekeepers, and creating the conditions for peace to hold and flourish — four points, so a 4-mark question on the UN's role is straightforward.

  • The Security Council has primary responsibility. It determines whether there is a threat to peace or an act of aggression, can call on parties to settle disputes peacefully, can help draw up the terms of a settlement, and can enforce measures including economic sanctions and military action.
  • The General Assembly plays a complementary role, giving member states a forum and making recommendations to the Security Council in the form of resolutions.
  • Ukraine, 2022 — a usable example. The UN mobilised agencies for humanitarian relief, particularly for those fleeing. On 2 March 2022 the General Assembly held a special session and approved a resolution deploring Russia's actions by 141 votes to 5, prompting Secretary-General António Guterres to say: "End hostilities in Ukraine now. Silence the guns now. Open the door to dialogue and diplomacy now."
  • Peacekeeping examples: policing the "green line" in Cyprus between the Turkish north and Greek south; and peacekeeping in South Sudan, monitoring human rights abuses, delivering aid and enforcing the law where necessary.

The 12-marker here is almost always a form of "Christians should always forgive", so the two columns are worth memorising:

subsections.heading: Bullying
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3 · Lesson 8, Revision Booklet 3 p.14

  • Three defining features — intentional harm, unequal power between the parties, and repeated over a period of time.
  • Five types — physical, verbal, social, psychological and cyber; the spec names cyberbullying, so define it rather than list it.
  • Why it happens — the bully's craving for power or lack of empathy, a society venerating strength, and the need to belong.
  • No direct biblical teaching — Christians argue from God's image (Genesis 1:26–27), agape, the Good Samaritan and the Golden Rule.
  • Communication is the strongest solution — bullies rely on secrecy, so witnesses must be upstanders rather than bystanders.
  • The wider harm — damage to mental health and self-esteem, and unchallenged it creates a culture nobody feels able to stop.
  • Inclusion is the positive form of the same teaching — the body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12), Galatians 3:28, and Jesus eating with outcasts.
Argument — it can be stoppedCounter-argument — it cannot
Communication breaks it, because bullies rely on secrecy: the victim needs someone to talk to, and witnesses can be encouraged to be an upstander rather than a bystanderThe causes are in human nature — the bully enjoys the feeling of power and lacks empathy — and Christians would add that because of sin every person has the potential to harm another
Education works: teaching children to be open to difference and nurturing empathy and compassion, with campaigns such as the ABC campaigns in schoolsA society that venerates strength and assertiveness keeps endorsing the behaviour, whatever an individual school teaches
Christian teaching gives a reason to stop: everyone is made in God's image (Genesis 1:26–27), the Golden Rule is the test a bully fails, and "repay no one evil for evil" stops the cycle continuingCyberbullying is anonymous and constant, so supervision, a word with a teacher and zero-tolerance policies reach far less of it
Zero tolerance in schools, workplaces and churches, therapy for bullies and positive role models change what a community treats as acceptableThe need to belong keeps witnesses silent rather than speaking out, so the secrecy bullying depends on is easy to maintain
Christians join campaigns against bullying as part of their stewardship, and pray — the sheep and goats make indifference to a victim indifference to ChristHuman rights law and decades of anti-bullying policy have not removed it, which suggests it can be reduced but not ended
More detail

Bullying has three defining characteristics: it is intentional, with the aim of causing harm or distress; it occurs between two parties who have different degrees of power; and it happens repeatedly over a period of time. All three are needed — a single argument between equals is not bullying.

Type of bullyingWhat it involves
PhysicalThe victim is physically assaulted, or their property is damaged
VerbalLanguage is used to tease or taunt the victim
SocialThe victim is excluded from group activities or publicly embarrassed
PsychologicalPurposeful mental abuse aimed at undermining the victim's self-confidence
CyberHarassment by electronic means — sending, posting or sharing negative, harmful, false or mean content, or sharing private information to cause embarrassment or humiliation

The spec names cyberbullying explicitly, so define it rather than just listing it.

  • Why it happens — the nature of the bully: they enjoy the feeling of power; it makes them feel strong; it compensates for feelings of inadequacy; or they lack the empathy that would prevent it.
  • Why it happens — the environment: a society that venerates strength and assertiveness can endorse bullying behaviour.
  • Why it happens — the need to belong: fear of social rejection can drive bullying, or an unwillingness to speak out against it.

The Bible does not refer directly to bullying, so Christians argue from general teachings — say that explicitly, because it shows understanding rather than invention:

SourceTeachingWhat it is used to argue
Genesis 1:26–27"God created humans in his own image"; humans are God's stewardsEveryone deserves respect and equal treatment, so bullying attacks something God made
Jesus — agape"Love your neighbour" (Mark 12:31), the Golden Rule, and the parable of the Good SamaritanCare is owed even to the stranger, let alone the classmate — and the Samaritan helps rather than relishing another's misfortune
Jesus — the sheep and goatsCaring for those in need is caring for Christ himselfTurns indifference to a victim into indifference to God
Jesus — the Beatitudes"Blessed are the meek"Jesus overturned the world's values: weakness is not contemptible
St Paul"Repay no one evil for evil"Victims should not retaliate; the cycle has to stop somewhere
Ephesians 4:29 and Psalm 139:23–24Honour God with your words; assess your words and behaviour against God's expectationsJudgement — Christians are accountable for how they speak, which should make them think twice
The Golden RuleTreat others as you wish to be treatedThe simplest test a bully fails

Solutions. The strongest single point is communication, because bullies rely on secrecy: the victim needs someone to talk to, whether known to them or reached through a charity, and witnesses should be encouraged to speak out — to be an upstander rather than a bystander. Then: education, teaching children to be open to difference and nurturing empathy and compassion; positive role models; therapy for bullies; zero tolerance in workplaces and churches; campaigns such as the ABC campaigns in schools; and prayer. Christians may join campaigns against bullying in schools and workplaces as part of their stewardship.

The 12-marker here is usually a form of "bullying can never be stopped", and the Christian teaching sits on both sides:

Non-religious objections: bullying does not lead to happiness, it is a form of violence, and it is against human rights. Note the wider harm as well — bullying damages mental health, self-esteem and social relationships, and if it is not challenged it creates a culture in which it is tolerated and everyone feels powerless to stop it.

Inclusion. The spec asks about inclusion as well as bullying, and it is simply the same teaching stated positively — so learn it as teachings, because the question comes as "outline two teachings about why inclusion is important". (1) Everyone is made in God's image (Genesis 1:26–27), so excluding anyone denies the worth God gave them. (2) Galatians 3:28 — "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus" — removes every ground on which people are usually sorted. (3) 1 Corinthians 12:12–27 makes the Church a body whose parts need each other: "the body is one and has many members", and the weaker parts are treated with greater honour — so a community is incomplete when anyone is left out. (4) Agape and the Golden Rule both require treating the excluded person as you would want to be treated. (5) Jesus' own practice is the strongest example: he ate with tax collectors and sinners, touched lepers and talked with the Samaritan woman, each time including the person his society had pushed out — which is also the model behind Jean Vanier's L'Arche communities. The non-religious case reaches the same place by a different route: inclusion follows from human rights and equality before the law, and an inclusive society is more stable and makes better use of everyone's abilities.

subsections.heading: Sin and crime
subsections.html:
Spec 3.4 · Lesson 9, Revision Booklet 3 p.16–17

  • Sin versus crime — a sin offends God; a crime is an illegal act punishable by law. Not every sin is a crime.
  • Hamartia — the Greek for sin, meaning to "miss the mark": humanity turned away and failed God's goals.
  • Original Sin and the Fall — Adam and Eve's disobedience banished them from Eden and separated humanity from God's grace.
  • The Catholic three — original sin; mortal sin, which loses the state of grace; venial sin, which rusts the soul.
  • Causes of crime — poverty, socialisation, prejudice, low self-esteem, drugs and politics; Christians add sin itself.
  • Street Pastors and Prison Fellowship — Les Isaac's 2003 street patrols, and 3,000 volunteers visiting prisoners because no one is beyond hope.

The consequences of sin

"But the cowardly, the unbelieving, the vile, the murderers, the sexually immoral, those who practice magic arts, the idolaters and all liars — they will be consigned to the fiery lake of burning sulphur. This is the second death."

— Revelation 21:8, describing what awaits sinners who have failed to repent. Used to argue that sin has eternal, not merely legal, consequences — the point of a 6-marker on "the consequences of sin". The phrase "the second death" is worth including.

More detail

A sin is an offence against God; a crime is an illegal act punishable by the law — so not all sins are crimes, but Christians would argue all crime has its source in sin. The Greek word for sin, hamartia, means to "miss the mark": God expected humanity to obey him in order to be in a relationship with him, and by turning away and becoming self-centred humanity has not fulfilled God's goals.

The Original Sin was committed by Adam and Eve, who gave in to the serpent's temptation and disobeyed God's command not to eat the fruit from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. They were banished from Eden and separated from God — the Fall, the Fall from God's grace (undeserved love). Christians believe all humanity is affected: for some it is a spiritual inheritance each person is born with; for others the story describes the universal human condition — however good our intentions, we are easily influenced into doing wrong.

Point of differenceSinCrime
SourceDetermined by GodIdentified by the government
EffectA violation of God's willBreaks the law
ConsequencesPunishment occurs after deathPunishment occurs in this life

Types of sin. Roman Catholics distinguish three.

  • Original Sin — the initial nature of people. All human beings begin life separated from God because of the actions of Adam and Eve, but can still be reconciled to him through the sacrament of baptism.
  • Mortal sin — grave immoral acts which imperil the soul; violations of the Ten Commandments are the examples, such as murder. All mortal sins result in the loss of the state of grace, and while outside it a Roman Catholic cannot fully participate in church activities.
  • Venial sin — minor infractions of God's commandments, such as lying. Less severe, but if ignored they weaken a person's inner moral strength and make greater sins more likely — they are said to rust the soul.

Protestants instead distinguish sins of commission — doing what one has been commanded not to do, such as violence — from sins of omission, failing to do what one should, such as not giving aid to those in need. Jesus said only blasphemy against the Holy Spirit cannot be forgiven.

Sins can be forgiven. Roman Catholics believe the effects of sin are erased through the sacrament of penance and reconciliation: by confessing to a priest, wholly desiring a return to God's grace and accepting an earthly punishment, the individual is reconciled to God.

Types of crime, with their usual seriousness: crimes against persons (GBH, violence, murder — life imprisonment); crimes against property (theft, arson — imprisonment); hate crimes (prejudice, racism); crimes against morality; white-collar crime (fraud and financial crime); and organised crime (people trafficking, county-lines drug gangs, prostitution rings — long sentences).

Why crime happens — the spec lists these, so a 4-marker wants two of them developed:

  • Poverty — need: many people convicted of shoplifting food were stealing to feed themselves or their family, and a lack of job opportunities or unrealised aspirations can lead to crime.
  • Socialisation — upbringing and family background: poor parenting or a troubled family life makes it harder to conform to society's expectations.
  • Prejudice — discrimination against particular social or racial groups reinforces negative perceptions, forcing people into isolation and possibly crime.
  • Low self-esteem — those who do not value themselves are more likely to have a low opinion of others too.
  • Drugs — a great deal of acquisitive crime is committed by heroin or crack cocaine users to pay for their drugs.
  • Politics, and, Christians would add, sin: because sin is part of human nature, all people have the potential to commit a crime.

Christian responses to crime — the spec names two organisations, so learn both:

  • Street Pastors. Pioneered in London in 2003 by Les Isaac. It sets up city projects in partnership with the local police and council, and trains volunteers to make the streets safer, offering reassurance, safety and support through caring, listening and helping — water for the drunk and distressed, a way home. It began in the night-time economy and now works in the daytime too, in parks, schools and colleges. It is ecumenical, with many different churches involved, and a group will spend the night praying for the town.
  • Prison Fellowship. Its mission is to show Christ's love to people in prison by visiting and supporting them, using prayer and practical help such as literacy teaching and someone to confide in. It has a network of over 3,000 volunteers working in almost all the prisons in England and Wales, and supports prisoners' families too. It works with people of all faiths or none, treating every person with respect and dignity, believing no one is beyond hope and every life can be transformed.

More broadly, Christians try to address the causes of crime: support groups for parenting and addiction, protest against social injustice, charities and food banks, and targeting the times and places where crime is most likely.

subsections.heading: Punishment — its aims, and why Christians disagree about them
subsections.html:
Spec 3.5 · Lesson 10, Revision Booklet 3 p.18–19

  • Punishment defined — the penalty inflicted for breaking the law; its main aim is to vindicate the law itself.
  • Five aims — protection, deterrence, retribution, reform and reparation. Learn the names and one line on each.
  • No official Christian opinion — neither Catholic nor Protestant churches have one, so all argue from biblical justice and forgiveness.
  • Most Christians prioritise reform — every offender is made in God's image, so rehabilitation matters more than payback.
  • Restorative justice — victim and offender meet, so the victim regains control and the offender sees the harm done.
  • A minority want harshness — reading the Old Testament retribution strand as avenging the crime and deterring reoffending.

Justice: the retributive strand

"Anyone who injures their neighbour is to be injured in the same manner: fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth. The one who has inflicted the injury must suffer the same injury."

— Leviticus 24:19–20. The classic retribution text.

"The one who sins is the one who will die. The child will not share the guilt of the parent, nor will the parent share the guilt of the child."

— Ezekiel 18:20, showing God's justice is fair and individual: nobody is punished for someone else's wrong. Also Genesis 3, where Adam and Eve are cast out of Eden in punishment for disobeying God.

Because God's justice is real, Christians believe they must monitor their own behaviour — the text the spec names for this is Galatians 6:1–5: "Brothers and sisters, if someone is caught in a sin, you who live by the Spirit should restore that person gently. But watch yourselves, or you also may be tempted. Carry each other's burdens, and in this way you will fulfil the law of Christ." Note that even this justice text says restore gently — which is why it is often used for reform rather than retribution.

Forgiveness: the reforming strand

"You have heard that it was said, 'Eye for eye, and tooth for tooth.' But I tell you, do not resist an evil person. If anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to them the other cheek also."

— Matthew 5:38–39. Jesus rewrites the Old Testament retribution law, quoting Leviticus 24 in order to overturn it.

He put it into practice in John 8:1–11, confronted by a crowd holding a woman charged with adultery, for which the sentence was death: he answered that whichever of them was without sin should cast the first stone, nobody would, and the woman was released with the instruction to sin no more.

Also: "Do not repay anyone evil for evil… Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good" (Romans 12:17ff), used to support reformation over retribution; the parable of the Prodigal Son, confirming God's willingness to forgive the truly penitent; and the parable of the unforgiving servant, warning that Christians must show mercy if they wish God to forgive them. Jesus taught that to be forgiven a person must repent — the word is metanoia, meaning a complete turnaround. It is an active word: the sinner has to do something that moves them away from the sin and towards a more God-like life.

Argument — reformCounter-argument — retribution and the other aims
Jesus rejected retribution — "Eye for eye, and tooth for tooth. But I tell you, do not resist an evil person" (Matthew 5:38–39) — and stopped an execution in John 8:1–11The Old Testament demands payback — "fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth" (Leviticus 24:19–20) — and a minority of Christians still follow that strand
Forgiveness requires metanoia, a complete turnaround, which is exactly what reform aims at; the Prodigal Son shows God forgives the truly penitentGod is the source of justice, and Christians as his stewards have a duty to keep society just — which means punishment must vindicate the law so everyone obeys it
Every offender is made in God's image and can be redeemed: the Salvation Army holds that Christ can transform lives, Prison Fellowship that no one is beyond hopeProtection comes first with a dangerous criminal, and reparation matters to the victim — neither is served by a punishment aimed only at the offender's future
Restorative justice brings victim and offender together, so the victim regains a sense of control and the offender understands the effects of their behaviourDeterrence requires punishment unpleasant enough to put others off, and soft prisons such as Bastoy in Norway arguably do not deter at all
Reform is the only aim that cuts reoffending, so it serves society as well as the criminalThere is no official Christian opinion on punishment, so a Christian may legitimately put retribution, deterrence or protection first — and Galatians 6:1–5 still says "watch yourselves" as well as "restore that person gently"

✗ "Christians think criminals should be forgiven." — ignores the justice strand, so it cannot reach the top level.
