✓ "Most Christians prioritise reform, following Jesus' rejection of retribution in Matthew 5 and the forgiveness shown in the Prodigal Son. However, some emphasise retribution, citing Leviticus 24, and argue justice requires payback."

More detail

Punishment is the penalty inflicted on a person for breaking the law, and it has five standard aims. Learn the five names and a one-line gloss for each; most of this spec area is built on them.

AimWhat it is forStrength and weakness
ProtectionTo protect society from a dangerous criminal and from reoffendingWorks while they are inside; does nothing about why they offended
DeterrenceTo deter other people from committing the same crimeOnly works if offenders expect to be caught
RetributionA fair and just payback for the crime — the "eye for an eye" ideaSatisfies the victim; risks becoming revenge
ReformTo change the criminal so they are less likely to reoffend — teaching a skill in prison, therapy, soft prisons such as Bastoy in NorwayCuts reoffending; can look soft on serious crime
ReparationTo pay society back for the crimeRepairs some damage; impossible for violent crime

Types of punishment: imprisonment, a suspended sentence, community service, probation, a fine, a compensation order, a restitution order, a hospital order, and in some countries death. The main aim is to vindicate or justify the law, thereby ensuring everyone obeys it — the other five aims sit underneath that.

Context the examiner likes: the European Convention on Human Rights gives the accused the right to a fair trial — carried out publicly, in an unbiased court, with an opportunity to defend oneself — and in the UK a person is considered innocent until proven guilty. A judge and jury weigh the evidence, and the sentence varies with the severity of the crime.

There is no official Christian opinion on punishment, but the Bible supplies two general principles — justice and forgiveness — and they pull in opposite directions.

So Christian attitudes split. Note first that neither the Roman Catholic Church nor the Protestant denominations have an official opinion on the general issues surrounding punishment — all Christians look to the Bible for principles. Upholding the law matters to all of them: God is the source of justice, and Christians as God's stewards have a duty to keep society just, which gives a smooth-running society and boundaries that keep people in check. But care must be taken that punishment is fair and that mitigating circumstances are considered.

For most Christians the main aim should be to reform the criminal so they can be rehabilitated. Many therefore prefer restorative justice, in which the criminal and the victim meet so each gains insight into the other's feelings and behaviour: the victim may regain a sense of control, and the offender may understand the effects of their behaviour, which helps them reform. A minority, focusing on the Old Testament, think punishment should be harsh, avenging the crime and making the offender think twice about reoffending.

"Reform should be the main aim of punishment" is the standard 12-marker, so have both columns ready:

subsections.heading: Capital punishment
subsections.html:
Spec 3.6 · Lesson 11, Revision Booklet 3 p.20–21

  • Capital punishment defined — taking a criminal's life; its aims are protection, deterrence and retribution for the victim's family.
  • The UK dates — last hangings 1964; abolished for murder in Great Britain 1965 and Northern Ireland 1973; completely in 1998.
  • Christian support — Article 37 of the Thirty-Nine Articles (1563), Aquinas, and the Council of Trent (1566); Genesis 9:6.
  • Christian opposition — the General Synod deplored reintroduction in July 1983, citing the sanctity of life and Jesus stopping an execution.
  • Popes against it — John Paul II's Evangelium Vitae (1995) allowed absolute necessity only; Francis' Fratelli Tutti (2020) called it inadmissible.
  • Humanists, 1989 — called for worldwide abolition because it denies the right to life in the Universal Declaration.
ArgumentCounter-argument
It is the ultimate retribution for the most serious crimes, and entails a natural justice — a life for a lifeIt is contradictory: taking a life because murder has been committed undermines the value of life too
It protects law-abiding citizens and prevents reoffendingMiscarriages of justice occur, and an execution cannot be reversed
It is a strong deterrentIt does not deter people from murder
It may give some comfort or closure to the victim's familyThe time between sentencing and execution is costly
Some crimes are so heinous the offender must be beyond reform — death is the only fitting responseIn the US it is effectively racist: it is poor Latino and Black defendants who face death. It also brutalises society and feeds a cycle of violence, and humans are never fully responsible for their actions

The text used to support the death penalty

"Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed; for in the image of God has God made man"

— Genesis 9:6. Used to argue that the taking of a life demands a life, precisely because humans bear God's image.

The text used against it

"If any one of you is without sin, let him be the first to throw a stone at her."

— John 8:1–11, where Jesus stops the stoning of a woman caught in adultery. Used to argue that Jesus halted an execution, because no sinful human is fit to judge.

More detail

Capital punishment, or the death penalty, involves taking the life of a criminal; its aims are to protect society, to deter people from committing the same crime, and, as retribution, to compensate the victim and the victim's family. A crime punishable by death is a capital offence.

The UK dates are worth getting right, because a vague "it was banned a while ago" throws away an easy mark. The last executions, by hanging, took place in 1964. Capital punishment for murder was abolished in Great Britain in 1965 and in Northern Ireland in 1973. It remained on the books for certain crimes such as treason until it was completely abolished in 1998.

Two further points from the booklet are worth having. Since abolition in the UK, many people have been pardoned and released years after the crime they allegedly committed — had the death penalty still been legal they would already be dead. And in the US there have been botched executions, where the drugs were not administered correctly and the prisoner suffered in agony before dying, alongside hundreds of convicts on Death Row for years, which is severe for the prisoner and their family and enormously expensive for the state.

Christian arguments for. Article 37 of the Thirty-Nine Articles of the Church of England (1563) states that the Laws of the Realm may punish Christian men with death for "heinous and grievous offences", and in the sixteenth century many ministers agreed. Until the Middle Ages all Christians believed capital punishment was part of God's plan of salvation; Aquinas agreed, as did Pope Innocent III (1161–1216), and in 1566 the Council of Trent reaffirmed its morality, calling the just use of the power "an act of paramount obedience to the Commandment which prohibits murder". Supporters today cite Leviticus 24:21, which recommends the loss of life for those who take a life, and Genesis 9:6; Natural Law, to create an ordered society; and St Paul, that everyone should "obey the ruling authorities". Calvin is cited both ways — that laws do not override forgiveness.

Christian arguments against. Most Anglican priests now disagree with its use: in July 1983 the General Synod of the Church of England carried a motion that it "would deplore the reintroduction of capital punishment into the United Kingdom's sentencing policy". They cite the biblical teachings on the sanctity of life — punishing someone by taking their life devalues life itself — and the teaching and example of Jesus, who stopped an execution and rejected retribution ("love your enemies", Matthew 5:44; "turn the other cheek"). They also question whether it deters at all, and prefer imprisonment, which allows an opportunity for reform.

The Roman Catholic position changed across the twentieth century. In 1980 the National Conference of Catholic Bishops in America approved a statement criticising the death penalty. In 1995, in his encyclical Evangelium Vitae (the Gospel of Life), Pope John Paul II argued that execution should be used only in cases of absolute necessity, and that progress in penal systems had made such cases a rarity. On 3 October 2020, in the encyclical Fratelli Tutti (All Brothers), Pope Francis ratified the Church's opposition, declaring there can be no stepping back: "Today we state clearly that 'the death penalty is inadmissible' and the Church is firmly committed to calling for its abolition worldwide." The Salvation Army believes in reformation — Christ can transform lives.

Non-religious attitudes. In 1989 the International and Ethical Union, the worldwide group for Humanists, called for abolition across the world on the grounds that the death penalty denies the right to life as recognised by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Humanists also doubt that it deters — and argue it may exacerbate crime, since a murderer who knows he will be killed if caught has an incentive to kill more people to avoid capture — and note that an incorrect conviction and execution cannot be reversed, whereas a wrongly imprisoned person can be released and compensated. Some non-religious people support it where the crime is so heinous that there is little chance of reforming the offender, applying Utilitarianism or Situation Ethics case by case.

The facts you cannot sit the paper without

Five causes of conflict: politics, resources, history, culture, religion. Three current conflicts: Ukraine (2014, full invasion Feb 2022), Israel/Palestine (annexation 1948, Gaza May 2021), Ethiopia (civil war since 2020, Tigray v Abiy Ahmed).

Key verses — peace: Matthew 5:9 peacemakers · Matthew 5:44 love your enemies · Matthew 5:39 turn the other cheek · John 14:27 "peace I leave with you" · Isaiah 9:6–7 Prince of Peace · Micah 4:3 no more training for war. Key verses — war: Deuteronomy 7:22–24 · Joel 3:9–10 ploughshares into swords · 1 Samuel 15:3 Amalekites · Mark 11:15–16 the Temple.

Just War: Augustine (354–430) → Aquinas (1225–1274) → Francisco de Vitoria (c.1483–1546, jus post bellum). Jus ad bellum — just cause, legitimate authority, right intention, last resort, strong chance of success. Jus in bello — proportionate, no attacks on the innocent, prisoners treated fairly, no WMD. Jus post bellum — treat the losers humanely and help them rebuild.

Holy war: religious goal, authorised by a religious leader or God, spiritual reward. Example: the First Crusade (1095–1099), called by Pope Urban II, promising heaven to those who fought. OT: Numbers 21:14 wars of Yahweh · Exodus 17:8–16 Amalekites and Moses' rod · Joshua 6 Jericho.

WMD: nuclear, chemical, biological. Hiroshima 6 Aug 1945, ~84,000 dead; Nagasaki ~40,000. Hydrogen bomb 1,000× stronger; neutron bomb 1970s. 2015: nine nations, ~15,700 warheads. Chemical Weapons Convention 1993; Biological Weapons Convention, 180 states. Pacem in Terris; Pope Benedict XVI — "no victors, only victims"; Stephen Cottrell, Archbishop of York, 2020 — use or possession never a just use of arms.

Bullying: intentional, aiming to cause harm or distress · unequal power · repeated over time. Types: physical, verbal, social, psychological, cyber. Verses: Genesis 1:27 · Mark 12:31 · Ephesians 4:29 · Psalm 139:23–24.

Five aims of punishment: protection, deterrence, retribution, reform, reparation. Verses: Ezekiel 18:20 · Leviticus 24:19–20 · Galatians 6:1–5 · Matthew 5:38–39 · John 8:1–11 · Romans 12:17ff.

Sin vs crime: hamartia = "miss the mark". Source (God / government), effect (God's will / the law), consequences (after death / in this life). Revelation 21:8 — the fiery lake, "the second death".

Named examples: Corrymeela (Ray Davey, 1965, Ballycastle, county Antrim), the UN (1945; 2 March 2022 resolution 141–5), the Quakers (Declaration to Charles II, 1661), Gandhi, Martin Luther King, Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission (1996; apartheid abolished 1994), Gee Walker, Rev Julie Nicholson, Street Pastors (Les Isaac, London, 2003), Prison Fellowship (3,000+ volunteers), the IRA's Brighton bombing (1984, Patrick Magee, five dead, 31 injured), the Army of God (1982).

Capital punishment: last UK executions 1964; abolished for murder in Great Britain 1965 and Northern Ireland 1973; completely abolished 1998. Article 37 of the Thirty-Nine Articles (1563); General Synod motion July 1983; Evangelium Vitae 1995 (John Paul II); Fratelli Tutti 3 October 2020 (Francis) — "the death penalty is inadmissible"; Humanists' International and Ethical Union, 1989.

The 12-mark frame

Five paragraphs, in this order. The top band needs Christian teaching in every one of them and a conclusion that actually decides, so write the conclusion you are heading for before you start.

  1. Restate the statement and say what turns on it. One or two sentences naming the real question — whether war can ever be just, whether forgiveness has limits, whether punishment should reform or repay.
  2. The strongest case for, with teaching and scripture. Not a list: one argument developed, then appraised. If the statement is pro-peace, this is Matthew 5:9 and 5:44, Micah 4:3 and Jesus' refusal to resist arrest in Gethsemane; if it is pro-force, Deuteronomy 7, 1 Samuel 15:3 and the Temple cleansing.
  3. The strongest case against, with teaching and scripture. Same again from the other side, and say which of the two arguments is stronger and why — the appraisal is where the AO2 marks are, not the listing.
  4. Where Christians disagree with each other. This is the paragraph that reaches the top level, because it shows the disagreement is internal to the religion: Quaker absolute pacifism against Just War theory; Gee Walker against Rev Julie Nicholson; Leviticus 24 against Matthew 5. Add a non-religious view for perspective — Utilitarianism, Situation Ethics or a Humanist position — but remember it does not count as the reference to a religion.
  5. A conclusion that decides. Name the winning argument, say why it outweighs the other, and tie it back to the words of the statement.

Sentence starters that earn the evaluation marks:

  • "Most Christians would agree with this statement, because…"
  • "An absolute pacifist, such as a Quaker, would argue…"
  • "However, a Christian who accepts Just War theory would respond that…"
  • "This argument is the stronger of the two, because…"
  • "Christians themselves are divided here: those who follow the Old Testament's retributive strand… whereas those who follow Jesus' teaching on forgiveness…"
  • "A Utilitarian would weigh this differently, since…" / "A situation ethicist would ask only what is most loving, and so…"
  • "On balance, I disagree with the statement, because the teaching of Jesus… outweighs…"

subsections.heading: Quotes to learn
subsections.html:
The marks in this section live in the quotations. These are the ones worth knowing word-for-word; the front of the card is the topic and the reference, so you can test whether you can produce the words from the prompt alone.

Peacemaking — Matthew 5:9"Blessed are the peacemakers."Used to argue: peacemaking, not fighting, is the Christian vocation — the first quotation in any answer on Christian attitudes to war
Love of enemies — Matthew 5:44"Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you."Used to argue: even an enemy is owed agape, which rules out killing them
The end of war — Micah 4:3"Nation will not take up sword against nation, nor will they train for war any more."Used to argue: God's ideal world is disarmed, so war can never be God's will
The Messiah's title — Isaiah 9:6–7"For to us a child is born, to us a son is given… And he will be called Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. Of the greatness of his government and peace, there will be no end."Used to argue: peace is not incidental to the Messiah's work but his title
God commands war — Deuteronomy 7:22–24"The LORD your God will drive out those nations before you… He will give their kings into your hand, and you will wipe out their names from under heaven."Used to argue: God himself has commanded war, so the Bible is not uniformly pacifist
Prepare for war — Joel 3:9–10"Proclaim this among the nations: Prepare for war! Rouse the warriors! Let all the fighting men draw near and attack. Beat your ploughshares into swords and your pruning hooks into spears. Let the weakling say, 'I am strong!'"Used to argue: the prophets commanded the people to fight on God's behalf — and it is the exact inversion of Micah 4:3, which is why quoting both wins the point
The Amalekites — 1 Samuel 15:3"Go now and fall on the Amalekites and destroy them, and put their property under ban. Spare no one: put them all to death, men and women, children and babes in arms, herds and flocks, camels and asses"Used to argue: the Old Testament has God ordering total war — the sharpest evidence that the Bible cuts both ways
Pacifism as doctrine — the Quaker Declaration, 1661"We utterly deny all outward wars and strife and fighting with outward weapons for any end or under any pretence whatsoever. And this is our testimony to the whole world."Used to argue: absolute pacifism is a settled Christian position and not a modern opinion — the Society of Friends' Declaration to Charles II
Non-violence as power — Gandhi"Non-violence is the greatest force at the disposal of mankind. It is mightier than the mightiest weapon of destruction devised by the ingenuity of man."Used to argue: passive resistance is not weakness but a different and stronger kind of power
Nuclear war — Pope Benedict XVI"In nuclear war there would be no victors, only victims."Used to argue: weapons of mass destruction can never satisfy jus in bello — pair it with Pacem in Terris and with Archbishop Stephen Cottrell (2020), who rules out possession as well as use
Justice — Amos 5:24"But let justice roll on like a river, righteousness like a never-failing stream!"Used to argue: justice is a demand of God, not an optional extra — the basis for saying there is no peace without justice first
Limitless forgiveness — Matthew 18:21–22"Peter came to Jesus and asked, 'Lord, how many times shall I forgive my brother when he sins against me? Up to seven times?' Jesus answered, 'I tell you, not seven times, but seventy-seven times.'"Used to argue: Christian forgiveness has no limit, which is why most Christians favour reform over revenge
What reconciliation costs — Desmond Tutu"Forgiving and being reconciled to our enemies or our loved ones are not about pretending that things are other than they are… True reconciliation exposes the awfulness, the abuse, the hurt, the truth. It could even sometimes make things worse. It is a risky undertaking but in the end it is worthwhile, because in the end only an honest confrontation with reality can bring real healing."Used to argue: forgiveness is risky and painful rather than easy — the best answer to "forgiveness is weakness"
Bullying — Genesis 1:26–27"God created humans in his own image"Used to argue: everyone deserves respect and equal treatment, so bullying attacks something God made — say openly that the Bible does not mention bullying and that Christians argue from imago Dei, agape and the Beatitudes
The consequences of sin — Revelation 21:8"But the cowardly, the unbelieving, the vile, the murderers, the sexually immoral, those who practice magic arts, the idolaters and all liars — they will be consigned to the fiery lake of burning sulphur. This is the second death."Used to argue: sin has eternal, not merely legal, consequences — and the phrase "the second death" is worth quoting
Retribution — Leviticus 24:19–20"Anyone who injures their neighbour is to be injured in the same manner: fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth. The one who has inflicted the injury must suffer the same injury."Used to argue: justice requires payback — the text the minority of Christians who prioritise retribution rely on
Jesus rewrites retribution — Matthew 5:38–39"You have heard that it was said, 'Eye for eye, and tooth for tooth.' But I tell you, do not resist an evil person. If anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to them the other cheek also."Used to argue: Jesus quotes Leviticus 24 in order to overturn it, so reform outranks retribution for most Christians
Capital punishment, for — Genesis 9:6"Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed; for in the image of God has God made man"Used to argue: the taking of a life demands a life, precisely because humans bear God's image
Capital punishment, against — John 8:1–11"If any one of you is without sin, let him be the first to throw a stone at her."Used to argue: Jesus halted an execution, because no sinful human is fit to judge
The death penalty today — Pope Francis, Fratelli Tutti"Today we state clearly that 'the death penalty is inadmissible' and the Church is firmly committed to calling for its abolition worldwide."Used to argue: the modern Roman Catholic position is outright abolition — 3 October 2020, hardening John Paul II's "absolute necessity" in Evangelium Vitae (1995)

subsections.heading: Examples to learn
subsections.html:
The 12-markers in this section are won with concrete examples, so learn them the same way as the quotations: the name on the front, what it was and what it shows on the back. An unnamed charity or an undated conflict earns nothing.

Reconciliation — CorrymeelaFounded by Ray Davey in 1965 at Ballycastle, county Antrim; inter-denominational, bringing Catholics and Protestants together. Visitors stay two days to a week, share the chores and join discussion groups that challenge prejudice; much of the work is school and youth workshops on conflict resolution. Davey's line as people leave: "Corrymeela begins when you leave."Used to argue: Christians put the Bible's teaching on forgiveness into action because Jesus is the Prince of Peace — the named organisation for any question on Christian peacemaking
Pacifism — the QuakersThe Religious Society of Friends, who take the absolutist position: there is evil in the world, but it cannot be overcome by weapons that harm and kill, so Christians should use the "weapons of the Spirit" — truth, love and peace. In both World Wars they were conscientious objectors, many serving as medics, stretcher-bearers or fire-watchers; some were imprisoned and fined.Used to argue: absolute pacifism is practised, not just preached — and that refusing to fight still carries a cost, which answers the charge that pacifism is hypocritical
Passive resistance — Gandhi and Martin Luther KingPassive resistance is opposition without violence: strikes, boycotts, creative disorder, demonstrations and marches. Mahatma Gandhi (1869–1948) and Martin Luther King are the two named campaigners, and the fall of apartheid is the third standard example.Used to argue: non-violent protest works, so war is not the last resort it is claimed to be — the counter is that it is weak against a determined aggressor who is not watching public opinion
Restorative justice — the Truth and Reconciliation CommissionChaired by Desmond Tutu in 1996 to deal with what had happened under apartheid, abolished in 1994. Witnesses identified as victims of gross human rights violations were invited to give statements; perpetrators of violence could also testify and request amnesty from civil and criminal prosecution.Used to argue: restorative justice reconciled a divided community and helped the transition to a full and free democracy — forgiveness working at national scale
Forgiveness — Gee WalkerForgave her son's murderers; as a Christian she felt it was Jesus' command and will.Used to argue: Christian forgiveness is unconditional, following Matthew 18:21–22 and the Lord's Prayer — the "for" side of any forgiveness question
Refusing to forgive — Rev Julie NicholsonRefused to forgive the terrorists who killed her daughter in the 7/7 bombings: the guilty party had not repented, so she saw no point.Used to argue: forgiveness follows repentance — metanoia — and that Christians genuinely disagree; pair it with Gee Walker and the 12-marker evaluates itself
Christian response to crime — Street PastorsPioneered in London in 2003 by Les Isaac. City projects run in partnership with the local police and council, with trained volunteers making the streets safer by caring, listening and helping — water for the drunk and distressed, a way home. It began in the night-time economy and now works in daytime too, in parks, schools and colleges, and it is ecumenical, with a group spending the night praying for the town.Used to argue: Christians address the causes of crime rather than only its punishment, as an expression of agape and stewardship
Prisoners — Prison FellowshipShows Christ's love to people in prison by visiting and supporting them, with prayer and practical help such as literacy teaching and someone to confide in. Over 3,000 volunteers work in almost all the prisons in England and Wales, and prisoners' families are supported too; it works with people of all faiths or none.Used to argue: Christians prioritise reform over retribution, because no one is beyond hope and every life can be transformed
Terrorism — the IRA and the Brighton bombingThe Provisional IRA broke away towards the end of the 1960s, deciding physical force was necessary, and ran a bombing campaign aiming to force a British withdrawal. About a month before the 1984 Conservative Conference, Patrick Magee planted a bomb in The Grand Hotel, Brighton, timed for the last night of the conference with the explicit aim of assassinating Margaret Thatcher. She survived; five people were killed and at least 31 injured.Used to argue: terrorism uses atrocity against civilians to intimidate a government, so it can never meet the Just War conditions of legitimate authority or proportionate force
Christian terrorism — the Army of GodAn American Christian terrorist organisation formed in 1982 and committed to reducing abortions in America; it has committed kidnap, attempted murder and murder, and has been associated with abortion clinic bombings and arsons.Used to argue: Christians have been on both sides, so being honest about it strengthens the point that the majority hold terrorism cannot be justified morally
Holy war — the First CrusadeCalled by Pope Urban II, 1095–1099, to free Jerusalem from Muslim control so Christian pilgrims could visit sites such as the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. Urban promised those who took part the reward of heaven — a plenary indulgence, their sins forgiven if they died on Crusade. They were known as milites Christi.Used to argue: all three marks of a holy war are present at once — a religious goal, authorisation by a religious leader, and a spiritual reward — which is why this is the example to use
Peacekeeping — the United NationsCreated in 1945 after the Second World War to maintain international peace and security: preventing conflict, helping parties make peace, deploying peacekeepers, and creating the conditions for peace to hold. The Security Council can impose economic sanctions and military action; the General Assembly passes resolutions — on 2 March 2022 it deplored Russia's actions by 141 votes to 5. Peacekeepers police the "green line" in Cyprus and serve in South Sudan.Used to argue: the non-religious response to conflict is to give international institutions stronger powers rather than to fight — and Christians support it, the Roman Catholic Church holding a non-voting UN membership

equations.formula: Called by Pope Urban II, 1095–1099, to free Jerusalem from Muslim control so Christian pilgrims could visit sites such as the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. Urban promised those who took part the reward of heaven — a plenary indulgence, their sins forgiven if they died on Crusade. They were known as milites Christi.
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: all three marks of a holy war are present at once — a religious goal, authorisation by a religious leader, and a spiritual reward — which is why this is the example to use

equations.name: Peacekeeping — the United Nations
equations.formula: Created in 1945 after the Second World War to maintain international peace and security: preventing conflict, helping parties make peace, deploying peacekeepers, and creating the conditions for peace to hold. The Security Council can impose economic sanctions and military action; the General Assembly passes resolutions — on 2 March 2022 it deplored Russia's actions by 141 votes to 5. Peacekeepers police the "green line" in Cyprus and serve in South Sudan.
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: the non-religious response to conflict is to give international institutions stronger powers rather than to fight — and Christians support it, the Roman Catholic Church holding a non-voting UN membership

questions.promptHtml: Why do Christians disagree about war when they all read the same Bible?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the Bible itself contains both strands. The Old Testament has God commanding the destruction of the Amalekites (1 Samuel 15:3) and the taking of Jericho by supernatural means; the New Testament has Jesus blessing the peacemakers and telling his followers to love their enemies.

Christians then weigh those strands differently. Pacifists treat Jesus' teaching as the final revelation that supersedes the older material. Supporters of Just War argue that Jesus' commands were addressed to individuals rather than states — St Bernard's position — and point to his righteous anger in the Temple.

The exam point: every 12-marker here is won by showing that the disagreement is internal to Christianity, not between Christians and everyone else.

questions.promptHtml: What is the strongest objection to Just War theory, and how would a supporter answer it?
questions.answerHtml:
The strongest objection: modern war can never be just. Modern weaponry causes devastation that is neither proportionate nor discriminate, so jus in bello is unsatisfiable in practice — Dresden and the atomic bombs are the standard illustrations, and around a million civilians died in Iraq.

The answer: the theory is a restraint, not a permission. Its purpose is to make most wars unjustifiable and to limit the ones that happen. Abandoning it does not produce peace; it removes the only criteria by which a Christian can criticise a war at all.

The objection about soldiers' conduct is weaker, because bad conduct breaks the theory rather than disproving it.

questions.promptHtml: Why do Christians find weapons of mass destruction harder to justify than conventional weapons?
questions.answerHtml:
Because of jus in bello. WMD kill indiscriminately, so they cannot avoid attacking the innocent, and their scale makes any response disproportionate. Just War theory explicitly says WMD should not be used.

They also offend the sanctity of life and destroy God's creation — "the earth is the Lord's". Pacem in Terris called for an end to the arms race, and Pope Benedict XVI said a nuclear war would have "no victors, only victims".

The counter-position worth knowing: some Christians distinguish possessing from using. A deterrent that is never fired kills nobody — which is why states with strong Christian affiliations hold nuclear arsenals.

questions.promptHtml: Rev Julie Nicholson refused to forgive her daughter's killers. Gee Walker forgave her son's murderers. Which is the more Christian response?
questions.answerHtml:
For Gee Walker: Jesus set no limit on forgiveness — "not seven times, but seventy-seven times" (Matthew 18:21–22) — and the Lord's Prayer makes being forgiven conditional on forgiving. The Prodigal Son's father forgives before anything is earned.

For Julie Nicholson: Jesus taught that forgiveness follows repentance — metanoia. Her position was that the guilty party had not repented, so forgiveness would be empty. Romans 12:19 also leaves vengeance to God rather than demanding the victim resolve it.

Use it like this: this pair is the cleanest way to show a 12-marker that Christians genuinely disagree, and that both positions are grounded in teaching rather than feeling.

questions.promptHtml: If the Bible never mentions bullying, how can Christians have teachings about it?
questions.answerHtml:
They argue from general principles rather than a specific verse, and saying so openly is itself worth credit.

Genesis 1:26–27 — humans are made in God's image, so every person deserves respect. Agape and the Good Samaritan — love extends even to the stranger. The Beatitudes — "blessed are the meek" overturns a culture that venerates strength, which the lesson identifies as one cause of bullying. "Repay no one evil for evil" — the victim should not retaliate. Ephesians and the Psalms — honour God with your words.

The spec also asks about inclusion, which is why "everyone deserves equal treatment" is the central Christian claim here.

questions.promptHtml: Why do Christians say all crime comes from sin, but not all sin is crime?
questions.answerHtml:
All crime from sin: crime is a breach of God's will as well as the law, because it harms a neighbour made in God's image. Christians trace it to the self-centredness that began with Original Sin.

Not all sin is crime: the two have different sources. Sin is determined by God; crime is identified by the government. So lying, greed and hatred are sins but not crimes, and a law could in principle make something criminal that God does not forbid.

The consequences differ too: crime is punished in this life, sin after death. That is the answer to "Which is worse?" — a crime has visible consequences, a sin has eternal ones.

questions.promptHtml: Why do most Christians think reform is the most important aim of punishment?
questions.answerHtml:
Because reform is the aim that matches Jesus' teaching. He rejected retributive justice — "an eye for an eye… but now I tell you: do not take revenge" (Matthew 5:38–39) — and demonstrated it with the woman taken in adultery (John 8). He taught that forgiveness follows repentance and change, metanoia, which is exactly what reform aims at.

Christians also hold that every offender is made in God's image and can be redeemed; the Salvation Army's position is that Christ can transform lives. Practically, reform is the only aim that reduces reoffending, so it serves the stewardship duty to keep society just.

The balance to include: Christians do not abandon justice. Punishment must still be fair, must take mitigating circumstances into account, and a minority citing Leviticus 24 still prioritise retribution.

questions.promptHtml: Genesis 9:6 and John 8:1–11 are both used in the capital punishment debate. How can one religion hold both?
questions.answerHtml:
Genesis 9:6 — "Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed; for in the image of God has God made man." Supporters read the imago Dei as making murder so grave that only a life answers for it.

John 8:1–11 — "If any one of you is without sin, let him be the first to throw a stone at her." Opponents read Jesus as stopping an execution outright, because no sinful human is fit to pass that judgement.

The resolution most Churches have reached is developmental: the Thirty-Nine Articles once supported it and the Roman Catholic Church once regarded it as part of God's plan, but Pope John Paul II restricted it to absolute necessity and Pope Francis rejected it in 2020. The same imago Dei that once justified execution is now used to forbid it.

questions.promptHtml: Choose one religion and explain its attitudes to weapons of mass destruction. (6)
questions.answerHtml:
Most Christians believe WMD can never be justified, because nuclear, chemical and biological weapons kill indiscriminately 1; this breaks the Just War condition of jus in bello, which forbids attacking the innocent and requires proportionate methods, and explicitly rules out weapons of mass destruction 1

Christians also appeal to the sanctity of life: life is God-given, so destroying it on this scale usurps God's authority 1; WMD also destroy God's creation, which Christians are stewards of — "the earth is the Lord's" — and the Roman Catholic Church in Pacem in Terris demanded "that the arms race should cease", while Pope Benedict XVI said a nuclear war would have "no victors, only victims" and Stephen Cottrell, Archbishop of York, held in 2020 that even possession could never be a just use of arms 1

A minority of Christians accept possession as a deterrent 1; they argue that mutually assured destruction means the weapons will never be used, so holding them protects a country from attack without anyone being killed — which is why several nations with strong Christian affiliations hold nuclear arsenals 1

A 6-marker is level-marked on explanation, not on counting. Three developed points like these, with the religious terms used correctly, reach the top level.

questions.promptHtml:
"There is no such thing as a Just War."

Evaluate this statement, showing you have considered different points of view. In your answer, you should refer to at least one religion. (12)
questions.answerHtml:
Arguments for the statement.

Modern weaponry causes devastation that is neither proportionate nor discriminate, so jus in bello can never actually be met — Dresden and the atomic bombs on Japan are the standard examples 1

Controlling soldiers' conduct in the heat of war is impossible, so the rules collapse in practice even where they are accepted in principle 1

Deciding who is an innocent bystander and who is involved is a subjective judgement, so the condition protecting the innocent has no clear content 1

Even a "just" war produces horrors afterwards — around a million civilians died in Iraq — so jus post bellum is routinely failed 1

Arguments against the statement.

The conditions can be met: WWII had a legitimate authority (Chamberlain with the backing of Parliament), a just cause (stopping Hitler) and was a last resort after negotiation failed 1

The theory functions as a restraint rather than a permission — it exists to make most wars unjustifiable and to limit the conduct of the rest 1

Without it, resisting an aggressor becomes impossible, and some evil can only be met with force; pacifism also arguably relies on others fighting on your behalf 1

Christian teaching.

Augustine and Aquinas developed the theory precisely so Christians could resist evil without abandoning conscience, and many Christians accept war as a last resort to defeat a greater evil 1

Against this, pacifist Christians such as the Quakers argue the theory compromises Jesus' teaching — "blessed are the peacemakers", "love your enemies" — and Micah's vision of swords hammered into ploughs shows God's ideal world is disarmed 1

Supporters reply that Jesus showed righteous anger in the Temple, and that St Bernard held his peace commands applied to individuals rather than states 1

Conclusion.

Judgement: the theory's conditions are genuinely satisfiable at the point of going to war, which is why WWII is so widely accepted as just, but modern weapons make the conditions on fighting it very hard to satisfy 1

So the statement is too strong: a just war is possible but has become rarer, and the theory remains the only standard by which Christians can criticise a particular war at all — which is a reason to keep it rather than abandon it 1

✗ A long description of the conditions with "so it depends" at the end.
✓ Appraise each argument as you give it — say which is strong and why — then reach a conclusion that decides. Level 4 wants "a fully justified conclusion".

questions.promptHtml: Explain the work of one Christian organisation that works for peace. (6)
questions.answerHtml:
Corrymeela was founded by Ray Davey in 1965 at Ballycastle in county Antrim, Northern Ireland, which is divided along Protestant and Catholic lines 1; its work is inter-denominational, and people of any religious persuasion can stay at the centre for two days to a week, sharing the domestic chores and living alongside other visitors, which breaks down the segregation that keeps the division alive 1

Visitors take part in discussion groups that challenge their prejudices, and the centre runs team-building and community relations work, including an international peace conference 1; it works closely with schools and youth groups and runs workshops on conflict resolution, so the next generation does not inherit the hostility 1

It also supports victims of violence and social injustice, which matters because justice prevents the resentment that restarts conflict 1; the motivation is religious — Jesus is the Prince of Peace who blessed the peacemakers, so Corrymeela puts the Bible's teaching on forgiveness into practice, and Ray Davey's reminder that "Corrymeela begins when you leave" shows the aim is changed behaviour at home, not a pleasant week away 1

questions.promptHtml:
"Capital punishment is never justified."

Evaluate this statement, showing you have considered different points of view. In your answer, you should refer to at least one religion. (12)
questions.answerHtml:
Arguments for the statement.

It is self-contradictory: taking a life to punish the taking of a life undermines the very value it claims to defend 1

Miscarriages of justice occur and an execution cannot be reversed, so the system guarantees that innocent people will eventually be killed 1

It does not deter murder, so it fails on its own terms, and in the US it falls disproportionately on poor Black and Latino defendants 1

It brutalises society and feeds a cycle of violence, and the long wait between sentence and execution is costly as well as cruel 1

Arguments against the statement.

It is the ultimate retribution for the worst crimes and embodies a natural justice — a life for a life 1

It protects law-abiding citizens absolutely, since an executed offender cannot reoffend 1

It may give the victim's family comfort or closure that no other sentence can, and some crimes are so heinous that the offender appears beyond reform 1

Christian teaching.

Supporters cite Genesis 9:6 — "whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed; for in the image of God has God made man" — and Leviticus 24; the Thirty-Nine Articles of the Church of England allowed it for the most heinous offences, and St Paul told Christians to obey the ruling authorities 1

Opponents cite the sanctity of life and John 8, where Jesus stops an execution with "if any one of you is without sin, let him be the first to throw a stone at her", and Matthew 5, where he rejects "an eye for an eye" 1

The Churches have moved: Pope John Paul II restricted it to cases of absolute necessity, Pope Francis opposed it outright in 2020 as fostering vengeance, and the Salvation Army argues Christ can transform any life — while Humanists reached the same conclusion from the right to life, calling for worldwide abolition in 1989 1

Conclusion.

Judgement: the retributive case is the strongest argument for, but it rests on a reading of imago Dei that Jesus himself set aside in John 8 when he refused to join a lawful stoning 1

Since the deterrent claim is unsupported and the risk of irreversible error is real — many people in the UK have been pardoned years after conviction — I agree with the statement, which is also the direction the Churches themselves have moved in, from Article 37 of the Thirty-Nine Articles to Fratelli Tutti 1

questions.promptHtml: Explain the differences between sins and crimes. (6)
questions.answerHtml:
The two differ in source: a crime is an illegal act identified by the government, whereas a sin is determined by God 1; this matters to Christians because the law can change while God's will does not, so an act can be legal and still sinful — which is why Christians sometimes campaign against laws they regard as unjust 1

They differ in effect: a crime breaks the law of the land, while a sin is a violation of God's will, rooted in disobedience and being self-centred rather than God-centred, as Adam and Eve were in the Original Sin 1; this gives sin a relational dimension a crime does not have, because it damages the sinner's relationship with God 1

They differ in consequences: a crime is punished in this life, by imprisonment, a fine or community service, whereas the punishment for sin comes after death 1; Revelation 21 warns that liars, murderers and idolaters will find their place "in the fiery lake of burning sulphur", which is why Christians regard repentance — metanoia — as more urgent than any court appearance, and why not all sins are crimes while Christians would argue all crime has its source in sin 1

questions.promptHtml:
"Passive resistance is more effective than fighting."

Evaluate this statement, showing you have considered different points of view. In your answer, you should refer to at least one religion. (12)
questions.answerHtml:
Arguments for the statement.

It has a record of success: Gandhi's campaigns and Martin Luther King's bus boycotts, marches and speeches achieved change that violence had not 1

It wins public sympathy, which converts opponents instead of hardening them, so the settlement lasts — as in South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission 1

It breaks the cycle of violence rather than continuing it, and it costs no lives, which matters if human life is treated as having absolute value 1

Gandhi's claim that non-violence is "mightier than the mightiest weapon of destruction devised by the ingenuity of man" is at least arguable, given how often military victories have had to be re-fought 1

Arguments against the statement.

It is a weak response to a determined aggressor who is not susceptible to public opinion — appeasement did not stop Hitler 1

It can be hypocritical: pacifists still benefit from the protection of those who do fight on their behalf 1

It rules out a pre-emptive strike that might have saved more lives than it cost, so on a straightforward count of lives it can be the costlier option 1

Christian teaching.

Many Christians are pacifists because of the biblical teachings of peace, love and forgiveness; the Quakers use the "weapons of the Spirit" — truth, love and peace — and became conscientious objectors in both World Wars, serving as stretcher-bearers or going to prison 1

Jesus' own teaching supports this: "blessed are the peacemakers", "love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you", and Micah's vision of swords hammered into ploughs 1

Against this, conditional pacifists and supporters of Just War argue that extreme cases leave no option, citing "greater love has no man than this that he lay down his life for his friends" and Jesus' righteous anger in the Temple 1

Conclusion.

Judgement: effectiveness depends on the opponent. Against a government that needs public legitimacy, passive resistance is demonstrably more effective; against a regime indifferent to opinion and willing to kill, the evidence is much weaker 1

So I partly agree: passive resistance should always be tried first and is usually more effective, but the claim that it is always more effective is not supported — which is why most Christians are conditional rather than absolute pacifists 1

drill.intro:
What each part of the question actually wants

Section 3 sits on Paper 1 — 1 hour 45 minutes, four sections, each with a choice of two questions, each question worth 25 marks. The four parts are marked in completely different ways, so answer each in its own shape.

  • a) 3 marks — AO1. Three focused and distinct points. The answer does not require explanations; brief, clear reasons are ideal. Number them and stop.
  • b) 4 marks — AO1. Two points of information which require some development — point (1) + development (1), twice. The development must add value to the point while still answering the question posed; an example is often the quickest way to develop it.
  • c) 6 marks — AO1 and AO2. An explain question, marked in levels rather than by ticking points. Explain and develop the issue, drawing out the influence and significance of the religion, beliefs and values, with religious terms used appropriately. Aim to explain more than one reason even when no number is given, make sure every point is fully explained, and balance breadth against depth.
  • d) 12 marks — AO1 and AO2. The synoptic assessment, also level marked. It wants fully evaluated arguments underpinned with knowledge and understanding, drawn from across the course: consider the alternative viewpoint no matter how weak it is, refer to at least one religion, appraise the quality of each argument as you give it, and reach a fully justified conclusion. Humanist and atheist views add perspective but do not on their own count as the reference to a religion.

Twelve questions in the shape of the real thing: three each of the 3-, 4-, 6- and 12-mark parts. The 12-mark answers are written as plans — the real paper marks them in levels, not by ticking points, so treat the twelve mark points as a target for coverage rather than a tick list.

modules.title: Rights, Equality and Social Justice
modules.standfirst: Section 4 of Paper 1 Beliefs and Values — human rights and whether they can be restricted, equality for women and for disabled people, the multi-ethnic and multi-faith society, ecumenism, and the relationship between rich and poor. One 25-mark question (3, 4, 6 and 12 marks) that wants named people — Desmond Tutu, Eleanor Roosevelt, Martin Luther King, Jean Vanier, Oscar Romero, Toby Ord — and the four words proselytisation, exclusivism, inclusivism, pluralism used correctly.

subsections.html:
Five spec areas: human rights (4.1), equal rights and equal opportunities — women and disability (4.2), the multi-ethnic society and racial harmony (4.3), the multi-faith society and interfaith relationships (4.4), and relationships between rich and poor (4.5). Almost every Christian answer in this section is built from the same three foundations — the doctrine of creation (everyone is made in God's image), stewardship (Christians are responsible for the world and each other), and agape (selfless love of neighbour). Learn those three, and most 6-markers write themselves. The paper then expects you to contrast them with non-religious views, and the non-religious case has its own named thinkers.

What they actually ask

From the seven June papers 2019–2025, Paper 1 Section 4 (Questions 7 and 8 — you answer one). Four stems appear in every year, and poverty and human rights usually turn up twice in the same paper.

  • The poor — charity, justice and whose duty it is — all seven years. "two non-religious beliefs about the treatment of the poor" and "It is more important to work for justice than give charity" (2019); "three practical ways religious people can help the poor" (2020); "three ways society could support the poor" (2021); "religious attitudes to the treatment of the poor" and "the responsibilities many religious people believe they have to the poor" (2022); "two teachings about the treatment of the poor" and "different non-religious responses to the treatment of the poor" (2023); "three ways people may respond to the poor" and "two ways religious people can support the poor" (2024); "why wealthy countries should support the poor" and "Charity is the best way to help the poor" (2025).
  • Human rights — and whether they can be restricted — all seven years. "why some of its followers support human rights" (2019); "two reasons why many of its followers support human rights" and "why religious people may disagree with some human rights" (2020); "three ways religious people may support human rights" and "Religious people should uphold all human rights" (2021); "three reasons why some religious people may not support human rights" (2022); "two reasons why some of its followers may disagree with some human rights" and "Freedom of speech is dangerous for society" (2023); "Everyone deserves human rights" (2024); "three ways non-religious people can support human rights" and "two reasons why equality before the law is important" (2025).
  • Women, gender bias and equality — all seven years. "three ways women's rights have improved in society" and "what its followers believe about the status of women" (2019); "Women should be religious leaders" and "two of its attitudes towards the role of women in society" (2020); "Religions are biased in favour of men" and "the responses religious people may have to changes in women's role in society" (2021); "Women and men should be equal in all things" (2022); "Men and women are equal in society" (2023); "the attitudes its followers may hold towards equal rights for women" (2024); "three attitudes to the role of women in society" and "two examples of gender bias" (2025).
  • The multi-faith and multi-ethnic society, interfaith relationships and conversion — all seven years. "three ways religious people may promote the development of a multi-faith society" (2019); "different religious attitudes to living in a multi-faith society" (2020); "two attitudes its followers may have towards people of other religions" and "two attitudes towards living in a multi-faith society" (2021); "three religious attitudes to proselytisation", "two responsibilities its followers have in a multi-ethnic society" and "two attitudes towards interfaith relationships" (2022); "why some religious people may not want to live in a multi-faith society" (2023); "three attitudes non-religious people may have to living in a multi-faith society", "the responsibilities its followers have in a multi-ethnic society" and "Religious people should only mix with others of the same faith" (2024); "It is wrong to try to convert people to a religion" and "the benefits a religious person may experience in a multi ethnic society" (2025).
  • Racism, prejudice and racial harmony — five of seven. "two examples of racial harmony in society" and "Religious people are the best hope for racial harmony" (2019); "three examples of discrimination" and "Prejudice and discrimination are the biggest problems facing society today" (2020); "non-religious attitudes to racial harmony" (2021); "three ways those of a different race should be treated" and "three non-religious beliefs about racial harmony" (2023); "two ways society tries to overcome racism" (2024).
  • Disability — only once: "Disabled people have the same rights as others in society" (2022). Thin, but it is a named spec topic, so keep Jean Vanier and L'Arche ready.

Note how often the non-religious side is asked on its own — 2019, 2021, 2023, 2024 and 2025 each had at least one part that could only be answered from non-religious material. Ecumenism has not been asked directly in these seven years.

subsections.heading: What human rights are
subsections.html:
Spec 4.1 · Lesson 2, Revision Booklet 4 p.6

  • Human rights defined — basic freedoms everyone is entitled to; they are universal, inalienable, and indivisible or interdependent.
  • Rights carry duties — the right not to be tortured brings the duty to respect it; due legal process can remove rights.
  • The Universal Declaration (1948) — written by the UN after the camps and Hiroshima; 30 articles, affirmed by 58 countries.
  • Guidelines, not law — the Declaration is not itself enshrined in law, though many countries have since passed their own.
  • The four named rights — liberty (Article 3), equality before the law (7), freedom of religion (18), freedom of speech (19).
  • Abuse is widespread — Amnesty International and UNICEF report torture in over eighty countries and speech limited in seventy.
More detail

Human rights are basic freedoms to which all human beings are entitled, and they have three defining characteristics. The three characteristics are a reliable 3-marker.

  1. Universal — everyone has them.
  2. Inalienable — people are entitled to them regardless of nationality, language, religion or ethnic origin; they cannot be taken away.
  3. Indivisible and interdependent — all the different rights are needed together for human beings to flourish and participate in society.

Rights must be balanced with duties: if I have the right not to be tortured, I have a duty to respect other people's right not to be tortured. Rights can be removed as a result of due legal process — being sent to prison.

They were codified in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, produced by the United Nations in 1948 after the world had seen the Nazi concentration camps, the treatment of Japanese prisoners of war and Hiroshima and Nagasaki. It contains 30 articles, and 58 countries — including African, Asian and Latin American ones — assembled to affirm it. If someone believes their rights have been abused they can have their case heard in international courts of appeal. Crucially, the Declaration only offers guidelines and is not itself enshrined in law, although many countries have since passed laws of their own.

The spec names four basic rights you must be able to discuss, and each has an article number worth quoting:

RightArticleWhere it gets contested
LibertyArticle 3 — "Everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of person"Abortion: a woman's freedom to choose, against the sanctity of life
Equality before the lawArticle 7 — "All are equal before the law and are entitled without any discrimination to equal protection of the law"Same-sex marriage on the same terms as heterosexual marriage
Freedom of religionArticle 18 — freedom of thought, conscience and religion, including freedom to change religion and to manifest it in teaching, practice, worship and observanceWearing visible signs of religious affiliation in public; praying for those in your care; Christians executed in the Middle East for not converting
Freedom of opinion and speechArticle 19 — freedom to hold opinions without interference and to seek, receive and impart information through any mediaWhether writers may use religious beliefs and figures in their stories; the Charlie Hebdo affair

The history is also examinable, and a date is cheap evidence. Originally people had rights only through membership of a family or tribe. Then: 539 BC, Cyrus the Great frees Babylon's slaves and declares that all may choose their own religion — the Cyrus Cylinder is held to be the first declaration of human rights. 1215 Magna Carta makes the king subject to the law. 1628 the Petition of Right to Charles I. 1776 the US Declaration of Independence — life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. 1789 the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. 1948 the Universal Declaration. 1953 the European Convention on Human Rights, enforceable at Strasbourg. 1998 the UK Human Rights Act, which brought those rights into UK law.

Abuse of human rights is the other half. Many countries that agreed to uphold the Declaration do not: people are "disappeared", tortured and executed for disagreeing with their governments, while those with power or money carry on criminal activity and the poor and uneducated have no recourse to a fair justice system. Amnesty International and UNICEF suggest torture occurs in over eighty countries, freedom of expression is limited in at least seventy, and slavery and forced labour are common in many.

The lesson's case study is from The Times, 26 July 2021: a 29-year-old woman, believed to be an evangelical Christian, wearing a Charlie Hebdo t-shirt was stabbed in the face at Speakers' Corner in Hyde Park by a man who fled the scene. Use it for the collision between freedom of speech (Article 19) and freedom of religion (Article 18) — the point being that two rights can conflict with each other, not only with the state.

subsections.heading: Christianity and human rights
subsections.html:
Spec 4.1 · Lesson 3, Revision Booklet 4 p.6–8

  • Three foundations — creation, stewardship and agape: everyone bears God's image, so rights are recognised rather than granted.
  • Galatians 3:28 — "neither Jew nor Greek… neither male nor female": the verse that makes freedom from discrimination Christian.
  • Authority comes from God — not from a state law or an agreement between countries, which is the key contrast with non-religious views.
  • Not every article unconditionally — for some Christians rights hold only where they do not contradict Christian teaching, as with abortion.
  • Oscar Romero — the Salvadorean archbishop shot dead at the altar in 1980 for defending the rights of the poor.
  • Desmond Tutu — the "voice of the voiceless", Nobel Peace Prize 1984, who called abusing someone made in God's image blasphemy.

Romero on why abusing rights is a religious offence

"There is no dichotomy between man and God's image. Whoever tortures a human being, whoever abuses a human being, whoever outrages a human being, abuses God."

— Oscar Romero. The sharpest one-line link between imago Dei and human rights, and a natural pair with Tutu's "blasphemy".

Desmond Tutu — the human rights quotations to learn

"I am not interested in picking up crumbs of compassion thrown from the table of someone who considers himself my master. I want the full menu of rights."

Used to argue that rights are owed, not granted as charity.

"When will we learn that human beings are of infinite value because they have been created in the image of God, and that it is a blasphemy to treat them as if they were less than this and to do so ultimately recoils on those who do this?"

The single best line for linking imago Dei to human rights: abusing rights is not merely unkind, it is blasphemy.

More detail

Christians support human rights because of the nature and teachings of God — the doctrine of creation, stewardship and agape. Many Christians think the Universal Declaration reflects Christian principles.

FoundationThe reasoningTeaching
The doctrine of creationAll humans are created in the image of God, so all deserve respect — rights are not granted by the state but recognisedGenesis 1:27, "the image of God"
StewardshipChristians are responsible for the world and for one another, which includes defending the rights of the vulnerableGenesis — humanity given care of creation
AgapeSelfless love of neighbour requires supporting rights such as equality before the law"Love your neighbour"; the Good Samaritan; the Golden Rule
Equality in ChristDistinctions of race, status and sex do not determine worth, so freedom from discrimination is a Christian principleGalatians 3:28 — "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus"
The sanctity of lifeThe right to life is already a commandmentExodus 20:13 — "you shall not kill", the sixth commandment
JusticeThe Old Testament prophets insisted on social justice, which is what rights are forIsaiah 1:17 — "Learn to do good; seek justice, correct oppression; bring justice to the fatherless, plead the widow's cause"

The key difference from the non-religious case: Christians argue human rights get their authority from God, not merely because countries agreed a set of guidelines or a state passed a law. Every human being has worth and dignity because every human being has been created by God — the first two chapters of Genesis teach that God created humanity in his image, set apart from the rest of creation to be in a relationship with him and to care for it. "The human rights to life, freedom, community and self-determination mirror God's right to the human being because the human being is destined to be God's image in all conditions and relationships of life" — Jürgen Moltmann.

Agape is specifically commanded: "you shall love your neighbour as yourself. There is no other commandment greater than these" (Mark 12:30–31), and the Golden Rule — "whatever you wish that men would do to you, do so to them" (Matthew 7:12). Jesus set the example by treating outcasts with kindness, healing people with leprosy and healing the Samaritan woman's daughter.

But Christians do not accept every article unconditionally: for some, rights are only valid if they do not contradict Christian teaching. A right to abortion, for example, collides with the sanctity of life, and conservative Christians dispute a right to same-sex marriage.

Christians who have fought for human rights. Followers of Liberation Theology hold that they have a duty to speak out against unjust governments and abuses of rights, and that a country run on structured violence should be challenged and changed to prevent continued oppression and poverty. Oscar Romero, a Roman Catholic archbishop in El Salvador, believed Christians must defend the weak and make a stand against social injustice; in his sermons he spoke about the rights of the poor and openly criticised the government. In 1980, while he was celebrating Mass, armed men burst into the cathedral and shot him dead in front of the altar.

Tutu (1931–2021) was born in Klerksdorp, Transvaal, and became the first Black Anglican Archbishop of both Cape Town and Johannesburg. Known as the "voice of the voiceless", he was an outspoken critic of apartheid and supported the economic boycott of South Africa, urging the UK government to use sanctions, while constantly encouraging reconciliation. He won the 1984 Nobel Peace Prize for his part in ending apartheid, and when Nelson Mandela became the nation's first Black president he appointed Tutu chairperson of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. He stated his objective as "a democratic and just society without racial divisions", demanding equal civil rights for all, a common system of education and an end to forced deportation. His reasons were explicitly religious: "all are God's children", we are a "human family", and Jesus was a man.

subsections.heading: Non-religious views of human rights
subsections.html:
Spec 4.1 · Lesson 4, Revision Booklet 4 p.6, 8

  • The split — are rights natural, or created by the state? The spec expects the named philosophers.
  • John Locke (1632–1704) — rights are self-evident and existed before civil society: life, liberty and property.
  • Jeremy Bentham (1748–1832) — natural rights are "nonsense on stilts"; the state creates rights and endorses them through law.
  • Hobbes and Rousseau — a social contract: surrender some freedom and accept obligations, and society protects your rights.
  • Amnesty International — founded by Peter Benenson in 1961; frees prisoners of conscience by letter-writing, publicity and protest.
  • Eleanor Roosevelt — chaired the UN Human Rights Commission and was instrumental in formulating the Universal Declaration.

Eleanor Roosevelt on where rights begin

"Where, after all, do universal human rights begin? In small places, close to home — so close and so small that they cannot be seen on any maps of the world… Unless these rights have meaning there, they have little meaning anywhere."

Used to argue that rights are practised in the home, school and workplace before they mean anything in law — the standard answer to "rights are just paperwork".

More detail

Non-religious thinkers divide over whether rights are natural or created by the state — and the spec expects the named philosophers.

ThinkerPositionWhy it matters
John Locke (1632–1704)Certain rights self-evidently apply to human beings because they naturally existed before people entered civil society. The main natural rights are to life, liberty and propertyThe classic secular case for universal rights without God
Jeremy Bentham (1748–1832), the father of UtilitarianismNatural rights are "nonsense on stilts" — "a natural right is a son that never had a father". The concept is a fiction invented by revolutionaries to undermine real laws, and following it would lead to anarchy; the state creates rights and endorses them through lawThe strongest objection to the whole idea of inalienable rights
Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679)Left unchecked, people would maximise their own well-being with no obligations to anyone else; a world of unlimited rights means chaos and a war against all, so a social contract is neededRights are the price of security, not a gift of nature
Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712–1778)Also argued for a social contract: surrender basic freedoms and accept moral obligations, and society can protect your rights. "Each of us puts his person and all his power in common under the supreme direction of the general will"Pairs with Hobbes for a 6-marker on non-religious arguments

Non-religious people also argue that rights are enshrined in law: it is a legal requirement in both international and national law to respect them, and the UK Human Rights Act 1998 asserts in Article 4 that "no one should be held in slavery or servitude". They add that all humans have reason and free will to determine their own future, and that nobody — not church nor state — should intervene in that.

Named non-religious campaigners.

  • Amnesty International, founded by Peter Benenson in 1961 after he learned of two Portuguese students imprisoned for seven years for raising their glasses in a toast to freedom in a Lisbon bar. He believed that if enough people protested together, governments could not get away with such intimidation. Its four aims: to free prisoners of conscience; to gain fair trials for political prisoners; to end torture, political killings and "disappearances"; and to abolish the death penalty throughout the world. Its methods are letter-writing, publicity and protest, plus practical help — persuading governments to let doctors visit prisoners, and raising money for food and clothing on release — and campaigning to change laws, including the international ban on torture and the abolition of the death penalty in the UK. It won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1977 and the United Nations Human Rights Prize in 1978.
  • Eleanor Roosevelt (1884–1962), wife of President Franklin D Roosevelt and called the "First Lady of the World" by President Truman. She advocated equal rights for women, African-Americans and Depression-era workers; when the Black singer Marian Anderson was denied Washington's Constitution Hall in 1939 because of her race, Roosevelt saw to it that she performed on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial instead. Appointed a UN delegate in 1946, as Chair of the United Nations Human Rights Commission she was instrumental in formulating the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, submitting it with the words that it "may well become the international Magna Carta for all men everywhere".

subsections.heading: Can human rights be restricted?
subsections.html:
Spec 4.1 · Lesson 5, Revision Booklet 4 p.8

  • Article 29.2 — the Declaration itself allows limits, on two grounds: the rights of others, and public order and general welfare.
  • Accepted examples — CCTV, wartime censorship, conscription, rationing, prison, and 28-day detention under the 2006 Terrorism Act.
  • The Utilitarian case — restriction is justified where more people benefit than suffer, such as torturing one terrorist to save many.
  • The Christian objection — worth comes from being created in God's image, so no one may limit the rights of a child of God.
  • Three problems with the concept — cultural neo-imperialism, impracticality, and the charge that it stifles progress.
  • Nietzsche (1844–1900) — "slave morality" protects the weak against a "master morality" of power and ambition: sheep against tigers.

The article that makes restriction arguable

"In the exercise of his rights and freedoms, everyone shall be subject only to such limitations as are determined by law solely for the purpose of securing due recognition and respect for the rights and freedoms of others and of meeting the just requirements of morality, public order and the general welfare in a democratic society."

— Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 29.2. Note the two grounds it gives: the rights of others, and public order and general welfare.

ArgumentCounter-argument
Utilitarian: restriction is justified if more people benefit from the limitation than suffer it — torturing one terrorist to save manyRights are universal and inviolable; the moment they are negotiable they are not rights at all. Amnesty International completely opposes torture and the death penalty and holds that other ways of solving problems must be sought
The UN Declaration itself permits it for public order and to protect others' rights (Article 29.2)Guidelines that allow exceptions are exactly what abusive governments exploit
Natural Law: an ordered society is a precondition of any rights being enjoyedChristian teaching: based on the doctrine of creation, human beings get their worth from being created by God in his image, so no human being has the right to abuse or limit the rights of a child of God
Christians may appeal to agape — restriction can be the most loving thing to do — and may want limits on rights that clash with the teachings of the Bible or the ChurchTerrorism and torture are always wrong, so neither can be a reason to abandon rights
ObjectionReply
Cultural neo-imperialism: the rights originated in the West, reflect Western interests and values, and are a weapon in an attempt at Western dominanceImperialism means imposing values on other nations, but the Declaration only provides guidelines; laws passed to enforce them operate within a state. And the 58 countries that affirmed it in 1948 included African, Asian and Latin American ones
Impracticality: it is logistically very hard to provide adequate food, clean water, education and shelter for people in poor, remote areas — and nearly impossible to force a country with a bad record to change. If rights cannot be universally accepted or enforced, the concept is arguably meaninglessA standard that is imperfectly met is still a standard, and international courts of appeal do exist
Stifling progress: Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) argued traditional morality benefits the weak but harms the strong, who could do better unconstrained. He contrasted "slave morality", which protects the weak by championing compassion and altruism, with "master morality", which values power, success, ambition and ruthlessness — the "sheep" against the "tigers"Christians answer directly from imago Dei: worth is not earned by strength, so protecting the weak is not a weakness in the system but its point

✗ "Human rights should never be taken away because they are human rights." — circular, no teaching, no development.
✓ "Article 29.2 of the Declaration itself allows suspension to protect others, and a Utilitarian would accept it where the outcome is better for the majority. However, Christians who ground rights in the image of God argue dignity must be respected at all times, because a right that can be withdrawn is only a privilege."

More detail

The Universal Declaration itself allows it: Article 29.2 states that human rights may be suspended in order to protect people. That single reference turns a vague answer into a precise one.

Situations the lesson lists: using the army to enforce a lockdown during a pandemic; imprisoning terrorist suspects without charge; preventing a face veil when giving testimony in court; torturing a terrorist suspect; censoring subversive newspapers; testing chemical agents on an unsuspecting public; preventing a known extremist from speaking publicly.

Accepted examples in practice: CCTV — limiting liberty, but a fair price for feeling safer. Wartime censorship, to preserve the secrecy of military plans, conscription, to keep the armed forces strong, and rationing. Detention of terrorists without arrest or trial — in Britain the 2006 Terrorism Act allowed police to detain terror suspects for up to 28 days without arrest, because evidence of terrorist activity is often on encrypted files and takes time to build into a case, while the risk to large numbers of people is high. Loss of liberty as punishment — prison, and the loss of the vote while a prisoner. And restraint in speech and religious practice so society can function: having freedom of speech does not mean using it to offend or abuse.

The spec also expects the problems with the concept itself — three of them, each with a reply:

subsections.heading: Gender bias, the growth of women's rights, and feminism
subsections.html:
Spec 4.2 · Lesson 6, Revision Booklet 4 p.11

  • Gender bias defined — stereotypes about how the genders should behave, limiting their capabilities and so their opportunities and rights.
  • It cuts both ways — women get less pay and promotion; men stereotyped as emotionally strong are reluctant to ask for help.
  • Six reasons rights grew — the suffragettes, the World Wars, contraception, the feminist movement, economic growth and education.
  • Mary Wollstonecraft (1792) — A Vindication of the Rights of Women argued educated women decide as capably as men.
  • The milestones — the vote at 30 in 1918, equal votes 1928, the Sex Discrimination Act 1975, the Equality Act 2010.
  • Emma Watson's HeForShe (2014) — the modern example: her UN speech argued gender equality is men's issue too.
More detail

Gender bias, or sexism, means preconceived ideas or stereotypes about how the genders should behave and think, and placing limitations on their capabilities — which restricts their opportunities and rights. "Showing preference to one sex over the other" is the short version.

Two points that lift an answer above the obvious. First, discrimination can be negative (a group is disadvantaged) or positive (a group is treated more favourably for what are believed to be good reasons) — so positive discrimination is itself contested. Second, gender bias cuts both ways: typically women are offered fewer options, receive less pay and are more likely to be judged by appearance, and are overlooked for promotion in favour of less qualified men, while suffering "everyday sexism". But men may struggle to get jobs in roles perceived as feminine such as nursing and primary school teaching, and the stereotype that men are more confident and emotionally stronger damages men's mental wellbeing by making them reluctant to express emotion or voice insecurity.

The spec wants both the history of how women's rights grew and the reasons it happened, so learn the six factors as a list.

  1. The suffragettes — campaigned for women's vote before WWI.
  2. The World Wars — women were employed in all areas, and there was no turning back afterwards.
  3. Contraception — the pill gave women control over their bodies, and so freedom and choice. The Abortion Act had the same effect.
  4. The feminist movement — campaigning for equal rights since the 1960s.
  5. Economic growth — women work, and societies generally become more liberal as they grow richer.
  6. Education — greater access has opened up opportunities.

The movement began in the eighteenth century with Mary Wollstonecraft (1759–1797), who published A Vindication of the Rights of Women in 1792. Influenced by the French Revolution, she argued that if all men were entitled to liberty, equality and fraternity then so were women, and that educated women would be just as capable of decision-making as men. Harriet Taylor Mill (1807–1858) added that women needed job opportunities and the vote.

The campaign for female suffrage was taken up by suffragists, who used non-violent methods, and suffragettes, who thought violence permissible given the urgency — public civil disobedience, rallies and acts of vandalism as well as leaflets.
