Many were arrested and went on hunger strike in prison, and the government's "Cat and Mouse Act" (1912) let hunger strikers out to recover before rearresting them. The milestones:

DateWhat changed
1870The Married Women's Property Act lets married women own their own property; previously it transferred to their husbands on marriage
1903The Women's Social and Political Union is founded in Manchester by Emmeline Pankhurst and her daughters Christabel and Sylvia
1918Women over 30 are granted the vote, and the Parliamentary Qualification of Women Act lets women stand as MPs
1928All women gain equal voting rights with men
1967The Abortion Act decriminalises abortion on certain grounds; the contraceptive pill arrives in the 1960s
1975The Sex Discrimination Act makes it illegal to discriminate against women in work, education and training; the Employment Protection Act introduces statutory maternity provision
1979Margaret Thatcher becomes the first female Prime Minister
1994Rape in marriage is made a crime, after fifteen years of campaigning
2010The Equality Act replaces previous anti-discrimination laws with a single Act, protecting people from discrimination in the workplace and wider society

During the two World Wars women filled the jobs normally done by men and showed they could be more than wives and mothers; economic growth and inflation made it acceptable to carry on working, and by the 1960s women made up 40% of the workforce. Motherhood became a choice rather than, in Queen Victoria's phrase, an "occupational hazard of being a wife".

But the job is not finished — needed for the "against" side of a 12-marker. Women still tend to earn less than men and hold far fewer positions of power: they are at least half the voting population but only a small percentage of MPs. Some argue it is unreasonable for women to expect the same careers as men because pregnancy and childbirth take up time and energy; others reply that parenting should be shared and employers should support family life with flexible hours. Elsewhere in the world women face unequal access to divorce and education, forced marriage and domestic violence — in 2012 the Pakistani schoolgirl Malala Yousafzai was shot in the head by the Taliban for blogging in favour of education for girls.

Kind of feminismAim
Liberal feminismChange institutions and governments to give women equal access to positions men have traditionally dominated
Radical feminismReshape society and restructure its institutions so they are no longer hierarchical and authoritarian
Cultural feminismPromote the feminine and nurturing qualities of women rather than trying to make women more like men

Feminism is the belief in the social, economic and political equality of the sexes. The movement largely originated in the West but is manifest worldwide. Non-religious views note that gender bias is embedded in society — few women head FTSE 100 companies, and "glass ceilings" persist in business — even though it is illegal to discriminate on gender.

Emma Watson's 2014 speech to the United Nations, launching HeForShe, is the usable modern example. Her argument is that gender equality is men's issue too: she has seen a father's role as a parent valued less by society, and young men unable to ask for help with mental illness "for fear it would make them less of a man" — suicide is the biggest killer of UK men between 20 and 49. "If men don't have to be aggressive in order to be accepted, women won't feel compelled to be submissive." She also noted that at current rates it will be 2086 before all rural African girls can have a secondary education.

subsections.heading: The role and status of women in the Christian community
subsections.html:
Spec 4.2 · Lesson 7, Revision Booklet 4 p.10–11

  • Equal worth, two readings — all Christians agree both sexes bear God's image, and disagree over what equality then requires.
  • Different but complementary — conservatives give the husband headship (Ephesians 5:23) and priesthood to men, citing 1 Timothy 2:11–15.
  • Vocation and ability — liberals assign roles by skills and talents, not gender, citing Genesis 1:27 and Galatians 3:28.
  • Denominations and dates — Church of England priests since 1994 and bishops since 2015; Baptists from the 1920s; Catholic and Orthodox never.
  • Mulieris Dignitatem (1988) — John Paul II named motherhood and virginity as women's vocations; many women found it patronising.
  • Why they disagree — the authority of the Bible, and how each church balances scripture, tradition and modern life.

The teachings quoted on both sides

"There's neither male nor female… all are one in Christ." — St Paul, Galatians 3:28. The liberal case in one line.

"Each of the two sexes is an image of the power and tenderness of God, with equal dignity though in a different way." — the Catechism of the Catholic Church. Note the exact move: equal dignity, different way.

"to remain at home, sit still, keep house and bring up children" — Luther, on a woman's role. Pope John Paul II: "the family comes first" — women should not be pressurised into working. A Roman Catholic declaration speaks of women's "special ability to humanize the family".

The document to name is Mulieris Dignitatem (1988), a letter in which Pope John Paul II described motherhood and virginity as the two great vocations of women, with the Virgin Mary as the supreme example of both: motherhood as a way of sharing God's creative purpose, virginity as a way of dedicating oneself to God. His aim was to show how highly the Church respects women — but many women have found the document patronising and narrow-minded, which is exactly the kind of appraisal a 12-marker rewards.

Argument — it is biasedCounter-argument
1 Timothy 2:11–15 — "I permit no woman to teach or to have authority over a man; she is to keep silent" — is in scripture, and Ephesians 5:23 makes "the husband... the head of the wife"Those texts were written in a patriarchal society and must be read in context; Galatians 3:28 — "all are one in Christ Jesus" — is the teaching most Christians now treat as decisive
Genesis 2:18 makes Eve "a helper as his partner", Adam is created first, and Genesis 3:16 says "he shall rule over you" — read as Eve being morally weaker and needing male guidanceGenesis 1:27 has both created at the same time and both in God's image, and Eve made from Adam's rib can equally mean God wanted them side by side
The Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches still refuse to ordain women, holding that the priest represents Christ and so should be male, and Jesus chose twelve male apostlesThe religion has changed: the United Reformed Church and Salvation Army always ordained women, the Baptists from the 1920s, and the Church of England has had women priests since 1994 and bishops since 2015
Mulieris Dignitatem (1988) names motherhood and virginity as women's two great vocations, which many women have found patronising and narrow-minded; Luther told women "to remain at home, sit still, keep house and bring up children"Its stated purpose was to show how highly the Church respects women, and the Catechism insists on "equal dignity though in a different way" — equal worth, differing roles, which is not a claim of inferiority
Assigning authority to men and domestic duty to women has the practical effect of bias, whatever the stated intentionJesus broke through the prejudice of his day: many of his followers were women, and in John 4 he reveals to a Samaritan woman that he is the Messiah — and the Bible has strong women such as Deborah and Mary Magdalene

✗ "Christianity is sexist because women can't be priests." — true of some denominations only, and it ignores the reasoning.
✓ "The Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches restrict priesthood to men, holding that the priest represents Christ and citing 1 Timothy 2:11–15 and Jesus' choice of male apostles. The Church of England has ordained women as priests since 1994 and bishops since 2015, and the Salvation Army and United Reformed Church always have. Naming the denomination and the date is what moves this from assertion to understanding."

More detail

All Christians agree men and women are of equal worth because both are created in the image of God — but they interpret "equality" in two different ways, and that is the whole of this topic. Jesus was sent to save all from sin, men and women alike; all will be judged at the Eschaton; and St Paul emphasised equality in Galatians 3:28. The split is over what follows.

PositionWhat it saysEvidence used
Different but complementary roles (traditional / conservative)Equal worth, differing roles — partly because of different biological composition: men are generally physically stronger and so expected to go out to work, while women can bear and feed children and so are best suited to rearing them. In the home the husband is head of the family; in the Church, Roman Catholic and Orthodox denominations hold that women cannot be priests because the priest represents Christ and so should be male, but women can take pastoral duties, care for the building and contribute to worship — many belong to the Mother's UnionGenesis 2:18 — "I will make him a helper as his partner", and Adam created before Eve; Genesis 3:16 — "he shall rule over you"; Genesis 3 read as Eve being morally weaker and needing male guidance; Ephesians 5:23 — "the husband is the head of the wife just as Christ is the head of the church"; 1 Timothy 2:11–15 — "I permit no woman to teach or to have authority over a man; she is to keep silent"; Jesus chose only men as apostles
Vocation and ability (liberal)Role in home and church should be decided by skills and talents, not gender. Husband and wife share equally the roles of providing and caring, listening, compromising and deciding togetherGenesis 1:27 — Adam and Eve created at the same time, both in God's image; Genesis 2 — Eve from Adam's rib, which can mean God wanted them side by side; Galatians 3:28; Jesus broke through prejudice by recognising the worth of women — many of his followers were women, and in John 4 he reveals to a Samaritan woman at a well that he is the Messiah. The patriarchal texts must be read in context: both Testaments were written in a patriarchal society, Jesus was bound to choose men, and Paul was concerned not to upset Roman society while Christianity sought legal recognition. The instruction that women keep silent may reflect the fact that the home — the wife's domain — doubled as the place of worship

Where the denominations actually stand — this is the detail that separates a top answer from a vague one:

  • The United Reformed Church and the Salvation Army have always accepted women on equal terms with men.
  • The Baptists began ordaining women in the 1920s.
  • The Church of England has ordained women as priests since 1994 and as bishops since 2015.
  • The Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches do not ordain women, holding that the priest represents Christ.

Why do Christians disagree? Two reasons, and they are worth stating explicitly: the authority of the Bible — conservatives take the patriarchal texts seriously, liberals regard them as of their time — and the fact that different churches balance scripture, tradition and modern life differently. Points often added: conscience; the strong women in the Bible such as Deborah and Mary Magdalene; and the Church of England's position that it is up to a couple to decide, provided children are taken seriously. The family is also called the "domestic church".

"Christianity is biased in favour of men" is the standard 12-marker, and both columns have scripture behind them:

subsections.heading: Disability — attitudes, rights and Christian action
subsections.html:
Spec 4.2 · Lesson 8, Revision Booklet 4 p.11–13

  • Two Christian attitudes — compassion and equal worth, against a minority reading of disability as punishment for sin.
  • John 9 — Jesus denies that the blind man or his parents sinned: the direct refutation of the punishment view.
  • Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9) — David gave Jonathan's lame son his grandfather's lands and a permanent place at the king's table.
  • Jean Vanier and L'Arche (1964) — he shared his house at Trosly-Breuil with two disabled men; now 120 communities in 30 countries.
  • L'Arche has no clients or staff — disabled people are core members, assistants live in the houses, and all share responsibility.
  • Prejudice persists — disabled employment is 44% against 75%, and 66% report aggression, hostility or name-calling.

Jean Vanier on why L'Arche exists

"Jesus is the starving, the parched, the prisoner, the stranger, the naked, the sick, the dying. Jesus is the oppressed, the poor. To live with Jesus is to live with the poor. To live with the poor is to live with Jesus."

Used to argue that serving the marginalised is not charity added onto faith — it is the faith. Compare the parable of the sheep and goats.

Argument — they do enoughCounter-argument
L'Arche: Jean Vanier shared his own home from 1964, and there are now over 120 communities in 30 countries where disabled people are core members rather than clients, with no shift work and no staffMany churches admit they do not do enough to welcome disabled people, and access to some buildings is still limited
In worship: accessible buildings, large-print hymn books and service sheets, hearing loops, communion taken to the housebound, services of healing, chaplains who minister to the deaf and blind, and pilgrimages to LourdesSome of the tradition pulls the other way: Leviticus 21:17–20 barred the disabled from the priesthood, and Jesus' healing miracles can be read as implying disability is something to be removed rather than included
Liveability runs care homes, provides accessible holidays and rehabilitates people with brain injuries; Through the Roof makes the Christian message accessible and advises churches on practical projectsThe figures show what has not been fixed: employment 44% against 75%, 66% having faced aggression or name-calling, and poverty twice the rate for non-disabled adults
The teaching is unambiguous: all are made in God's image, "all are one in Christ", love your neighbour, David's care for Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9), and in John 9 Jesus denies that disability is punishment for sinChristians have sometimes made it worse: in 1999 Glenn Hoddle, a born-again Christian, claimed disabled people were being punished for sins from a former life
Christians defend disabled life before birth on the sanctity of life, as Joanna Jepson did in 2001 in challenging a late abortion for cleft lip and palateAround 90% of couples told their unborn baby has a disability still abort, and 92% of Down's syndrome pregnancies are terminated — so the Christian argument is not winning in practice
More detail

Christian attitudes to disability split sharply: some texts treat disability as punishment, while the dominant modern view treats it as calling for compassion and equal worth. Give both, because the spec asks for "reasons for differing attitudes".

AttitudeReasoning and evidence
PositiveEveryone, able-bodied or disabled, is created in the image of God; "all are one in Christ"; love your neighbour and the Good Samaritan, whose example Jesus tells his listeners to copy. King David showed compassion to Jonathan's disabled son Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9): though lame in both feet, David saw to it that he inherited his grandfather's lands and invited him to eat at the king's table for life. Deuteronomy 27:18 — "cursed be anyone who misleads a blind person on the road". And in John 9, asked whether a blind man or his parents had sinned, Jesus answered "neither this man nor his parents sinned; he was born blind so that God's works might be revealed in him" — the direct refutation of the punishment view. Pope Francis kissed a severely disabled man
NegativeSome texts suggest God uses physical and mental ailments to punish: Leviticus 21:17–20 states that the disabled cannot be priests, and Deuteronomy 28:28–29 warns Israel that breaking the covenant will bring "madness, blindness, and confusion of mind". Jesus' cure of a paralysed man, where he declared the man's sins forgiven, has been read as implying a connection; Matthew 12:22 links muteness and blindness to demon possession. In 1999 the England coach Glenn Hoddle, a born-again Christian, claimed people with disabilities were being punished for sins from a former life — the modern example, and one most Christians reject. Note that Jesus' miracles sit on both sides: healing implies compassion, but also that disability is something to be removed

Jesus' healing ministry is the single strongest piece of evidence for the compassionate reading. He healed the blind, the lame, those with withered arms, lepers, the deaf and the paralysed — people whose condition had made them outcasts — and treated them as equals needing practical help and inclusion. Mark 1:40–44: a leper begs him, "If you choose, you can make me clean", and "moved with pity, Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him". The touch is the detail worth noting — touching a leper was itself forbidden.

The sanctity of life follows from creation and stewardship: all life comes from God, who created all people in his image, able-bodied and disabled, so all life must be respected. This is why the Roman Catholic Church and many other Christians oppose abortion on the grounds of disability. The figures make the issue live: around 90% of couples told their unborn baby has a disability choose to abort, and 92% of mothers diagnosed with a Down's syndrome pregnancy terminate. In 2001, Joanna Jepson, an Anglican priest with a jaw deformity herself, legally challenged the late abortion of a 28-week-old foetus with a cleft lip and palate, arguing this did not constitute a "serious handicap" under the 1967 Abortion Act. Some argue aborting disabled foetuses is a form of eugenics and breaches the Disability Discrimination Act.

The history. For much of it there was no social welfare for those unable to work; in the medieval period monasteries and convents cared for the sick and disabled, which ended with the dissolution of the monasteries. The Elizabethan Poor Law of 1601 specified that those unable to work — the "deserving poor" — should be helped in their local parish poorhouses. By the nineteenth century philanthropists established charities, but in the early-to-mid twentieth century many disabled children did not attend mainstream schools, mothers of disabled children were encouraged to place them in institutions, and shops, cinemas, theatres and workplaces rarely provided access.

Why attitudes changed: injured servicemen returning from the World Wars, who were thought to have a right to care given their sacrifice and who also changed the perception of disability — many remained fit, healthy and able to contribute fully; recognition of human rights generally; momentum from the feminist and civil rights movements; campaigns by individuals and charities such as Leonard Cheshire; changing healthcare and the end of the asylum; more mixing in society, with disabled children taught in mainstream schools; more openness about mental health; and the Paralympic movement. The shift in the later twentieth century was from looking after disabled people to helping them live independent lives.

DateWhat changed
1920The Blind Persons' Act promotes the welfare of blind people, allowing a pension at 50 rather than 70
1944The Disabled Persons' Employment Act makes better provision for disabled people to secure employment
1952Scope is founded, aiming to ensure disabled children have equal rights to education
1970MP Alf Morris' Chronically Sick and Disabled Persons' Act: local authorities must provide for disabled people's needs, with equal rights to education and recreation, and public buildings should be accessible with disabled parking and toilets
1995The Disability Discrimination Act prohibits discrimination in employment, education and the provision of goods and services — ramps in shops, support for disabled staff
2000The Disability Rights Commission is founded to stop discrimination and promote equality of opportunity
2010The Equality Act unifies previous anti-discrimination law

But prejudice persists — figures for the "against" side of an evaluation. More than one billion people worldwide experience some form of disability, and 10.9 million live in Great Britain. The employment rate for disabled people is 44% against 75% for people without disabilities. 66% say they have experienced aggression, hostility or name-calling, and 46% experience discrimination daily or weekly. The poverty rate for disabled adults is twice that for non-disabled adults, and 98% of disabled children in developing countries have no access to basic services. Stigma around mental health is fuelled by stereotypes — that such people are dangerous or violent — when in fact they are at greater risk of being attacked or of harming themselves.

The named Christian example: Jean Vanier and L'Arche. In 1964, Jean Vanier (1928–2019), a Canadian academic, invited Raphaël Simi and Philippe Seux, two men with intellectual disabilities, to share his life in an old house at Trosly-Breuil in France. They called the home L'Arche — "the Ark", after Noah's: the biblical symbol of deliverance, and of God's covenant with humanity, a refuge from a prejudiced world. Inspired by the Beatitudes, which begin "Blessed are the poor" (Matthew 5:1–12), Vanier was among the first in the modern age to say it is not right to lock people up in institutions, believing instead that those the world would rather lock away have much to teach us and can even heal us.

Today there are over 120 communities in 30 countries, each of 2 to 8 houses, many running day programmes, workshops and retreat centres. The detail that earns the marks is how L'Arche differs from a group home: there are no "clients" and "staff" and no shift work. Disabled people are core members, those who assist them are assistants, the assistants live in the houses as they would with any family, and everyone is equally responsible for the life of the community. The Charter of L'Arche says the members "are called to be one body. They live, work, pray and celebrate together, sharing their joys and their suffering and forgiving each other, as in a family. They have a simple life-style which gives priority to relationships."

Other Christian work: Liveability runs care homes, provides accessible holidays and rehabilitates people with brain injuries; Through the Roof ensures the Christian message is accessible to people with any type of disability and advises churches on practical projects.

In worship — five practical actions, enough for a 6-marker on putting belief into action: buildings are made accessible with suitable facilities; large-print hymn books and service sheets are provided for the visually impaired and hearing loops for those hard of hearing; clergy visit the housebound, taking them the sacrament of communion; churches hold services of healing and prayers for the sick and disabled; and many have chaplains or trained individuals who minister to the deaf and blind, with special services to support them. Pilgrimages are made to places of healing such as Lourdes.

Many churches admit they do not do enough to welcome disabled people. In wider society there is still prejudice and discrimination, a lack of equality in employment, and limited access to some buildings, though clubs such as PHAB (Physically Handicapped and Able Bodied) bring disabled and non-disabled young people together.

The 12-marker here is usually "Christians do enough to support disabled people", so the two columns are worth having:

subsections.heading: The multi-ethnic society — benefits and problems
subsections.html:
Spec 4.3 · Lesson 9, Revision Booklet 4 p.16

  • Multi-ethnic society defined — many ethnic groups living together; Britain always has been, from the Romans to the Windrush Generation.
  • Census evidence — White fell from 91% in 2001 to 85.4% in 2011 while Asian rose to 7.8%: quote the change.
  • Benefits against problems — diversity, tolerance, skills and new ideas, against segregation, the 2001 Bradford and Oldham riots and strained infrastructure.
  • Enoch Powell — the named critic, whose "Rivers of Blood" speech (1968) warned of a lack of integration.
  • Three terms kept apart — prejudice is pre-judging, discrimination is prejudice acted on, racism is both against another ethnicity.
  • Laws do not change attitudes — the pivot of most 12-markers, so education, role models, shared values and campaigns are needed too.
More detail

A multi-ethnic society is one in which people of many different ethnic groups live together. Britain always has been one: the Romans invaded the Celts, then the Germanic tribes collectively called the Anglo-Saxons, then the Normans in 1066; the slave trade brought increasing numbers of people from different ethnic groups; and in the twentieth century people from the Commonwealth came to fight for Britain in the World Wars and then to fill the post-war labour shortages — the Windrush Generation. Diversity is uneven: London and Leicester are among the most diverse areas, while rural Devon, Cornwall, parts of Wales and the Lake District are much less so.

The census figures turn "Britain is diverse" into evidence, and the change between censuses is the better detail:

Ethnic group2001 census2011 census
White91%85.4%
Asian5.4%7.8%
Black2.3%3.5%
Mixed1.4%2.0%
Other0.4%1.0%
BenefitProblem
Cultural diversity — different food, music, clothing, beliefs, customs and the artsSegregation and divided communities: the "herd instinct" means people stick to those they identify with
It removes ignorance about people from different backgrounds, and so builds greater tolerance of differenceSegregation can lead to racial tensions that erupt into violence — in 2001 Bradford and Oldham experienced race riots, with petrol bombs, bricks and bottles thrown at police
A greater skill set and economic benefitLanguage and cultural barriers within communities, and a lack of integration
It sparks new ideas — fusions that enhance creativityStrain on infrastructure such as education
It puts the ideals of equal rights and opportunities into practiceConcern that it undermines national heritage and identity

The named critic is Enoch Powell, a Conservative politician, whose "Rivers of Blood" speech in 1968 warned about a lack of integration and the fragmentation of society: "As I look ahead, I am filled with foreboding: like the Roman, I seem to see the River Tiber foaming with much blood." He also claimed increased diversity would leave English people feeling "strangers in their own country". Segregation has been documented since — Ed Hussain's Among the Mosques (2021) noted separate white and Asian areas in Bradford and Blackburn. On language, there is evidence that pupils who speak English as a second language underperform in primary education but mostly catch up in secondary school, though poor communication remains a barrier to integration and employment.

The three technical terms must be kept apart — this is a standard 3-marker and a standard source of lost marks:

ConceptDefinitionHow to overcome it
PrejudicePre-judging — making up your mind without the full factsEducation, empathy, experience, protest, prayer
DiscriminationPutting prejudice into action — doing something negative that shows your prejudiceLegislation, direct action, example
RacismPrejudice and discrimination against people of another ethnicityLegislation, example, action (King, Tutu), forgiveness, prayer, events promoting understanding

Why racism occurs: socialisation — children brought up by racist parents or influenced by racist adults; fear of difference in appearance, language or customs, and low self-esteem leading people to single out a perceived weaker group to boost their own sense of worth; and poverty — a shortage of resources and jobs leading people to blame ethnic minorities rather than poor government. The consequences are worth stating too: resentment and division, less trust and community cohesion, isolated minority groups withdrawing, fewer opportunities and poorer physical and mental wellbeing — social tensions that can erupt into violence and rioting.

How racial harmony is promoted. Laws and sanctions, so that prejudiced or discriminatory behaviour can be punished:

DateLegislation
1976The Race Relations Act makes direct or indirect discrimination on grounds of race, colour or nationality illegal, and creates the Commission for Racial Equality
1986The Public Order Act bans inciting racial hatred
2000The Race Relations Act is amended: public bodies have a duty to encourage good race relations
2010The Equality Act unifies all previous anti-discrimination law; discrimination on grounds of race, nationality and ethnicity is forbidden, and employers must ensure employees are not subject to discriminatory behaviour by third parties

But laws do not change attitudes — say that, because it is the pivot of most 12-markers here. So also: education, teaching children about different religions, nations and ethnicities to remove ignorance, ideally by meeting and mixing with people from other cultures; positive role models in the public eye, to counteract negative stereotypes; shared values — in November 2014 the Department for Education published guidance on promoting British values in schools, naming democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, and mutual respect and tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs; campaigns such as football's Show Racism the Red Card; and the United Nations' continuing work against racism. Churches were instrumental in bringing in the Race Relations Act — the Church of England has bishops in the House of Lords. In August 2021 Stephen Cottrell, Archbishop of York, argued for an expansive vision of English and regional identity as a route to national unity, pointing to the monarchy, the Church, the NHS and the World Service as institutions that share a sense of public service and the common good.

subsections.heading: Christian teachings on racism and racial harmony
subsections.html:
Spec 4.3 · Lesson 10, Revision Booklet 4 p.15–17

  • The doctrine of creation — if one God made all the nations (Acts 17:26), no nation can be superior.
  • Galatians 3:28 — covers race, class and sex at once: the single most useful verse in the module.
  • The Dutch Reformed Church and apartheid — it backed Malan's 1948 laws, using Noah's curse of Canaan (Genesis 9:18–27) to justify inferiority.
  • The religion corrected itself — the World Alliance of Reformed Churches declared apartheid a heresy in the early 1980s and expelled that church.
  • Named Christians — Martin Luther King's 382-day bus boycott, Tutu's "rainbow nation", Trevor Huddleston in the townships, Pope Francis on immigrants.
  • Leicester (BBC, 2001) — a harmony role model: council intolerance of racism, local dialogue, ethnic representation in government, religious leaders co-operating.
  • The non-religious case for racial harmony — one human species, the UDHR and the Equality Act, Humanist "one life, one world", and the practical gains of a diverse society.

The texts that promote racial harmony

"From one man he made all the nations, that they should inhabit the whole earth; and he marked out their appointed times in history and the boundaries of their lands."

— Acts 17:26. Used to argue that all ethnic groups share one origin, so racial hierarchy is a denial of creation.

"As for those who were held in high esteem — whatever they were makes no difference to me; God does not show favouritism — they added nothing to my message."

— Galatians 2:6. Used to argue that God is impartial, so Christians must be too.

"There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus."

— Galatians 3:28. The single most useful verse in the whole module: it covers race, class and sex at once.

"When a foreigner resides among you in your land, do not mistreat them. The foreigner residing among you must be treated as your native-born. Love them as yourself, for you were foreigners in Egypt."

— Leviticus 19:33–34. Used to argue the duty to the outsider is in the Law itself, with a reason attached: Israel had been the outsider.

"Stop judging by mere appearances, but instead judge correctly." — John 7:24, the most direct text against prejudice. And "A new command I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you must love one another" — John 13:34.

"Let justice flow down like a river" — Amos. Used to argue racial equality is a demand of justice, not of politeness.

Argument — Christianity has promoted racial harmonyCounter-argument — Christians have done harm
Acts 17:26 — "from one man he made all the nations" — and Galatians 3:28 make a racial hierarchy a denial of the doctrine of creation itselfThe Dutch Reformed Church supported apartheid from 1948, using Genesis 9:18–27, Noah's curse of Canaan, to claim Black people were inferior
Leviticus 19:33–34 puts the duty to the foreigner in the Law, with a reason attached — "for you were foreigners in Egypt" — and John 7:24 forbids judging by appearancesDeuteronomy 7:1–3 has God telling Israel to "destroy them totally" and "do not intermarry with them", so the covenant strand can be read as exclusive
Jesus' example: the Good Samaritan makes the ethnic outsider the hero rather than the helpless victim; he healed the Roman centurion's servant (Luke 7:1–10) and discussed theology with a Samaritan woman (John 4)In the Crusades thousands were killed in the name of Christianity, tens of thousands were massacred in South America to force conversion, and missionaries during colonialisation were patronising towards those they converted
Named Christians acted on it: Martin Luther King, Desmond Tutu, Trevor Huddleston, Pope Francis on immigrants — "God will judge us on how we treated the most needy" — and William Wilberforce against the slave tradeMany Christians were themselves involved in the slave trade, and churches were instrumental in the Race Relations Act only after centuries in which they were not
The religion corrected itself: in the early 1980s the World Alliance of Reformed Churches declared apartheid a heresy and expelled the Dutch Reformed Church, which has since expressed repentanceThat it took until the 1980s is itself the objection: scripture can be bent to whatever a culture already believes, so religion is as much a mirror of a society's racism as a cure for it
More detail

The doctrine of creation is the foundation: if one God made all nations, no nation can be superior.

Also used: Genesis 1:27, all created in God's image; the Good Samaritan (Luke 10), where the neighbour to be loved is the ethnic outsider — and note the second point, that by making the Samaritan the helper rather than the victim, Jesus refuses to stereotype other ethnic groups as helpless, presenting them instead as dignified members of society with their own positive qualities; Jesus' example — he healed the Roman centurion's servant (Luke 7:1–10) and discussed theology with a Samaritan woman (John 4); Ruth, a foreigner in the line of David; and Moses leading the Israelites out of slavery in the Exodus, the model of liberation that Martin Luther King's "promised land" imagery draws on.

Be honest about the other side — the examiner rewards it. The main theme of the Old Testament is the covenant between God and his chosen people, so some passages have God helping them conquer neighbouring peoples and discouraging mixing: Deuteronomy 7:1–3 — "then you must destroy them totally. Make no treaty with them, and show them no mercy. Do not intermarry with them."

And Christians have used their faith to oppress. In the Crusades thousands were killed in the name of Christianity. When the Spanish navy invaded South America, tens of thousands of local people were massacred in attempts to force conversion and steal their wealth. During colonialisation many missionaries were patronising towards the people they tried to convert. Many Christians were involved in the slave trade — though William Wilberforce campaigned against it.

The fullest case is apartheid, and the whole arc is worth learning because it shows the religion correcting itself. In 1948 the South African Prime Minister Daniel François Malan, a Dutch Reformed minister, introduced the apartheid legislation, supported by the Dutch Reformed Church, which used Genesis 9:18–27 — Noah's curse of his grandson Canaan — to claim that treating Black people as inferior was justified. In the early 1980s the World Alliance of Reformed Churches declared apartheid a heresy and expelled the Dutch Reformed Church; in 1986 all its congregations were desegregated; in 1994 apartheid was abolished; and the Church has since expressed repentance.

Christians who actively promoted racial harmony:

  • Martin Luther King (1929–1968) — born in Atlanta, Georgia, to a Baptist minister and ordained a Baptist minister himself in 1947; a Doctor of Philosophy at 26. He learnt at home and in church that God had created everyone in his own image, but on the streets he was refused permission to play with white children and saw the Ku Klux Klan beating Black people. As pastor in Montgomery, Alabama, he became president of the Montgomery Improvement Association in 1955 and led a 382-day bus boycott after the arrest of Rosa Parks — the bus companies lost more than half their income, and the American Civil Rights Movement began. He followed a policy of non-violent protest — petitions, demonstrations and sit-ins — influenced by Jesus' teachings and the example of Gandhi, while being harassed by police, having his house bombed and receiving constant threats. In August 1963 he led a march of 250,000 to Washington and delivered the "I have a dream" speech at the Lincoln Memorial; the Civil Rights Bill passed in 1964, the year he won the Nobel Peace Prize, donating the $54,000 to the movement. He was shot dead on 4 April 1968 in Memphis. "We must not allow our creative protest to degenerate into physical violence. Again and again, we must rise to the majestic heights of meeting physical force with soul force." "I have a dream that one day on the red hills of Georgia, the sons of former slaves and sons of former slaveowners will be able to sit down together at the table of brotherhood."
  • Desmond Tutu (1931–2021) — former Archbishop of Cape Town, who opposed apartheid, campaigned for racial harmony and used his high profile to challenge human rights injustices; he led the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which allowed South Africa to discuss its past and move forward. He calls South Africa a "rainbow nation".
  • Trevor Huddleston (1913–1998) — an Anglican priest who worked in a South African township and was an early opponent of apartheid.
  • Pope Francis — campaigns to end prejudice and discrimination against immigrants to Italy: "God will judge us on how we treated the most needy".

Racial harmony in practice — the spec wants examples, including local ones.

  • South Africa after apartheid, through the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.
  • Southwark Cathedral in London has many Zimbabwean members who read the lessons in a Zimbabwean dialect and support the church in Zimbabwe — churches in cities often have diverse congregations.
  • Leicester. On 29 May 2001 the BBC reported that the city should be seen as a role model in racial harmony, having transformed a poor reputation over about thirty years through: a clear message from the local council that racism would not be tolerated; local people creating dialogue so problems could be discussed and solved; a wide variety of ethnic groups represented in local government so all felt they had a voice; and religious leaders meeting to discuss issues in a spirit of co-operation. Those four points make a strong 6-mark answer on how harmony is achieved.
  • The London 2012 Olympics, which brought British people together with a common aim and a shared sense of achievement.

The 12-marker is usually "religion has done more harm than good in race relations", and the honest answer uses both columns:

Non-religious attitudes to racial harmony — asked directly and more than once, so it needs its own answer rather than "they agree with Christians". (1) Science: there is one human species and race has no biological basis, so racism rests on a factual mistake — the human genome shows all modern humans share a recent African origin. (2) Rights and the law: the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) opens with everyone being "born free and equal in dignity and rights", and in the UK the Race Relations Act 1976 and the Equality Act 2010 make racial discrimination illegal; non-religious campaigners therefore treat harmony as a matter of enforceable equality rather than of charity. (3) Humanism: with one life and one world, there is no reason to divide it by ancestry, and Humanists UK campaigns against discrimination of every kind; Utilitarians add that prejudice reduces total happiness, and the social contract argument of Hobbes and Rousseau says a society only works if its members accept each other as equals. (4) Practical benefits: a diverse society gains skills, labour, trade, food, music and ideas, while segregation costs it — the 2001 Bradford and Oldham riots are the example to cite. (5) How they would promote it: education and the curriculum, anti-racism in sport and the media, mixed schools and workplaces, and prosecuting racist crime — essentially the same programme as the churches, minus the theology. A non-religious person may also be the critic here: Rowan Atkinson argued that criticising a religion must stay lawful even though criticising a race must not, and the same voices sometimes say religion itself divides communities and that a secular public space is the better route to harmony.

subsections.heading: The multi-faith society and interfaith relationships
subsections.html:
Spec 4.4 · Lesson 11, Revision Booklet 4 p.18–19

  • Multi-faith society defined — several religions co-existing in one community; the UK is one, Saudi Arabia is not.
  • The 2011 census — Christian 59.4%, no religion 24.7%, Muslim 5.0%: the figures that turn the claim into evidence.
  • Benefits — greater tolerance, free choice of religion, creativity from dialogue, and a powerful united voice for social justice.
  • Difficulties — meeting every believer's needs, practices clashing with UK law, diluted national identity, and strain on interfaith marriages.
  • How it is promoted — Isaac Poobalan lending his church to Muslim neighbours, interfaith networks, the Equality Act 2010, and compulsory RE.
  • Rowan Atkinson's objection — criticising a religion is a freedom, unlike criticising a race; the 2006 Act passed without that clause.
More detail

A multi-faith society is one in which a number of different religions co-exist in one community. Historically most people lived where a single faith dominated and was tied to the law, marriage customs and education. The UK is now multi-faith; Saudi Arabia is not.

Factors that produced multi-faith societies: migration from one country to another, foreign travel, easy and speedy access to information, intercultural marriage, and increased tolerance of religious diversity.

Religion (2011 census)Percentage of the UK population
Christian59.4%
No religion24.7%
Not stated7.2%
Muslim5.0%
Hindu1.5%
Sikh0.8%
Jewish0.5%
Buddhist0.4%

In some local areas Christians and atheists are in the minority. The visible signs are everywhere: churches, mosques, synagogues, mandirs and gurdwaras in most towns and cities; religious education in the basic curriculum; and local businesses catering to faith communities — kosher butchers, religious bookshops, travel agents offering hajj packages.

BenefitDifficulty
Increased tolerance of different beliefs and practices, because living among people of many faiths removes the ignorance and fear of difference that heightens tensionIt may be difficult to meet the needs of all believers — not every community can have its own place of worship, not every religion can be covered in a school RE syllabus, and employers may struggle to let all staff be absent for their festivals and holy days
It provides choice — people can practise the religion of their choice freely, because a local faith group exists to practise it with. Colourful festivals and celebrations make for an interesting communitySome beliefs and practices may be incompatible with the laws or customs of a country — bigamy is forbidden in the UK, and kosher and halal slaughter are regarded by many as cruel
Greater creativity — interfaith dialogue leads to new ideas and practices and enhances people’s lives; many people, religious and not, find the Buddhist practice of meditation and mindfulness usefulIt may dilute national identity and make community cohesion harder, or cause social division
When united, the faiths can be a powerful voice for social justiceInterfaith marriage may add to the stresses of married life and parenthood: couples may find it hard to agree how to raise their children, and studies show children of a mixed-faith marriage are much less likely to be brought up as observant members of either religion
People can learn from each other, sharing their own faiths and customsSome believers regard their own faith as exclusively true and may refuse to mix with members of other faiths or let their children learn about them — which leads to social division and raised tensions

Responsibilities of living in a multi-faith society: tolerance; respecting others' freedom of speech and religion; allowing freedom of worship and making allowances for holy days and festivals; setting aside prejudice; government legislating to protect all religions; and all faiths supporting shared values.

How the development of a multi-faith society is promoted.

  • Religious. The Revd Isaac Poobalan, a parish priest in Scotland, let Muslim worshippers from the mosque next door use his church for their prayers after seeing them worshipping in the street on a cold winter's day for lack of space: "Jesus taught his disciples to love your neighbour as yourself and this is something I cannot just preach to my congregation, I had to put it into practice." The Church of England supports the Council of Christians and Jews, the Inter Faith Network for the UK and the Christian Muslim Forum. The congregation of Southwark Cathedral visits mosques and synagogues regularly and discusses issues of mutual interest. A national Interfaith Week is supported by most churches.
  • Legislation. The Racial and Religious Hatred Act 2006 makes it illegal to do anything that might be perceived as inciting religious hatred; the Equality Act 2010 reiterates that discriminating on the basis of religion is illegal.
  • Government initiatives. In 2008 the Government published Face to Face and Side by Side, built on three core principles — partnership, empowerment and choice — aiming to encourage interfaith dialogue, increase collaborative social action between faith communities, maintain good relations with wider civil society, and overcome barriers facing young people and women. The Inter Faith Network for the UK, founded in 1987, promotes understanding and co-operation between people of different faiths and organised the UK's first Multi-Faith Week in 2009.
  • Education. Religious education is part of the basic curriculum and compulsory for pupils aged 5 to 18 in maintained schools unless withdrawn by their parents; since a change of policy in 2016, all students taking GCSE RS must explore the beliefs and practices of at least two world religions.

The counter-view, held by some non-religious people, is that religion should be a private matter: signs of religious affiliation should not be evident in public, and religious organisations and beliefs should receive no special treatment. When the racial and religious hatred bill was first proposed it would have been an offence to use insulting language about a religion; writers, comedians and actors objected, and Rowan Atkinson argued: "to criticise a person for their race is manifestly irrational and ridiculous but to criticise their religion, that is a right. That is a freedom." The Act passed in 2006 without that clause, and the advocacy group Liberty held that "free speech is far more precious than protection from being offended". Use this for any 12-marker on limits to freedom of speech.

subsections.heading: Ecumenism — unity within Christianity
subsections.html:
Spec 4.4 · Lesson 12, Revision Booklet 4 p.19

  • Ecumenism defined — the movement for unity and co-operation between denominations, from the Greek oikoumene, "whole, inhabited world".
  • It began in 1910 — the World Missionary Conference in Edinburgh: bickering would hinder the Gospel and contradict agape.
  • The World Council of Churches (1948) — about 400 million Christians, 340 churches, 120 countries; Rome sends observers but has not joined.
  • The Lima Document (1982) — mutual recognition of baptism, a weekly Eucharist, and a role in ministry for all Christians.
  • Taizé — Brother Roger's 1940 community in France where Catholic and Protestant monks live, and young pilgrims pray in chant.
  • Churches Together and Street Pastors — local denominations co-operating in joint worship, social action and street patrols.
More detail

Ecumenism is the movement to promote unity and co-operation between the different Christian denominations. The word comes from the Greek oikoumene, meaning "whole, inhabited world". It accepts the diversity of Christians but strives to bring the different communities together in one fully committed fellowship to serve God's purpose in the world. The spec counts interdenominational relationships as a form of interfaith work, so this topic answers questions about Christians "promoting unity within their faith community".

  • Why it is necessary, and how it began. The modern movement began at the World Missionary Conference in Edinburgh in 1910. It was designed to help Christians work together in spreading the Gospel, on the view that bickering between denominations would inhibit that work — and that division would itself undermine the Christian message of agape. Division has also fed sectarian conflict, as in Northern Ireland.
  • The World Council of Churches, established in 1948, to pray for and pursue the visible unity of Christ's Church, preach the Gospel and promote justice and peace. It represents approximately 400 million Christians in more than 340 churches and denominations across 120 countries, and meets every seven years with around a thousand delegates. The Roman Catholic Church has not joined, but recognises the need to move towards mutual understanding and sends observers. In 1982 the WCC produced the Lima Document, with three conclusions: mutual recognition of each other's baptism, since all are baptised into the body of Christ; all churches should celebrate the Eucharist at least once every Sunday; and all Christians should have a role in the Church's ministry.
  • Churches Together groups — local co-operation between denominations, committing to an ongoing relationship: joint acts of worship, social gatherings, discussion groups and shared charity projects.
  • Taizé — an ecumenical monastic order founded by Roger Louis Schutz-Marsauche (Brother Roger) in 1940 in south-east France, to provide a place of reconciliation in view of the Second World War. About a hundred Roman Catholic and Protestant monks belong, living at Taizé or in poor areas of Asia, Africa and South America; they earn their own keep and give the rest of their time to the needy. After the war it became a major site of pilgrimage, and tens of thousands of young people now come to study the Bible, join discussion groups, share the chores and take part in worship three times a day. The worship uses the community's distinctive music — simple phrases, usually from the Psalms, set to music and repeated as a prayer chant to aid prayer and meditation. All are welcome regardless of religious affiliation, so unity is practised rather than merely discussed.
  • Street Pastors is also explicitly ecumenical, with many different churches involved — a useful example of denominations working together in practice.

subsections.heading: Christianity and other religions — the four attitudes
subsections.html:
Spec 4.4 · Lesson 13, Revision Booklet 4 p.19

  • Exclusivism — only Christianity saves: "No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6).
  • Inclusivism — other faiths hold real truth; Karl Rahner's "anonymous Christians", and "My Father's house has many rooms" (John 14:2).
  • Pluralism — all religions are equally valid routes to one Reality; John Hick's blind men and the elephant. No biblical support.
  • Proselytisation — converting others, commanded in the Great Commission: "Go into all the world and proclaim the good news" (Mark 16:15).
  • The baseline is tolerance — rejected by a Samaritan village, Jesus rebuked James and John and simply moved on (Luke 9:52–56).
  • Conversion and colonisation — missionary work travelled with colonisation, reshaping whole cultures: the strongest objection, and a historical fact.

The three salvation texts

"For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save the world through him." — John 3:17. Used by inclusivists and pluralists: God's purpose is saving, not condemning.

"Jesus answered, 'I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.'" — John 14:6. The exclusivist text.

"Salvation is found in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to mankind by which we must be saved." — Acts 4:12. Also exclusivist, and worth having as a second reference.

ArgumentCounter-argument
Proselytisation is a duty: Jesus commanded it, and if exclusivism is true then withholding the gospel condemns peopleIt can be disrespectful and coercive, and it treats another person's faith as merely a mistake
Pluralism produces harmony in a multi-faith society and reflects God's transcendenceIt has no biblical support, and it empties the incarnation of its significance — why send the Son if any path will do?
Inclusivism keeps Christian truth claims while allowing a loving God to save the good, and is the basis of the Church of England's interfaith work"Anonymous Christians" arguably patronises other faiths by relabelling them
Conservative and evangelical Christians argue preaching to non-believers is itself an expression of love for neighbour, since they believe salvation requires accepting Jesus' sacrificeMany liberal Christians reply that there are better ways to love a neighbour — practical support such as food, clothing and shelter — and that shared beliefs make dialogue the better route
Exclusivism takes Jesus' own words at face valueIt condemns those who lived before Christ or never heard of him, which looks incompatible with a loving God
More detail

Christian attitudes to other religions come in four named positions, and using the four words correctly is the single clearest way to reach the top level in this spec area. They all start from salvation — being saved from sin — which Christians believe was made possible by Jesus' death and resurrection. The three-way division was identified by the theologian John Hick (1922–2012).

Begin from the general position, because it frames the rest: Christians believe in human rights, including the right to religious freedom, and using Jesus' Golden Rule — "do unto others as you would have them do unto you" — most think they must respect other people's faith if they expect theirs to be respected. They can also follow Jesus' example: when his message was rejected he simply moved on. In Luke 9:52–56, when a Samaritan village would not welcome him, James and John asked, "Lord, do you want us to call fire down from heaven to destroy them?" — and "Jesus turned and rebuked them", then went to another village. So the baseline Christian attitude is tolerance and mutual understanding.

PositionWhat it claimsWho holds it, and the key teaching
ExclusivismChristianity is the only path to salvation. The incarnation was a unique revelation of God; Original Sin placed a barrier between God and humanity, and Jesus' sacrifice paid the debt of sin, so accepting it is what makes atonement possible. Those who reject Christ are damnedConservative Christians, Roman Catholics and some Anglicans. "I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6); "Salvation is found in no one else" (Acts 4:12)
InclusivismChristianity has unique doctrines, but other religions' truth claims and good works have real validity: followers of other religions genuinely believe in God, and the points of overlap are where interfaith dialogue becomes possible. A loving God would not condemn good people who never heard of ChristKarl Rahner (1904–1984), a Roman Catholic theologian, who coined "anonymous Christians" for those who live like Christians without identifying as such. John 14:2 — "My Father's house has many rooms" — is the text. The Church of England's interfaith work follows from this position
PluralismAll religions are equally valid — different expressions of one Ultimate Reality. God is so vast and so far beyond human understanding that we can only have limited knowledge of him, so every religion offers real truths through the revelations it has received without having a complete knowledge. Christ's teaching, like the teachings of other religions, encourages personal transformation from self-centred to God-centred, so all religions can lead to GodLiberal Christians; the theologian John Hick, who used the analogy of the elephant and the blind men: one felt a leg and reported "a great living pillar", another the trunk and reported "a great snake", another a tusk and reported "a sharp plough-share" — "of course they were all true, but each referring only to one aspect of the total reality". Also 2 Peter 3:9 — "He is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish, but everyone to come to repentance". Critics note it has no support in the Bible, so many Christians reject it
ProselytisationConverting a person from one faith to another. Christianity is an evangelical religion: Christians are taught to follow Jesus' example and preach the Gospel so that others have the possibility of salvation. A missionary is someone sent out by a church to a particular area to encourage people to join the Christian community; evangelical work is proclaiming the message with the aim of converting peopleTechnically most Christians, but practised most by evangelical Protestants. Instigated by Jesus himself in the Great Commission: "Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation" (Mark 16:15–16), and "As the Father has sent me, so I send you" (John 20:21–22)

How it actually works, for a 6-marker. Much local missionary work centres on the parish church — the building and its worship bear witness in the area, while the congregation visits people at home, distributes leaflets about services, and runs outreach for families, legal or financial advice and food banks. Nationally, Evangelism UK coordinates: the Alpha Course, introducing non-Christians to the basics of the faith through talks and discussions, run in local churches by all denominations; Hope, providing resources for local evangelism; Urban Saints, running youth groups, events, holidays and mission trips; Scripture Union, encouraging use of the Bible; and Youth for Christ, resourcing churches and schools. In Lent 2012 the Roman Catholic Church established Mission Metropolis to revive the faith in Europe's major cities. Evangelical Protestants committed to global evangelism at the Lausanne International Congress on World Evangelisation in Switzerland in 1974, and modern missionary efforts have been more sensitive to local cultures, helping local people organise their own church life and appoint their own leaders.

Historically, conversion often went hand in hand with colonisation, where Europeans tried to reshape a country's customs, culture, language and religion in their own image — which is why much of south and central America is Catholic and much of north America and sub-Saharan Africa Protestant. That is the strongest objection to missionary work, and it is a historical fact rather than an opinion.

subsections.heading: Relationships between the rich and the poor
subsections.html:
Spec 4.5 · Lesson 14, Revision Booklet 4 p.21

  • The real question — not whether wealth is wrong, but whether its distribution obliges the rich to help the poor.
  • Absolute poverty (UN, 1995) — severe deprivation of food, safe water, sanitation, health, shelter, education and information.
  • The Brandt Report (1980) — the developed world holds 25% of the world's population and around 80% of its wealth.
  • Two sets of causes — low pay, unemployment and family breakdown everywhere; unfair trade, debt, war and disasters in developing countries.
  • The Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation (2000) — over $49 billion, run by venture philanthropy: business methods aimed at disease and poverty.
  • Toby Ord's Giving What We Can (2009) — 6,000+ members pledge a tenth of their income to the most effective charities.
Religious argumentNon-religious argument
Isaiah 58 — "Share your bread with the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house: and when you see the naked cover him"The UK committed to the UN in the 1970s to spend 0.7% of gross national income on foreign aid; the target was met in 2013 and enshrined in law in 2015. In 2020 Britain spent £14.5 billion, mostly in African and Asian countries on humanitarian aid and health. In 2021 the government cut the budget to 0.5% — around £10 billion — calling it temporary and blaming Covid-19; aid groups warned it would harm the world's poorest and damage Britain's reputation
The parable of the rich man and Lazarus — the rich man goes to hell because he did not help the poor man at his gateHuman rights — everyone has a right to life, which is empty without the means to live
The parable of the sheep and goats — you will be judged on how you helped the poor, and in helping the poor you help GodPoverty slows economic development, so reducing it benefits everyone
The rich young man — "sell all you have and give to the poor"; "it's easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the Kingdom of God"Many global corporations exploit low wages in developing countries and so have an obligation to help
Argument — they have a dutyCounter-argument
The sheep and goats — "just as you did it to one of the least of these… you did it to me" (Matthew 25:31–40) — makes it a matter of judgement, not choiceWealth itself is not wrong; the module's own point is that it is the distribution of wealth that is the concern, so someone who earns honestly and gives has nothing to answer for
The parable of the rich man and Lazarus: the rich man goes to hell because he did not help the poor man at his gateGiving can create dependency, which is why Christian Aid works on skills and education for self-reliance rather than aid alone — so the duty is not simply to hand over money
The rich young man is told to "sell all you have and give to the poor", and "it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for someone who is rich to enter the kingdom of God" (Mark 10:25)Jesus warned his disciples to give for the love of God rather than public acclaim, so giving out of obligation misses the point — and John Wesley's "earn all you can, save all you can, give all you can" assumes earning comes first
Justice, not only charity: "let justice flow down like a river" (Amos), and Amos 8:4–6 condemns those diligent in ritual while cheating the poor — so the duty is to change unjust structures, as Liberation Theology arguesThe causes in developing countries are structural — unfair trade, debt, war, over-population, natural disasters — so individual generosity cannot fix them and the duty really falls on governments
Non-religious arguments agree: everyone has a right to life, which is empty without the means to live, and global corporations that exploit low wages owe something backToby Ord's point cuts both ways — what matters is effectiveness, not amount — and the UK cut aid from 0.7% to 0.5% in 2021 with public support, which suggests most people treat it as optional
More detail

The spec's central question is whether wealthy individuals and countries have a responsibility towards the poor. Wealth in itself is not a bad thing; it is the distribution of wealth that is the concern. Absolute poverty was defined by the United Nations in 1995 as "a severe deprivation of basic human needs, including food, safe drinking water, sanitation facilities, health, shelter, education and information".

The headline evidence is the 1980 Brandt Report, which identified an imbalance between developed and developing countries: the developed world contains 25% of the world's population but around 80% of its wealth. The Report advocated long-term action on the causes of poverty, requiring changes in both the developing and developed worlds — and little has changed since.

Causes of poverty — keep the two lists separate, because the spec distinguishes them:

In many countriesAdditional factors in developing countries
Low paid work; unemploymentUnfair trade
Family breakdowns and illnessDebt to developed countries
Inadequate social benefitsOver population
Discrimination and social inequalityWar and political instability
GamblingA lack of education and opportunity
Alcoholism and other drug dependencyEnvironmental problems and natural disasters

Examples of practical generosity.

  • Religious: the clergy and congregation of Southwark Cathedral support the Robes Project, which shelters London's homeless from November to April each year. Many churches run food banks.
  • Bill and Melinda Gates were moved to act by a newspaper article about millions of children dying of preventable diseases, and set up the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation in 2000. With assets of over $49 billion it is the second largest charitable foundation, and works by venture philanthropy — applying business techniques to fight disease, poverty and inequity, identifying the world's most pressing problems and then using investment, grants and partnerships to bring resources and expertise together. Gates has encouraged other billionaires to pledge the same.
  • Toby Ord (b.1979), an Australian philosopher based in Oxford, founded Giving What We Can in 2009; its 6,000+ members pledge at least 10% of their income over their careers, and the aim is not just to give but to research the most effective charities so the money has the greatest impact. His own reasoning: "if my money could help others much more than it helps me, then why not?" — he calculated that donating to the most efficient charities could save tens of thousands of years of healthy life.

"The rich have a duty to help the poor" is the 12-marker, and the teaching is heavily on one side — which means the counter-arguments have to be found rather than guessed:

subsections.heading: Christian teachings on poverty — charity, justice and compassion
subsections.html:
Spec 4.5 · Lesson 15, Revision Booklet 4 p.22

  • Answer in three words — charity, justice and compassion, each with a teaching and an example, all resting on creation, stewardship and agape.
  • Charity — loving kindness beyond self-interest, close to agape: "Sell your possessions and give to the poor" (Luke 12:33).
  • Christian Aid (1947) — the agency of over 40 denominations, in 70 countries: emergency relief, then skills and education for self-reliance.
  • Justice — a fair distribution of resources, not merely law and order; Amos condemned ritual alongside cheating the poor.
  • Liberation Theology — South American base communities with no hierarchy; Romero protested peacefully, Camilo Torres took up a gun.
  • Compassion must act — Albert Schweitzer's hospital at Lambaréné grew to 500 patients, and his 1952 Nobel money started a leprosarium.

✗ "Christians help the poor because they are nice people." — no teaching, no term, no example.
✓ "Christians help the poor out of agape and because of stewardship. The parable of the sheep and goats teaches that they will be judged on how they treated the needy, and in helping the poor they help God — which is why Christian Aid works for long-term development, not only emergency relief."

More detail

The spec asks how the poor should be treated "as expressed in the ideals of charity, justice and compassion" — so answer in those three words, each with a teaching and an example. All three rest on creation, stewardship and agape.

IdealTeachingExample in practice
Charity — acts of loving kindness that go beyond self-interest; in the Bible the word is often interchangeable with agape, so charitable acts are a way of emulating God's grace. In practice, helping with aid or by teaching new skillsThe early Christians shared everything: "No one claimed that any of his possessions was his own, but they shared everything they had"; the rich young man, prompting Jesus to say "it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for someone who is rich to enter the kingdom of God" (Mark 10:25); "Sell your possessions and give to the poor. Provide purses for yourselves that will not wear out, a treasure in heaven that will never fail" (Luke 12:33); John Wesley, founder of the Methodists — "Earn all you can, save all you can, give all you can"; "Faith without good works is dead" (James); "He who gives to the poor will lack nothing" (Proverbs 28:27). Jesus warned his disciples to give for the love of God rather than public acclaim. Many Christians in England paid tithes — a tenth of income — to their parish church until 1936; today most services include collections, and Christians also give time (charity shops, food banks, soup kitchens) and skillsChristian Aid — the official aid agency of over 40 denominations in the UK and Ireland, founded in 1947 to help those who had lost homes, families and possessions in WWII; through the 1950s and 60s its focus moved from Europe to other countries facing poverty and injustice. It works in over 70 countries with more than 500 partner organisations, aims to "strengthen the poor", and does not force religion on anyone. Short term: emergency relief after natural disasters. Long term: skills and education so people become self-reliant, plus health education, immunisation, training local nurses and midwives, and in recent years the education of women. Campaigning: for fair wages and fair-trade conditions, and lobbying government to drop developing-world debt, as in Jubilee 2000
Justice — a fair society: not just law and order but a fair distribution of resources so all have a comfortable and productive lifeIsaiah 61:8 calls God a lover of justice, and Psalm 24:1 reminds people that the earth is owned by the Lord and everything in it — the basis of stewardship. "Learn to do good, seek justice" (Isaiah 1); "A righteous man knows the rights of the poor" (Proverbs); "Let justice flow down like a river" (Amos). The Old Testament prophets had to ensure social justice as well as deliver God's message: Amos condemned people who were diligent in religious ritual while cheating the poor — "skimping on the measure, boosting the price and cheating with dishonest scales, buying the poor with silver and the needy for a pair of sandals" (Amos 8:4–6). Christians today think global inequality is unjust and against God's will, and that they must raise awareness and campaign for changeLiberation Theology, which emerged in South America to end the poverty produced by oppressive structures — partly influenced by Marxism and mostly by Jesus' teaching and example. Catholics set up base or grass-roots communities, with no hierarchy, in which every member is valued and has a role in worship and organisation, and worship is informal, spontaneous and joyful — so the community itself does not reflect the unjust social order. Liberation theologians advocate protest, mostly non-violent but confrontational. Peaceful: Oscar Romero. Violent: Camilo Torres — "I took off my cassock and picked up a gun"
Compassion — the ability to feel what someone else is feeling. But compassion is more than feeling another's pain: it should lead to action"The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim freedom for the prisoners and recovery of sight for the blind, to set the oppressed free, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favour" (Luke 4:18–19) — Jesus' mission statement at the start of his ministry. The parables of the Good Samaritan and the Sheep and Goats: "for I was hungry and you gave me food… just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me" (Matthew 25:31–40). The epistles press the same point: "rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep" (Romans 12:15); bear one another's burdens to fulfil the law of Christ (Galatians 6:2); and since Jesus laid down his life for humanity, Christians should lay down theirs for their brothers and sisters (1 John 3:16)Mother Teresa. Albert Schweitzer (1875–1965), a theologian and concert organist who funded his medical training with his concert earnings, took his M.D. in 1913 and founded a hospital at Lambaréné in French Equatorial Africa, expanding it with his royalties and donations to seventy buildings caring for over 500 patients at a time. He received the Nobel Peace Prize for 1952 and used the $33,000 to start a leprosarium

Why Christians might prefer some charities to others: they may choose ones founded on Christian ideals, such as the Salvation Army and Christian Aid, which help the homeless, those with addictions and those in poverty — the point the Model Answer makes when explaining differing attitudes to giving.

The facts you cannot sit the paper without

Three foundations of every Christian answer here: the doctrine of creation (imago Dei), stewardship, agape.

Rights: universal · inalienable · indivisible and interdependent. UDHR 1948, UN, 30 articles, 58 countries — guidelines, not law. The four named rights and their articles: liberty (3), equality before the law (7), freedom of religion (18), freedom of opinion and speech (19). Article 29.2 permits suspension to protect others' rights and for public order. History: Cyrus Cylinder 539 BC · Magna Carta 1215 · Petition of Right 1628 · US Declaration of Independence 1776 · Declaration of the Rights of Man 1789 · UDHR 1948 · European Convention 1953 · UK Human Rights Act 1998.

Christian grounds: creation (imago Dei), stewardship, agape. Galatians 3:28 · Exodus 20:13 · Isaiah 1:17 · Mark 12:30–31 · Matthew 7:12. Moltmann; Romero — "whoever abuses a human being, abuses God"; Tutu — "a blasphemy".

Non-religious thinkers: Locke (1632–1704, natural rights to life, liberty and property), Bentham (1748–1832, "nonsense on stilts", "a natural right is a son that never had a father"; the state grants rights), Hobbes (1588–1679) and Rousseau (1712–1778) — social contract. Nietzsche (1844–1900) — slave morality v master morality, rights stifle the strong.

Named campaigners: Desmond Tutu (1931–2021; Nobel Peace Prize 1984; TRC; "rainbow nation"), Oscar Romero (shot at the altar, El Salvador, 1980), Martin Luther King (1929–1968; Montgomery bus boycott 382 days; march of 250,000, Aug 1963; Nobel 1964; shot 4 April 1968), Eleanor Roosevelt (1884–1962; Chair of the UN Human Rights Commission; "small places"), Amnesty International (Peter Benenson, 1961; Nobel 1977), Jean Vanier (1928–2019; L'Arche, 1964), Mother Teresa, Albert Schweitzer (Lambaréné; Nobel 1952), Bill and Melinda Gates (Foundation, 2000), Toby Ord (Giving What We Can, 2009).

Women: Galatians 3:28 and Genesis 1:27 against Genesis 2:18, Genesis 3:16, Ephesians 5:23 and 1 Timothy 2:11–15. Six reasons rights grew: suffragettes, the World Wars, the pill, the feminist movement, economic growth, education. 1870 Married Women's Property Act · 1903 WSPU (Emmeline Pankhurst) · 1918 vote at 30 · 1928 equal vote · 1967 Abortion Act · 1975 Sex Discrimination Act · 1979 Thatcher · 2010 Equality Act. Three feminisms: liberal, radical, cultural. Mulieris Dignitatem 1988. Ordination: Salvation Army and United Reformed always; Baptists 1920s; Church of England priests 1994, bishops 2015; Roman Catholic and Orthodox not.

Disability: positive — imago Dei, Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9), Deuteronomy 27:18, John 9 ("neither this man nor his parents sinned"), Mark 1:40–44, Pope Francis. Negative — Leviticus 21:17–20, Deuteronomy 28:28–29, Matthew 12:22 (possession), Glenn Hoddle 1999. Law: 1601 Poor Law · 1944 Disabled Persons' Employment Act · 1952 Scope · 1970 Chronically Sick and Disabled Persons' Act (Alf Morris) · 1995 DDA · 2000 Disability Rights Commission · 2010 Equality Act. Figures: 1bn+ worldwide, 10.9m in GB, employment 44% v 75%, 66% faced hostility, 92% of Down's pregnancies terminated. L'Arche (core members and assistants), Liveability, Through the Roof, Lourdes, PHAB.

Multi-ethnic UK: 2011 census — White 85.4%, Asian 7.8%, Black 3.5%, Mixed 2.0%, Other 1.0% (2001: 91 / 5.4 / 2.3 / 1.4 / 0.4). Race Relations Act 1976 (+ Commission for Racial Equality) · Public Order Act 1986 · RRA amended 2000 · Equality Act 2010 · British values guidance Nov 2014. Enoch Powell's "Rivers of Blood" 1968; Bradford and Oldham riots 2001; Leicester as a role model (BBC, 29 May 2001); London 2012. Acts 17:26 · Leviticus 19:33–34 · Galatians 2:6 · John 7:24 · Luke 7:1–10 · John 4 · Luke 10. Negative: Deuteronomy 7:1–3; Genesis 9:18–27 used by the Dutch Reformed Church; apartheid 1948–1994, declared heresy in the early 1980s.

Multi-faith UK: 2011 census — Christian 59.4%, no religion 24.7%, Muslim 5.0%, Hindu 1.5%, Sikh 0.8%, Jewish 0.5%, Buddhist 0.4%. Racial and Religious Hatred Act 2006 · Equality Act 2010 · Face to Face and Side by Side 2008 (partnership, empowerment, choice) · Inter Faith Network for the UK 1987, first Multi-Faith Week 2009 · two religions at GCSE from 2016. Revd Isaac Poobalan; Council of Christians and Jews; Christian Muslim Forum; Southwark Cathedral.

The four attitudes (the three-way division is John Hick's): exclusivism (John 14:6, Acts 4:12), inclusivism (Karl Rahner, "anonymous Christians", John 14:2), pluralism (John Hick, the elephant and the blind men, 2 Peter 3:9), proselytisation (the Great Commission, Mark 16:15–16; John 20:21–22; Alpha Course; Lausanne 1974). Ecumenism (Greek oikoumene): Edinburgh 1910 · World Council of Churches 1948, 400m Christians, 340+ churches, 120 countries, Lima Document 1982 · Churches Together · Taizé (Brother Roger, 1940).

Rich and poor: absolute poverty defined by the UN in 1995. Brandt Report 1980 — 25% of people, 80% of the wealth. UK foreign aid 0.7% (met 2013, in law 2015, £14.5bn in 2020, cut to 0.5% in 2021). Christian Aid (1947; 40+ denominations; 70+ countries; 500+ partners; Jubilee 2000). Liberation Theology and base communities; Camilo Torres. Charity (Mark 10:25, Luke 12:33, tithes until 1936), justice (Isaiah 61:8, Psalm 24:1, Amos 8:4–6), compassion (Luke 4:18–19, Matthew 25:31–40, Romans 12:15, Galatians 6:2, 1 John 3:16).

The 12-mark frame
