Five paragraphs, in this order. The top band needs Christian teaching in every one of them, at least one named example, and a conclusion that actually decides — so write the conclusion you are heading for before you start.

  1. Restate the statement and say what turns on it. One or two sentences naming the real question — whether rights may ever be restricted, whether the Church is biased against women, whether all religions are equally true, whether the rich owe the poor anything.
  2. The strongest case for, with teaching and scripture. One argument developed, then appraised. Build it from the three foundations — the doctrine of creation (imago Dei), stewardship and agape — and anchor it in a verse: Galatians 3:28, Acts 17:26, Matthew 25:31–40, Isaiah 1:17. Attach a named example, because this section rewards them more than any other: Tutu, Romero, King, Roosevelt, Vanier, Amnesty, Christian Aid.
  3. The strongest case against, with teaching and scripture. Same again from the other side — 1 Timothy 2:11–15, Leviticus 21:17–20, Genesis 9:18–27 as the Dutch Reformed Church used it, John 14:6 — and say which of the two arguments is stronger and why. The appraisal is where the AO2 marks are, not the listing.
  4. Where Christians disagree with each other. The paragraph that reaches the top level, because it shows the disagreement is internal to the religion: complementary roles against vocation and ability; Roman Catholic and Orthodox practice against the Church of England since 1994 and 2015; exclusivism, inclusivism and pluralism — use the technical words. Then add a non-religious view for perspective: Locke, Bentham, Hobbes and Rousseau on rights, Nietzsche on protecting the weak, Utilitarianism, Toby Ord on effective giving. Remember it does not count as the reference to a religion.
  5. A conclusion that decides. Name the winning argument, say why it outweighs the other, and tie it back to the words of the statement.

Sentence starters that earn the evaluation marks:

  • "Most Christians would agree with this statement, because the doctrine of creation teaches…"
  • "A Christian who follows Natural Law would argue…"
  • "However, a Utilitarian would respond that…" / "A situation ethicist would ask only what is most loving, and so…"
  • "This argument is the stronger of the two, because…"
  • "Christians themselves are divided here: a conservative Christian citing 1 Timothy… whereas a liberal Christian citing Galatians 3:28…"
  • "An exclusivist would reject this outright, while an inclusivist such as Rahner would…"
  • "A Humanist, who grounds rights in reason rather than God, would say…"
  • "On balance, I agree with the statement, because the teaching that every person bears the image of God outweighs…"

subsections.heading: Quotes to learn
subsections.html:
The marks in this section live in the quotations and the named examples. These are the quotations worth knowing word-for-word; the front of the card is the topic and the reference, so you can test whether you can produce the words from the prompt alone.

Equality in Christ — Galatians 3:28"There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus"Used to argue: race, status and sex do not determine worth, so freedom from discrimination is a Christian principle — the single most useful verse in the module, because it covers race, class and sex at once
Abusing a human abuses God — Oscar Romero"There is no dichotomy between man and God's image. Whoever tortures a human being, whoever abuses a human being, whoever outrages a human being, abuses God."Used to argue: an abuse of human rights is a religious offence, not merely a political one — the sharpest one-line link between imago Dei and human rights
Rights and the image of God — Desmond Tutu"When will we learn that human beings are of infinite value because they have been created in the image of God, and that it is a blasphemy to treat them as if they were less than this and to do so ultimately recoils on those who do this?"Used to argue: abusing rights is not merely unkind but blasphemy — pair it with Tutu's "I want the full menu of rights", that rights are owed and not charity thrown from a master's table
Natural rights denied — Jeremy Bentham"a natural right is a son that never had a father"Used to argue: the strongest objection to inalienable rights — they are "nonsense on stilts", a fiction invented by revolutionaries, and it is the state that creates rights and endorses them in law
When rights may be limited — Universal Declaration, Article 29.2"In the exercise of his rights and freedoms, everyone shall be subject only to such limitations as are determined by law solely for the purpose of securing due recognition and respect for the rights and freedoms of others and of meeting the just requirements of morality, public order and the general welfare in a democratic society."Used to argue: the Declaration itself permits restriction, on two grounds — the rights of others, and public order and the general welfare
Where rights begin — Eleanor Roosevelt"Where, after all, do universal human rights begin? In small places, close to home — so close and so small that they cannot be seen on any maps of the world… Unless these rights have meaning there, they have little meaning anywhere."Used to argue: rights are practised in the home, school and workplace before they mean anything in law — the standard answer to "rights are just paperwork"
Equal dignity, different roles — the Catechism"Each of the two sexes is an image of the power and tenderness of God, with equal dignity though in a different way."Used to argue: the traditional Christian position is equal worth with differing roles, not female inferiority — note the exact move, equal dignity in a different way
Women to keep silent — 1 Timothy 2:11–15"I permit no woman to teach or to have authority over a man; she is to keep silent"Used to argue: the conservative case for male leadership in home and church — liberals reply that it was written in a patriarchal society, and that the home, the wife's domain, doubled as the place of worship
Gender equality as men's issue — Emma Watson"If men don't have to be aggressive in order to be accepted, women won't feel compelled to be submissive."Used to argue: gender bias harms men too, so equality is not a women's cause only — her 2014 HeForShe speech to the United Nations, the usable modern non-religious example
Disability is not punishment — John 9"neither this man nor his parents sinned; he was born blind so that God's works might be revealed in him"Used to argue: the direct refutation of the view that disability is punishment for sin — quote it against Leviticus 21:17–20 and Glenn Hoddle
Why L'Arche exists — Jean Vanier"Jesus is the starving, the parched, the prisoner, the stranger, the naked, the sick, the dying. Jesus is the oppressed, the poor. To live with Jesus is to live with the poor. To live with the poor is to live with Jesus."Used to argue: serving the marginalised is not charity added onto faith — it is the faith; compare the parable of the sheep and goats
One origin for all nations — Acts 17:26"From one man he made all the nations, that they should inhabit the whole earth; and he marked out their appointed times in history and the boundaries of their lands."Used to argue: all ethnic groups share one origin, so a racial hierarchy is a denial of creation itself
The duty to the foreigner — Leviticus 19:33–34"When a foreigner resides among you in your land, do not mistreat them. The foreigner residing among you must be treated as your native-born. Love them as yourself, for you were foreigners in Egypt."Used to argue: the duty to the outsider is in the Law itself, with a reason attached — Israel had been the outsider
Non-violent protest — Martin Luther King"We must not allow our creative protest to degenerate into physical violence. Again and again, we must rise to the majestic heights of meeting physical force with soul force."Used to argue: racial justice is pursued without violence, following Jesus' teaching and Gandhi's example — pair it with "I have a dream… the table of brotherhood"
Exclusivism — John 14:6"Jesus answered, 'I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.'"Used to argue: Christianity is the only path to salvation — the exclusivist text, with Acts 4:12, "Salvation is found in no one else"
Inclusivism — John 14:2"My Father's house has many rooms"Used to argue: other religions' truth claims have real validity and a loving God would not condemn those who never heard of Christ — Karl Rahner's "anonymous Christians", and the basis of Church of England interfaith work
The Great Commission — Mark 16:15–16"Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation"Used to argue: proselytisation is a duty instigated by Jesus himself, which is why Christianity is an evangelical religion — with John 20:21–22, "As the Father has sent me, so I send you"
Judged on the needy — Matthew 25:31–40"for I was hungry and you gave me food… just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me"Used to argue: Christians will be judged on how they treated the poor, and in helping the poor they help God — the parable of the sheep and goats, the central text for compassion
Wealth and the kingdom — Mark 10:25"it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for someone who is rich to enter the kingdom of God"Used to argue: wealth is a spiritual danger, so charity is expected rather than optional — the rich young man is told to "sell all you have and give to the poor"
Social justice — Amos 8:4–6"skimping on the measure, boosting the price and cheating with dishonest scales, buying the poor with silver and the needy for a pair of sandals"Used to argue: the prophets demanded social justice as well as ritual, so poverty is an injustice against God's will — which is why Christians campaign for change and do not only give

subsections.heading: Examples to learn
subsections.html:
More than any other section this one wants named people and organisations, and the 12-markers are won with them. Learn them the same way as the quotations: the name on the front, what it was and what it shows on the back.

Human rights campaigning — Amnesty InternationalFounded by Peter Benenson in 1961, after he learned of two Portuguese students imprisoned for seven years for raising their glasses in a toast to freedom in a Lisbon bar. Four aims: free prisoners of conscience, gain fair trials for political prisoners, end torture, political killings and "disappearances", and abolish the death penalty worldwide. Methods: letter-writing, publicity and protest, plus practical help and campaigning to change laws. Nobel Peace Prize 1977; UN Human Rights Prize 1978.Used to argue: ordinary people acting together can stop a government getting away with intimidation — and because Amnesty opposes torture absolutely, it is the counter to the Utilitarian case for suspending rights
The Universal Declaration — Eleanor Roosevelt(1884–1962) Wife of President Franklin D Roosevelt and called the "First Lady of the World" by President Truman. As Chair of the United Nations Human Rights Commission she was instrumental in formulating the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, submitting it with the words that it "may well become the international Magna Carta for all men everywhere". In 1939, when the Black singer Marian Anderson was denied Constitution Hall because of her race, Roosevelt saw to it that she performed on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial instead.Used to argue: the non-religious case that rights are built by human agreement and campaigning — and a named individual for the 1948 Declaration, which otherwise sounds like a committee
Liberation Theology — Oscar RomeroA Roman Catholic archbishop in El Salvador who held that Christians must defend the weak and make a stand against social injustice; in his sermons he spoke about the rights of the poor and openly criticised the government. In 1980, while he was celebrating Mass, armed men burst into the cathedral and shot him dead in front of the altar.Used to argue: Christians have a duty to speak out against unjust governments, and that defending rights can cost a life — the peaceful face of Liberation Theology, against Camilo Torres' violent one
Women's suffrage — Emmeline Pankhurst and the WSPUThe Women's Social and Political Union was founded in Manchester in 1903 by Emmeline Pankhurst and her daughters Christabel and Sylvia. Suffragettes thought violence permissible given the urgency — civil disobedience, rallies and vandalism as well as leaflets; many were arrested and went on hunger strike, and the government's "Cat and Mouse Act" (1912) released strikers to recover before rearresting them. Women over 30 got the vote in 1918, and all women equally in 1928.Used to argue: rights are won by campaigning rather than granted — and the suffragist/suffragette split is the exact parallel to the pacifism debate about whether force is ever justified in a just cause
Disability — Jean Vanier and L'ArcheIn 1964 Jean Vanier (1928–2019) invited Raphaël Simi and Philippe Seux, two men with intellectual disabilities, to share his life in an old house at Trosly-Breuil in France. They called it L'Arche — "the Ark", after Noah's: deliverance, and a refuge from a prejudiced world. Now over 120 communities in 30 countries. The detail that earns the marks: no "clients" and "staff" and no shift work — disabled people are core members, those who assist them are assistants who live in the houses as family, and everyone is equally responsible for the life of the community.Used to argue: inclusion rather than institutions; inspired by the Beatitudes, Vanier was among the first in the modern age to say it is not right to lock people away, and that they have much to teach us
Apartheid and scripture — the Dutch Reformed ChurchIn 1948 the South African Prime Minister Daniel François Malan, a Dutch Reformed minister, introduced the apartheid legislation, supported by the Dutch Reformed Church, which used Genesis 9:18–27 — Noah's curse of his grandson Canaan — to claim that treating Black people as inferior was justified. In the early 1980s the World Alliance of Reformed Churches declared apartheid a heresy and expelled the Church; in 1986 its congregations were desegregated, in 1994 apartheid was abolished, and the Church has since expressed repentance.Used to argue: scripture can be bent to justify racism — the strongest single example for "religion has done harm on race", and, because the Church repented, for a religion correcting itself
Racial harmony — Martin Luther King(1929–1968) A Baptist minister, ordained in 1947, who became president of the Montgomery Improvement Association in 1955 and led a 382-day bus boycott after the arrest of Rosa Parks — the bus companies lost over half their income and the Civil Rights Movement began. Non-violent protest throughout: petitions, demonstrations and sit-ins, influenced by Jesus' teachings and Gandhi, while his house was bombed and he was threatened constantly. In August 1963 he led a march of 250,000 to Washington and gave the "I have a dream" speech; the Civil Rights Bill passed in 1964, the year of his Nobel Peace Prize. Shot dead on 4 April 1968 in Memphis.Used to argue: Christian teaching translated into political change, and that non-violent protest works — his reasons were religious, that God created everyone in his own image
Reconciliation after apartheid — Desmond Tutu(1931–2021) The first Black Anglican Archbishop of both Cape Town and Johannesburg, known as the "voice of the voiceless". An outspoken critic of apartheid, he supported the economic boycott of South Africa and urged the UK to use sanctions, while constantly encouraging reconciliation; Nobel Peace Prize 1984. Nelson Mandela appointed him chairperson of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. He calls South Africa a "rainbow nation", and gave his objective as "a democratic and just society without racial divisions".Used to argue: the religious grounds for racial equality — all are God's children, a human family — and that reconciliation rather than revenge is the Christian route after injustice
Racial harmony in a city — LeicesterOn 29 May 2001 the BBC reported that Leicester should be seen as a role model in racial harmony, having transformed a poor reputation over about thirty years through four things: a clear message from the council that racism would not be tolerated; local people creating dialogue so problems could be discussed and solved; a wide variety of ethnic groups represented in local government, so all felt they had a voice; and religious leaders meeting to discuss issues in a spirit of co-operation.Used to argue: how harmony is actually achieved — those four points make a complete 6-mark answer, and they are the evidence for the claim that laws alone do not change attitudes
Interfaith in practice — the Revd Isaac PoobalanA parish priest in Scotland who let Muslim worshippers from the mosque next door use his church for their prayers, after seeing them worshipping in the street on a cold winter's day for lack of space: "Jesus taught his disciples to love your neighbour as yourself and this is something I cannot just preach to my congregation, I had to put it into practice."Used to argue: agape obliges practical interfaith co-operation — naming him is the difference between an example and a rumour
Ecumenism — TaizéAn ecumenical monastic order founded by Roger Louis Schutz-Marsauche (Brother Roger) in 1940 in south-east France, to provide a place of reconciliation in view of the Second World War. About a hundred Roman Catholic and Protestant monks, who earn their own keep and give the rest of their time to the needy. It became a major site of pilgrimage: tens of thousands of young people study the Bible, share the chores and worship three times a day, using simple repeated chants usually taken from the Psalms. All are welcome regardless of religious affiliation.Used to argue: unity between denominations is practised rather than merely discussed — the example to use when a question asks how Christians promote unity within their own faith community
Poverty, long-term aid — Christian AidThe official aid agency of over 40 denominations in the UK and Ireland, founded in 1947 to help those who had lost homes, families and possessions in the Second World War; through the 1950s and 60s its focus moved from Europe to other countries facing poverty and injustice. It works in over 70 countries with more than 500 partner organisations, aims to "strengthen the poor", and does not force religion on anyone. Short term: emergency relief after natural disasters. Long term: skills and education so people become self-reliant, health education, immunisation and training local nurses and midwives. Campaigning: fair wages and fair-trade conditions, and lobbying to drop developing-world debt, as in Jubilee 2000.Used to argue: Christian charity is justice as well as compassion — the answer to "charity creates dependency" is the long-term, self-reliance half of the work
Effective giving — Toby Ord and Giving What We CanToby Ord (b.1979), an Australian philosopher based in Oxford, founded Giving What We Can in 2009; its 6,000+ members pledge at least 10% of their income over their careers, and the aim is not only to give but to research the most effective charities so the money has the greatest impact. His own reasoning: "if my money could help others much more than it helps me, then why not?"Used to argue: the non-religious duty to the poor, reached by reason rather than scripture — and that effectiveness matters as much as generosity, which is the sharpest challenge to ordinary church collections
Compassion — Albert Schweitzer(1875–1965) A theologian and concert organist who funded his medical training with his concert earnings, took his M.D. in 1913 and founded a hospital at Lambaréné in French Equatorial Africa, expanding it with royalties and donations to seventy buildings caring for over 500 patients at a time. He received the Nobel Peace Prize for 1952 and used the $33,000 to start a leprosarium.Used to argue: compassion is more than feeling another's pain — it must lead to action, and his whole career is the example of a Christian who turned belief into a hospital

equations.name: Human rights campaigning — Amnesty International

Four aims: free prisoners of conscience, gain fair trials for political prisoners, end torture, political killings and "disappearances", and abolish the death penalty worldwide. Methods: letter-writing, publicity and protest, plus practical help and campaigning to change laws. Nobel Peace Prize 1977; UN Human Rights Prize 1978.

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
Human rightsBasic freedoms to which all human beings are entitled
UniversalA right that belongs to everybody in the world
InalienableA right people are entitled to regardless of nationality, language, religion or ethnic origin; it cannot be taken away
Indivisible and interdependentAll rights are needed together for human beings to flourish and participate in society
Imago DeiThe belief that humans are made in the image of God, which gives every person equal and infinite worth
StewardshipThe duty to care for creation and for one another on God's behalf
AgapeSelfless, unconditional love of neighbour, taught by Jesus
Social contractAn agreement to surrender some freedoms so that society can protect everyone's rights (Hobbes, Rousseau)
EqualityTreating people as having equal worth and equal entitlement, regardless of race, sex, faith or disability
PrejudicePre-judging — making up your mind about someone without the full facts
DiscriminationPutting prejudice into action — treating someone less favourably because of it
RacismPrejudice and discrimination against people of another ethnicity
Positive discriminationFavouring a disadvantaged group deliberately, in order to correct past inequality
Gender biasPreconceived ideas or stereotypes about how the genders should behave and think, which place limitations on their capabilities
Absolute povertyA severe deprivation of basic human needs — food, safe drinking water, sanitation, health, shelter, education and information (UN, 1995)
Anonymous ChristiansRahner's term for good people who live like Christians without identifying as Christians
MissionarySomeone sent out by a church to a particular area to encourage people to join the Christian community
FeminismThe belief in the social, economic and political equality of the sexes
Multi-ethnic societyA society in which people of many different ethnic groups live together
Multi-faith societyA society in which members of different religions live side by side
Racial harmonyPeople of different ethnicities living together with respect and without discrimination
EcumenismThe movement promoting unity and co-operation between Christian denominations
Interfaith dialogueDiscussion between different religions to build understanding, without trying to convert
ProselytisationConverting atheists or members of other religions to one's own religion
ExclusivismThe belief that only Christianity leads to salvation
InclusivismThe belief that the Christian God saves, but will be kind to good members of other religions — Rahner's "anonymous Christians"
PluralismThe belief that all religions are equally valid expressions of one Ultimate Reality
SalvationBeing saved from sin and its consequences, made possible for Christians through Jesus
PovertyLacking the money and resources needed for an adequate standard of living
JusticeA fair society and the fair distribution of resources — people getting what they deserve
CompassionThe ability to feel what someone else is feeling, which should motivate action
CharityHelping those in need in practical terms, with aid or by teaching new skills
TitheGiving a tenth of one's income to God's work or to the poor
Liberation TheologyA Christian movement that sides with the poor against oppression, structuring communities so all are empowered
Sanctity of lifeThe belief that life is holy and God-given, so every person must be respected

questions.promptHtml: Why do Christians believe in human rights, when the phrase never appears in the Bible?
questions.answerHtml:
They derive them from three doctrines rather than a verse. Creation: all humans are made in the image of God, so every person has worth that no government conferred and none can revoke. Stewardship: Christians are responsible for one another, which includes defending the vulnerable. Agape: loving your neighbour requires wanting for them what you want for yourself — the Golden Rule.

Galatians 3:28 — "there's neither male nor female… all are one in Christ" — is the nearest thing to a text, and it is why many Christians think the 1948 Declaration reflects Christian principles.

The qualification to include: for some Christians rights are only valid where they do not contradict Christian teaching, which is why the same believers can champion equality before the law and still reject a right to abortion.

questions.promptHtml: What is the strongest objection to the idea of natural human rights, and how would a supporter answer it?
questions.answerHtml:
The strongest objection is Bentham's: natural rights are a fiction — "nonsense on stilts". Nothing in nature confers a right; if everyone simply followed their natural rights the result would be anarchy. Rights exist because the state creates and enforces them through law.

Locke's answer: people are born with natural rights and dignity — life, liberty and property — and a state that denies them is unjust rather than merely unusual. Without something prior to the law, there is no standpoint from which to call a legal system evil.

The Christian answer is stronger still: rights rest on the image of God, so they are recognised rather than granted. Tutu's line is the one to quote — treating people as less than infinitely valuable is "a blasphemy".

Hobbes and Rousseau occupy the middle: rights are real but need a social contract to be secured.

questions.promptHtml: Both sides of the women's ordination debate quote scripture. How can the same Bible produce opposite conclusions?
questions.answerHtml:
Because they differ on the authority and interpretation of the texts, not on the texts themselves.

Conservatives read 1 Timothy's "no woman to have authority over a man" and Genesis 2 (Adam first, Eve as companion) as permanent instruction, supported by Jesus choosing no female disciples. Equality then means equal worth, different roles — the Catechism's "equal dignity though in a different way".

Liberals read those texts in the context in which they were written, and give priority to Galatians 3:28 and Genesis 1:27, where male and female are created at the same time. Equality then means roles decided by vocation and ability.

The deeper reason is denominational: churches balance scripture, tradition and modern life differently. The Salvation Army and United Reformed Church always accepted women on equal terms, the Baptists began ordaining them in the 1920s, and the Church of England ordained women as priests in 1994 and as bishops in 2015 — while the Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches do not, holding that the priest represents Christ.

Liberals also point to historical context: both Testaments were written in a patriarchal society, Jesus was bound to choose male apostles, and Paul was concerned not to upset Roman society while Christianity sought legal recognition. The instruction that women keep silent may reflect the fact that the home — the wife's domain — doubled as the place of worship in the earliest churches.

questions.promptHtml: Jesus healed disabled people. Why is that evidence on both sides of the Christian debate about disability?
questions.answerHtml:
For the positive view: he spent much of his ministry healing people whose illness or disability had made them society's outcasts. That shows compassion, inclusion and the worth of people the rest of society had written off.

For the negative view: healing implies disability is a defect to be removed rather than a way of being human. Read alongside Leviticus 21:17 and the texts treating ailments as punishment for sin, the miracles can be used to suggest disability is a problem God fixes rather than a state God blesses.

The text that settles it: in John 9, asked whether a man born blind had sinned or his parents had, Jesus answered "neither this man nor his parents sinned; he was born blind so that God's works might be revealed in him" — an explicit rejection of the punishment reading. Deuteronomy 27:18 also curses "anyone who misleads a blind person on the road".

How to use it: this is the cleanest example in the whole section of a single piece of evidence being appraised two ways — exactly what a 12-marker's level 4 descriptor asks for. The modern Christian resolution is the sanctity of life and imago Dei: Jean Vanier's L'Arche, founded in 1964, treats disabled people as core members rather than clients, with no staff and no shift work.

questions.promptHtml: Why do Christians who hold exclusivism and Christians who hold pluralism both claim to be following the Bible?
questions.answerHtml:
Exclusivists take Jesus at his word: "I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6), and "salvation is found in no one else" (Acts 4:12). Add Original Sin as a barrier and the crucifixion as the payment, and the logic is tight — which is also why they regard missionary work as urgent rather than rude, and as itself an expression of love for neighbour.

Pluralists start from God's transcendence: if God is beyond human comprehension, every religion's knowledge is partial, so each may be true but incomplete — the blind men and the elephant. They cite 2 Peter 3:9, that God does not want anyone to perish, and John 3:17, that the Son came to save rather than condemn.

The honest assessment: pluralism has no direct biblical support, which is why many Christians reject it; exclusivism has strong textual support but struggles with the fate of those who never heard of Christ. Inclusivism — Rahner's "anonymous Christians", with John 14:2's "my Father's house has many rooms" — exists precisely to keep John 14:6 while letting a loving God save the good.

Both sides can also appeal to Jesus' own conduct: in Luke 9 a Samaritan village refuses to welcome him, James and John ask whether to "call fire down from heaven to destroy them", and Jesus rebukes them and moves on. That is evidence for tolerance from an exclusivist text.

questions.promptHtml: Ecumenism and interfaith dialogue are often confused. What is the difference, and why does the spec treat both as relevant here?
questions.answerHtml:
Ecumenism — from the Greek oikoumene, "whole, inhabited world" — is unity between Christian denominations: the World Council of Churches (1948), Churches Together groups, Taizé, the ecumenical make-up of Street Pastors. Interfaith dialogue is between different religions: the Council of Christians and Jews, the Christian Muslim Forum, Southwark Cathedral's visits to mosques and synagogues.

The spec asks for "interfaith (including interdenominational) relationships", so both count. The connection is practical, and it is the ecumenical movement's own stated reason: the movement began at the World Missionary Conference in Edinburgh in 1910 on the view that bickering between denominations would inhibit their work and that division would itself undermine the Christian message of agape. A Christianity visibly divided against itself has little credibility asking a multi-faith society to live in peace, and Northern Ireland shows denominational division producing the same harms as interfaith division.

questions.promptHtml: Why do Christians distinguish charity from justice when helping the poor, if both end up giving money away?
questions.answerHtml:
Charity relieves the symptom: practical help, hand-outs or new skills, motivated by compassion. Justice attacks the cause: it says the poor are not unlucky but wronged, and that the distribution of resources is itself unfair — the Brandt Report's 25% of people holding 80% of the wealth.

The teachings differ accordingly. Charity: "he who gives to the poor will lack nothing", Wesley's "give all you can". Justice: "let justice flow down like a river" (Amos), "a righteous man knows the rights of the poor".

So does the action. Charity funds a food bank; justice campaigns to drop developing-world debt (Jubilee 2000), or builds base communities with no hierarchy so the poor can fight for themselves — Liberation Theology. Amos is the model for the justice strand: he condemned people who performed every religious ritual diligently while "cheating with dishonest scales, buying the poor with silver and the needy for a pair of sandals" (Amos 8:4–6), which is exactly the charge that charity without justice invites.

The evaluation question "It is more important to work for justice than to give to charity" turns entirely on this: charity helps now but can leave the system intact and the poor dependent; justice changes the system but is slow and political. Christian Aid does both, which is the strongest line for a conclusion.

questions.promptHtml: Many Christians have opposed racism — and many Christians defended slavery and apartheid. How should an answer handle that?
questions.answerHtml:
Head on. Pretending otherwise loses marks; acknowledging it gains them, because the level descriptors reward considering different viewpoints and appraising evidence.

The teaching is unambiguous: Acts 17:26 — "from one man he made all the nations"; Galatians 2:6 — "God does not show favouritism"; Genesis 1:27; the Good Samaritan; Jesus healing Gentiles. And it produced King, Tutu, Huddleston and Pope Francis on immigration.

The failures are real: Deuteronomy 7 has God driving out other nations and discouraging intermarriage; Christians ran the Crusades, colonised, profited from the slave trade, and the Dutch Reformed Church supported apartheid.

The judgement: these were failures to follow the teaching rather than applications of it — the same scripture that was misused also produced the movement that ended apartheid, and it was Tutu's Christianity, not his politics, that produced the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

questions.promptHtml: Choose one religion and explain why there are different attitudes to giving to charity. (6)
questions.answerHtml:
Most Christians believe they should give to charity, because it shows compassion for others and helps ensure justice within society 1; these qualities are cherished because Jesus advocated them, encouraging his followers to care for those in need and to promote social justice 1; his parable of the sheep and goats goes further still, linking care for those in need to care for God himself, so giving becomes an act of worship rather than mere kindness 1

questions.promptHtml:
"Prejudice and discrimination are the biggest problems facing society today."

Evaluate this statement, showing you have considered different points of view. In your answer, you should refer to at least one religion. (12)
questions.answerHtml:
Arguments for the statement.

Acting on superficial judgements is detrimental to the smooth running of society: assuming skin colour or gender defines a person leads to inequality, resentment and ultimately conflict — most visibly in South Africa under apartheid 1

Prejudice and discrimination are not confined to one country or era: they appear in racism, gender bias, disability bias and religious hatred alike, which is why so much legislation has been needed, from the Race Relations Act 1976 to the Equality Act 2010 1

They underlie other problems rather than sitting alongside them — most conflicts occur because of prejudice and discrimination 1

Arguments against the statement.

The environmental crisis may be greater: if global warming is not dealt with now, there will be no people left to experience prejudice 1

Current conflicts may usurp it: the war in Ukraine is devastating for those who live there and has international repercussions, and support for Ukraine could ultimately lead to a wider war and even the use of weapons of mass destruction 1

Poverty is arguably more urgent still — the Brandt Report found the developed world holds around 80% of the wealth with 25% of the population, and poverty kills directly 1

However, these can be connected back: those most affected by global warming are usually those who already face discrimination 1

Christian teaching.

Christians may well agree the statement is true, because of their teachings on creation and stewardship: God created all of humanity in his image, and the duty to care for all people obliges Christians to work against prejudice and discrimination 1

Desmond Tutu worked tirelessly against apartheid and continued afterwards with the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, showing that discrimination's consequences outlast the laws that created it 1

Christian leaders have also spoken on the other issues, urging forgiveness and compassion rather than vengeance in response to conflict, which suggests Christianity does not treat prejudice as the only great problem 1

Conclusion.

There are several very important problems — the environmental crisis, discrimination and conflict — and all of them have a global impact from which anyone can suffer 1

I agree that prejudice and discrimination are likely to be the biggest, because they not only produce social injustice directly but lie behind localised conflicts and, in the case of global warming, cause further suffering to people already singled out by race or social status 1

✗ Three paragraphs describing prejudice, then "so it is a big problem".
✓ Compare it against named rivals, concede the strongest point against you, then decide — the Model Answer concedes the environment and conflict before explaining why prejudice still wins.

questions.promptHtml: Explain Christian teaching on racial harmony. (6)
questions.answerHtml:
Christian teaching begins with the doctrine of creation: all people are made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), so no ethnic group can be superior 1; the book of Acts states it directly — "from one man he made all the nations, that they should inhabit the whole earth" (Acts 17:26) — which makes racial hierarchy a denial of how God made the world, and Leviticus 19:33–34 applies it to the outsider: "the foreigner residing among you must be treated as your native-born" 1

Agape extends the duty of love beyond one's own group: in the parable of the Good Samaritan the neighbour to be loved is the ethnic outsider, and Jesus himself healed and talked with Gentiles, including the Centurion's servant 1; St Paul reinforces it — "God does not show favouritism" (Galatians 2:6) — so partiality on grounds of race is incompatible with imitating God 1

Christians therefore treat racial equality as a demand of justice, following Amos' call to "let justice flow down like a river", and put it into practice: Martin Luther King led non-violent protest for civil rights, and Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission helped South Africa move beyond apartheid 1; Christians also acknowledge failures to follow this teaching — the slave trade and the Dutch Reformed Church's support for apartheid — which is why they regard racial harmony as something to be actively worked for rather than assumed 1

questions.promptHtml:
"All religions are equal."

Evaluate this statement, showing you have considered different points of view. In your answer, you should refer to at least one religion. (12)
questions.answerHtml:
Arguments for the statement.

God is transcendent, so human knowledge of him is necessarily limited; each religion may therefore offer a true but incomplete understanding — the blind men and the elephant 1

What matters, pluralists argue, is being God-centred rather than self-centred, and the truth claims of all religions can produce that personal transformation 1

In a multi-faith society treating religions as equal produces tolerance, choice and co-operation on social justice, whereas ranking them produces division 1

Equality before the law already requires the state to treat all religions equally, whatever their truth claims 1

Arguments against the statement.

Religions make incompatible claims — they cannot all be straightforwardly true at once, so "equal" must mean something weaker than "equally true" 1

Pluralism has no support in the Bible, so many Christians regard it as unacceptable 1

If any path leads to God, the incarnation and crucifixion lose their point — which is a serious cost for a Christian to accept 1

Christian teaching.

Exclusivists reject the statement outright, citing John 14:6 — "I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me" — and Acts 4:12; for them proselytisation is a duty rather than an insult 1

Inclusivists take a middle position: Karl Rahner argued a loving God would not condemn good people who never heard of Christ, calling them "anonymous Christians", so other religions contain real truth even though Christianity understands God best 1

Pluralists such as John Hick accept the statement, arguing from God's transcendence with the analogy of the elephant and the blind men — each report was true but partial — and citing 2 Peter 3:9 and John 3:17 that God wants to save rather than condemn 1

Conclusion.

Judgement: as a claim about truth the statement is weak, since religions contradict one another and pluralism cannot be derived from Christian scripture 1

As a claim about respect and treatment it is strong, and the inclusivist position is the most defensible — it keeps Christian conviction while recognising the good in other faiths, which is why interfaith dialogue, rather than either proselytisation or indifference, is the response most churches now take 1

questions.promptHtml: Choose one religion. Outline two of its attitudes to the role of women. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
Traditional Christians hold that men and women have equal worth but complementary roles 1 — the Catechism speaks of "equal dignity though in a different way", so women may take pastoral duties and contribute to worship but, in Roman Catholic teaching, cannot be priests, citing St Paul's instruction that no woman should have authority over a man 1

questions.promptHtml: Explain why many Christians feel they have an obligation to help the poor. (6)
questions.answerHtml:
Christians believe they are stewards of a world God created and of the people in it, so wealth is held in trust rather than owned outright 1; agape then requires that it be used for the neighbour in need — Isaiah 58 commands believers to "share your bread with the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house" 1

Jesus' teaching makes the obligation unusually sharp: in the parable of the sheep and goats, people are judged on how they helped the poor, and in helping the poor they help God himself 1; the parable of the rich man and Lazarus shows the rich man condemned for ignoring the poor man at his gate, and Jesus told the rich young man to sell all he had, warning it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the Kingdom of God 1

Christians also treat poverty as an issue of justice, not only kindness: the prophets demanded that justice "flow down like a river", and today Christians regard global inequality as unjust and campaign for change 1; this is why Christian Aid, founded in 1947, works for long-term development and lobbies governments to drop developing-world debt rather than only providing emergency relief, and why Liberation Theology set up base communities so the poor could fight for justice themselves 1

questions.promptHtml:
"Religions are biased in favour of men."

Evaluate this statement, showing you have considered different points of view. In your answer, you should refer to at least one religion. (12)
questions.answerHtml:
Arguments for the statement.

The structures are patriarchal: the Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches restrict ordination to men, holding that the priest represents Christ, so the most senior roles are closed to women by rule rather than ability 1

The texts are used to support it: St Paul instructs that no woman should have authority over a man (1 Timothy), Genesis 2 has Eve created as Adam's companion, and Jesus chose no female disciples 1

Teaching about the home has pushed women towards domestic roles — Luther's "to remain at home, sit still, keep house and bring up children", Ephesians 5:23 making the husband the head of the wife, and Pope John Paul II's "the family comes first" 1

Society has moved faster than the churches: the Equality Act 2010 made gender discrimination illegal, yet some denominations retain exemptions 1

Arguments against the statement.

Christianity's foundational claim is equality of worth: both sexes are made in the image of God, Jesus came to save men and women alike, and all will be judged equally at the Eschaton 1

Galatians 3:28 — "there's neither male nor female… all are one in Christ" — is an explicit statement of equality from the same apostle cited on the other side 1

Practice is changing: the Salvation Army and United Reformed Church have always accepted women on equal terms, the Baptists began ordaining women in the 1920s, and the Church of England ordained women as priests in 1994 and bishops in 2015 1

The Bible contains strong women — Deborah, Mary Magdalene — and Jesus and Paul treated women with respect in a culture that did not 1

Christian teaching.

Traditionalists do not claim women are inferior: the Catechism's formula is "equal dignity though in a different way", and a Roman Catholic declaration speaks of women's "special ability to humanize the family" — so the claim is difference, not bias 1

Liberals reply that the patriarchal texts must be read in the context in which they were written, and that Genesis 1:27 has men and women created at the same time, with Eve made from Adam's rib so that they work side by side 1

Conclusion.

Judgement: "complementary roles" is a coherent position — the Catechism's "equal dignity though in a different way" is not a claim of inferiority — but where it consistently assigns authority to men and domestic duty to women, the practical effect is bias whatever the stated intention, which is why many women found Mulieris Dignitatem patronising 1

So I partly agree: Christianity's teaching is not biased in favour of men, but some of its institutions historically have been — and the fact that churches have changed, ordaining women on the basis of the same scripture, shows the bias lies in interpretation rather than in the religion itself 1

drill.intro:
What each part of the question actually wants

Section 4 sits on Paper 1 — 1 hour 45 minutes, four sections, each with a choice of two questions, each question worth 25 marks. The four parts are marked in completely different ways, so answer each in its own shape.

  • a) 3 marks — AO1. Three focused and distinct points. The answer does not require explanations; brief, clear reasons are ideal. Number them and stop.
  • b) 4 marks — AO1. Two points of information which require some development — point (1) + development (1), twice. The development must add value to the point while still answering the question posed; an example is often the quickest way to develop it.
  • c) 6 marks — AO1 and AO2. An explain question, marked in levels rather than by ticking points. Explain and develop the issue, drawing out the influence and significance of the religion, beliefs and values, with religious terms used appropriately. Aim to explain more than one reason even when no number is given, make sure every point is fully explained, and balance breadth against depth.
  • d) 12 marks — AO1 and AO2. The synoptic assessment, also level marked. It wants fully evaluated arguments underpinned with knowledge and understanding, drawn from across the course: consider the alternative viewpoint no matter how weak it is, refer to at least one religion, appraise the quality of each argument as you give it, and reach a fully justified conclusion. Humanist and atheist views add perspective but do not on their own count as the reference to a religion.

Twelve questions in the shape of the real thing: three each of the 3-, 4-, 6- and 12-mark parts. The 12-mark answers are written as plans — the real paper marks them in levels, not by ticking points, so treat the twelve mark points as a target for coverage rather than a tick list.

subsections.html:
This section asks one question of the authority half of the topic and one of the Jesus half — but not always in the same place, so both have to be solid. The exam technique guide is blunt about what the parts want: the 4-mark answer is two pieces of information with "a little development"; the 6-mark answer must "draw out the significance" of two or three points; the 10-mark answer needs arguments for, arguments against, Christian teaching, your own reasoned opinion and a balanced conclusion.

What they actually ask

Paper 2 Section 1, Religion B: Christianity, every June paper from 2019 to 2023 — fifteen parts in all, always shaped (a) 4, (b) 6, (c) 10. (The 2024 and 2025 Paper 2 papers held in this app are the Buddhism option booklets, so there is no Christianity question from those two years to check.) Only two things are ever asked here: the Bible and authority, and the life of Jesus. Every paper took one of each.

  • The Bible — how it is used, and how far its authority goes — in all five years. "Outline two ways the Bible is used in Christian worship" (2019a); "Explain the importance of the Bible for Christians" (2020b); "Explain how the Bible is used in worship within any one Christian denomination" (2021b); "The Bible has the same importance for all Christians" (2022c). Note the pattern: the 4- and 6-markers ask about use, the 10-marker about divergent authority.
  • The life of Jesus — in all five years, and it has worked steadily through the spec list. Death: "Explain why the death of Jesus is important for Christians" (2019b); "The main purpose of Jesus' life was to die on the cross" (2023c). Temptations: "Outline two temptations experienced by Jesus in the wilderness" (2020a). Healing: "Outline two examples of Jesus' ministry of healing" (2021a). Resurrection: "For Christians, Jesus' resurrection is the most important event of his life" (2021c). Baptism: "Outline two features of the baptism of Jesus" (2023a).
  • Authority — ordained ministry, the laity and the conscience — "The individual conscience is the only moral guide a Christian needs" (2019c); "Ordained ministers are important for all Christians" (2020c); "Outline two examples of authority in any one Christian denomination" (2022a); "Explain different attitudes to the ordained ministry within Christianity" (2022b).
  • One other significant Christian — "Explain the contribution to Christianity of one significant Christian other than Jesus" (2023b). Asked once, and it is the part that catches people out, so have Dietrich Bonhoeffer ready in enough detail to fill six marks.

What has not been asked: the three ethical theories, and the Bible's use in private devotion and meditation specifically. Both are still spec content and both feed the stems above.

subsections.heading: Ethics first: the three theories the course starts with
subsections.html:
Spec 1.1 · The basis of human decision-making, before Christian sources of authority

  • Ethics — the study of how people behave, the reasons they give and the rationale behind their decisions.
  • Moral absolutism — objective principles true for all people in all situations, e.g. deontological ethics.
  • Moral relativism — morality related to the particular situation, e.g. consequentialism.
  • Kant — do your duty whatever the consequences; test it by the categorical imperative. Absolutist.
  • Bentham — the Greatest Happiness Principle: the greatest happiness of the greatest number. Relativist.
  • Fletcher — situation ethics: do the most loving thing here; the easiest to link to agape.
More detail

Ethics is the study of how people behave — what they do, the reasons they give, and the rationale behind their decisions — and it divides into two families before it divides into theories.

  • Moral absolutism — there are objective moral principles that hold true for all people in all situations, e.g. deontological ethics (duty-based).
  • Moral relativism — morality should be related to the particular situation people find themselves in, e.g. consequentialism (results-based).
TheoryWho, and the test they apply
Kantian ethicsImmanuel Kant (1724–1804): the most important thing is to do your duty, irrespective of the consequences. You find your duty by the categorical imperative — an act is right if you could expect everyone else to act the same way in the same situation, establishing a universal law. Absolutist.
UtilitarianismJeremy Bentham (1748–1832): decisions should be based on the Greatest Happiness Principle — a good action is the one that brings the greatest happiness to the greatest number of people. Relativist.
Situation ethicsJoseph Fletcher (1905–1991): decisions should be made on the basis of what is the most loving thing to do in that particular situation. Relativist, and the easiest to connect to Christian agape.

These are worth three lines in an answer about why Christians disagree with each other: a fundamentalist reading of the Bible is absolutist, while a liberal reading that weighs context and consequences looks much more like situation ethics.

subsections.heading: The Bible — what it is and why it has authority
subsections.html:
Spec 1.1 · "The Bible and its authority for Christians"

  • The Bible is Scripture — an agreed, authoritative collection Christians believe reveals God's word.
  • 66 books, two halves — the Old Testament (Jewish scriptures) and the New Testament (Christian scriptures).
  • The New Testament — four Gospels, Acts, the letters and Revelation; the canon was agreed in AD 367.
  • Catholics add the Apocrypha — the cleanest denominational difference about the Bible itself; Protestants do not.
  • Authority comes from its origin — 2 Timothy 3:16, "all scripture is inspired by God".
  • It contains all that is needed for salvation — and is a way of encountering God, not just information about him.

The verse that carries the argument

"All scripture is inspired by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work."

2 Timothy 3:16–17

Used to argue the Bible's authority comes from God, not from human authorship. Fundamentalists lean on the first clause ("inspired by God", or "God-breathed"); others lean on the last ("for teaching") — that it is useful, which does not require it to be literally true in every detail.

More detail

The Bible is Scripture: an agreed, authoritative collection of texts which Christians believe is the revelation of God's word. Its authority rests on where Christians believe it came from — not on how old it is or how well it is written.

  • 66 books, in two halves: the Old Testament (the Jewish scriptures) and the New Testament (the Christian scriptures).
  • The New Testament contains four Gospels — the life and teaching of Jesus; Acts — a history of the early church by St Luke; letters — mostly Paul's, answering theological and ethical problems in the early church; and an apocalypse, the book of Revelation, about the coming of God's kingdom.
  • It is believed to contain everything needed to lead a good life and attain salvation.
  • It is a way of encountering God, not only a source of information about him.
  • The Holy Spirit is believed to guide its interpretation.

"Bible" comes from the Greek biblia, meaning books: it is a library written between about 1200 BC and AD 200, and the list of books accepted as the genuine word of God — the canon — was finally agreed in AD 367.

PartWhat it contains
Old Testament — 39 books, originally in Hebrew and Aramaic, later translated into GreekTorah (Law) — the first five books: the early history of the Jews, their relationship with God, the laws God wanted them to follow and the rituals they were to perform. Nevi'im (Prophets) — the messages the prophets received from God, giving more information about his nature, reminding the Jews to keep the covenant and foretelling a messiah. Ketuvim (Writings) — history, poetry and liturgy, giving insight into God's nature and how to worship him
New Testament — 27 books, originally in GreekGospels ("good news") — the life and teachings of Jesus. Mark, Matthew and Luke are similar in style and use common sources, so they are called the synoptic Gospels; John's reads more as a series of sermons interpreting the significance of Jesus. All four say little about his childhood and concentrate on the last few years, and especially the last week. Acts of the Apostles — the beginnings of the Christian community, focusing on the work of Peter and Paul. The Epistles — 21 letters from early Christian leaders to the new churches, giving advice, guidance and encouragement. Revelation — written towards the end of the first century AD, full of visions and symbols; its theme is that good will finally win over evil and Jesus will return in victory
The Apocrypha — written between about 300 BC and AD 100Books about Jewish ancestors, Jewish freedom fighters and wise sayings. Some Christians, most notably Roman Catholics, include them in the Bible and Protestants generally do not — the cleanest denominational difference you can name about the Bible itself

Why each half matters. The Old Testament is important to Christians because it gives the context in which to understand Jesus and his significance: the New Testament writers used the Jewish scriptures to show that Jesus is the messiah the prophets foretold. The New Testament is the account of God sending his son to willingly sacrifice his life so that humanity could return to God — so it is a set of books focused on the love of God, with Jesus's teaching and example showing how to respond to that love, summed up in the two great commandments to love God and love your neighbour (Mark 12:30–31).

Two more facts for a first line: Christianity is the most widely practised religion in the world, with more than two billion followers; roughly 42 million Britons regard themselves as Christian and about 6 million actively practise.

Also note that Revelation itself splits Christians the way the rest of the Bible does: some interpret it literally as a forecast of the End Time, while others read it as symbolic — written to reassure Christians during Roman persecution and encourage resilience.

subsections.heading: Divergent Christian attitudes to the Bible
subsections.html:
Spec 1.1 · "Differences among Christians in their attitudes to its authority and interpretation"

  • Fundamentalist — the direct, inerrant word of God; Genesis 1 literally happened in six days.
  • Conservative — inspired, not dictated; Genesis 1 is a poem about why, not how. Probably most Christians.
  • Liberal — the writers were inspired rather than the words; Genesis 1 is largely symbolic.
  • The two test cases — the Feeding of the Five Thousand on miracles, 1 Timothy 2:9–15 on women.
  • Name the three positions — unnamed "some Christians" answers stay in the bottom level.
  • 10-marker — "The Bible is the literal word of God"; both columns carry Christian teaching.

✗ "Some Christians think the Bible is true and some think it isn't."
✓ "Fundamentalists hold the Bible to be the literal, inerrant word of God, while liberals hold it to contain the word of God within writings shaped by their human authors' context."

Name the three positions. Unnamed "some Christians" answers stay in the bottom level.

ArgumentCounter-argument
2 Timothy 3:16–17 — "all scripture is inspired by God", so the words themselves come from God through the Holy Spirit and cannot contain errorThe same verse ends "profitable for teaching" — useful, which does not require every detail to be literally true; liberals hold that the writers were inspired, not the words
It is the ultimate authority on God, the world, human behaviour and the afterlife, so anything contradicting it must be rejected — the fundamentalist positionThe Church of England holds Scripture alongside Tradition and Reason (Articles 6 and 20), and Roman Catholics alongside the Magisterium; neither treats the text alone as sufficient
Adam, Eve, Noah, Jonah and Jesus were real people at actual points in history; treating Genesis 1 as six literal days keeps God's account of creation intactConservative Christians read Genesis 1 as a poem about why, not how; liberals read it as symbolic. Both still call it the revealed word of God
A God-given text that changes with the age cannot guide anyone — if the reader decides what counts, the authority has moved from God to the reader1 Timothy 2:9–15 — "I permit no woman to teach… she is to keep silent" — shows the cost of literalism, and Reason is what lets Anglicans set it aside as a first-century instruction
Jesus himself answered each of the three temptations with "it is written", treating scripture as decisive (Matthew 4:3–10)Jesus also broke the written Law to touch the leper (Mark 1:40–44) and cleared the Temple against the practice of his day, so he is not a straightforward literalist
More detail

All Christians believe the Bible is the revealed word of God; they disagree about how exactly it is so, and that disagreement produces three recognisable positions. The exam loves this because the three views are easy to compare and hard to muddle if you learn the Genesis 1 test case.

ViewWho holds itWhat it meansGenesis 1
FundamentalistEvangelical Protestants. The view arose as a reaction to the Age of Enlightenment and the rise of modern science in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, when people began to question religion and scientific discoveries seemed to contradict religious teachingsThe Bible is the direct word of God, passed down through the Holy Spirit to the writers, and so free from all errors and the ultimate source of authority on God, the world, human behaviour and the afterlife. There is poetry and allegory in it, but it gives an accurate account of history — Adam, Eve, Noah, Jonah and Jesus were real people at actual points in history. Anything contradicting it must be rejectedIt literally happened: God commanded the world into existence in six days and rested on the seventh, so the Big Bang and Darwinian evolution are simply wrong
ConservativeMany Catholics and some Anglicans — probably most ChristiansThe Bible is the inspired word of God rather than dictated. Writers added their own interpretation, personality and context, allowing some error on factual matters, so the Gospel accounts of Jesus are historical and accurate while the stories of Adam, Eve, Noah and Jonah may be myths. Further guidance is needed from the Holy Spirit and Church leaders. The view is clearest in the Roman Catholic Church, which holds that the Holy Spirit inspired both the people who wrote the books and the Church leaders who decided which books belonged in the New Testament — so both the Bible and the Magisterium (the teachings of the Pope, Cardinals and Bishops) carry authorityIt is a poem explaining why the world was created, not necessarily how
LiberalLiberal Anglicans and members of other denominationsThe Bible is a record of the experiences of people seeking God in their own lives, situations and cultures. It was the writers who were inspired, not the words themselves, so they could make mistakes and use the ideas and world views of their own times. It contains the word of God within it but is not directly the word of God, so it must be read with care and in context, open to the guidance of the Holy Spirit and one's own conscience in looking for the spiritual meaning. Much of it is myth or symbolic poetry — the miracles express Jesus' power but may not have happenedIt is largely symbolic, pointing to God as the author of the universe guiding it through its formation; scientific explanations of origins are preferable

Two passages are the standard test cases. The Feeding of the Five Thousand (Matthew 14:14–21) divides Christians over miracles: a literal multiplication, or a symbol of Christ feeding the world. 1 Timothy 2:9–15 — "I permit no woman to teach or to have authority over men; she is to keep silent" — divides them over ethics: a standing command, or a first-century instruction that reason should now set aside.

Read across the table below and the 10-marker "The Bible is the literal word of God" writes itself — both columns carry Christian teaching, which is what the top band requires.

subsections.heading: The Bible in worship, devotion and instruction
subsections.html:
Spec 1.1 · "Its use in worship: devotion/meditation and instruction/education within any one Christian denomination"

  • Answer on one denomination — the Church of England, and say so in the first line.
  • Worship — three lectionary readings at the Eucharist, from an eagle lectern; the congregation stand for the Gospel.
  • Devotion and meditation — daily private reading with Bible notes, or the Book of Common Prayer's Daily Office.
  • Instruction and education — Sunday school, confirmation classes and Bible study groups, especially in Lent.
  • Three uses, three paragraphs — a ready-made structure for a 6-marker.
More detail

The spec asks about one denomination, so answer on the Church of England and say so in the first line. The three uses are a ready-made three-paragraph structure for a 6-marker.

UseWhat actually happens
WorshipAt the weekly Eucharist the Bible is the basis of the prayers, including the Lord's Prayer. During the liturgy of the Word three passages are read — one from the Old Testament, one from the epistles and one from the Gospels — chosen from a lectionary so that they share a common theme. The Bible rests on a lectern, often carved as an eagle standing on a sphere, signifying God's wisdom sent out to the world, and placed centrally or near the congregation to indicate the immanence of God. The congregation stand for the Gospel reading to acknowledge its significance, and the acolytes stand either side with candles to recall Jesus as the light of the world. A sermon, from the minister or a lay preacher, explains the significance of the passages just heard and their relevance to everyday life. In the second part, the liturgy of the sacrament, the eucharistic prayer retells the story of the Last Supper as the bread and wine are consecrated. In Protestant services the Bible is centre stage — a service of the Word
Devotion and meditationMany Christians set aside time each day for private prayer and study, opening the Bible at random or working through a section using Bible reading notes written by Christian leaders. Passages may be read slowly and repeatedly so the deeper meaning becomes clear — a meditation — and then prayed over. Others use the Book of Common Prayer and its Daily Office of morning and evening prayer, with its collections of prayers, Psalms and readings. The Holy Spirit is believed to aid interpretation
Instruction and educationThe Bible is the authority behind much Church teaching — divorce is held to be wrong because Jesus says so in Mark's Gospel. Sunday school is held each week for children, usually during the first part of the Eucharist in the church hall, with Biblical stories as the basis for discussion and activities. Confirmation classes meet with the minister for a couple of months before the confirmation service to talk about the person and work of Christ, with the Bible as the basis of the instruction. Bible study groups of a few people meet to read passages and discuss their relevance, sharing knowledge and asking questions; they are especially encouraged in Lent, to prepare for Easter. The Gideon Bible even carries a "where to find help when…" guide at the front

subsections.heading: Authority in the Church of England
subsections.html:
Spec 1.1 · "The nature and form of authority in any one Christian denomination"

  • Scripture, Tradition and Reason — three sources held in creative tension; that triad is the whole answer.
  • Scripture is primary — Article 6: it "containth all things necessary to salvation".
  • Tradition — Fathers, councils, saints and bishops, so long as they agree with the Bible (Article 20).
  • Reason — applies both to today's problems, and is what lets Anglicans set aside "women should be silent".
  • Why three — a guide both fixed and dynamic, preventing complacency and forcing constant review.
  • The structure, in order — monarch, Canterbury, York, diocesan bishops, priests, deacons and laity.
More detail

The Church of England answers moral questions from three sources held in creative tension: Scripture, Tradition and Reason. That triad is the whole answer to "explain your chosen denomination's sources of authority".

  1. Scripture is the primary source. "Holy Scripture containth all things necessary to salvation; so that whatsoever is not read therein, nor may be proved thereby, is not to be required of any man, that it should be believed as an article of the faith" — the 39 Articles of Religion, Article 6. Through prayer and the guidance of the Holy Spirit its teachings can be applied in daily life. But Anglicans themselves disagree how to read it: the full range of fundamentalist, conservative and liberal understandings is found inside the denomination — Leviticus calls homosexuality an abomination; liberals think that is out of date, conservatives think it stands.
  2. Tradition. The teachings of the Church Fathers, the early ecumenical councils, the saints and senior Anglican bishops offer insight and wisdom on how problems have been solved before — as long as those teachings agree with the contents of the Bible. "The Church hath the power to decree rites or ceremonies and authority in controversies of Faith. And yet it is not lawful for the Church to ordain anything that is contrary to God's Word written" — the 39 Articles of Religion, Article 20. Charles Gore called Tradition a "living witness to a once-spoken voice".
  3. Reason. Thought and reflection let Christians evaluate and measure Scripture and Tradition and apply them to today's problems. "Reason increases and enlarges human understanding of divine revelation through its own workings, so long as reason is used in humble dependence upon the God who gave it" — Michael Ramsey (1904–1988), former Archbishop of Canterbury. Reason is what lets Anglicans reject "women should be silent in church" as the product of a patriarchal age.

Why three and not one. Using the three in tandem is meant to give a guide that is both fixed and dynamic, preventing complacency and arrogance: having to refer to the Bible, to respected Christians of the past, and to your own rationality forces a Christian constantly to review their relationship with and knowledge of God, and how best to act in each situation. That is the sentence to use if a question asks why the triad is a strength.

The key beliefs are set out in the 39 Articles of Religion, and the distinctive ideas are a ready-made list: that the Bible contains the core of all Christian faith and thought; loyalty to the way of worship and life first set out in the Book of Common Prayer; celebration of the two sacraments ordained by Jesus, Baptism and the Eucharist; a system of Church order from ancient times focused on the ordained ministry of bishop, priest and deacon; a firm commitment to the ministry of the whole people of God, lay and ordained; and Scripture, Tradition and Reason held together in creative tension.

Two things the Church of England rejects: the authority of the Pope — the monarch is Supreme Governor of the Church of England, appointing archbishops and bishops — and the primacy of Natural Law over Scripture. Its origins explain why: it is part of the Anglican Church and separated from the Roman Catholic Church in the sixteenth century for political and doctrinal reasons, the main one being the rejection of papal authority, aiming at a middle way between Roman Catholicism and Puritanism. It embraces Protestant themes such as the importance of Scripture while keeping the Roman Catholic respect for the ancient Church and the Church Fathers (unless they contradict the Bible), and it accepts the decisions of the first four ecumenical councils on the Trinity and the Incarnation. Like the Roman Catholic and Orthodox Churches it ordains bishops, priests and deacons. That middle position produces real internal variety: some Church of England communities follow Roman Catholicism closely (High Church) while others are much closer to evangelical Protestantism (Low Church) — naming that distinction is an easy mark on "differences among Christians".

Structure, in order, because "outline two forms of leadership" is a real 4-marker: the monarch as Supreme Governor; the Archbishop of Canterbury, Primate of All England; the Archbishop of York; diocesan bishops, who oversee the priests in their dioceses; priests or vicars, who run parishes; deacons and the laity, who assist.

subsections.heading: The individual conscience as a source of authority
subsections.html:
Spec 1.1 · "The role of the individual conscience in matters of belief and practice"

  • The inner voice of God — St Paul and Aquinas; to act against conscience is itself a sin.
  • A means of self-restraint — Butler: conscience must control the passions and balance self-love against benevolence.
  • The super-ego — Freud: acquired in infancy from parents' morals, so not innate and not divine.
  • A false idol — Bonhoeffer: after the Fall it cannot be God's voice, so trusting it is idolatry.
  • Romans 2:15–16 — the law "written on their hearts" is the strongest biblical support for the inner voice.
  • Where it bites — Catholics following conscience against Church teaching on contraception and homosexuality.

St Paul on the conscience

"They show that what the law requires is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness and their conflicting thoughts accuse or perhaps excuse them on that day when according to my gospel, God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus."

Romans 2:15–16

Used to argue that everyone has a conscience, given by God, and that God will judge by it — the strongest Biblical support for the "inner voice" view.

ArgumentCounter-argument
It is the voice of God, written on the heart (Romans 2) — so it carries God's own authorityFreud and modern psychology: it comes from upbringing and socialisation, so it is not universal and not divine
Everyone has one, so it is a guide available to every person, Christian or notIt can be distorted by sin, so it may confidently command the wrong thing
Aquinas: to act against it is itself a sin, so it must be obeyedBonhoeffer: trusting it is idolatry; follow the example of Christ instead
It allows moral decisions in situations the Bible never addressesIt can be just an excuse for doing what you already wanted to do
More detail

Christians disagree about what the conscience actually is, and that is the whole question — four named positions, two for and two against trusting it.

Account of the conscienceWhoThe claim
The inner voice of GodSt Paul; Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274)An innate conviction of what is good or bad — like the voice of God speaking within the person and guiding their moral decision-making. Aquinas treated it as a rational person's natural ability to understand the difference between right and wrong, but was aware it can be distorted by one's emotions or limited by ignorance or habit, so it should be guided by accepted moral principles — those found in the Bible and in Church teachings. His own words: "Every conscience, whether it is right or wrong, whether it concerns things evil in themselves or things morally indifferent, obliges us to act in such a way that he who acts against his conscience sins."
A means of self-restraintBishop Joseph Butler (1692–1752)There are two sides to a person: passions, appetites and affections on one side, and the thoughtful aspects of benevolence towards others, self-love and conscience on the other. For a moral life the conscience must take priority: it is the controlling influence over the passions, balancing self-love against benevolence. "There is a superior principle of reflection or heart… which passes judgement upon ourselves and them; pronounces determinably our actions to be in themselves just, right, good; others to be in themselves evil, wrong, unjust."
The super-egoSigmund Freud (1856–1939)Explaining the link between conscience and guilt, Freud concluded the conscience originates in the values acquired in early upbringing from parents and other significant adults. The mind is ego (rational, balancing), id (basic needs — hunger, self-preservation; amoral and merely seeking to express itself) and super-ego: the restraining part formed in infancy from parents' morals, acting as censorship. It can be too severe, demanding perfectionism and producing guilt and acute self-criticism. So conscience is not innate but acquired, influenced by psychological and sociological factors, and therefore not fully independent
A false idolDietrich Bonhoeffer (1906–1945)The conscience only grapples with what is permitted and forbidden within a narrow understanding of the world. As a result of the Fall humanity lost its connection with God, and with it any possibility that the conscience is God's voice; it is formed only of one's own self-knowledge. To call it the voice of God is idolatry: "Conscience pretends to be the voice of God and the standard for the relation to other men… man has become the origin of good and evil." The example of Jesus is the better moral guide

Bonhoeffer's scepticism has a context worth one sentence: he had watched a large number of Protestant churches in Germany accept the Nazi regime and its atrocities, which is a powerful piece of evidence that private conscience is not a reliable guide. His alternative is Christ: "Who is pure in heart? Only those who have surrendered their hearts completely to Jesus that he may reign in them alone… their hearts are not ruled by their conscience, but by the will of Jesus."

Where it bites in practice: Roman Catholic teaching holds that contraception is wrong, but a Catholic couple who do not yet want children may follow their conscience against it; the Church holds homosexual acts to be sinful, and gay Catholics may judge that teaching outdated on grounds of conscience. Catholic teaching is that a conscience must always be obeyed — and also that a good conscience will be in line with the Bible and Natural Law, and can be distorted by sin.

subsections.heading: The ordained ministry, the laity and leadership in the community
subsections.html:
Spec 1.1 · "Differences among Christians in their attitudes to the roles of the ordained ministry, the laity and religious leadership in local communities"

  • Ordination — the ceremony appointing ministers; the Holy Spirit passes by the "laying on of hands".
  • A sacrament for Catholics — Protestant groups do not regard the ceremony itself as important.
